\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\tx720\tx2280\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore stated the Florida Department of Health and the State Surgeon General were recommending that municipalities stop adding fluoride to their public water systems.\par
\par
Hassan Hadjimiry, Director of Public Utilities, emphasized that choosing to fluoridate or not fluoridate the City\rquote s water is essential as the City constructs its new Water Treatment Plant. He noted that raw water already contains a small percentage of fluoride before any additional fluoride is added. He also mentioned neighboring municipalities have eliminated fluoridating their water, and some never practiced it at all.\par
\par
The City Commission asked that more information be provided prior to making a decision regarding fluoridation. \par
\par
Mr. Moore stated he would reach out to professionals to identify the pros and cons of this issue and schedule a meeting for them to address the Commission in February.\par
\par
The Commission thanked Mr. Hadjimiry for bringing this to their attention.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\tx720\tx2280\f0\fs24 Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, provided an overview of the Live Local Act and an update on the project submitted. She identified the requirements for development and the administrative approval process, discussed preemptive land use zoning and the proposal for Alton Delray, and described the architectural plans for the project. She noted that once the project is approved and if the project meets the standards of the Act, then it would not come before the Commission as an appealable.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Casale spoke about the preemption and being a home rule state. She suggested the City send a letter to the State Legislature expressing concerns.\par
\par
There was discussion regarding the parking spaces. Ms. Gianniotes stated the parking has been addressed. \par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Long suggested contacting the Florida League of Cities to voice any concerns.\par
\par
There was consensus among the Commission to draft a letter. Mr. Moore stated he would begin working closely with Mat Forrest to write a letter addressed to the Florida League of Cities and the State Legislature outlining concerns related to the Live Local Act.\cf1\f1\par

action_text: A motion was made by Commissioner Burns, seconded by Vice-Mayor Casale, to eliminate fluoride in the City's water. The motion carried by the following vote:
minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red255\green0\blue0;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Hassan Hadjimiry, Director of Utilities, introduced Dr. Joseph Ladapo, the Surgeon General of Health for the State of Florida. Dr. Ladapo discussed the future of fluoridating the City\rquote s drinking water in light of the construction of the new Water Treatment Plant. He shared the latest findings from the National Toxicology Department regarding water fluoridation, which have indicated potential neurotoxic harm to individuals, particularly children and pregnant women, who consume fluoridated water. Dr. Ladapo stated that since fluoride became available in toothpaste and mouthwash in 1975, his recommendation would be to discontinue fluoridating\cf1 \cf0 the drinking water. \par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item.\par
\par
\ul Dr. Jeffrey Ganeles\ulnone , 2365 NW 46th Street, Boca Raton\par
Mentioned he has an extensive 35-year career in periodontal care and education. He emphasized the importance of growing up with fluoridated water, which contributes to healthier teeth and fewer cavities in adulthood. Dr. Ganeles proposed hosting a workshop to discuss further findings and suggested reaching out to other dental publications for their input.\par
\par
\ul Dr. Richard Kitt\ulnone , 6100 Glades Road, Boca Raton\par
Referenced recent publications recommending that fluoridation should continue in the water supply, particularly for underprivileged communities.\par
\par
\ul Angela Hill\ulnone , 1103 NW 3rd Terrace, Delray Beach\par
Preferred to obtain fluoride from toothpaste and mouthwash for her family.\par
\par
\ul Dr.Bruce Tandy\ulnone ,100 Macfarlane Drive, Delray Beach \par
Teaches dentistry at Nova University and practices charity dental work.\par
\par
Stated that after 30 years of dental practice, he has observed a noteworthy difference in patient outcomes between those consuming fluoride and those using unfluoridated water. He mentioned his concerns that removing fluoride from the water supply would lead to an increased need for dental specialists, thereby putting more strain on patients.\par
\par
\ul Jean Marie Nacer\ulnone , (registered nurse) 9473 Glider Way, Boca Raton \par
Stated each individual should have a choice regarding fluoride intake, and adding it to the water supply removes that choice.\par
\f1\fs22\par
\f0\fs24 Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comments.\f1\par
\par
\f0 Discussion ensued with the Commission concerning this matter.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Long acknowledged the overwhelming information on this topic but stated that he would support a \ldblquote yes\rdblquote vote that evening. \par
\par
Commissioner Burns stated she conducted a survey, revealing most individuals oppose having fluoride forced upon them in their water.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Casale acknowledged that over the past 25 years, numerous studies have supported the addition of fluoride to drinking water, along with endorsements from various health organizations. She expressed a desire to see more recent data before considering a vote against adding fluoride to the water.\par
\par
Dr. Ladapo advised that disregarding warnings about fluoride levels in drinking water was irresponsible, according to the evidence.\par
\par
Commissioner Markert suggested holding a workshop on this issue due to significant division among the City Commission.\par
\par
Mayor Carney expressed his discomfort with mandating fluoride for those who can access it through other means, such as toothpaste and mouthwash.\par
\b\par
\b0 The Commission thanked Dr. Lapado for his efforts and for coming to Delray Beach.\cf2\f1\par
}

Pursuant to Section 3.12 of the Charter of the City of Delray Beach, the Mayor has instructed me to announce a Workshop Meeting of the City Commission to be held for the following purposes:

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\tx431\kerning2\fs24 The February 11, 2025, City Commission Workshop was called to order at 3:07 p.m. \kerning0\f1 City Clerk, Alexis Givings, called the role, and the following were present:\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx29 Terrence Moore - City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin - City Attorney\par
\par
\b\f0 Present: 5\b0\f1 - Commissioner Angela Burns, Commissioner Tom Markert, Vice Mayor Juli Casale, Deputy Vice Mayor Rob Long and Mayor Thomas F. Carney Jr. \par
\pard\kerning2\par
Michelle Hoyland, Senior Planner, presented information from the Commission Meeting held on May 17, 2022. During that meeting, the Commission approved the submission of an application to the State of Florida Historical Resources for a Small Matching Grant (SMG) to complete a historic resource survey of the Delray Beach Memorial Gardens Municipal Cemetery. Since the City has maintained its status as a Certified Local Government (CLG), it was not required to provide matching funds for this grant. Other grants were funded by the Florida Legislature, the Historic Preservation Fund, and a grant administrated by the National Park Service. \par
\par
Ms. Hoyland mentioned that for the first time, a city\rquote s application for a small grant was funded by a federal grant, which was a testament to the project\rquote s goodness. She discussed what the Historic Survey covered on the northeastern corner of the cemetery, which evaluated areas that were 50 years or older to determine whether the cemetery qualified for a historic designation. Achieving this designation would make the City eligible for grants to improve the historical section of the cemetery. Many individuals buried in this graveyard were pioneers from diverse families. \par
\par
Ms. Hoyland concluded her presentation by summarizing the report\rquote s recommendations. She outlined the criteria for historical eligibility, stating that the City met all of the necessary requirements. Additionally, she noted there were numerous grants available to cemeteries that satisfied these criteria. \par
\par
On January 15, 2025, the Historic Resource Survey was presented to the Historic Preservation Board. The board recommended listing the historic section of the Delray Beach Memorial Gardens Municipal Cemetery on the Local Register of Historic Places and suggested continuing the research identified in the report to gather more information.\par
\par
Ms. Hoyland asked the Commission for guidance on proceeding with the designation of the cemetery and whether they should continue seeking grants to enrich the community further. There was a consensus among the Commission to pursue both local and national grants, as well as to enhance research efforts for future reports. \par
\par
The Commission thanked Ms. Hoyland and her team for their efforts.\cf1\kerning0\f0\par
}

\par
\ul Joyce Mauney\ulnone , 516 NE 8 Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Expressed her support for the Historic Designation of the discussed areas and highlighted the issue of affordable housing in relation to developers.\par
\par
\ul Linda Oxford\ulnone ,148 Coconut Road, Delray Beach\par
Discussed maintaining the charm of Delray Beach.\par
\par
\ul Price Patton\ulnone , 102 Tamarind Road\par
Discussed the role of the Delray Beach Preservation Trust as it relates to the preservation of historic areas in Delray Beach.\par
\par
\ul Joy Howell\ulnone , 25 NW 24 Court, Delray Beach\par
Discussed preserving Atlantic Avenue and maintaining property values through the creation of Conservation Districts.\par
\par
\ul Stephaine Immelman\ulnone , Chamber of Commerce, Delray Beach\par
Supports keeping the charm of Delray Beach and the Historic District.\par
\par
\ul Irene Rivelas\ulnone , 331 East Atlantic Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Discussed the boundaries of a Conservation/Heritage District and acknowledged the diversity of each historic building.\par
\par
\ul Michael Weiner, Esq.\ulnone 44 East Atlantic Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Supports charm and eclectic style. \par
\par
\ul Sandy Zeller\ulnone , 209 NW 12 Street, Delray Beach\par
Discussed the designation of Veteran\rquote s Park as a Historic District and suggested strengthening deed restrictions on nearby properties.\par
\par
\ul Kelly Barrette\ulnone ,1201 Seaspray Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Requested the Commission, especially the newly elected members, to uphold their campaign promise in support of the Atlantic Avenue Historic District.\par
\par
\ul John Miller\ulnone , 1502 Fenton Drive, Delray Beach\par
Requested the Commission consider the merits of the opinions expressed by all stakeholders involved.\par
\par
\ul Laura Simon\ulnone , Executive Director of the Downtown Development Authority\par
Requested that the Downtown Development Authority participate in discussions about preserving Delray Beach\rquote s East Atlantic Avenue historic charm. She noted that property and business owners encounter challenges when their parcels are designated as historic due to the City\rquote s processes.\par
\par
\ul Greg Snyder\ulnone , 3324 Lakeview Drive, Delray Beach\par
Expressed his support for maintaining a Historic District, acknowledging its role in stimulating economic spending within the city.\par
\par
\ul George Long\ulnone , 46 North Swinton Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Stated he supported maintaining a Historic District.\par
\par
\ul Jim Chard\ulnone , 401 SE 4 Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Suggested adding incentives to encourage residents to support the establishment of a Historic/Heritage District.\par
\par
\ul David Harden\ulnone , 1395 NW 22 Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Stated his first choice would be to have a Historic District, and if that weren\rquote t possible, he would support having a Conservation District.\par
\par
\ul Matt Gracey\ulnone , 255 NE 255 6 Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Expressed his concern about property rights for people who live in the downtown area.\par
He referenced the Atlantic Crossings Project.\par
\par
\ul Steve Cohen\ulnone , 1140 Bauhinia Road, Delray Beach\par
Stated the town was functioning well and the Commission should not interfere with the property owners.\par
\par
Mayor Carney closed public comments.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes noted that with the success of the City\rquote s software improvements, applications for projects have accelerated. She emphasized that the City only accepts complete project applications, and every communication regarding the process was documented.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion regarding the presentation.\par
\par
\ul Vice Mayor Casale\ulnone :\par
Emphasized that Conservation Districts should function as a zoning tool but should only be implemented in cities that have experienced a significant loss of historic structures due to inappropriate alterations. She pointed out that the City has not reached that point and highlighted the many advantages of maintaining Historic Districts within a city.\par
\par
\ul Commissioner Burns\ulnone :\par
Thanked the staff for their excellent work on this matter. She acknowledged that the City\rquote s Code maintains safeguards on what was allowable and suggested looking into a Conservation District as an option. She mentioned the importance of a demolition review process.\ul\par
\par
Mayor Carney\ulnone :\par
Emphasized the importance of preserving the scale, charm, and ambiance of Atlantic Avenue along with the need to protect everyone\rquote s interests.\par
\par
He noted that evidence supporting property values often pertains to residential neighborhoods. He also mentioned suggesting stricter guidelines for Conservation Districts, asserting that such measures protect property rights. He proposed involving aggregation in property matters, granting the Commission control over the facades, and tightening the guidelines regarding demolition. Mayor Carney stated that the only way to ensure Veteran\rquote s Park remains a park is through a deed restriction. \par
\par
\ul Commissioner Markert\ulnone :\par
Stated that he campaigned extensively and heard from residents that they overwhelmingly support the Historic District. He added that the time has come to approve the Historic Designation, and there shouldn\rquote t be any leeway moving forward. \par
\par
\ul Deputy Vice Mayor Long\ulnone :\par
Recognized the staff, residents, and advocates for their dedicated efforts on this important issue. He proposed the creation of a Conservation District as a fair compromise for all parties involved. He pointed out that the primary concern was aggregation, which permitted developers to construct large, monolithic structures in the downtown area. Establishing a Conservation District would enable the City to address ongoing design issues effectively.\par
\par
Mayor Carney concluded the meeting by directing staff to begin developing plans for a Conservation District/Ordinance, which he, Commissioner Burns, and Deputy Vice Mayor Long supported.\par
\par
There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 5:03 p.m.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\tx2379\expndtw-2\kerning2\f0\fs24 Hassan Hadjimiry, Public Utilities Director, was accompanied by Henry Dachowitz, CFO; Daryll Parker, Principal Consultant with Willdan Financial Services; Gregory Roy, Project Manager with CDM; and Jay Glover, Director of PFM Financial Advisors. Together, they presented a comprehensive overview of the updated estimated project costs for the new water treatment plant, along with information on funding sources, user rates, and the timeline for completion.\par
\par
\pard\expndtw0 Mr. Roy stated the original project cost in June 2023 was $129 million. However, in April 2024, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) updated water treatment regulations, necessitating changes to the project to comply with the newly proposed maximum concentration levels for Forever Chemicals. As a result, the cost of the project increased to $280 million.\par
\par
Mr. Glover discussed the financing plan/debt services, which included proceeds from bond issuances. He mentioned there were several options for capitalized interest. Additionally, he noted the City was exploring grant opportunities and utilizing reserve funding if needed. \par
\par
Mr. Parker explained that his company's role in this project was to develop financial projections and establish a rate path for the new utility system. He discussed the necessity to increase residents\rquote water bills, but emphasized these increases would be implemented gradually.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a brief discussion on the presentation.\par
\par
Commissioner Markert expressed his concern about the safety of the new Water Treatment Plant. Mr. Roy mentioned that multiple security measures would be integrated into the facility\rquote s entire design. \par
\par
Police Captain Ferrari stated his team would work with the Utilities Department to integrate a software camera system for real-time monitoring. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Casale thanked everyone for their time and reminded residents that there had not been a water rate increase since the early 2000s.\par
\par
The Commission unanimously agreed to proceed with the outlined plans.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\tx820\expndtw-2\kerning2\f0\fs24 Stephen Emory, Citrin Cooperman Advisors, along with Henry Dachowitz, delivered a presentation on Citrin Cooperman's assessment of budget transfers for the period of October 1, 2021, to September 30, 2024. They also analyzed the adjusted journal entries identified in the external audit for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2023. During their assessment, they identified opportunities to improve the purchase order rollover process and enhance transparency in financial reporting throughout the year. They recommended implementing procedures to ensure costs were accurately and promptly allocated to the appropriate fund. Additionally, they advised conducting a review of the account numbers included in the proposed budget amendment before notifying the Commission.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion on the presentation on fund usage across departments to ensure each department\rquote s budget was accountable and transparent.\par
\par
\pard\expndtw0\kerning0 Vice Mayor Casale expressed concern that earlier journal entries may not have provided Citrin Cooperman with the clarity needed to deliver the most accurate report.\f1\fs22\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx820\expndtw-2\kerning2\f0\fs24\par
Mr. Dachowitz stressed the need for departments to communicate with each other to ensure the accuracy of budget amendments. He also mentioned the City would be migrating to a more advanced accounting software program.\par
\par
Mayor Carney acknowledged that funds may have been allocated incorrectly, but they were spent appropriately. He expressed full confidence in the Finance Department moving forward.\cf1\expndtw0\kerning0\f2\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 The March 18, 2025, Budget Workshop Meeting was called to order at 4.00 p.m. City Clerk, Alexis Givings, called the roll, and the following were present:\par
\par
\b Present: 5 - \b0 Vice Mayor Juli Casale, Deputy Vice Mayor Rob Long, Mayor Thomas F. Carney, Jr., Commissioner Tom Markert, Commissioner Angela Burns.\par
\par
Others present were:\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk \par
\par
\b I.\b0 Mr. Moore opened the meeting by informing the Commission about changes to the budget process, which will start on April 8, 2025, earlier than previous years. He stated Chief Financial Officer Henry Dachowitz was focused on working with him to develop a future proposed annual budget process that will include a more detailed review of operational revenue and expenditure considerations. Additionally, these exercises will allow elected officials more time to review budget data.\par
\par
\b II.\b0 Henry Dachowitz presented the budget for the last quarter of the previous year and the first quarter of the current fiscal year. He explained that, in government, a fund was a subset of accounts that balances itself. He also mentioned the City does not manage the accounting for the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) or the Downtown Development Authority (DDA).\par
\par
He stated in the fiscal year 2024 budget, there was a deficit of $5 million dollars in the General Fund, with expenses exceeding revenues. He discussed the importance of having separate funds within a department to improve the tracking of expenses and ensure compliance with the allocated funds. Mr. Dachowitz mentioned that there were three types of accounts:\par
\par
1. Cash Accounts\par
2. Modified accruals - Government funds were mostly modified accruals\par
3. Accrual accounts\par
\par
He presented an analysis of various funds and departments based on the last fiscal year and expressed his desire to implement monthly or quarterly reviews of each fund and budget by department moving forward. He also mentioned that he would provide more up-to-date figures by the second quarter of the current year, following discussions with department heads.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz concluded his presentation by mentioning the City will be upgrading its utility billing and payroll software, which will include the payroll systems for the Police and Fire Departments. He emphasized that he would be holding regular meetings with departments and sharing reports regarding the budget, which would provide more granular outcomes to the Commission and residents.\par
\par
\b III.\b0 Missie Barletto, Director of Public Works, presented data from the Capital Improvement Budget Program by fund type. She stated that the significant increase in dollars was mainly due to priority projects progressing from the design phase to the construction phase. She also noted there would be more substantial construction improvements to the City\rquote s facilities in the future. Additionally, she stated that funding from the County, State, and Federal levels would be crucial for funding these projects. In the coming years, her department would be more aligned with the State by including a dedicated fund for each 5-year Capital Improvement Plan.\par
\par
\b IV.\b0 Direction Regarding Implementation of Fire Rescue 24/72 Workshift\par
\par
Fire Chief Ronald Martin provided a presentation on implementing a 24/72 Workshift for the Fire Rescue Department. He discussed the contractual requirements of the International Association for Fire Fighters (IAFF). Chief Martin noted that implementing the 42-hour work schedule would require a mid-year budget adjustment of $619,534.78 for the fiscal year 2024-2025, and the creation of a 4th platoon of firefighters. The total cost for the City to meet these contractual obligations would be $2,584,725.68 starting October 1, 2025. He stated these calculations were based on the salary of a firefighter/paramedic. Fire Chief Martin mentioned this model would theoretically see a global reduction in overtime and leave usage. He advised the Commission that if they decide to change the Fire Rescue service model, Fire Rescue would implement the following:\par
\par
Implement a Hillsborough Model of Staffing\par
\par
3 - Person Rescue Staffing will remain, but;\par
\par
The third Person would not be supported with overtime. Staffing decisions will be based on data.\par
\par
Chief Martin noted that efficiency in Fire and Special Operations would be reduced, and the risk profile of these incidents would increase. \par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion about the appropriate staffing for a fire truck when responding to a 911 call. They all agreed on the importance of having an adequately staffed fire emergency truck when responding to a potentially life-threatening situation.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated the City was close to local hospitals, allowing rescue trucks to reach the hospital more quickly.\par
\par
Dr. Craig Kushnir, the Medical Director for the City of Delray Beach Fire Department, informed the Commission that the County was transitioning to a 3-person response truck to improve service quality and reduce mortality rates among the residents. \par
\par
The Commission thanked Chief Martin for his presentation.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated all City departments were expected to come back with their recommendations for efficiency as they prepare their 2025-2026 budgets.\par
\par
\b V.\b0 City Commission Input, Direction, and Guidance \par
\par
Vice Mayor Casale requested an agenda item be added to discuss preferences for local small businesses interested in responding to a bid solicitation.\par
\par
Mayor Carney mentioned having a small business portal on the City\rquote s website.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Long suggested postponing this discussion until after May, when the legislative session would conclude.\par
\par
Mr. Moore recommended adding this item to the April 8, 2025, meeting, separate from the Disparity Study. \par
\par
There was consensus to approve this request and add it to the April 8, 2025, agenda.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Long informed everyone that Rita Ellis, the second female Mayor of the City of Delray Beach, had recently passed and requested to have a certificate of recognition written in her honor. There was consensus to approve this request.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 The March 27, 2025, Commission Workshop Meeting was called to order at 4:00 p.m. City Clerk, Alexis Givings, called the role, and the following were present:\line\par
\b Present: 5 -\b0 Deputy Vice Mayor Rob Long, Vice Mayor Juli Casale, Commissioner Angela Burns, Commissioner Tom Markert, Mayor Thomas F. Carney, Jr.\par
\par
Others present were:\par
\par
Terrence Moore - City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin - City Attorney\par
\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney, began by reviewing the Florida Statute, Section 163.3177, as it relates to the City of Delray Beach's Comprehensive Plan, also known as the Always Delray Comprehensive Plan. She stated that this document serves as a blueprint for the City's future residential and commercial development. It was intended to guide the area's economic, social, physical, environmental, and fiscal growth, reflecting the community's commitment to implementing the plan and its various components.\par
\par
Janai Bowens, the Education and External Opportunities Manager, noted that the goal of this workshop was to use the collected data to assist the Commission in developing key initiatives that promote early childhood success, family engagement, grade-level reading, and workforce development through the Education Element of the Comprehensive Plan. \par
\b\par
\b0 She delivered a presentation on the schools in the City of Delray Beach, highlighting their current status and proposed policy improvements for the future. She focused on city-wide strategies to enhance academic performance and addressed the barriers faced by many families in the community. Ms. Bowens emphasized the necessity for the schools to align with the Palm Beach County School District, especially given the increasing number of non-English-speaking residents, economically disadvantaged families, and children with special needs.\par
\par
Ms. Bowens presented her proposed additional policies and amendments to the City\rquote s Always Delray Comprehensive Master Plan, which aims to improve early childhood literacy through collaboration and funding from the City and County\rquote s partners. She stressed the importance of including the City\rquote s non-profit organizations in these plans. \par
\par
In addition, this data was intended to be used to develop key initiatives that promote early childhood success, family engagement, grade-level reading, workforce development, and other societal influences.\par
\par
The Commission discussed the presentation and acknowledged the importance of gaining support from local non-profit organizations and the Palm Beach County School Board. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Casale expressed her gratitude to several non-profit organizations that have been serving the children of the city without receiving any funding from the City. She emphasized that to create an equitable budget, the Commission should receive a comprehensive list of all non-profits that are receiving financial support from various departments within the City, along with the respective amounts.\par
\par
Mayor Carney suggested meeting with the School Board annually to review progress under the new goals and priorities established by the updated interlocal agreement.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to public comments on this subject.\par
\par
\ul Stephaine Immelman\ulnone , Delray Beach Chamber of Commerce\par
Stated the Chamber of Commerce is willing to assist the City in achieving its educational goals.\par
\par
\ul Allison Turner\ulnone , Chairman of the Delray Beach Chamber of Commerce Education Fund\par
Discussed grant opportunities available to schools, teachers, and organizations to help make a direct impact on schools in the City of Delray Beach.\par
\par
\ul Barbara Stark\ulnone , President and CEO of the Milagro Center, Delray Beach\par
Discussed the academic achievements that the Milagro Center has helped make for local students.\par
\par
\ul Janet Meeks\ulnone , 2782 Hampton Circle South, Delray Beach\par
Provided her suggestions to improve education in the City as the former Education Coordinator.\par
\par
\ul Jim Chard\ulnone , 401 SE 4 Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Suggested implementing goals for education instead of focusing on policies to help ensure they are ready for college or the workforce after high school.\par
\par
\ul Did Not State Her Name\ulnone \par
Recognized learning challenges children face and parents who work extended hours not being available engage in the child's schoolwork.\par
\par
\ul Irene Rivelas\ulnone , 331 East Atlantic Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Discussed mandating the interlocal agreement for coordinated planning that governs capital improvements in the city schools.\par
\par
\ul Rita Rona\ulnone , 50 East Road, Delray Beach\par
Thanked Ms. Bowens for her dedicated work and suggested the City meet with the Rotary Club to assess their educational needs and identify any monetary shortfalls.\par
\par
\ul Montre Bennett\ulnone , 323 NW 2 Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Mentioned some parents struggle to assist their children with homework and suggested that children walk and meditate before school in the morning.\par
\par
\ul Janice Hill\ulnone , 309 SW 15 Terrace, Delray Beach\par
Congratulated Ms. Bowens for her work and acknowledged the language and economic barriers that have plagued the city's schools for years.\par
\par
\ul Chuck Ridley\ulnone , 210 NW 2 Avenue, Delray Beach\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Janai Bowens and Jeff Oris, Assistant City Manager, delivered a presentation on the Historic Carver/Delray Full Service Campus Revitalization Plan. She stated that in February 2019, the Division of Historical Resources designated the Historic Carver Campus as eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places, deeming several buildings significant contributing resources. She also mentioned that in September 2023, the School Board approved the fiscal year Capital Plan, which included $20 million to revitalize Buildings 1 and 12. The School District of Palm Beach County is seeking the support of the City of Delray Beach in developing a proposed Historic Carver Revitalization Plan/ Phase II, which includes additional education programs and a community clinic.\par
\par
Joseph Sanches from the School District of Palm Beach County was present to request the City\rquote s support for the proposed Phase II of the Historic Carver Revitalization Plan. This phase includes the development of a technical center and a community clinic, as well as the demolition of Building 2 to create a parking lot.\par
\par
The Commission discussed the significance of students who choose not to attend college but instead enroll in a technical school, allowing the students to enter the workforce promptly with valuable skills. They expressed their concern that the on-site clinic should serve as a learning center instead of a medical treatment facility. \par
\par
There was a consensus to allow the demolition of Building 2.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to provide public comment on this item.\par
\par
\ul Michele Gitu\ulnone , 1020 Citrus Way, Unit 201, Delray Beach\par

\ul Janet Meeks\ulnone , 2782 Hampton Circle South, Delray Beach\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 The April 1, 2025, Special Meeting was called to order at 3:00 p.m. City Clerk, Alexis Givings called the role, and the following were present: \par
\par
\b Present: 4 - \b0 Mayor Thomas F. Carney, Jr., Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns, Commissioner Tom Markert, Commissioner Juli Casale.\par
\par
\b Absent: 1 -\b0 Vice Mayor Rob Long.\par
\par
Others present were:\par
\par
Terrence Moore - City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin - City Attorney\par
\par
Duane D\rquote Andrea, Human Resources Director, began the meeting by announcing that the final two Internal Auditor candidates were present for in-person interviews with the Commission. Before proceeding, he introduced Anne Lewis and Serena Wright Black, representatives from Raftelis Financial Consultants, Inc., whom the City hired to provide professional consulting services for this executive search. \par
\par
\b\f1 David Medrano,\b0\f0 CPA,CFA,CIA,CISA,CFE,CCEP,FRM,CTP\par
Thanked the Commission for the privilege of selecting him for an in-person interview.\par
\par
Each Commissioner participated in a brief discussion with Mr. Medrano regarding how his skills could assist the City in defining the requirements for the internal auditor position. Mr. Medrano provided several examples of innovative initiatives he had developed in his previous roles, including implementing best practices for compliance and internal controls across departments and managing investigations into cases reported to a whistleblower hotline that he established. Mr. Medrano stated that if selected, his priorities for the first six (6)months would be to educate the departments on the role of an internal auditor, provide guidance on what would be expected, and establish positive working relationships. \par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion and asked Mr. Medrano to elaborate on his philosophies and procedural practices.\par
\par
Mayor Carney thanked Mr. Medrano for his time and for making the trip from Texas.\par
\par
Mr. D\rquote Andrea led Mr. Medrano into the conference room, bringing in the next candidate.\par
\par
\b\f1 Elena Georgiev,\b0\f0 CPA, CGMA, CIA, CISA, CRMA\par
Thanked the Commission for the opportunity to interview for the internal auditor position and thanked the staff and recruiters for their seamless assistance.\par
\par
Ms. Georgiev noted that most of her career has been in municipal government. She provided several examples of her achievements for each of her employers. \kerning0 She noted that she is interested in obtaining her license as a Certified Fraud Examiner (CFE).\par
\f2\par
\kerning2\f0 The Commission engaged in a discussion with Ms. Georgiev about her methodology. She discussed her creation of a city-wide risk assessment plan, which was later adopted as the model for that municipality's annual audit. Furthermore, she shared her findings from an audit of a municipality's purchasing cards (P-Cards) and made several recommendations that generated significant savings. Ms. Georgiev noted that while reviewing the City\rquote s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) from 2023, she discovered an outstanding finding from a previous year. She stated that if selected for the position, a priority would be to assist the City\rquote s external auditor in resolving this issue so that it may be closed out. Additionally, she outlined her strategies for fostering positive relationships with department heads to enhance problem-solving when issues arise. Mayor Carney thanked Ms. Georgiev for her time.\par
\par
\kerning0 Vice Mayor Casale mentioned that if selected, she would like to make it a condition of her employment that Ms. Georgiev obtain her Certified Fraud Examiners (CFE) License. \kerning2 Ms. Gelin indicated that if Ms. Georgiev is selected, obtaining her CFE certification could be included in her contract. She suggested adding this item to the agenda for approval on April 22, 2025.\par
\par
The Commission discussed the presentations made by both candidates. All agreed that both candidates were impressive and would bring the high-level skills the City is seeking. They recognized that Ms. Georgiev had several innovative strategies that could benefit the City in ways they had not previously considered.\par
\kerning0\f2\par
\kerning2\f0 A motion was made by Commissioner Casale, seconded by Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, to select Elena Georgiev and to allow Human Resources to negotiate within the salary range already provided.\par
\par
\b all were in favor\par
\par
\b0 There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 4:32 p.m.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 The April 8, 2025, City Commission Budget Workshop was called to order at 3:02 p.m. City Clerk, Alexis Givings, called the roll, and the following were present:\par
\par
\b Present: 5 -\b0 Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns, Commissioner Tom Markert, Commissioner Juli Casale, Vice Mayor Rob Long (arrived at 3:06 p.m.), and Mayor Thomas F. Carney Jr.\par
\par
Others present were:\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\par
Chief Financial Officer, Henry Dachowitz, stated each department would undergo three (3) budget reviews this year, a departure from previous years. He explained that this change aims to provide the Commission with greater granularity in the numbers and enhance their participation in the process. Mr. Dachowitz cautioned the Commission that this was a preliminary budget request from each department. \par
\par
\ul\f1 Fire Chief Ronald Martin\ulnone\f0 announced that his department had begun the budget process for the fiscal year 2025-2026 by adopting a zero-based budgeting approach. This method aims to identify opportunities for greater budgetary efficiency while maintaining the current level of operations. He provided examples of cost savings achieved through collaboration with local labor partners. For instance, some collective bargaining positions have been reclassified as exempt executive roles. This change would expand the City\rquote s span of control, helping to reduce the department\rquote s service costs. Overall, it will provide the City with greater oversight, which is expected to decrease expenses for the department further. He stated that his preliminary budget anticipates an inflation rate increase of 5-6 percent for its projections and operational costs. \par
\par
In conclusion, Chief Martin advised Mr. Moore that the Fire Department's primary goal should be to achieve long-term fiscal control by conducting community risk assessments related to the fire-rescue strategic plan. This plan has been submitted by the Commission to the City Manager and is intended for adoption, ultimately aiming to establish long-term budgetary controls.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion on the fire department's strategy for maintaining the current level of service while ensuring a balanced budget. Since this was a preliminary budget meeting, they\fs32 \fs24 recognized the importance of making key decisions moving forward, particularly when the tax roll is determined.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz reminded the Commission that this is the very early stage of the budget process, which was initiated earlier at the Commission\rquote s request.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that the department must explore alternatives to prevent increasing taxes on residents.\par
\par
\ul Chief of Police Russ Mager\ulnone presented the proposed budget for the Police Department and explained that the budget reflects a continuous commitment to ensuring safe and secure community-focused policing. He noted that the budget was organized into two (2) main divisions: operations and support. Each division's budget was further categorized into personnel services, operating expenses, and capital outlay. Chief Mager stated that last year's amended budget was $50.3 million. In comparison, this year's preliminary budget was initially set at $55.5 million but has since been revised to $55.7 million, a difference from last year's budget of $5.4 million. He emphasized that these figures reflect a 10.8% increase compared to the current year's fiscal amended budget.\par
He stated that out of the $5.4 million difference, $4.4 million was in personnel services. \par
\par
Assistant Police Chief Darrell Hunter outlined the strategies for enhancing the efficiency and allocation of resources within the Police Department. \par
\par
Administrative Services Manager Kristina Maricic provided a list of units and services within the police department and the community patrol units.\par
\par
The Commission expressed their gratitude to the Police Department for their efforts and requested to be provided with an executive summary for the budget meetings moving forward.\par
\fs32\par
\pard\qj\kerning0\ul\fs24 Director of Neighborhood and Community Services, Jeri Pryor\ulnone outlined the budget criteria for the fiscal year budget for 2025-26 to effectively manage the Neighborhood and Community Service Department. She requested funding for new radios to ensure the safety of code enforcement officers, enabling them to communicate with other officers and police. Additionally, she proposed increasing funds for code enforcement officers' training. She requested the General Fund Budget include financing for new vehicles for the Community Redevelopment Agency and Clean and Safe Staff. Furthermore, she emphasized the need for a dedicated irrigation maintenance person and a Clean and Safe program administrator. She mentioned that the overall budget had increased by 8 to 9 percent compared to the previous year.\par
\par
The Commission praised Ms. Pryor for her leadership during her three (3) months with the City.\par
\par
As the presentations lasted shorter than anticipated, Mr. Moore proposed rescheduling the upcoming budget workshops to begin at 3:30 p.m. instead of 3:00 p.m. There was a consensus to reschedule the budget workshops on April 22nd, May 6th, and May 20th to begin at 3:30 p.m.\par
\par
There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 7:37 p.m.\kerning2\ul\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mr. Moore briefly discussed the item which concerns the City acquiring several segments of Atlantic Avenue from Florida Department of Corrections (FDOT.) He expressed that he believes this is a positive idea.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\cf0\f1 Missie Barletto, Director of Public Works, stated that on January 30, 2025, and March 7, 2025, the City of Delray Beach Public Works Department and FDOT staff met to discuss the possibility of transferring ownership of several segments of Atlantic Avenue within Delray Beach city limits. Ms. Barletto stated that since then, FDOT has been willing to officially begin negotiations for the transfer of West Atlantic Avenue (State Road 906) from NW/SW 12\super th\nosupersub Avenue to N/S Swinton Avenue from the FDOT to the City of Delray Beach. She mentioned that the City already performs a great deal of the maintenance. She explained further that approving this item would align with the City\rquote s redevelopment plans for projects, including the Set Transformation Plan and the Community Redevelopment Agency's Expansion Plan. Ms. Barletto stated that this evening's presentation was to secure the Commission's permission to move forward with preliminary negotiations and to have the Mayor sign a letter asking FDOT to begin the process formally.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion about the costs of assuming the proposed area of land.\par
\par
Ms. Barletto stated that since there have been no negotiations yet, there were no concrete facts regarding the actual costs involved. The Commission agreed that moving forward with this plan has been overdue.\par
\par
There was consensus for the Mayor to send a letter granting permission to proceed with the proposed project.\f0\par
\par
\f1 During the discussion of this item, Mr. Moore added the following comments:\par
\par
- Announced that Delray Beach received the Blue Flag Beach Designation Award for the third consecutive year. He also noted that on Thursday, May 1, 2025, at 10:00 a.m., there would be a waterfront celebration.\f0\par
\par
\f1 - Mentioned there would be a community engagement session on Thursday, April 24, 2025, at 6:00 p.m., which will be held at the Delray Beach Municipal Golf Course Clubhouse. \par
\par
- Announced that the City of Delray Beach has confirmed its bid for the Davis Cup through the Palm Beach County Sports Commission.\cf1\f0\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\fs24 The April 22, 2025, Budget Workshop Meeting was called to order at 3:34 p.m. City Clerk, Alexis Givings, called the roll, and the following were present:\par
\par
\b Present: 4\b0 - Mayor Thomas F. Carney, Jr., Vice Mayor Rob Long, Commissioner Tom Markert, and Commissioner Juli Casale.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns arrived at 3:42 p.m.\par
\par
Others present were:\par
Terrance Moore, City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Director of Development Services, provided an overview of her department, which consists of four different divisions. She mentioned that in the upcoming budget year, personnel positions in the Code Enforcement Division related to the Florida Building Code will be fully or partially funded by the Building Fund. This change aims to decrease the department's dependence on the General Fund. Additionally, adjustments will be made to other divisions based on the recommendations from the upcoming Fee Study.\par
\par
The Commission thanked Ms. Gianniotes for her report.\par
\par
Missie Barletto, Director of Public Works, presented the department\rquote s proposed operating budget for the fiscal year 2025-2026. She stated that the Department of Public Works consists of eight (8) different divisions with seventy-one (71) full-time employees and three (3) part-time employees. She detailed the responsibilities of each of the eight (8) divisions. She stated that the General Fund Revenue was projected for $6.5 million dollars for the parking division, which was a 27.4% increase over the previous year. This number reflects the level of service as the status quo.\par
\par
Other revenues not included in the general fund are grants, contractual obligations, contributions from the Community Redevelopment Agency, legislative appropriations, and federal grants. She stated that in the upcoming months, the Commission will consider several items, including the adoption of a city-wide valet service and the implementation of metering for downtown parking lots. She presented another scenario that her department would like to propose, which represents a 22.6% overall increase in the department's budget. It includes transferring the costs of roadway restoration and preservation from the Capital Improvement Project to maintenance expenses, as well as other improvements. She also reviewed the Stormwater Fund expenses, which were expected to decrease by 7.5%, and the Garage Fund expenses, which included a 3% increase overall.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion of the importance of understanding departmental expenses before determining tax rates for residents.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that his office would provide a preliminary budget outlook after meeting with the department directors at the June 10, 2025, Commission Meeting.\par
\par
The Commission thanked Ms. Barletto for her report.\par
\par
Hassan Hadjimiry, the Director of Utilities, presented a preliminary budget forecast for the fiscal year 2025-2026. He explained that the Utilities Department consists of nine (9) divisions and employs a total of 146 full-time staff members. Additionally, he shared the annual performance report for 2024, highlighting that there have been no violations reported in the past five (5) years. Mr. Hadijimiry provided a breakdown of the increases:\par
\par
1. Personnel & Operating Budget - Increase of $52,809,043\par
2. Utilities Capital Fund 442 - Increase of $ 52,706,475 (5-Year Plan) Combined with Public Works.\par
3. Capital Improvement Project 443 - Increase of $269,3000,000 \cf1 (Water Plant Treatment Plant- 5 year plan.)\cf2\par
\cf0\par
The Commission expressed their gratitude to Mr. Hadjimiry for his dedication.\par
\par
There being no further business, Mayor Carney adjourned the Workshop Meeting at 4:37 p.m.\cf1\kerning0\par
}

Pursuant to Section 3.12 of the Charter of the City of Delray Beach, the Mayor has instructed me to announce a Workshop Meeting of the City Commission to be held for the following purposes:

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Calibri;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574\expndtw-2\up3\f0\fs24 The May 20, 2025 Budget Workshop Meeting was called to order at 3:33 p.m. Alexis Givings, City Clerk, called the roll, and the following were present:\up0\par
\fs18\par
\pard\expndtw0\kerning2\b\fs24 Present: 4\b0 - Mayor Thomas F. Carney, Jr., Commissioner Tom Markert, Commissioner Juli Casale, Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns.\par
\par
\b Absent: 1 \b0 - Vice Mayor Rob Long\par
\par
Others present were:\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574\expndtw-2\kerning0 Lynn Gelin, City Attorney\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\par
\b Department of Communications\par
\b0 Gina Carter, Director of Communications\b ,\b0 presented the 2026 fiscal year proposed budget for her department. She stated that her department oversees more than 13 social media platforms, as well as digital displays and billboards located at City facilities, beach pavilions, and along I-95. Additionally, her team manages many other internal and external communications. She proudly informed the Commission that the Department of Communications received the Florida Municipal Communication Certificate of Excellence in Governmental Communications and was recognized as the Local Government Communicator of the Year in 2025.\par
\par
In summary, Ms. Carter indicated that 87.1% of her proposed budget for the fiscal year 2026 is allocated for personnel services, while 12.9% is for operating services, which marks a slight increase from the previous year due to staff pay increases. In total, she stated that she was requesting a 4% decrease from the previous year.\par
\par
\pard\expndtw0\kerning2 The Commission engaged in a discussion on the presentation and inquired about the Creative Art School\rquote s programs.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar Ms. Carter stated that she was seeking to hire a part-time culinary arts professional to manage a cooking program. The total cost for this position would be $30,000, with an additional $10,000 allocated for properly stocking the kitchen.\kerning0\fs22\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574\fs24 The Commission expressed their gratitude to Ms. Carter for her accomplishments\expndtw-2 .\par
\par
\pard\expndtw0\kerning2\b Office of the City Manager\par
\b0 Mr. Moore presented the preliminary proposed budget summary for the 2026 fiscal year for his department. He stated that the overall budget decreased by 7.61%, compared to the previous year. This decrease was partly due to the phasing out of a Sustainability and Resiliency position, as well as a reduction in grant funding by $145,000. \kerning0 He provided an overview of the divisions under the City Manager's Office, which includes the Department of Economic Development, Education and External Opportunities, Special Events, and the Office of Sustainability and Resiliency. He noted the Office of Sustainability and Resiliency was recently reduced from two (2) to one (1) staff member, as the department's goals and objectives were determined to be achievable with a single-person operation.\f1\fs22\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 \par
The Commission engaged in a discussion on the presentation and inquired about the sustainability position being eliminated.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale expressed her concern that in the previous year\rquote s goal setting meeting, it was determined that the office of Sustainability and Resiliency was identified as a vital department and should be further developed, especially in relation to the City\rquote s Climate Action Plan.\par
\par
Mayor Carney mentioned he would address his concerns in writing to Mr. Moore before the next Budget Workshop.\par
\par
\b Office of Information Technology (IT)\par
\b0 Jay Stacy, Chief Technology Officer and Don Marese, Assistant Information Technology Director,\b \b0 presented their department's preliminary proposed budget summary for the 2025-2026 fiscal year. \par
\par
Mr. Stacy presented a detailed list of the responsibilities managed by his department. He noted that through strategic contract negotiations, they successfully reduced certain expenses; however, employee costs have increased by 4%. He also mentioned that the IT network system supports the infrastructure of the Fire and Police Departments.\par
\par
Mr. Stacy acknowledged that although the budget has increased in the past five (5) years, significant measures have been implemented to protect the City and enrich the lives of its residents and business owners. Additionally, he recognized that the Center for Digital Government and Government Technology Magazine has ranked Delray Beach among the top 10 Digital Cities for two (2) consecutive years. He reported a budget increase of 4%, due to merit increases, expanded meeting support, reclassifications, and adjustments in compensation.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion regarding the presentation and commended Mr. Stacy for the exceptional expertise and leadership he has brought to the IT department.\par
\fs18\par
\fs24 Mayor Carney proposed that the since the City's IT personnel is now live streaming the Downtown Development Authority's (DDA) meetings, the City should be compensated because the DDA is an independent taxing agency.\par
\par
\b Office of the City Clerk\par
\b0 Alexis Givings, City Clerk, presented her department's preliminary proposed budget summary for the 2025-2026 fiscal year. She mentioned the wide range of professional services that the Clerk\rquote s Office was responsible for.\par
\par
Ms. Givings reported that the total personnel and operating expenditures for 2025 amounted to $685,000. She explained that the proposed budget for 2026 reflects an increase of $173,000, primarily due to the costs associated with the upcoming election and the necessary adjustments in personnel expenses to maintain the expected level of service.\par
\par
\b Finance Department \par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Jeff Oris, Assistant City Manager, along with Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, provided an updated report since the last Commission Meeting.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 On Tuesday, May 6, 2025, staff visited the Subculture site to meet with the owner, Mr. Rodney Mayo, to address issues raised during the Commission Workshop Meeting on April 29, 2025. The attendees included representatives from the City Manager\rquote s Office, Neighborhood and Community Services, Development Services, and the Fire Rescue Department. During the meeting, Mr. Oris explained the specific areas where Mr. Mayo was found to be non-compliant. He highlighted parking concerns, noting that the business currently have 10 vehicles on-site, arranged in a tandem configuration for employees. He pointed out that the roadway is under the jurisdiction of the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT), which has stringent space requirements for parking. Consequently, additional on-street parking is not feasible in the area without reducing either the size or the number of curb cuts. Mr. Oris noted that Mr. Mayo has attempted to stripe the parking lot, but had not applied for a permit to do so.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 Ms. Gianniotes provided a staff report on the physical arrangement of the site. She noted that to date, Mr. Mayo has received 3 notices of violation, which provided him with 60 days to come into compliance. The violations were for the parking spaces not being demarcated, the absence of a handicapped space, and the lack of a life safety plan. She stated a Special Magistrate meeting has been scheduled for July 18, 2025, if these issues have not been resolved by then. She mentioned that when the previous Commission approved this item, they did not foresee significant events being held there, particularly since the venue was not located in the entertainment district. She added that once the owner provides a life safety plan, the entire operation will be reviewed and come back before the Commission.\par
\par
Mr. Oris concluded by stating that the City will closely monitor the area, and the Police will issue tickets to cars parked illegally or on the property of other businesses.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\kerning0\f2 A discussion ensued amongst the Commission regarding the parking issues and the type of special events that should be permissible at the location. It was noted that these matters should be addressed by Code Enforcement and not be discussed on the dais.\par
\f3\par
\f2 Mayor Carney emphasized the need for a clear definition distinguishing a coffee shop from a restaurant. He pointed out that when the original approval was granted, the owner mentioned having a parking agreement with the nearby business, Putting Around, but that agreement did not materialize. Ms. Gelin stated that she would investigate this issue further.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f0 The Commission thanked Ms. Gianniotes and Mr. Oris for their work.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Ms. Gelin entered Ordinance No. 15-25 into the record and reminded the Commission that they had received a presentation on this item during the meeting on May 6, 2025.\par
\par
Mayor Carney inquired if the Commission had any questions. Seeing no response, he opened the floor for public comments regarding this item.\par
\par
\ul Mitch Katz,\ulnone 1618 Classical Blvd, Delray Beach\par
Suggested that the Commission explore ways to slow down the rate increases and reconsider the fluoridation of water.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comments.\par
\par
Mayor Carney addressed Hassan Hadjimiry, Utilities Director, regarding the proposed water rate increase in comparison to rates in surrounding municipalities.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f1 Mr. Hadjimiry stated that before 2022, the City had not increased its water rates in fifteen years, whereas other municipalities had an average annual increase of 3 to 4%. He noted that initiating water service in surrounding areas is considerably more expensive than in Delray Beach. He emphasized that if the City of Delray Beach had raised its rates each year, the Water Treatment Plant could have already been completed. He pointed out that the underground infrastructure still requires improvements.\cf1\kerning0\f2\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f1 Discussion ensued amongst the Commission regarding the increase in water rates and the potential use of settlement funds from the PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) lawsuit to help offset the construction costs for the Water Treatment Plant. They acknowledged that the City was significantly behind in rate increases and that action needed to be taken.\cf1\kerning0\f2\par
}

{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Aptos;}{\f2\froman\fprq2\fcharset0 Times New Roman;}{\f3\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Ms. Gelin entered Ordinance No. 37-24 into the record.\par
\par
Russ Mager, Police Chief, stated that this item enables the City to install automatic speed measuring devices in school zones.\par
\par
Matthew Naparstek, Lieutenant, noted that a traffic study revealed a heightened safety risk at 10 city schools where speeding was prevalent. He mentioned that once the system goes live, a 30-day grace period will be in effect before actual violations are issued. He also provided a breakdown of how the funds from the violation penalties would be allocated. He mentioned that any non-payment of a violation would result in the issuance of a uniform traffic citation (UTC).\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to provide public comments on this item. \kerning2\f1 Seeing no one present, Mayor Carney closed public comments.\par
\par
\kerning0\f0 A discussion ensued amongst the Commission about starting a media campaign to inform residents about this program as soon as possible. Mayor Carney inquired about the hours that the devices would be operational.\f2\par
\par
\kerning2\f1 A representative from Red Speed (the Camera Device Company) was present to answer any questions. He stated that the cameras would turn on half an hour before school starts and shut down half an hour after school ends. He mentioned that the only thing that changes between those time periods is the speed limit, which is being enforced. He stated that there wouldn\rquote t be enforcement on weekends or holidays.\cf1\kerning0\f3\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mayor Carney asked his colleagues to disclose any ex-parte communications for Item No. 7.B.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\kerning0\ul\f1 Mayor Carney\ulnone : Spoke with Mr. Schiller.\par
\ul Vice Mayor Long\ulnone : Spoke with Mr. Schiller.\par
\ul Deputy Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone : Spoke with Mr. Schiller.\par
\ul Commissioner Casale\ulnone : Spoke with Mr. Schiller, the applicant's representative, and what was on the server.\par
\pard\kerning2\ul\f0 Commissioner Markert: \ulnone Spoke with Mr. Schiller.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\kerning0\f1 Ms. Gelin entered Resolution No. 93-25 into the record.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f0 Ms. Gianniotes entered File No. 2024-104 into the record.\par
\par
Neil Schiller, attorney for the applicant, introduced the developer for this project, Mr. Jerry Batoff, 109 5\super th\nosupersub Avenue, Delray Beach.\par
\par
Mr. Schiller presented a request to use contemporary functionalism architectural design for this project. He provided examples of how this design was being utilized throughout South Florida and how it seamlessly integrates into the surrounding area.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\kerning0\f1 Ms. Gianniotes provided a staff report for this item. She stated the applicant does not have sufficient documentation to show that the style is contextually and historically appropriate for use within Downtown Delray Beach. She mentioned direction has been given to consider removing Masonry Modern from the design guidelines. She stated the Planning and Zoning Board (PZB) recommended approval of this request on April 21, 2025, by a 4-2 vote, and deemed the elevations and landscaping to be contextually appropriate, contributing positively to the area. She cautioned the Commission whether the proposed design was a well-executed example of Contemporary Functionalism as outlined in the report.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f0 Seeing no one present, Mayor Carney closed public comments.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\kerning0\f1 Mr. Schiller provided a rebuttal, stating that his client had initially wanted to collaborate with staff to make modifications but was rebuffed. He noted his client had intentionally not designed a building in the Masonry Modern style and confirmed that his client was amenable to continue working with staff on any modifications to refine the definition.\par
\par
A discussion ensued amongst the Commission about the style of the building and its conformity. \par
\par
Rafik Ibrahim, Principal Planner, noted the site plan would be returned to the Planning and Zoning Board, and changes to the design were anticipated as both parties worked together.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes emphasized the importance of adhering to the seven approved architectural designs established by the City in 2015, noting that disregarding them undermines their intended purpose.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f0 Peggy Fitzgerald, architect for the project, mentioned the various iterations that this design had previously undergone.\cf1\kerning0\f2\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore discussed the collaborative efforts between his office and that of Henry Dachowitz, Chief Financial Officer, which were aimed at achieving a balanced budget. He outlined the steps that could be taken to reach this goal. Additionally, he briefly addressed the Fire Department's transition from a 24/48-hour shift schedule to a 24/72-hour shift schedule and the financial implications this change would have on the City\rquote s budget.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz presented the amended budget for 2025, which totals $189,220,303 as of May. He noted that, through workshops, individual meetings, and other interactions with departments, the proposed budget for 2026 revenues is estimated to be $177,895,910. This resulted in a shortfall of $11,324,393, primarily due to a $10 million drawdown from reserves. He stated that the 2026 budget does not include the drawdown, which was included in the amended budget from the previous year. He compared the departmental expenses for 2025 with those proposed for 2026. He also provided the City Manager\rquote s recommendations for balancing the budget, which included not filling all vacancies across departments in a single year. He then discussed the expenses, which totaled $189,220,303 in 2025. The projected revenues for 2026 were $201,832,744, representing a shortfall of $12,612,441. He stated that once the Commission sets the millage rate, it will affect the revenue for the City.\par
\par
Mr. Moore discussed the Fire Department's 3/3 staffing model and mentioned potential revenue sources that the City could utilize to fund this additional expenditure, which will begin on October 1, 2025. He asked Fire Chief Martin to present the next items regarding the Fire Department and strategies to fund the budget.\par
\par
Ronald Martin, Fire Chief, noted that the SAFER Grant is a program administered by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), designed to enhance or maintain the number of firefighters in local communities. He emphasized that the program is highly competitive, and the application process typically begins in January. Chief Martin pointed out that the SAFER Grant application has specific guidelines regarding staffing requirements. During the discussion, he shared the funding and payout schedule related to the grant. He highlighted that the City has two weeks left to submit the application, pending approval from the City Commission, and indicated that there was less than a 9% chance of securing funds.\par
\par
There was consensus among the Commission to proceed with the application for the SAFER Grant. Mr. Moore stated he would add this item to the agenda for the June 17th Commission Meeting for consideration. \par
\par
Discussion ensued among the Commission regarding the City's delay in applying for the grant. Mayor Carney stated that not all fire emergency calls require advanced life support. In many cases, basic life support was sufficient. He also mentioned that other counties are contracting with private ambulance services to alleviate the burden on firefighters who would otherwise respond to basic life support calls.\par
\par
Chief Martin presented information on fire suppression coverage, indicating that this is a risk-based recommendation. The proposal involves shutting down a fire suppression unit, which would enable the reallocation of those resources to the rescue unit. This approach would maintain minimum fire services by having at least a two-person search-and-rescue crew with limited to no suppression capabilities in one zone of the city. However, it would ensure that the City remains in a constant state of readiness for emergencies in other areas. He addressed the potential risks linked to this decision.\par
\par
The Commission discussed the importance of being adequately staffed when responding to fire or emergency calls. They noted that the City is experiencing significant growth, highlighting the need for long-term budget solutions rather than year-to-year planning. \par
\par
The Commission acknowledged that the City relies heavily on its property taxes to fund its operations, as Delray Beach does not assess its residents for other services like neighboring municipalities do.\par
\par
Mr. Moore proposed holding meetings with each Commissioner over the next two weeks to discuss the possibility of converting more parking lots into paid ones, in an effort to generate revenue for the City and to gather their thoughts.\par
\par
He then presented a detailed schedule outlining the budget topics to be discussed each month in preparation for finalizing the fiscal year 2025-2026 budget, which will be presented at the Regular Meeting on September 16th. He mentioned hosting a live-streamed Town Hall Meeting on July 24th to keep residents informed about ongoing budget considerations and parking considerations at the July 8th Regular City Commission Meeting.\par
\par
Mr. Moore requested the Commission's consensus to develop a proposal with a 3/3 staffing model aimed at securing $1.4 million. This funding would ensure that fire response trucks remain staffed with three personnel, ready to respond to emergencies. He noted that, according to the firefighters' collective bargaining agreement negotiated in 2023 and approved by the Commission, their hours would follow a 24/72 schedule, as outlined in the contract.\par
\par
\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 The June 17, 2025 Workshop Meeting was called to order at 4:07 p.m. Alexis Givings, City Clerk, called the roll, and the following were present:\par
\kerning2\f1\par
\kerning0\b Present 4\b0 - Commissioner Tom Markert , Mayor Thomas F. Carney Jr., Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns and, Commissioner Juli Casale\par
\par
\b Absent: 1\b0 - Vice-Mayor Rob Long\kerning2\f0\par
\par
Others present were:\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the meeting by discussing the Comprehensive Plan and the need to amend it to improve the educational components for the City\rquote s public schools. He emphasized that the first step would be to identify the various City departments that allocate funding for education to determine the actual amount being spent. He specifically highlighted Carver Middle School, Village Academy, and the International Baccalaureate (IB) program at Atlantic High School as underperforming institutions. He mentioned that the Chairman of the School Board shares this concern, as she had expressed during their meeting. He also referenced a competitive assessment and cluster study conducted by the Greenway Strategy Group in 2018, which evaluated the City\rquote s schools and suggested engaging Greenway to perform an updated analysis.\par
\par
\kerning0 Commissioner Casale proposed that a productive first step would be for the School Board to visit the schools, beginning with Carver Middle, Atlantic High, and Village Academy, to evaluate any shortcomings. Following this assessment, they should meet with the Commission to share their findings and discuss the Commission's requests for enhancing school performance. At that time, the Commission would have a strong basis for amending the Comprehensive Education Plan.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that his goal was to request at a future meeting $25,000 from the Commission to conduct an updated assessment by Greenway Strategy Group and an additional $25,000 to fund another comprehensive review/education study conducted by Florida International University (FIU). He stated that these two studies would provide independent analyses.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale proposed contacting the County School Board for their latest assessments on the schools before engaging in other studies.\par
\par
Mr. Moore suggested revisiting this item at the Commission Meeting on July 15\super th\nosupersub , after he and the relevant staff have contacted the School District of Palm Beach County for any relevant information they can provide on the matter. He noted that the Commission might also consider the possibility of engaging external consultants at that time.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns requested that the School Board's report include an update regarding the early prevention and wrap-around services. \cf1\f1\par
}

minutes_note:
