\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\tx2279\expndtw-2\f0\fs24 The July 8, 2025 City Commission Budget Workshop was called to order at 3:33 p.m. Alexis Givings, City Clerk, called the roll, and the following were present:\par
\par
\b\f1 Present: 5\b0\f0 - Mayor Thomas F. Carney, Jr., Vice Mayor Rob Long, Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns, Commissioner Juli Casale, Commissioner Tom Markert \par
\par
Others present were:\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Kelly Brandon, Assistant City Attorney\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\par
Mr. Moore informed the Commission that this workshop aimed to highlight the considerations presented at the June 10th Budget Workshop Meeting for achieving a balanced budget by presenting various scenarios based on proposed millage rate options. He provided his recommendations for the General Fund only and advised that the Capital Improvement Program would be presented separately. \par
\par
Henry Dachowitz, Chief Financial Officer, provided the Commission with millage rate scenarios for FY 2025-26, which would aid in determining the City\rquote s revised potential shortfall based on the City\rquote s proposed \f1 revenues and expenditures \f0 as of July 3, 2025. He stated that increasing the millage rate allows the City to fund the Fire Department's Rescue Model of 3/3 and the A-Guide (funding for non-profits). He noted that while reviewing revenues and expenses, they were being mindful of the policy regarding the fund balance. He explained that the City\rquote s residential taxes are based on the taxable value of a home, rather than its market value. He provided a breakdown of the projected citywide operating expenses for FY 2025-26 by fund type and weight:\par
\par
Internal Services:\tab $ 42,731,958 (12.26%)\par
Enterprise:\tab $ 79,731,934 (22.87 %)\par
Debt Services:\tab $ 0 (0.00 %)\par
General:\tab $ 200,411,824 (57.49%)\par
Special Revenue:\tab $ 25,731,286 (7.38 %)\par
\par
\ul Total Budget\ulnone :\tab\b $ 348,607,002.00 (100%)\par
\par
\b0\f1 Mr. Moore \f0 presented the increases and rate adjustments that were driving each type of fund within the aggregated proposed budget. He outlined the timeline and the next steps in the budget process.\par
\par
\ul July 1\ulnone - Property Appraiser certifies taxable value to municipalities.\par
\ul July 8\ulnone - Budget workshop to discuss the recommended budget and tentative millage. \par
\ul July 24\ulnone - Town Hall Meeting on Budget.\par
\ul Late July\ulnone - The Florida Department of Revenue provides estimates for state-shared revenue sources.\par
\ul August\ulnone - Additional budget workshop conducted (if necessary) - City submits tentative millage rate and non-ad valorem information to the Property Appraiser.\par
\ul September\ulnone - Public hearings held to adopt millage and budget.\par
\ul\f1 October 1 \ulnone\f0 - Fiscal year begins.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that significant changes to the proposed budget were not expected based on the trend analysis from the past 3 years.\par
\par
The Commission provided their thoughts on the presentation.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\expndtw0\ul\b Mayor Carney\ulnone\b0 expressed concerns that the City had not thoroughly examined potential areas for implementing budget cuts. He proposed various strategies for generating additional revenue to include employee contributions to health insurance and increasing parking fees for City-owned lots. Additionally, he mentioned that specific departmental responsibilities could be reassigned to other areas to help achieve budgetary savings.\par
\par
\ul\b Deputy Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone\b0 raised concerns that the millage rate options presented did not adequately address the budget shortfall. She pointed out increases that residents would face in the upcoming year and expressed her desire to avoid placing further financial burdens on taxpayers. She opposed raising the millage rate at this time, and suggested the City explore more comprehensive solutions to achieve a balanced budget.\par
\par
\ul\b Vice Mayor Long\ulnone\b0 mentioned that most of the City's road resurfacing projects have been put on hold due to budget constraints. He noted that the rollback rate from last year has contributed to the current situation and that the proposed maximum rate increase of 6.211 is still lower than the rate set for 2024. He added that increasing the millage rate would help stabilize the budget shortfalls while the City continues to look for ways to offset expenses.\par
\par
\ul\b Commissioner Casale\ulnone\b0 noted that the budget cuts presented would necessitate further depletion of the City\rquote s reserve funds. Additionally, she recommended the Mayor outline his proposed cuts before the Commission votes on the ad valorem tax. She noted that despite the City receiving funds from the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), there was still a shortfall in the City fulfilling the level of service that residents require and that the actual budget amount needed was $11.5 million to maintain the status quo.\par
\par
\ul\b Commissioner Markert\ulnone\b0 mentioned that during discussions with the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), they stated there were significant cuts to government funding. He emphasized that Florida needs to be prepared to manage a catastrophic event independently. Additionally, he noted that maintaining high reserves is beneficial, as it generates interest, and suggested that revenue generated from in-lieu parking fees be allocated towards parking improvements.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz stated the Finance Department has provided the Commission with different scenarios based on the current rate, as per their instructions. He noted the next 8 to 10 months would provide valuable insights for analyzing the budget for the next fiscal year.\par
\par
Mr. Moore emphasized that achieving a balanced budget is an ongoing process, and the Commission must continue to provide feedback, as this process is not yet complete.\cf1\f1\par
}

\par
\pard\nowidctlpar Jon Kinsman with the VAP Group provided a presentation on the site plan for the Maxwell project.\par
\par
Peggy Fitzgerald, architect for the proposed Maxwell project, discussed the Elevated Art Deco Design for this mixed-use development. She highlighted that the site design features a spacious civic area that engages the corner of NE 2nd Street and NE 4th Avenue, which connects to a covered arcade. The arcade provides covered sidewalk spaces next to the retail stores on the ground floor. The residential component of the design offers different-sized condominiums. Ms. Fitzgerald noted that after gaining staff approval for this project, they made some revisions based on feedback they received. She concluded by stating that the design would elevate the neighborhood and the Central Business District.\par
\par
\pard Mr. Kinsman discussed the applicant\rquote s request to operate the site without a designated off-street loading space. They proposed using the Railroad Street for strictly controlled loading and unloading during specified times. Additionally, he mentioned that they were seeking the Commission's approval for a reduction in the required 5-foot landscape buffer along the west side of the parking lot. He provided the summary of approvals to date:\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar August 17, 2023 - The Development Services Management group (DSMG) approved the right-of-way (ROW) reduction.\par
\par
July 10, 2024 - The Downtown Development Authority (DDA) recommended approval of the project.\par
\par
October 1, 2024 - The City Commission approved the Art Deco style, streetscape reduction waiver, front setback waiver, and civic space waiver.\par
\par
June 16, 2025 - Planning and Zoning Board recommended approval of the landscape strip reduction and no off-street loading requests.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes presented a staff report for this item, which included an aerial view of the site plan. She stated that the project met all the provisions of the code. She noted that Resolution No. 177-24 had been approved for the streetscape reduction, and Resolution No. 179-24 was approved for the Civic Open Space. \par
\par
\pard Vice Mayor Long opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item.\cf1\f1\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\cf0\ul Carta Van Voris\ulnone\f0 , representing the VAP Group \par
Noted that the railway alley is currently used only by garbage trucks and for the moving in and out of the Ocean City Lofts. She mentioned that the landscape buffer waiver would run alongside the railroad tracks.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Vice Mayor Long closed public comments.\par
\par
\pard A discussion ensued amongst the Commission regarding the physical limitations of the alley and loading area, and a consensus was reached that these were manageable issues.\cf1\f1\par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Missie Barletto, Public Works Director, and Ms. Gianniotes provided the Commission with a comprehensive overview of the proposed parking system.\par
\par
Ms. Barletto reported that the City had already implemented most of the outlined goals, except for the coordinated valet app. She discussed the performance-based parking program, which aims to guide people to price-based, tiered parking locations. The goal of this program is to increase downtown parking utilization from the current 55 percent to 85 percent. Additionally, she mentioned that this presentation focused on parking located west of the Intracoastal.\par
\par
Ms. Barletto shared an analysis of the current parking program and those in nearby municipalities. She discussed a performance-based parking system that aims at increasing parking turnover to support the success of the downtown merchants. She mentioned that this plan includes adjusting the parking times and rates. \par
\par
Ms. Barletto then presented the concept of a centralized valet parking model. She stated that there were currently 5 valet parking stations on Atlantic Avenue. The holder of the license agreement, which is an adjacent restaurant owner, pays $189.09/ month for each public parking space they have reserved for the valet queue; the City receives nothing. She mentioned that parking studies over the years have recommended moving valet queues from Atlantic Avenue onto side streets. The results of traffic modeling associated with the Swinton/Atlantic Avenue Intersection Improvement Project indicate that this project would help address congestion issues and that the current model is not conducive to working with valet operators to achieve compliance. This system would also involve communicating with the valet through an app to arrange the client's preferred pick-up time and location. She suggested that staff follow the parking model used by Coral Gables, as it\rquote s the only city in South Florida that utilizes a Centralized Valet Parking Program. She proposed engaging in a single Request for Proposal (RFP) to operate the entire parking program, with one central drop-off and 3-4 satellite stands for pickup. She mentioned that this model would include additional revenue from leasing city-owned lots for vehicle storage. She noted the possibility of store operators leasing lots for their employees.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx2279\par
Ms. Barletto stated that the Parking and Curbside Management Master Plan recommends establishing a Parking Benefits District\b , \b0 which would provide several benefits and\b \b0 support the City\rquote s operations by taking an active management approach. She stated that the Downtown Development Authority was in favor of establishing a Parking Benefits District, and it would become an element of the City\rquote s overall Transportation and Mobility Plan.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes discussed the Development Services aspect of this plan. She stated that the Parking Management Advisory Board has become obsolete due to the inability to establish a quorum, and decisions are now made directly before the Commission. \par
\par
Ms. Barletto mentioned designating a pilot program for an employee parking lot on the 4th and 5th floor levels of the Old School Square parking garage. Lastly, she concluded the presentation by stating that staff needed direction from the Commission on how to proceed with the information presented.\par
\par
A discussion ensued amongst the Commission regarding the presentation and how the elements of this program would ultimately address the City\rquote s parking issues.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar Ms. Barletto stated that this program would utilize the in-lieu fees the City collects from businesses, which would be used to maintain and repair the parking areas, thereby alleviating some of the burden on the general fund.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx2279 Ms. Gianniotes asked for a consensus on charging for the electric vehicle spaces. There was a consensus to charge for the electric charging spaces.\par
\par
The Commission thanked Ms. Barletto and Ms. Gianniotes for their hard work on this matter.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sb23 There was consensus to move forward with the proposed parking plan and tiered rate structure as outlined.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx2279 Mr. Moore instructed the staff to proceed with the plan presented.\cf1\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\expndtw-2\f0\fs24 The July 15, 2025 City Commission Meeting was called to order at 3:07 p.m. Alexis Givings, City Clerk, called the roll, and the following were present:\f1\par
\par
\pard\expndtw0\b Present: 4 \b0 - Mayor Thomas F. Carney, Jr., Vice Mayor Rob Long, Deputy Vice Mayor Angela\fs22 Burns, Commissioner Juli Casale\par
\par
\b\fs24 Absent: 1\b0 - Commissioner Tom Markert\par
\fs22\par
\fs24 Others present were:\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Kelly Brandon, Assistant City Attorney\par
\pard\nowidctlpar Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\pard\cf1\par
\cf0 Missie Barletto, Director of Public Works, and Henry Dackowitz, Chief Financial Officer, presented the Commission with the preliminary budget for the Capital Improvement Plan (CIP) budget for Fiscal Years 2026-2030. Ms. Barletto outlined the CIP budget by fund type, which totaled $295,412,650, and noted that this represented an increase of $45 million from last year. Additionally, she pointed out that a significant portion of the budget was dedicated to the City\rquote s new water treatment plant. She also presented the CIP budget by department, highlighting that the Utilities Department accounts for the majority of the expenses. She stated that numerous individual projects were included in the CIP, which this year included a Special Projects Fund that totaled $848,098. Funding for these projects will come from in-lieu parking fees and recouped litigation fees. She discussed the General Construction Revenue Fund, which included grants that support the CIP projects as well as funds appropriated by legislation. The Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) also funds several large-scale projects in the CIP. This year, the City will begin utilizing the funds from the Parks Safety General Obligations Bond, which will support the Fire Stations and Ocean Rescue initiatives. She discussed the Water and Sewer Revenue Fund, for which the City was awarded $1.5 million from the House Committee for the Tropic Isle Neighborhood Improvement Project.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar The Municipal Golf Course and clubhouse secured financing of $24,500,000 for renovations this year and an additional $2,500,000 for the 2026-2027 fiscal year. She discussed the Stormwater Utility / Revenue Fund, which the Commission voted to increase. She stated that this increase would generate an additional $2,224,615 for the upcoming fiscal year. Additionally, she mentioned that the City is exploring various loan and bond options to cover the total expense for this initiative over the next 5 years, which amounts to $6,820,000. \par
\par
The Commission discussed the presentation and expressed their gratitude to Ms. Barletto for her efforts. Ms. Barletto acknowledged that the list of capital improvement projects was crucial for the City\rquote s progress. She stated that she was working to find a source to cover the $6.6 million deficit in the General Construction fund and hoped to have it identified by the next presentation.\cf1\par
}

\par
\pard\b BOYS AND GIRLS CLUB OF PALM BEACH COUNTY\expndtw0\b0\f1\fs22\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx2279\expndtw-2\f0\fs24 Pablo Tejada, Chief Impact Officer, shared the club's accomplishments over the past year. He emphasized that their primary goal is to create a safe and positive environment for the youth and teens in the communities that need support the most. He stated that they achieved this by fostering a welcoming atmosphere, building healthy and supportive relationships, and providing meaningful experiences. They aim to equip children with strong character, leadership skills, and academic success to prepare them for life and future careers. Mr. Tejada also noted that Delray Beach has seen the fastest growth in membership within Palm Beach County.\f2\par
\par
\f0 Frankie Pierre-Paul, Executive Club Director, shared that they have partnered with various organizations to teach the children about sports and fitness, cultural arts, mental health, workforce readiness, and other essential life skills. He mentioned that since January, they have been providing food to families on Fridays and the last Saturday of each month, so the families have food over the weekend.\par
\par
Mr. Tejada noted that more than 40 organizations collaborate with the club to help the children. He expressed gratitude to the City for its support.\f2\par
\par
\pard\b\f0 SPADY CULTURAL HERITAGE MUSEUM\expndtw0\b0\f1\fs22\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\expndtw-2\f0\fs24 Charlene Farrington, Executive Director, was present to discuss this year's exhibits, workshops, and lectures\f2 .\f0 She outlined the museum\rquote s plans for the fiscal year 2025-2026, emphasizing their continued commitment to being good partners and stewards of Delray Beach. The museum's goals include maintaining programs and events that foster personal growth for the diverse community of Delray Beach and the surrounding municipalities. She mentioned that management has been challenged to mitigate the loss of national and state funding cuts. She presented the Commission with the museum's year-to-date profit and loss statement, detailing how this year\rquote s funding from the City and the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) was utilized\f2 .\par
\par
\f0 The Commission expressed their gratitude to Ms. Farrington\f2 .\f0 Mayor Carney noted that the Spady Cultural Museum is the only museum in Palm Beach County dedicated to Black history.\f2\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx2279\par
\pard\b\f0 ACHIEVEMENT CENTER FOR CHILDREN AND FAMILIES\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\b0 Stephanie Siebel, Chief Executive Officer and Strategic Advisor, along with Jalesa Huggins, Chief Operating Officer,\b \b0 were present to discuss their ongoing mission, which is to nurture a collaborative community where children are inspired to reach their full potential. Ms. Siebel noted that they work under an agreement with the City of Delray Beach and the School District of Palm Beach County. She also stated that they serve over 750 children annually, with 63% of them residing in Delray Beach. The families they work with are multicultural, with 45% of the children speaking Creole, and most households earning less than $800 per month. Additionally, many of the students come from single-parent households. The Center offers scholarships and affordable programs to remove financial barriers for families to enable children to receive a quality education and quality out-of-school care. She noted that they hold the highest accreditation in both schooling and non-profit organizations. She stated that they recently launched their EmpowerED Program, which aims to close the learning gap by supporting under-resourced K-12 students in Southern Palm Beach County through personalized academic support, test preparation, mentorship, and social and emotional learning to help them reach their full potential. Finally, she mentioned that the facilities are showing signs of wear and require improvement. They will be implementing a new strategic plan for the next 3-5 years. They thanked the City staff for their trust, collaboration, and shared vision.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx2279 The Commission thanked Ms. Siebel, Ms. Huggins, and the Achievement Center for their positive impact on children and families.\f2\par
\par
\pard\b\f0 SANDOWAY HOUSE NATURE CENTER\expndtw0\b0\f1\fs22\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\expndtw-2\f0\fs24 Danica Sanborn was present to discuss the facility\rquote s accomplishments over the past year, including receiving the All-America City Award. She stated that the center's mission is to inspire students and visitors through experiential conservation. She also mentioned that the center welcomed 17,000 visitors and hosted students from various schools on field trips. She discussed multiple programs that are offered free of charge to children, including the Science Leadership Academy, which focuses on helping students struggling in specific areas of science. Ms. Sandborn stated that the center has taught hundreds of children by collaborating with the City\rquote s partner organizations. She highlighted their partnership with the City in efforts to protect the coastal ecosystem, which includes activities such as beach cleanups, sea turtle nest excavations, and environmental education initiatives aimed at securing Blue Flag Certification. She mentioned that they won the medium non-profit of the year award this year, and were nearing the completion of their new renovations. Lastly, she thanked the City for their continued support of the Sandoway House Nature Center and for allowing them to serve the community by teaching thousands about the importance of our coastal ecosystems.\par
\par
The Commission expressed their gratitude to the Sandoway House Nature Center and its staff for their exceptional efforts in providing educational programs for children who might not otherwise have access to such opportunities. They also recognized the center's important role in preserving the City\rquote s ecosystem.\par
\par
\pard\b DELRAY BEACH HISTORICAL SOCIETY\expndtw0\b0\f1\fs22\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\expndtw-2\f0\fs24 Winnie Edwards, Executive Director, was present to discuss their annual update. She mentioned that the upcoming year will mark the Historical Society\rquote s 40th year partnering with the City. She emphasized that their mission is to inspire and encourage everyone to reflect on the City's history by inviting residents to study and discover the remarkable achievements and milestones that have made Delray what it is today. She mentioned that they strive to be mindful of both the past and the present to foster community connections through their programming and engagement initiatives. They interact with over ten thousand people each year through their programming and events, on and off-site. Ms. Edwards stated that they have invested in upgrades and improvements to their aerial projects, which will aid City planners in future city initiatives. She also discussed their latest historical archive collaboration with PEB Capital that involves identifying historical markers in Sundy Village. \par
\par
The Commission expressed its gratitude to Ms. Edwards, along with the entire staff and volunteers of the Delray Beach Historical Society.\par
\par
\pard\b DELRAY BEACH PUBLIC LIBRARY\expndtw0\b0\f1\fs22\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\expndtw-2\f0\fs24 Mykal Banta, Executive Director, provided a presentation that highlighted the essential free services and benefits the library offers to residents and visitors of the City. Mr. Banta shared the history of the library that was established in 1913. He stated that since 1950, the library's patrons have received library service through a successful public/private partnership between the City of Delray Beach and the Library Association. Mr. Banta discussed the numerous programs offered to children and adults, including a technology training and instruction lab. He noted that since Delray Beach directly funds the library, there has been no library tax since 1967. However, if the City were to stop funding the library, residents would face an additional tax burden of $9.7 million per year.\par
\par
The Commission thanked Mr. Banta for his 31 years of dedicated service to the library and for all that the library offers to residents and visitors.\cf1\expndtw0\f2\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\tx2279\expndtw-2\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore provided the Commission with an executive summary based on the current position, reflecting the feedback and guidance given during the July 8th Budget Workshop. He stated that the proposed operating millage rate of 6.1611 was a difference of 0.2548 from the previous year's rate. He noted that the majority of the City Commission had previously expressed their desire to maintain the current level of service, and achieving this goal required raising the millage rate.\par
\par
Mayor Carney proposed that staff be given a rate of 5.9% and develop a budget that complies with this rate. He informed the Commission that the government recommended that cities review their expenses carefully because if the City seeks funding from the state, officials will want to know what measures the City took to make the necessary budget cuts. He suggested that the Downtown Development Authority (DDA) absorb the costs of specific City events, as they benefit most from these events. He reiterated that he favored keeping the millage rate unchanged. He provided examples of how the City could save money. \par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion on the millage rate and emphasized the importance of maintaining service levels for both City stakeholders and visitors. It was mentioned that adjusting the current millage rate to 6.1611 would provide citizens with a strong police presence, well-paved roads, and properly equipped emergency vehicles, along with other essential services. \f1\par

\pard\expndtw-2\up3\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that Hassan Hadjimiry, Utilities Director, would discuss this item and recommend ways to utilize the funds from the PFAS settlement for the construction of the new water treatment facility.\par
\par
\expndtw0\up0 Mr. Hadjimiry, stated that, in response to public concerns and to ensure complete transparency, the Utilities Department proactively and voluntarily tested for PFAS in the City\rquote s drinking water in August 2020. He noted that the results were posted on the City\rquote s website and shared with the Department of Health. He explained that it was believed Delray was testing its water due to a local issue. However, on December 27, 2021, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) mandated that all municipalities in the United States begin testing for unregulated contaminants between 2023 and 2025. \par
\par
The results indicated that PFAS contamination was widespread across the country. He also mentioned that the new water treatment plant would be equipped with a nano-filtration system designed to remove all PFAS. He stated that in mid-2022, the City Attorney\rquote s Office requested Delray Beach join the national class-action lawsuit against PFAS manufacturers and worked diligently with the Utilities Department to gather and submit all relevant data. The cities prevailed in winning the national class-action lawsuit. Payment installments would be paid quarterly from 2026 to 2033. He requested that these funds be protected from general fund absorption and deposited solely for the use of the Utilities Department to achieve a long-lasting, positive impact on public health and regulatory compliance.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar The Commission expressed its gratitude to Mr. Hadjimiry and Ms. Gelin for their diligent efforts on this matter and agreed to use the settlement funds exclusively for improvements to the Utilities Department.\cf1\f1\par
}

\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that representatives from Public Financial Management (PFM) were present to provide an updated financial analysis of the golf course renovation program's rate structure. He mentioned that the City was also in line to select a contractor for the project.\par
\par
Joe Buckshon, Senior Managing Consultant with PFM, provided an overview of the preliminary new rate structure for the Delray Beach Municipal Golf Course, which aligns with surrounding courses based on a statistical analysis of those rates. Mr. Buckshon highlighted the course's rich history in the area and its popularity among local leagues. However, he also pointed out some of the course's weaknesses, including the lack of a maintenance and a capital budgets. He noted that the rates for a round of golf had not increased in many years, which would be a factor in the proposed rate increases, especially with the extensive renovations anticipated for the course. He recommended an initial rate of $80 for residents and $105 for non-residents, with a resident discount of approximately 25%. He suggested that rates should continue to increase by 5% through 2031, after which they would revert to an inflation-adjusted increase of 2%. He emphasized that these increases would help compensate for the years without any rate adjustments. He noted that in 2027, the course would be cash positive and would generate funds to support savings and investments in future capital expenditures.\par
\par
Jay Glover, Managing Director with PFM, stated that as the project moves forward, PFM will be bringing a bond resolution at a subsequent meeting to issue debt to finance these projects. He noted that the financing would be secured by non-ad valorem revenue from the City and would not require funding from the General Fund.\par
\par
The Commission thanked Mr. Glover and Mr. Buckshon for their presentation.\par

\par

Mayor Carney read the quasi-judicial rules into the record.\par
\par
Ms. Givings swore in those individuals who wished to provide testimony on this item.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked his colleagues to disclose any ex-parte communications for this item.\par
\par
\ul Mayor Carney\ulnone : What was on the server.\par
\ul Vice Mayor Long\ulnone : What was on the server.\par

\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Director of Development Services, entered File No. 2025-006 into the record.\par
\par
Christofer Bernardo, Attorney, provided an overview of the request for a waiver/relief of the Workforce Housing Requirement for the property located at 228 SE 3rd Avenue. He mentioned that the house, built in 1930, is currently uninhabitable. Additionally, he noted that the cost of rehabilitating the home was significantly higher than the cost of redeveloping the property. He stated that the Land Development Regulations require a waiver for a lot with less than 50 feet of frontage to build non-workforce housing. He noted that many of the neighboring lots had under 50 feet of frontage. He concluded his presentation by stating that the Commission had previously granted the same waiver for neighboring homes. \par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes presented a brief staff report on this item. She stated that granting this waiver would not result in a special privilege, as the same waiver would be given under similar circumstances to other properties for other applicants or owners.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item.\par
\par
\ul Christina Morrison\ulnone , 1000 Lowery Street, Delray Beach\par
Expressed concern that this neighborhood was intended for workforce housing. She requested that the Commission deny this request.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comments.\par
\par
Mr. Bernardo stated that his client was the original owner of this lot and had not made any modifications since purchasing it.\par
\par
There was no cross-examination or rebuttal from either side.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion regarding the need for regulatory changes concerning minor modifications. \par
\par
Mayor Carney requested that Ms. Gianniotes and her team look into a solution to this issue.\cf1\f1\par

Missie Barletto, Public Works Director, presented the annual Stormwater Utility Rate Tax Roll assessment for 2026 which established the budget for Stormwater Utility systems and rates for Stormwater Management that were approved in June.\up1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\sb1\tx2279\par

\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 The August 12, 2025 Workshop Meeting was called to order at 4:03 p.m. Alexis Givings, City Clerk, called the roll, and the following were present:\par
\par
\b Present: 4 -\b0 Mayor Thomas F. Carney, Jr., Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns, Commissioner Juli Casale, Commissioner Tom Markert \par
\par
\b Absent: 1 - \b0 Vice Mayor Rob Long\par
\par
Others present were:\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney \par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that, based on the Commission\rquote s directives from the July 15, 2025 Regular City Commission Meeting, this meeting's purpose aims to finalize discussions regarding amendments to the Education Element of the Delray Beach Comprehensive Plan. He mentioned that there would not be a formal presentation; however, leadership from the Director of Development Services was available to answer any questions.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked each Commissioner to share their thoughts on what they would like to see incorporated into the Education Element of the Comprehensive Plan to help drive and promote early childhood success, family engagement, grade-level reading, and workforce development.\par
\par
Some highlights of what the Commission expressed interest in were:\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Establish a task force to investigate successful practices in other communities to meet with parents, non-profits, and teachers.\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Meet more frequently with the School Board and representatives from each school to identify gaps, which would be addressed through a \ldblquote Sharing for Excellence\rdblquote plan. \par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Workshop with the residents through Town Hall Meetings.\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Adding a block of time to the school day.\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Formalize the City\rquote s liaison role with the School Board.\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Request additional assistance from the non-profits. \par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Strengthening the City\rquote s collaboration with the School Board by scheduling more frequent meetings to ensure the City was addressing their needs.\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Expand the wrap-around organizations that focus on children\rquote s mental health and wellness.\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Create career pathways through additional internship programs.\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Celebrate the achievements of our schools and students.\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 -\tab Advocate for dual language programming.\par
\pard\par
Mayor Carney stated that he had not received the requested education data from several individuals and, therefore, was not prepared to make any changes to the comprehensive plan until he obtained that information. He emphasized that a shared analysis would reveal trends in the education program rather than incomplete data and referenced the 2019 Always Delray Comprehensive Plan. He stressed that strengthening the City\rquote s schools would serve as an economic driver and attract companies to relocate to Delray Beach.\par
\par
Mr. Moore proposed that the City begin holding biannual meetings with School Board leadership. He stated that he would collect the specific data that some felt was lacking and use that to suggest any amendments to the Comprehensive Plan. Additionally, he would schedule a joint workshop meeting with the School Board in the coming weeks. He proposed the reinstatement of the Education Board that would serve as a Task Force, as recommended.\par
\par
There was consensus from the Commission to allow Mr. Moore to proceed as suggested.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\par
Missie Barletto, Public Works Director, provided an update on the implementation of the proposed Downtown Parking and Curbside Plan for employee parking. She mentioned that the Commission still needed to give feedback on specific aspects of the proposed plan that were discussed at a Commission meeting in July. She stated that the Parking and Curbside Management Master Plan recommended a month-to-month parking permit option for the downtown employees, which would cost $15.00 per month. She explained that this option would allow employees to park in any metered spot in the City, except for downtown.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion on the feasibility of this model and noted that the City might face financial losses under this structure.\par
\par
Mayor Carney suggested that store owners take responsibility for their employees' parking, similar to that in surrounding municipalities.\par
\par
The Commission suggested testing this proposal through a pilot program before adopting it.\par
\par
\kerning2\f1 There was consensus to initiate a six-month pilot program, charging employees $10 per month, starting on October 1, 2025, and concluding in April 2026. An update would be provided to the Commission in January 2026.\par
\par
\kerning0\ul\f0 Surface Parking Lots\ulnone :\par
\par
Ms. Barletto discussed the City\rquote s current parking program for surface lots, which were currently free but had time limits. She provided the projected revenues for the City based on the proposed rate structures for these lots. She stated that the City targets an 85% occupancy rate in these lots and could adjust the rates and hours as needed. She noted that the annual increase in rates was anticipated to bring the total to just over $8 million, given the newly proposed rate structure and timing model.\par
\par
\cf1 The Commission thanked Ms. Barletto for her efforts.\f2\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Mayor Carney asked anyone who had not been sworn in and wished to speak on this item to be sworn in by the Clerk.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked his colleagues to disclose any ex-parte communications.\par
\f1\par
\ul\f0 Mayor Carney\ulnone : Spoke with Jim Chard, Neil Schiller, members of the Historic Preservation Trust, Ann Whitehead, Gail Clark, Roger Cope, and Sandy Zeller, as well as what was on the server.\par
\ul Vice Mayor Long\ulnone : Spoke with Neil Schiller, Jordana Jarjura, Jim Chard, and emails on the server.\par
\ul Deputy Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone : Spoke with Neil Schiller, Price Patton, and emails on the server.\par
\ul Commissioner Casale:\ulnone Spoke with Neil Schiller, Jim Chard, the Historic Preservation Trust, and Kristin Finn, as well as emails on the server.\par
\ul Commissioner Markert\ulnone : Spoke with Neil Schiller, and emails on the server.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin entered Resolution No. 135-25 into the record.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes entered File No. 2024-133 into the record.\par
\par
Neil Schiller, attorney for the applicant, stated that for the record, he had sent a letter to Ms. Gelin on July 15\super th\nosupersub requesting that Commissioner Casale recuse herself from this hearing based on comments she made during the June 17\super th\nosupersub Commission meeting, where it appeared that she could not be objective on this item. He made this statement to preserve the record.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale discussed Mr. Schiller\rquote s request for her to recuse herself from this hearing. She expressed concern that the Mayor may have an appearance of impropriety on this project and how it affects the taxpayers' trust.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin asked Commissioner Casale if she could render a fair and impartial opinion on this item. Commissioner Casale confirmed that she could.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin stated that the Mayor secured a letter from the Commission on Ethics, dated July 29, 2025, confirming his eligibility to participate in this matter.\par
\par
Mr. Schiller delivered a presentation on this item, highlighting that the applicant intended to protect and preserve the property instead of demolishing it. He pointed out that the house was not situated at the proper grade, rendering it substandard. He noted that the developer had taken actions to modify the home based on the March 5\super th\nosupersub Historic Preservation Board Meeting. He stated that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) requires an elevation of 8 feet. In comparison, the Florida Building Code mandates an elevation of 9 feet, one foot higher than FEMA's requirement. He mentioned that the Secretary of the Interior\rquote s standards for rehabilitation also supported the elevation of historic homes, as flooding events could be particularly destructive to historic homes.\par
\par
Mr. Nguyen, with Affinity Architecture, discussed the project, stating that the home was currently uninhabitable in its current state. He noted that the house needed to be raised 6 \'bd feet to meet FEMA\rquote s minimum elevation and to maintain the home's structure.\par
\par
Michelle Hoyland, Principal Planner, provided a staff presentation on this item. She noted that the surrounding homes were also requesting a 9-foot vertical elevation but were awaiting the outcome of this matter. She expressed concerns that adding a structure on top of an existing historic structure could compromise the streetscape and the historic integrity of the building. Ms. Hoyland presented an analysis from City staff that outlined several concerns they had regarding the approval of this item.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item.\par
\par
\ul Price Patton\ulnone , on behalf of the Delray Beach Historic Preservation Trust\par
Expressed concern that the applicant's proposed plan would jeopardize the home's historical integrity to the extent proposed.\par
\par
\ul Sandy Zeller\ulnone\f1 ,\f0 209 NW 12\super th\nosupersub Street, Delray Beach\par
Expressed his support for considering the expert advice of the City\rquote s planners regarding this item.\par
\par
\ul Carolyn Patton\ulnone , 1020 Tamrind Road, Delray Beach\par
Discussed the history of the Marina District and emphasized the importance of preserving it by denying the applicant\rquote s request.\par
\par
\ul Jim Chard\ulnone , 401 SE 4\super th\nosupersub Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Suggested reaching a compromise between the City's recommendations and the applicant's requests for this project.\par
\par
\ul Daniele Edwards\ulnone , 46 Marine Way (owner of the property)\par
Stated that he was trying to preserve the home and mentioned that the surrounding properties could also be raised if their owners wished to do so.\par
\par
\ul Kristin Finn\ulnone , 102 George Bush Blvd, Delray Beach\par
Emphasized that the property owner doesn\rquote t want to demolish the home but rather renovate it to its maximum allowable capacity.\par
\par
\ul Roger Cope\ulnone , 701 SE 1\super st\nosupersub Street, Delray Beach\par
Expressed concern that the proposed elevation for this project was five feet higher than necessary, and the rationale for the design did not make sense to him as an architect.\par
\par
At approximately 10:57 p.m., Ms. Gelin proposed a motion to extend the meeting if the Commission wished to continue past 11:00 p.m.\par
\par
\b\f2\fs20 A motion was made by Commissioner Casale, seconded by Deputy Mayor Burns, to extend the meeting beyond 11:00 p.m.\par
\par
all were in favor\f0\fs24\par
\cf1\b0\f2\par
\cf0\f0 Ms. Gelin instructed the Commission not to consider the neighbors' comments, as they are hearsay, and the Commission was acting as a quasi-judge. \par
\par
Mayor Carney asked the applicant if he would like to provide a rebuttal.\par
\par
Mr. Nguyen expressed his gratitude to the staff for their dedicated work on the project over the past two years. Additionally, he pointed out that the site is not as large as it appears in the graphic representations.\par
\par
Mr. Schiller stated that this project exemplified adaptive reuse and pointed out that the Secretary of the Interior noted that when dealing with flood-prone areas, homeowners sometimes need to take additional steps to preserve the structure. He noted that his client would be amenable to revisions or suggestions from staff.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin stated that there were no revisions allowed for this project.\par
\par
Ms. Hoyland addressed inconsistencies between the applicant's presentation and the staff's findings. She mentioned that changes have to happen to be flood resistant, but the modifications should always be the one that minimizes changes to the home's historic character.\par
\par
A discussion ensued among the Commission about whether the modifications requested by the applicant were more appropriate than demolishing the home and rebuilding it. They acknowledged that if special privileges continue to be allowed, the City risks losing this particular Historic District.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes stated that demolishing the home would require Board approval and must comply with the necessary setbacks.\par
\par
Mayor Carney suggested bringing this project back with modifications made by the applicant.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin cautioned the Commission that what was before them was an appeal, and they had to decide that evening on the property\rquote s relocation, variances, waivers, and certificate of appropriateness.\par
\cf1\f2\par
\b\fs20 A motion was made by Commissioner Casale, seconded by Commissioner Markert, to deny Resolution No. 135-25. The motion carried by the following vote:\par
\par
Yes: \b0 3 - Commissioner Markert, Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, and Commissioner Casale\b\par
No: \b0 2 - Mayor Carney and Vice Mayor Long\b\par
\b0\fs24\par
At this time, Vice Mayor Long left the dais for the rest of the evening.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Brennan Keeler, Esq, of the Palm Beach County Police Benevolent Association (PBA) was present to represent both the Officers and Sergeants, as well as the Lieutenants and Captains. Mr. Keeler stated that this meeting would be conducted as a quasi-judicial hearing, which necessitates a strict duty of fairness and impartiality. Therefore, the Commission must consider the positions of both the City and the Union equally in order to reach a fair and impartial decision. He provided a PowerPoint presentation that reviewed the unresolved issues between the City and the PBA, along with the recommendations from the Special Magistrate. He noted that there was currently no contract between the City and the PBA. \par
\par
He suggested that when considering salaries, the City should look to the Palm Beach County Sheriff\rquote s office, rather than the surrounding municipalities, for comparisons. and that Delray Beach should mirror the City of Boynton Beach\rquote s Step Plan. He concluded by stating that the total costs for the PBA proposal versus the City\rquote s would amount to $600,000 to finalize the deal, and he provided the following breakdown of expenses.\par
\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\fi-360\li720\f1\'b7\tab\f0 $361,820.50 is the cost to hire, train, and officer, and then leave after 3 years. \par
\pard\nowidctlpar\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\fi-360\li720\f1\'b7\tab\f0 $9,045,512.50 is the amount of money lost by the City on the account of 25 officers leaving since June 2024.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\fi-360\li720\f1\'b7\tab\f0 $15.89 million is PBA\rquote s wage proposal cost for a 3-year collective bargaining agreement.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\par
Brett Schneider, Esq., was present as the City's outside labor counsel. He stated that the City had been negotiating with the Union\rquote s two bargaining units since June 2024, before reaching an impasse and presented a Power Point presentation that highlighted the recommendations from the Special Magistrate, received on July 7, 2025, which suggested adopting psychological fitness testing when deemed necessary by the City, through a licensed psychologist; mandating post-accident drug and alcohol testing; and accepting the City\rquote s wage proposal, in addition to the Union\rquote s pension proposal.\par
\par
He stated that the City modified its proposal in response to Mr. Kazanjian's (PBCPBA President) comments from the February 18, 2025Commission Meeting, where he noted that Delray Beach had the second-lowest pay and benefits in Palm Beach and Martin Counties. He mentioned that the modified proposal would provide more money to officers immediately and more funds to officers on the lower end of the pay scale. He noted that the City's modified proposal aims to help recruit and retain officers.\par
\par
The Special Magistrate\rquote s report noted that the Union\rquote s wage proposal does not increase starting pay to make the City competitive and does not address the issue of attrition. The Magistrate also mentioned that the City\rquote s wage proposal better addresses the significant problem of attracting and retaining officers than does the PBA proposal, and the resolution of this problem was undoubtedly in the best interest of the public.\par
\par
In conclusion, Mr. Schneider stated that the Union\rquote s proposal should be rejected because it adds additional costs for retaining highly paid senior employees, limits promotional opportunities, and the cost savings of the Deferred Retirement Options Plan (DROP) change are far less than the loss to the City of use of premium tax revenue.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion on the proposals presented by both attorneys. Mayor Carney reminded the Commission that they could ask questions to both parties.\par
\par
The Commission noted that based on the Commission's proposal made on July 22nd, most of the issues aligned with the recommendations of the Special Magistrate. However, they noted that there was no consensus on proceeding with changes to the 185 funds. Additionally, they recognized the importance of remaining competitive with the City of Boynton Beach regarding its police officers\rquote compensation. They stressed the importance of putting closure on this matter.\par
\par
Mayor Carney requested that everyone take a ten minute break.\par
\par
The meeting was recessed at 12:05 a.m. and reconvened at 12:25 p.m.\par
\par
Mr. Schneider stated that during the break, the counsel discussed a potentially mutually agreeable solution to the impasse.\par
\par
Mayor Carney suggested voting on the items/articles.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin entered Article 8, Section 13 into the record with modifications that stated:\par
\par
Motion to propose the City's impasse proposal with the proposed language being, \ldblquote The City has the right to require employees submit to a medical and or psychological examination by a physician or licensed psychological examination by a physician designated by the City when such examination or inquiry is shown to be job-related and consistent with business necessity.\rdblquote\fs22 \par
\par
\b\f2 A motion was made by Commissioner Casale, seconded by Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, to approve this item. The motion carried by the following vote:\par
\par
Yes: 5 - \b0 Mayor Carney, Vice Mayor Long, Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, Commissioner Markert, Commissioner Casale.\par
\b\par
\b0\f0\fs24 Ms. Gelin entered Article 27 for Lieutenants and Article 29\b \b0 for Police Officers / Sergeants into the record.\par
\f2\par
\pard\b\fs22 A motion was made by Commissioner Casale, seconded by Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, to approve Article 27 and Article 29. The motion carried by the following vote:\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\par
Yes: 5 - \b0 Mayor Carney, Vice Mayor Long, Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, Commissioner Markert, Commissioner Casale. \par
\b\par
\b0\f0\fs24 Commissioner Casale noted that approving this plan would impact the Department Directors and the Assistant Department Directors, who were already receiving substantial salaries. \par
\par
Duane D'Andrea, Human Resources Director, approached the presentation table and stated that these discussions are necessary to address as the pay scale moves up for the Police and Firemen\rquote s salaries.\par
\par
Mr. Moore noted that this would be considered accordingly.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin mentioned that a wage study conducted by the City recommended addressing the pay plans according to the Consumer Price Index to help keep up with the City\rquote s bargaining employees, who come before the Commission every three years.\par
\par
\pard\b\fs22 A motion was made by Vice Mayor Long, seconded by Commissioner Casale, to implement the Union\rquote s modified wage increase for officers and sergeants. \f2 The motion carried by the following vote:\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\b0\par
\fs24 Mr. Schneider reviewed the step structure that would be implemented for the pay rate\b .\par
\f0\fs22\par
Yes: 5 - \b0 Mayor Carney, Vice Mayor Long, Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, Commissioner Markert, Commissioner Casale.\b \par
\par
\b0\fs24 Ms. Gelin read the motion into the record for the modified Union Drop Proposal.\par
\par
Motion to impose a modified Union proposal that would provide an 8-year DROP, extending the DROP from 5 years to 8 years, members would contribute 3 percent of their salary during months 61 through 96, there would be no pension COLA while participating in the DROP, and the start date would be October 1, 2026.\par
\par
\b\f2\fs22 A motion was made by Vice Mayor Long, seconded by Vice Mayor Burns, to accept the modified Union DROP\rquote s proposal. The motion carried by the following vote:\b0\f0\fs24\par
\par
\b Yes: 3\b0 - Vice Mayor Long, Commissioner Markert, Deputy Vice Mayor Burns\par
\b No: 2\b0 - Mayor Carney, Commissioner Casale\par
\par
\b\f2\fs22 A motion was made by Vice Mayor Long, seconded by Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, to maintain the mutual consent as to the current use of Chapter 185 State Premium Tax Revenues. The motion carried by the following vote:\par
\b0\par
\b Yes: -\b0 Mayor Carney, Vice Mayor Long, Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, Commissioner Casale, Commissioner Markert\par
\par
\f0\fs24 Mayor Carney stated that this agreement will be presented to the Union for a vote. If it passes, the City will impose it starting on October 1, 2024 and continuing until September 30, 2027.\par
\par
Mayor Carney requested a motion to adjourn the meeting.\par
\par
\b\fs22 A motion was made by Vice Mayor Long, seconded by Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, to adjourn the meeting.\par
\par
all were in favor\par
\par
\b0\f2\fs24 Mayor Carney thanked everyone for participating.\par
\par
There being no further business to discuss, the meeting was adjourned at 12:50 p.m.\f0\par
\pard\cf1\f2\par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\froman\fprq2\fcharset0 Times New Roman;}{\f2\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Aptos;}{\f3\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Ms. Gelin entered Resolution No. 180-25 into the record.\par
\expndtw-2\f1\par
\f0 Mr. Dachowitz presented this item and discussed the impact that the proposed millage rate would have on the average homeowner, estimating it to be about $116. He pointed out that although this year\rquote s millage rate had increased, it was still lower than the rate in 2024. Additionally, Mr. Dachowitz presented the proposed operating budget and explained its effects based on fund type and department.\par
\expndtw0\f1\par
\f0 Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f2 Seeing no one present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\kerning0\f0 The Commission engaged in a discussion regarding the presentation and acknowledged that increasing the millage rate would enable the City to meet the costs of its contractual obligations and enhance resident safety. However, they noted that the City still faced a funding shortfall. title: PUBLIC COMMENTS

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f2\froman\fprq2\fcharset2 Symbol;}{\f3\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Aptos;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\tx2279\f0\fs24 The Commission engaged in a discussion on this matter, emphasizing that the Pride Streetscape does not pose any risks to public safety, as indicated by the State\rquote s justification for its removal. Additionally, the City was not given the chance to present evidence-based facts through due process before the State painted over the streetscape covertly in the middle of the night.\par
\f1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\f0 Lynn Gelin, City Attorney, discussed the petition filed by Miami Beach and Fort Lauderdale, which challenges the validity of the unadopted rule established by FDOT when they painted over the Pride Streetscapes throughout the state's municipalities, and suggested the Commission could take similar action. She stated that the Commission could either appeal the order issued on September 8\super th\nosupersub to remove the Pride Streetscape or join in the litigation with the cities of Miami Beach and Fort Lauderdale. She noted that litigation would be very costly, whereas an appeal would move quickly. \par
\par
Mayor Carney discussed the Commission\rquote s options and noted that challenging the State would be very costly to the taxpayers and that the City would most likely not succeed. He mentioned that the City had adopted the FDOT manual, which includes maintaining the City\rquote s roads as it see fit. He noted that Key West had decided to come into compliance with the FDOT, so as not to risk State funding and go through the expense of litigation. He voiced his support for exploring alternative ways that were just as meaningful in recognizing the LGBTQ community while ensuring compliance and maintaining State funding for roadwork, etc.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long expressed his concerns about the City\rquote s right to Fair Due Process and Home Rule. He noted that there would be cost-sharing benefits if Delray Beach joined other municipalities in petitioning the FDOT.\f1\par
\par
\f0 Mr. Moore shared that he had received a phone call earlier from a representative at the FDOT District 4 Headquarters. The representative acknowledged that FDOT had done a poor job overnight by painting over the streetscape, which resulted in partially smeared paint. They discussed their commitment to return to the City to conduct hydro blasting of the crosswalk to ensure compliance. Mr. Moore emphasized that if the City did not respond promptly to this offer, FDOT would come back immediately to carry out the hydro blasting, potentially as soon as the next day. He noted that this situation was unique because, regardless of the Commission's preferences, the FDOT was determined to proceed with its plans, which were to completely remove the Pride Crosswalk.\f1\par
\pard\cf1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\cf0\f0 Ms. Gelin presented the Commission with three options:\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\fi-360\li720\f2\'b7\tab\f1 Direct the City Manager to remove the Pride Streetscape and explore other areas in the City to acknowledge the LGBTQ community at the following week's meeting.\par
\f2\'b7\f1\tab Pursue either an appeal, which would be contesting the final order from the FDOT, that would give the City a stay.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\fi-360\li720\qj\f2\'b7\f1\tab Join the cities of Fort Lauderdale and Miami Beach in contesting the rule-making authority with a final hearing, via litigation.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\qj\par
\f0 A motion was made by Vice Mayor Long, seconded by Commissioner Markert, to join Fort Lauderdale and Miami Beach in a petition effort to the Department of Administrative Hearings (DOAH), and that for now, get a stay of enforcement and hydro blast the intersection to make it viable, rather than immediately sandblasting it. The motion carried by the following:\par
\par
\b Yes: 3 -\b0 Vice Mayor Long, Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, Commissioner Markert\par
\b No: 1\b0 - Mayor Carney\par
\par
\pard After the vote was taken, Commissioner Markert requested that Missie Barletto, Public Works Director, explain to the Commission the difference between sandblasting versus hydro blasting. She approached the presentation table and stated that hydro blasting is essentially sandblasting using water to keep the sand down.\par
\f3\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\qj\f0 There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 6:44 p.m.\cf1\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\fs24 The September 11, 2025 Special Meeting was called to order at 6:12 p.m. Alexis Givings, City Clerk, called the roll, and the following were present:\par
\par
\b Present: 5 -\b0 Mayor Carney, Jr., Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns, Vice Mayor Rob Long, Commissioner Juli Casale, Commissioner Tom Markert\par
\par
Others present were:\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\cf1\kerning0\par
\cf0\kerning2 Prior to Public Comment, Vice Mayor Long raised a point of order and read a letter he had written concerning the meeting. He stated that this meeting was noticed and calendared as a special meeting, not an emergency meeting. He referenced the City\rquote s Charter, which requires a minimum notice of 12 hours whenever practicable. He pointed out that only 5 hours of notice was given for this meeting, emphasizing that a 12-hour notice was not an unreasonable expectation, especially since this was not an emergency. He argued that by scheduling this meeting with such short notice, the City was deliberately compressing notice that blocked public input and invited Sunshine challenges and potential fee exposure, and the loss of public trust. He requested moving this meeting to a properly noticed meeting on Monday, September 15, at 3:00 p.m.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that the meeting was scheduled for 6:00 p.m. to accommodate the Commissioners' availability.\par
\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney, stated that the local rules do address special meetings and commented that the meeting was properly noticed and was postponed by 5 hours. She read the local rules regarding noticing special meetings into the record, which stated that the failure to provide a 12-hour notice did not affect the legality of this meeting.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long expressed concern that the public trust had been damaged.\par
\par
Mayor Carney read a personal letter into the record, raising the question of why the City of Delray Beach should not wait and see how the judge rules on other municipalities that were challenging the FDOT\rquote s decision to eliminate the Pride Streetscapes. He mentioned that the City could lose 60 million dollars in funding by challenging their action. Additionally, he pointed out that numerous forms of street art had been removed from cities across Florida. Mayor Carney recalled that the City had voted to join Fort Lauderdale in requesting a \ldblquote stay,\rdblquote which has since been lifted, and emphasized that the Commission\rquote s discussion was never about the legal analysis of the case, which he stated would be impossible to win.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale emphasized that there are other significant ways to support the LGBTQ community without risking crucial state funding or incurring costly legal fees. She recognized the importance of maintaining a good working relationship with a government entity.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin stated that this case was not a class action lawsuit; it is a petition, and if the cities that filed petitions were successful, the final verdict would apply to all municipalities, including those that did not file.\par
\par
PUBLIC COMMENT:\par
\par

\par

\par
\ul Nicholas Coppola\ulnone , 3930 Lowson Blvd, Delray Beach,\par
Suggested joining other cities that were challenging the State and setting a monetary cap on legal fees to support the Home Rule Bill.\par
\par
\ul George Long\ulnone , 46 North Swinton Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Shared his opinions on the state\rquote s painting over the various themed crosswalks.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\cf1\kerning0\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Sam Metott, Director of Parks and Recreation, was joined by Missie Barletto, Director of Public Works, to discuss possible options for the replacement of the Pride Intersection. Ms. Barletto mentioned that the City had received an abundance of suggestions, including those from the community, non-profit partners, and City staff. She stated that this was not an all-inclusive presentation, but one to spark some ideas. They presented several design options and proposed potential locations for pride recognition.\par
\par
Discussion ensued regarding the presentation, and some Commissioners expressed their concerns for a prompt solution to demonstrate the City\rquote s commitment to the LGBTQ community.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long proposed establishing a Pride Memorial in two phases. The first phase would involve implementing a temporary and cost-effective design. This approach would allow time for the Commission to engage with residents, organizations, and the Downtown Development Authority through workshops and public meetings to gather their input on what they envision for a permanent memorial design and location. \par
\par
Ms. Gelin stated that the Commission would need to discuss the funding arrangement for the memorial.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f1 The Commission discussed various funding options.\cf1\kerning0\f2\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f1 Vice Mayor Long expressed concern about the Commission's consideration of private funding, noting that in the previous meeting, it was stated that the memorial should be funded completely or at least partially by the City. \par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\kerning0\f0 Mr. Moore requested the names of organizations and individuals who expressed an interest in providing private donations to fund the monument so that he could contact them promptly.\par
\cf2\f3\par
\pard\cf0\kerning2\f1 There was a consensus to proceed with gathering more information and present this item at the October 14\super th\nosupersub workshop meeting for discussion.\cf1\kerning0\f2\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Duane D'Andrea, Human Resources Director, informed that the agreement before them represented the Collective Bargaining agreement for the Police Officers and Sergeants that had previously been ratified and agreed to by the Commission and the Police Benevolent Association (PBA) of Palm Beach County.\par
\par
\b\fs18 A motion to approve this item was made by Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, seconded by Vice Mayor Long. Commissioner Casale asked for a discussion on this item.\par
\b0\fs24\par
Commissioner Casale voiced her concern that the City was not achieving satisfactory returns on its investments as indicated in the fund compliance report dating back to before 2022, except for one instance. She suggested scheduling a workshop presentation to gain a better understanding of the factors contributing to the under performance of the City\rquote s mutual funds/investments within its peer group, as reported by an actuary. Commissioner Casale stated that the pension reports were based on a dollar amount that the City was not receiving. \par
\par
\kerning2\f1 Ms. Gelin requested a point of order to remind the Commission that the City had previously voted on the contract being presented with the Police Benevolent Association during the impasse.\par
\par
\kerning0\f0 Commissioner Casale proposed that the Commission hold a workshop to gain a better understanding of the City\rquote s investment performance. She acknowledged that the contract with the PBA could not be amended at that time.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long expressed his disappointment over the extended impasse, which resulted in the City losing numerous officers in a competitive environment. He mentioned that now, with a fair contract in place, he felt confident that the City would be able to recruit police officers to keep the City safe. He thanked Commissioner Markert and Deputy Vice Mayor Burns.\par
\par
\kerning2\f1 Mayor Carney stated that he was very clear on how he felt about the contract but would be voting in favor of the ratified contract.\cf1\kerning0\f2\par

\par

\par

Pursuant to Section 3.12 of the Charter of the City of Delray Beach, the Mayor has instructed me to announce a Workshop Meeting of the City Commission to be held for the following purposes:

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that the City Manager's Office, in collaboration with Henry Dachowitz, Chief Financial Officer, had been working closely with all departments that were heavily reliant on general funds to identify potential efficiencies before adopting the proposed final budget for the fiscal year 2025-2026, as discussed during the Commission Meeting on September 3, 2025. He stated that they had identified $507,000 in potential savings from the general fund account. Additionally, he noted that the Public Library\rquote s request for an additional $55,000 contribution from the City would be discussed that evening in response to their presentation on July 15, 2025.\par
\pard\cf1\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\cf0 Mr. Dachowitz provided a presentation of the individual departments and their adjusted budget considerations.\par
\par
\pard The Commission engaged in a discussion on the presentation and some expressed their concerns that cutting specific line items could negatively affect the efficiency of particular departments and the City overall.\par
\par
\kerning2 Mr. Moore stated that the proposed budget cuts would not compromise the City\rquote s departments and would expand the City\rquote s fund balance account from 21.1 percent to 21.4 percent.\par
\par
\kerning0 Commissioner Casale noted that the City had fixed contractual obligations that renew annually and consume a large portion of the budget, including payroll, insurance, and public safety services like Police and Fire. She pointed out that Delray\rquote s taxes are comparable to those of neighboring municipalities and stressed that the City\rquote s long-term financial health should be a top priority. Additionally, she mentioned that letters sent to residents by Mayor Carney reflect his personal viewpoint rather than the perspective of the entire Commission. She suggested that his letters be fact-checked before distribution.\par
\kerning2\par
Mayor Carney expressed his support for continuing to investigate the budget to identify additional cost-cutting measures.\par
\par
Amy Alarez, Assistant Development Services Director, and Jeri Pryor, Neighborhood and Community Services Director, were present to address the proposed budget efficiencies and its impact on their departments.\par
\par
Ms. Alvarez stated that the budget funds cut would affect professional studies, consultant fees, and directives issued by the Commission. She mentioned that there was also a minimum reduction in training services.\par
\par
Ms. Pryor stated that the Florida Association for Code Enforcement Officers does not currently offer free training for Code Officers, and the cost for sending an officer for training is $800. She explained that there were four levels of training, and presently, only nine code enforcement officers have completed training at various levels. Additionally, she mentioned that pressure cleaning is conducted twice a month, under the Department of Clean and Safe, and also covers the Community Redevelopment District. She suggested that the frequency of pressure cleaning could be reduced if the Commission wished. Ms. Pryor noted that Laura Simon, Executive Director of the Downtown Development Authority (DDA), has offered to help cover some of the costs associated with pressure cleaning the downtown area.\par
\par
Discussion ensued regarding the reduction of cuts in critical departments, the importance of having a cushion in the fund balance account to cover unexpected costs. Additionally, the 3% difference (City\rquote s fund balance account from 21.1% to 21.4%) wouldn\rquote t be worth the services that would be compromised, and that the City had fixed costs, which had significantly increased over the past few years. \par
\b\par
\kerning0\b0 Mr. Moore stated that, based on concerns expressed by the Commission, he would reinstate the $75,000 for pressure cleaning to the Neighborhood and Community Services Department. Additionally, he recognized that this would tweak the fund balance to an additional $425,000, rather than the $507,000 that had previously been identified.\kerning2\par
\par
Jay Stacy, Chief Technology Officer, was present in the audience and stated that he would be fine with eliminating the $75,000 request for his department's additional software. \par
\par
\kerning0 Mr. Dachowitz was thanked for his hard work.\par
\par
\kerning2 There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 5:06 p.m. and requested a five-minute break before the next meeting.\cf1\kerning0\par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that Jeff Oris, Assistant City Manager, was present to lead the discussion on this workshop item. He acknowledged that, as a Certified Economic Development Professional, Mr. Oris was the designated representative from the City Manager's Office to address this topic. Mr. Moore emphasized that the primary goal of the presentation was to gather the Commission's thoughts and expectations concerning the City's economic policy.\par
\par
Mr. Oris delivered a PowerPoint presentation on the City\rquote s current economic development activities. He mentioned that the City was looking into potential businesses that had either contacted the City or had been referred regarding starting or relocating their business to the City. He stated that the Economic Development Department is responsible for continually seeking ways to provide education to businesses through expos, educational programs, and maintaining relationships with the Chamber of Commerce, Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA), and the Downtown Development Authority (DDA). He mentioned that the City was in the process of formulating a more robust business seminar program in conjunction with the CRA and the Chamber of Commerce, where various business topics will be discussed. \par
\par
Mr. Oris stated that the Education and External Opportunities Manager and the Economic Development Manager was working together to meet the needs of Delray Beach residents in finding jobs and obtaining career skills through job fairs and connecting employers with training programs. He mentioned that the City was collaborating with Palm Beach State College to provide post-secondary education, which aims to fulfill the workforce needs of businesses in Delray Beach and assist residents in gaining job skills and training.\par
\par
The Commission discussed its vision for the City\rquote s Economic Development plans moving forward, and how to attract commerce to the City.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that on September 14, 2021, the sitting Commission conducted a detailed workshop on the City\rquote s Economic Development and mentioned that the workshop report had received favorable reviews. He noted that several of the programs mentioned in the presentation that evening were duplicated from the September report. Mayor Carney emphasized the importance of having a seat at the table to engage with businesses looking to relocate to Delray Beach, rather than just relying on the Business Development Board. He emphasized that attracting businesses to Delray Beach is a matter of Economic Development, as opposed to merely sustaining existing businesses in the City.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 Mr. Moore expressed his interest was to establish a consensus as to what the Commission would like to see the City achieve so that they could build the necessary resource structure for productivity.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 Commissioner Casale noted that during her time on the 2021 Commission, attracting businesses to the City was a key focus. However, there were votes taking place to convert twelve acres of commercial property into residential apartments, and she expressed her disapproval of this decision. She emphasized the importance of attracting large businesses but noted the City\rquote s limited availability of inventory for commercial properties. She recognized that the Commission could regulate the availability of its commercial land by denying requests for residential housing and suggested that the City network with the Chamber of Commerce or the DDA, which actively seeks resources for companies moving to Delray Beach. Additionally, she noted that the City\rquote s Economic Development section is a good tool to help businesses be successful once they are here.\par
\par
Mayor Carney noted that enhancements could be made to the Congress Avenue corridor to better attract businesses.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns recognized the importance of collaborating with establishments that provide educational training to the City\rquote s residents, ensuring a plentiful skilled workforce when new companies arrive. \par
\par
Commissioner Markert suggested that the most suitable companies to attract to the City are private equity firms and cyber start-ups, due to insufficient space for manufacturing plants.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long acknowledged the accomplishments made in the Development Services Department, specifically in streamlining its processes for businesses entering the City. He referenced the Congress Avenue Corridor Study that had been conducted earlier, which indicated that the area was more suitable for residential development rather than commercial use. Vice Mayor Long emphasized the importance of having quality schools and affordable housing to encourage young families to move to Delray. He provided feedback he received from attending various County meetings regarding their thoughts on Delray.\par
\par
Mayor Carney concluded by expressing his interest in leveraging the City\rquote s property inventory to attract new businesses. He also noted that the City may need to collaborate with other entities, if necessary, to bring businesses here.\par
\par
Mr. Moore proposed engaging in an updated Economic Development Study and then following up with a Workshop in December with the Commission and the City\rquote s partners such as the Delray Beach Chamber of Commerce, DDA, CRA, and key personnel from the City\rquote s leadership team to build the necessary structure as they relate to the City\rquote s Economic Development Plan.\par
\par
There was a verbal consensus for Mr. Moore to hire an external company to conduct a new Economic Development Study. The findings will be presented to the Commission and stakeholders during the workshop on Monday, December 1, 2025, at 3:30 p.m.\par
\par
Mr. Moore thanked the Commission for their feedback.\par
\par
The Commission thanked Mr. Oris for his contribution.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}
