\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that this item was intended to present the Commission with the public\rquote s feedback from the public engagement exercise conducted on October 1, 2025, regarding this matter. \par
\par
Sam Metott, Parks and Recreation Director, and Missie Barletto, Public Works Director, were present to provide a recap of this item and share public feedback from the public engagement.\par
\par
Mr. Metott shared that many comments and ideas from the public engagement had been presented to the Commission previously. He mentioned that someone had suggested the idea of greater inclusivity for other groups.\par
\par
The Commission discussed the numerous suggestions made by the residents and explored different funding options for the memorial.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long acknowledged his support for the City funding the memorial and pointed out that private funding would relieve taxpayers of the financial burden. He noted that displaying the pride colors on public property makes the statement that everyone is welcome and safe in Delray Beach, not just the LGBTQ community and proposed various design ideas that cater to different budget ranges. \par
\par
Commissioner Markert suggested assessing the proposed designs and locations, then seeking community feedback on the findings.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns expressed her happiness that every email she received indicated that Delray was a welcoming City. She stated that she hoped the idea decided upon would make the community happy.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale stated it was time for the City to excuse itself from this matter so that the City doesn\rquote t expose itself to any more liability and allow the memorial to be privately funded and placed on private property. She recognized that what started as a peaceful, loving idea had just the opposite effect. She suggested that the City should not be involved in private negotiations.\par
\par
\expndtw-2 Mayor Carney shared that he had received a plethora of emails expressing different opinions on whether the memorial should be funded by the City or privately. He recognized that any public art is at risk of vandalism. Additionally, he expressed his support for allowing the community to share their thoughts on the memorial, regardless of how it was funded.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long stressed the importance of placing the memorial on public property so that everyone could enjoy what had been lost in a shared space.\par
\par
In conclusion, Mayor Carney recommended that the City not participate in relocating the memorial to prevent any potential actions from the State. \par
\par
Ms. Barletto stated the Public Art Advisory Board would review all of the opportunities for placing art privately around the City.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that whatever design is chosen by the residents through public input and stakeholders, the Commission will determine its role and function.\par
\par
The Mayor indicated there was a consensus to proceed as outlined. He then opened the floor to public comments.\cf1\expndtw0\kerning0\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Edwin Ferguson, Esq., a member of the School Board, presented an overview of the performance of schools within the City of Delray Beach. He provided statistics on kindergarten readiness, as well as student performances across all subjects, comparing the schools\rquote results to the district's average. Mr. Ferguson stressed the importance of reading comprehension for understanding all subjects and pointed out that children who start school behind their peers often continue to struggle throughout their education. He also noted that these students were significantly influenced by their families and communities. \par
\par
Mr. Ferguson suggested promoting Village Academy because it will teach trades to motivated students who want to pursue a career and obtain a certification. He outlined his goals for 2026, which included relocating ESE (Exceptional Student Education) centers for students with disabilities to more central locations for easier access by low-income families. In conclusion, Mr. Ferguson expressed his willingness to work with the City to improve its schools.\cf1\f1\par
\par
\cf0\f0 The Commission thanked Mr. Ferguson for his efforts.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns recognized the significance of having dual language schools in promoting children\rquote s success.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale thanked Mr. Ferguson for his presentation and expressed her disappointment with the City\rquote s grades, stating that they indicated a failure to support the children. She mentioned that SouthTech Academy, a public, tuition-free technical school, has expressed interest in establishing a Charter School at the Historic Carver location in Delray Beach. She highlighted that SouthTech was an A-rated school with a 100% graduation rate. Furthermore, SouthTech serves students from kindergarten through eighth grade, helping them graduate with a certificate that prepares them for the ever-changing job market. Commissioner Casale emphasized the need for the Commission to find solutions to improve the City\rquote s schools.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long expressed his gratitude to Mr. Ferguson for his comprehensive presentation and his commitment to the education of students in Delray Beach. He noted that his colleagues were very dedicated to the City's schools and improving their ratings. He also noted that the State often overrides initiatives that the School Board wishes to implement.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2 Mayor Carney stated that the City has maintained an interlocal agreement (ILA) with the School Board since 2015, which outlines the meetings between the School Board and the Commission. He expressed his desire to revisit this agreement and adhere to its terms, and have the Commission collaboratively engage with the School Board. Additionally, he mentioned his vision for utilizing underused City facilities to provide training for high school students in technical education. This initiative would help students secure gainful employment after graduation. \par
\par
Mayor Carney emphasized the Commission's commitment to supporting the School Board in any way possible. He also suggested that the City implement various after-school programs that differ from those offered by other County Schools, considering the language barrier present in Delray Beach\f2 .\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Lynn Gelin, City Attorney, entered Resolution No. 257-25 and Resolution No. 231-25 into the record, as they were related.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that Jay Glover, with PFM Financial Advisors, Inc., the City\rquote s external financial advisor, was present, along with Steve Sanford, the City\rquote s Bond Counsel, who was available by telephone to discuss the most cost-effective ways to fund the City\rquote s renovation of the municipal golf course, clubhouse, and related facilities.\par
\par
Mr. Glover provided a slide presentation outlining the timeline and summarizing the financing for the golf course. He mentioned that the City\rquote s current financial ratings were robust, and that several months prior, a representative from his firm had been present to discuss various means of helping to cover the debt service for the capital improvement project, which included the renovations of the Delray Beach Municipal Golf Course, clubhouse and related facilities. He mentioned that his firm conducted a rate study of 29 comparable golf courses to ensure that the revenues generated from a round of golf for both residents and non-residents would be sufficient to cover the debt service, including both interest and principal. He outlined the project's financing timeline and emphasized that the General Fund would not be used to subsidize the golf course renovations or ad valorem revenues. \par
\par
Mr. Glover noted that, based on the Commission\rquote s approval, the City would enter a competitive bond sale through the marketplace the week of November 10, 2025, with pre-closing and closing activities scheduled for the week of November 24, 2025.\par
\par
\pard Commissioner Casale recognized that membership fees would necessitate an evaluation to ensure fairness for all players.\par
\par
Sam Metott, Parks and Recreation director, addressed Commissioner Casale\rquote s concerns regarding the rate structure for a round of golf. He explained that there is currently a permit holder rate for members who play mid-week and frequently, which helps offset costs for those who play less often. This group\rquote s rate would be locked in. Metott emphasized that they wanted to honor longtime members by securing their rate through 2037, with no additional members allowed to join that group. He also noted that this practice is typically an industry standard.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale acknowledged that the Tennis Center does not have a similar policy and suggested that the Commission discuss the matter further.\par
}

{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f2\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Aptos;}{\f3\froman\fprq2\fcharset0 Times New Roman;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Mayor Carney recused himself from this item and passed the gavel to Vice Mayor Long. He stated that he lives in the community affected by this item. \par
\par
Additionally, Vice Mayor Long recused himself in accordance with Florida Statutes Section 286.012 due to a potential conflict of interest.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long passed the gavel to Deputy Vice Mayor Burns.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns read the quasi-judicial rules into the record for this item.\par
\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk, swore in those individuals who wished to provide testimony on this item.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin entered Resolution No. 212-25 into the record.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns asked her colleagues to disclose any ex-parte communications for this item.\par
\par
\ul Deputy Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone : Spoke with Ms. Andrea Keiser and Ms. Sharon L\rquote Herrou and what was on the server.\par
\ul Commissioner Casale\ulnone : Spoke with the representative and what was on the server.\par
\ul Commissioner Markert\ulnone : None.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin stated that the City had collected all the emails related to this item and had entered them in Legistar.\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, entered File No. 2023-168 into the record.\par
\par
Andrea Keiser, Esq., was present on behalf of the homeowners who were seeking the Commission's approval for the abandonment of public access located in Old Palm Grove. She provided that this approval would allow residents to have shorter access to the park and a public right-of-way that leads to the beach. Ms. Keiser mentioned that there was a disagreement about the historical misinterpretation of why the burden was shifted from the dedicated access point into Old Palm Grove. She explained the impetus for this change, which included changes to the community and the surrounding area over the course of 20 plus years. \par
\par
Ms. Keiser concluded by recognizing that there was already a dedicated bike path on Federal Highway and that Old Palm Grove was not listed in the City\rquote s Comprehensive Plan\rquote s bike and pedestrian paths, nor any other map, and that the safety, security, and welfare of the residents of Old Palm Grove serves a greater public purpose than a bike path. Additionally, she addressed some of the opposition letters submitted to the Commission regarding this application, urging them not to abandon a public right-of-way. However, Ms. Keiser stated that this request is not for a public right-of-way, but rather for public roads that shoulder the burden of having a public amendment liability. \par
\cf1\f1\par
\cf0\f0 Ms. Gianniotes provided a staff report on the history of this item. She stated that the Old Palm Grove Community was initially designed as a comprehensive, multi-project strategy to create and maintain bicycle and pedestrian access in the neighborhoods. She noted that the City reconfigured public rights-of-way to create Old Palm Grove, which played a crucial role in the implementation of the North Federal Highway Redevelopment Plan, adopted by the City Commission on March 16, 1999. She stated that the plan aimed to facilitate pedestrian movement and neighborhood connections, while also creating new public spaces. The abandonment request would serve as pedestrian movement and neighborhood connections, creating an enclave with no public access. \par
\par
William Bennett, Assistant City Attorney, was present and called Tim Hernandez, AICP, with New Urban Communities, to the lectern to provide testimony regarding this matter. He stated that he was the planner, developer, and part-owner of the Old Palm Grove Project and answered questions posed by Mr. Bennett.\par
\par
Mr. Hernandez mentioned that the development of this site relied significantly on public rights-of-way, as well as waivers and variances. He stated that the abandonment was an integral part of the Old Palm Grove community\rquote s design. He noted that the community was created to be a beautiful, integral part of the community, keeping people out of harm's way from Federal Highway traffic.\par
\par
\kerning2\f2 Michelle Hoyland, Principal Planner, explained that the City, the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA), and various stakeholders collaborated closely to develop the site plan. The aim was to create safe pedestrian connections by guiding them through neighborhoods to the east for beach access, while reducing their exposure to Federal Highway. She emphasized that this community is one of several in which a private right-of-way allows public access.\par
\par
\kerning0\f0 Mr. Bennett had exhausted all his witnesses.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes commented that the City Engineer recommended denying this request, stating that if this item were approved, it would disregard the Always Delray Comprehensive Plan and the North Federal Highway Development Plan by restricting public access to the bicycle and pedestrian routes in Old Palm Grove and La Hacienda Gardens Park.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns opened the floor to anyone who wished to provide public comment on this item.\par
\par
\ul Anna Zukowski\ulnone ,1631 Old Palm Lane, Delray Beach\par
Expressed her displeasure over having public access roads/streets in her community and the liability they pose to its homeowners.\par
\ul\f3\par
\f0 Charles Springfield\ulnone , 812 Eastview Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Discussed the issues of having private sidewalks that allow the public to come through and do whatever they wish to.\par
\par
\ul Todd Harvey\ulnone ,1071 Kokomo Key Lane, Delray Beach\par
Requested that community access be preserved, as residents rely on it for safe navigation.\par
\par
\ul Robin Keller\ulnone , 717 South Lake Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Stated that she and her family enjoy the open access for biking and walking, and would like to see it continue, and requested that the Commission deny the request.\par
\par
\ul Evan Wdlitz\ulnone ,1639 Old Palm Lane, Delray Beach\par
Stated that staff reports on this item were over 25 years old and should not be used to determine whether to keep this access open. \par
\par
\ul Angela Chiara\ulnone , 786 Estuary Way, Delray Beach\par
Expressed her concern that this was a liability issue and that the residents of Old Palm Grove should not bear this burden. She mentioned that there was an alternative route.\par
\par
\ul Christine Jarjura\ulnone , 1604 Old Palm Grove\par
Discussed the risk of burglary in the community since her house was burglarized, and mentioned that pedestrians prefer walking in the community rather than in their own neighborhoods.\par
\par
\ul Maisie Vanhoggie\ulnone , 1045 Kokomo Key Lane, Delray Beach\par
Stated that she enjoys the access path to ride her bike to Church.\par
\par
\ul Evelyn Koutsouras\ulnone\f3 ,\f0 837 Kokomo Key Lane, Delray Beach\par
Expressed her desire to continue to allow Kokomo Key residents access through Old Palm Grove.\par
\par
\ul Lane Carlee\ulnone , 734 South Lake Drive, Delray Beach\par
Requested that the Commission follow the recommendations made in 2012 by the City\rquote s engineer and vote no.\par
\par
\ul Seth Gordon\ulnone , 932 Kokomo Key Lane, Delray Beach\par
Discussed the dangers of biking on Federal Highway and requested that it be maintained as public land, as was initially intended.\par
\par
\ul Sharon L\rquote Herrou\ulnone\f3 ,\f0 830 Kokomo Key Lane, Delray Beach\par
Urged the Commission to support the City Engineer\rquote s recommendation and not to give up the public access.\par
\par
\ul John Mc Avoy\ulnone , 1018 Kokomo Key Lane, Delray Beach\par
Stated that he has biked and walked through the Estuary neighborhood for 14 years and has never seen a problem. He would like to see both communities unified and be good neighbors.\par
\par
\ul Deborah Cianciotta\ulnone , 820 East View Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Discussed the liability concerns related to granting access to the Estuary community and holding its residents accountable for damages and repairs caused by individuals from other neighborhoods.\par
\par
\ul John Malodey\ulnone , 1636 Old Palm Lane, Delray Beach\par
Stated that the sidewalks and streets in the Estuary are private, and its residents are responsible for their maintenance and liable for any injuries or vandalism.\par
\par
\ul Clare Wheatley\ulnone , 829 East View Avenue, Delray Beach\par
Requested that the Commission abandon public access through Old Palm Grove due to legal liability concerns for residents and not make it a public amenity.\par
\par
\ul Mitch Katz\ulnone , 1618 West Classical Blvd, Delray Beach\par
\kerning2\f2 Emphasized that it was unfair for the Estuary residents to bear the burden of liability for injuries to non-residents of their community.\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Lynn Gelin, City Attorney, explained that any modifications to the City\rquote s Charter must go through a referendum. She stated that the process would begin with presenting an Ordinance to the City Commission. If the ordinance is adopted, it will be placed on the March ballot for voter approval.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 Mayor Carney stated that a Commission cannot remove a City Manager without proper justification. He suggested that City residents should have the opportunity to vote on this issue during a general election, rather than a municipal election, to boost voter turnout if such a situation arises. Mayor Carney acknowledged that the City has had the same City Manager for the past five (5) years and is inclined to keep the charter in its current form.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long emphasized that it was only fair to allow residents to vote on this matter, especially given the strong turnout at the public hearing that evening. He noted that during his campaign, residents frequently expressed their desire to reinstate a supermajority to ensure their voices are heard.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 Commissioner Casale noted that none of the surrounding municipalities, except for Boynton Beach, has a supermajority requirement. She noted that during the 2014 primary election, residents voted to remove the supermajority requirement.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns mentioned that a supermajority could have both positive and negative effects, but emphasized that the decision should lie with the residents.\par
\par
Commissioner Markert stated that the Commission discusses and debates everything on the dais and expressed his support for maintaining the current approach.\par
\par
Commissioner Burns clarified that this issue concerned the City Manager's position, not Mr. Moore directly.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long stated for the record that he and Mr. Moore never discussed this issue.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that the idea of reinstating a supermajority vote did not originate with him. He emphasized that his primary focus and commitment have always been to serve the best interests of residents and stakeholders in every municipality where he has worked, and that if the majority of the Commission wanted him to leave, he would do so voluntarily.\par
\par
There was a 3-2 consensus not to move this item forward at this time.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\par
Christina Bilinki, the applicant's attorney, was present for this item. She stated that this parcel, Kia Delray, had already been approved for general commercial land use as a car dealership along Federal Highway, where the vast majority of car dealerships are located in the City. She mentioned that the dealership aimed to modernize its property to better align with the surrounding dealerships. The first request was to change the required number of showers from 8 to 1. The second request was to reduce the required setback of the rear wall. She mentioned that this would improve the buffers by adding 25 feet of landscaping, which is in accordance with the City\rquote s Code.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes presented a staff report on this item. She stated that the existing structure is 20,040 square feet, and the proposed building is a 3-story, 143,672-square-foot full-service auto dealership. She discussed the landscape buffers and mentioned that other nearby car dealerships have had complaints about car wash noise, car alarms, and loading noise. Ms. Gianniotes emphasized that the applicant must not use the car alarms to locate a car, as it would be a tremendous nuisance to the surrounding residents. \par
\par
She concluded her presentation by mentioning that the Planning and Zoning Board recommended approval on October 20, 2025, by a 6-1 vote.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item.\par
\par
\ul Christina Morrison,\ulnone 1000 Lowery Street, Delray Beach\par
Mentioned that the car dealerships in that area are very mindful of the residents and keep the noise down, and suggested adding more trees to beautify Florida Blvd.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes requested additional information on the proposed garage turbo doors. The architect for this project approached the lectern and provided information on the turbo garage.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale asked for a description of the garage turbo door. The architect stated that the turbo doors were designed to open and close quickly to maintain the air conditioning in the area where customers receive their vehicles.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion on this item, and the majority supported the proposed upgrades to the dealership.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale expressed her concern about the landscaping buffers and the \kerning0 close proximity to the neighbors\f1\fs22 .\cf1\f0\fs24\par

{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mayor Carney requested that this item be discussed earlier in the meeting, acknowledging that many residents were present to hear it. It became Item No. 5.A.1.\par
\par
Mayor Carney recognized that Mr. Simon was the foremost architect of buildings throughout the City. He acknowledged that Ms. Rita Rena, President of the Rotary Club of Delray Beach, was present to read into the record the dedication of a bench in front of Old School Square to the Simon brothers, Roy and Earnie, on behalf of the Rotary Club of Delray Beach.\par
\par
Rita Rena, President of the Rotary Club of Delray Beach, expressed her gratitude to the Commission and the residents for their donations to support under served children, which she had discussed the previous week.\par
\par
\expndtw-2 Ms. Rena delivered a speech honoring Roy Simon and his family for their exceptional service and dedication in shaping the City. She discussed how their vision has guided the City and made it what it is today, and stated that in honor of Mr. Simon, a memorial bench would be dedicated to him in front of Old School Square.\par
\par
Laura Simon, Executive Director of the Downtown Development Authority, expressed her gratitude to the Rotary Club for their dedication to her father and family. She spoke about her family's legacy in the City and highlighted their significant impact on various organizations and architectural styles. Ms. Simon emphasized her father's pivotal role in shaping the community, including his efforts in establishing the Downtown Development \par
Authority in 1971.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale suggested that Laura Simon share her ideas on how the Commission could honor her father.\par
\par
Ms. Simon mentioned that one of her father\rquote s passions was parking; he developed several parking lots throughout the City. She provided several suggestions for locations for a memorial bench in his honor, including Veterans Park, the Railroad parking lot, and the Original Atlantic Plaza, which he designed.\par
\par
The Commission discussed how best to honor Mr. Simon. A suggestion was made to name the Railroad Lot as the Roy M. Simon Parking Lot. Ms. Simon supported that suggestion.\par
\par
The Commission proposed temporarily naming the lot the "Roy M. Simon Railroad Parking Lot" until new signs can be installed throughout the city to prevent confusion. Once the new signs are created, they will be updated to display the name "Roy M. Simon Lot."\par
\par

{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Aptos;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 The November 18, 2025 Commission Workshop Meeting was called to order at 3:34 p.m. Alexis Givings, City Clerk, called the roll, and the following were present:\par
\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\par
\pard\b Present: 5 - \b0 Commissioner Tom Markert, Mayor Thomas F. Carney Jr., Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns, Commissioner Juli Casale, and Vice-Mayor Rob Long\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574 Lynn Gelin, City Attorney, along with Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, presented this item.\f1\par
\f0 Ms. Gelin thanked everyone who worked diligently on this issue, noting that noise complaints are among the Commission's most significant concerns. She presented a slideshow detailing the timeline and scope of efforts to amend the noise ordinance, which began in 2022, when the previous City Commission approved hiring a consultant to conduct a noise study. That study included a Sound Walk throughout the Entertainment District. \f1\par
\par
\f0 Ms. Gelin stated that staff were seeking the Commission's approval to adopt the drafted ordinance, which will take effect in January - February 2026. This timeline will allow staff to be trained to use a sound meter. She noted that after the ordinance is adopted, a warning period will begin, followed by full enforcement in March, ideally. Ms. Gelin summarized the changes and continuities in the proposed amended ordinance, noting that the boundaries of the Entertainment District had been altered, as had the permissible noise hours and the penalties to businesses in violation. She mentioned that the proposed ordinance defines which activities are exempt from enforcement and which are prohibited.\par
\par
A discussion ensued amongst the Commission on the presentation and the extent to which a municipality should regulate noise in the Entertainment District and on private property.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2 Deputy Vice Mayor Burns acknowledged that expanding the West Atlantic Redevelopment District will effectively extend the existing Entertainment District. She noted that residents support this integration, even if it means hearing music nearby, because they believe it will help the area thrive alongside the rest of the City.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574\kerning0\par
\pard\kerning2 Commissioner Casale cautioned the Commission to be mindful when extending the Entertainment District.\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574\kerning0\f1\par
\pard\kerning2\f0 Commissioner Markert expressed concern that banning gas-powered landscaping equipment would harm companies that rely on it.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes acknowledged that not every resident uses lawn services and often mows their lawns on weekends. She mentioned that these services usually start early in the day because of the heat.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long thanked the Commission for bringing this to fruition, but he voiced concerns about implementing the new hours. He strongly supported the development of the West Atlantic area.\par
\par
Mayor Carney suggested installing noise cameras at key locations to identify vehicles that exceed noise limits. He stated that this would contain the noise downtown, allowing people to better enjoy their dining experience. He mentioned that he required additional time before discussing the expansion of the Entertainment District.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin emphasized that once a district is expanded, it cannot be reversed. She supported granting conditional uses along Atlantic Avenue until information on the effectiveness of the new noise ordinances is gathered.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574\kerning0 Mayor Carney proposed a conditional use agreement for the Entertainment District, valid until 1:00 a.m. This would allow the City to revoke it if necessary due to violations of the hours.\f1\par
\par
\f0 Ms. Gianniotes recommended that the City follow the same guidelines as the Community Redevelopment Agency.\par
\pard\kerning2\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574\kerning0 Ms. Gelin noted that if the Commission grants a conditional use agreement to a commercial facility that conducts outdoor activities, and that facility repeatedly violates the noise ordinance, the City can revoke the agreement. She mentioned that this item will be presented to the Commission for their approval in December.\par
}

{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Aptos;}{\f2\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574\expndtw-4\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that following the Commission\rquote s recommendation from the meeting on August 19, 2025, the Commission would seek community input regarding the expansion of the West Atlantic Improvement District. He acknowledged that this item was formalized and adopted by the State of Florida in 1988. Recently, the State of Florida conducted an audit of Neighborhood Improvement Districts throughout the State. During this audit, the City was asked about its intentions regarding the district. He noted that several steps need to be taken before formally considering funding for this initiative. He mentioned that the City was obligated to respond to the State by November 25, 2025.\f1\par
\par
\f0 Jeri Pryor, Neighborhood and Community Services Director, was joined by Terra Couzens, Neighborhood Planner, to present this item.\par
\par
\pard\expndtw0\kerning2 Ms. Pryor provided a brief history of the West Atlantic Neighborhood Improvement District, which was formed to encourage economic redevelopment in the West Atlantic Area, improve the physical environment, enhance public safety, create a welcoming neighborhood, support local businesses, attract new investments, and strengthen the community\rquote s identity and pride. She mentioned that the presentation would cover information shared with residents during their community outreach engagements.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574\expndtw-4\kerning0 Ms. Couzens presented information gathered from the Neighborhood and Community Services Outreach engagements and surveys conducted between August 2025 and September 2025, which aimed to determine whether the community wanted to proceed with developing the district or dissolve it. She mentioned that the Downtown Development Authority (DDA) and the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) attended meetings to assist with answering questions from businesses, landowners, and residents, since most properties in the district overlap their boundaries and each entity has its own funding and is taxed differently. Ms. Couzens presented the results of the community surveys, highlighting the improvements and priorities that residents want to focus on for the district's future. These priorities include installing more streetlights and enhancing sidewalks and streets.\f1\par
\par
\pard\expndtw0\kerning2\f0 Mr. Moore deferred to the Commission for guidance, reminding them that the City was obligated to respond to the State within one week if they were interested in exploring the feasibility of creating a taxing district.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\tx1574\expndtw-4\kerning0 Mayor Carney mentioned the City owes it to the community to explore options on how to make this work. He emphasized that accepting this measure would allow residents in that corridor to contribute to the area's development.\f1\par
\par
\expndtw0\kerning2\f0 Deputy Vice Mayor Burns proposed conducting a feasibility study to determine whether developing the district is viable. The majority of the Commission favored moving forward with conducting the study. \par
\expndtw-4\kerning0\par
Commissioner Casale pointed out that if the Commission moved forward with this tax or assessment, it would be taxing the City's most financially burdened residents. She emphasized that, according to the Statute, the City is required to provide these residents with the proposed services, infrastructure, etc., without imposing additional taxes. She also mentioned that the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) and the Downtown Development Authority (DDA) could obtain grants to improve this area of the corridor without increasing the tax burden on its residents.\cf1\expndtw0\f2\par
}

She stated that the crash was caused by an individual making an unsafe lane change, resulting in a side-swipe that flipped over another vehicle in front of the restaurant. She further explained that the Commission directed Public Works to conduct a warrant study for a traffic light in that area, and was present to provide some of the data collected.\par

He noted that other safety concerns included an existing bus shelter and high vegetation that blocks the sight line to the south.\par

Ms. Barletto stated that the City will coordinate with Palm Tran and the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT) to relocate the bus stop. Additionally, the City will work with Code Enforcement to either remove or lower the vegetation's height.\par

Mr. Moore suggested that the City first relocate the bus shelter and remove the vegetation. This would enable a more accurate statistical analysis of the area before conducting a study to determine whether a traffic signal is necessary.\par

\par

\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk, swore in those individuals who wished to provide testimony on this item.\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, entered Building Permit File No. 24-221112 and Planning and Zoning File No. 000336-2005 into the record.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f1 Mayor Carney asked his colleagues to disclose any ex-parte communications.\cf1\kerning0\f2\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\cf0\ul\f0 Mayor Carney\ulnone : None.\par
\ul Commissioner Casale\ulnone : Spoke with staff and drove by the project.\par
\ul Vice Mayor Long\ulnone : Spoke with staff.\par
\ul Commissioner Markert\ulnone : Spoke with staff.\par
\pard\kerning2\ul\f1 Deputy Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone : None.\par
\par
Albert Scartabello, 724 Sunshine Drive, Delray Beach, stated that he was present at the request of the Building Department regarding an internal audit conducted by the City. This audit revealed several errors in his permits related to the property at 417 Lake Drive. He noted that these permits had been reviewed and approved by the City Engineer and staff. Mr. Scartabello stated that he was informed that the permits did not account for the maximum allowed open-air space in the home. Although 99 percent of the work on the house has been completed, he was advised that he must appear before the Commission to request a waiver of lot coverage and floor area ratio to obtain a Certificate of Occupancy (CO) for the property at 417 Lake Drive.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\kerning0\f0 Ms. Gianniotes presented a staff report regarding this item. She explained that the zoning regulations for Lake Ida homes include additional requirements that other single-family homes in the area do not have to comply with. She provided the regulations that define lot coverage, previously known as the ground-floor building area. Ms. Gianniotes stated that these regulations were long-standing and were put in place to maintain the character expected of Lake Ida. These regulations were not fully calculated, but were identified during the audit. She mentioned that if these waivers are approved, a CO will be issued.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to provide public comment.\par
\par
Seeing no one present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
There was no cross-examination or rebuttal from either side.\par
\par
The Commission engaged in a discussion on this item, and the majority agreed that the City's engineer and staff were primarily responsible for approving the permits. They concluded that the builder should not be penalized, as redesigning the home would incur significant costs. \par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes emphasized the importance of comprehensive staff training on these issues. She also mentioned that the City no longer employs the engineer who approved this and other incorrect plans. Additionally, she noted that the IT department and the Director of Communications will update the City\rquote s website to include the Lake Ida District requirements to prevent similar problems in the future.\cf1\f2\par

Pursuant to Section 3.12 of the Charter of the City of Delray Beach, the Mayor has instructed me to announce a Workshop Meeting of the City Commission to be held for the following purposes:

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 After the conclusion of the presentation, Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this agenda item.\par
\ul\par
John Jasper\ulnone , 33444\par
Stated that he is a commercial office leasing agent with CBRE, and that he receives numerous calls from C-level executives from out of state wanting to establish their financial headquarters in Delray Beach. He suggested that the City be proactive by advertising to bring these companies to Delray Beach.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Long suggested including economic development in the City's Vision 2035 plan.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that he would allow the City\rquote s partners to engage with the Commission during public comment, rather than simply allowing them to speak for 3 minutes, to help foster a productive dialogue.\par
\par
\ul Kelly Smallridge\ulnone , President and CEO of the Palm Beach County Business Development Board, was present to share her expertise in bringing businesses to cities.\par
\par
She outlined effective strategies that the City should implement to attract companies and their executives to Delray Beach. Ms. Smallridge stated that her company is willing to collaborate with Delray Beach to develop a business plan and to strategize how to address the City's economic development challenges.\par
\par
The Commission discussed Ms. Smallridge\rquote s proposals, recognized the need to create an economic development plan, and thanked her for her assistance.\par
\par
Mr. Moore invited other City partners who were present and wished to speak to come forward.\par
\par
\ul Stephanie Immelman\ulnone , President and CEO of the Greater Delray Beach Chamber of Commerce, stated that the suggestions raised by Ms. Smallridge were included in the discussion items identified by the Greater Delray Beach Chamber of Commerce, the CRA, and the DDA. She mentioned that before the City\rquote s partners can reach out to businesses, they need to establish an updated database, expedited permitting, and address infrastructure needs, particularly for software companies.\par
\par
\ul Laura Simon\ulnone , Executive Director of the DDA, expressed her gratitude for organizing the workshop and highlighted that Delray Beach is a unique city that offers an ideal workspace for specific industries. She also mentioned that changing land use regulations could effectively attract more businesses to the area.\par
\par
\ul Renee Jadusingh\ulnone , Executive Director of the CRA, stated that their primary focus has been on the West Atlantic Redevelopment Program. Additionally, she mentioned that the CRA is open to exploring incentive programs for new businesses.\par
\par
The Commission unanimously agreed that the meeting was productive, and everyone felt encouraged that the City was finally addressing the economic development issue.\par
\par
Mayor Carney recognized that a city-wide referendum or ordinance might be required to determine the locations/perimeters involved. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale emphasized the importance of supporting small businesses, as they contribute significantly to the City's unique character. She also highlighted the need to improve school ratings to attract families with children who are considering relocation. Furthermore, she noted that when the Commission reviews projects, such as residential developments, it is essential to consider their future impact on the city.\par
\par
Mr. Moore concluded by stating that, based on feedback from the City\rquote s external partners and input from the Commission, he recommended returning in early January with updates on expedited permitting considerations, necessary regulatory structures, and resource commitments. These resources will support marketing, recruiting activities, and inventory availability. He informed the Commission that he would engage an outside firm to assist in executing this plan.\par
\par
There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 4:45 p.m.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Aptos;}{\f2\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 The December 1, 2025 Commission Workshop Meeting was called to order at 3:33 p.m. Alexis Givings, City Clerk, called the roll, and the following were present:\par
\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\li15\sb113\expndtw-2\kerning0\f1\par
\pard\kerning2\b\f0 Present: 5 - \expndtw0\b0 Commissioner Tom Markert, Mayor Thomas F. Carney Jr., Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns, Commissioner Juli Casale and Vice Mayor Rob Long (arrived on the dais at 3:34 p.m.)\par
\par
Mr. Moore began the meeting by stating that on November 17, 2025, he met with leaders from several organizations, including the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA), the Greater Delray Beach Chamber of Commerce, the Downtown Development Authority (DDA), and the Palm Beach County Business Development Board. The objective of this meeting was to explore ways to strengthen the City\rquote s economic development plan. He also mentioned that the City had engaged GRIP Solutions (Government Resource for Inspection and Planning) to update the City\rquote s economic data profile.\par
\par
Jeff Oris, Assistant City Manager, began by sharing the findings from the economic development data analysis conducted by GRIP since the last update in 2021. \par
\par
During the presentation, Mr. Moore indicated public comments should be heard before presentations, which aligned with the previously established consensus at an earlier workshop; however, Commission Casale interjected and proposed continuing the presentation to allow the public to make comments based it.\par
\par
There was consensus to proceed in this manner.\par
\par
Mr. Oris continued his presentation by updating the Commission on the study's findings, which included the City\rquote s current population, median household income, wages, and home values, all of which had increased significantly since 2021. He noted that the cost of living in Delray Beach is 17% higher than the national average. He stated that the revised livable wage calculator indicates that the required livable income before taxes to live in Delray Beach is still significantly below the livable wage for most families. He mentioned that some of the City\rquote s partners were present and available to answer any questions. \par
\par
Mr. Oris stated that his office was seeking the Commission\rquote s input on how to create a long-term economic development plan. He mentioned that a promising source of funds for the City could be the trade of imported goods, along with other untapped industries. He noted that business relocations and company expansions in Delray Beach are challenging due to insufficient available land. He stated that the City currently holds business assistance grants through the Urban Development Action Grant (UDAG) and maintains an economic development fund for incentives up to $500,000. He discussed the City\rquote s current incentives for businesses and residents, noting the need to review and update them to align with the Commission's desired outcomes.\cf1\kerning0\f2\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Mayor Carney stated that this presentation will showcase the ClearGov Inc. software, which aims to provide greater clarity and transparency for residents interacting with the City.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f1 Mr. Moore noted that the ClearGov software had been discussed during the budget proposal process. He stated that this software will provide residents and stakeholders with an easier platform to engage and access the City\rquote s budget information with greater transparency.\par
\par
Henry Dachowitz, Chief Financial Officer, was accompanied by Sabra Avery, Budget Manager, to provide a brief presentation on the ClearGov software program.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\expndtw-2\kerning0\f0 Ms. Avery stated that over 1,\expndtw0 300 communities, including local municipalities, utilize ClearGov. She described the software as a user-friendly, customizable digital budgeting program accessible via the web, enabling the budget team to collaborate efficiently through customizable pages without needing a developer or designer. Ms. Avery mentioned \kerning2\f1 that this program includes a built-in GFOA (Government Finance Officers Association) checklist to ensure the City meets the criteria for the association. She noted that the City had won this award 28 times. This approach streamlines collaboration and improves efficiency by providing customizable templates that team members can use to add content to their assigned sections of the budget easily. She stated that this program uses standardized, interactive charts, graphs, and tables that make complicated financial data easy to understand. \par
\par
\kerning0\f0 Mr. Dachowitz mentioned that this program allows for a highly interactive experience for users entering data. He explained that as information is input, all graphs and details update automatically with cross-referencing. This feature is designed to save staff considerable time when finalizing or making changes.\par
\par
\kerning2\f1 The Commission expressed gratitude to Mr. Dachowitz and Ms. Avery for their presentation and unanimously expressed eagerness to implement the program.\expndtw-2\kerning0\f0\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Mayor Carney requested that this item be pulled for discussion. It became Item No. 7.A.A. on the Regular Agenda.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin explained that the City has an Interlocal Agreement (ILA) with the Downtown Development Authority (DDA) to allocate a specific amount of funding on October 1st each year. She noted that because the City had requested an audit of the DDA, funding for the DDA has been temporarily withheld until the audit results are available.\f1\par
\par
\f0 Mayor Carney pulled this item because the DDA\rquote s audit revealed that several of their policies needed updating. He stated it would be unwise to provide the full funding amount until their policies were updated. He added, the complete funding should be contingent on the DDA\rquote s fulfilling its commitments.\f1\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f2 The Commission discussed this item, and most members expressed concern regarding the Mayor's criticism of the DDA.\par
\par
\pard\nowidctlpar\kerning0\f0 Ms. Gelin proposed an amendment to the ILA stating that by no later than December 31, 2025, and April 30, 2026, the City shall pay the DDA a management fee of $350,000. She emphasized that this timeline should allow ample opportunity for them to establish the necessary policies, and the DDA could easily adopt the City\rquote s policies.\par
\f1\par
\b\f0\fs20 A motion was made by Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, seconded by Commissioner Casale, for discussion and approval of Ms. Gelin\rquote s recommendations. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale inquired what a reasonable amount of time should be to withhold money to meet the City\rquote s expectations of the DDA\rquote s new policies.\par
\b0\f1\fs24\par
\f0 Elena Georgiev, Internal Auditor, approached the lectern and stated that the standard practice is to follow up on audit findings and their implementation within 6 to 12 months after an audit. In this instance, she noted that the DDA has committed to implementing the recommendations by March 2026. At that time, Ms. Georgiev will conduct her follow-up.\par
\par
\pard\kerning2\f2 Ms. Gelin stated that the dates that she proposed align with Ms. Georgiev\rquote s statement.\cf1\kerning0\f3\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\nowidctlpar\f0\fs24 Missie Barletto, Public Works Director, provided an overview of the Barwick Road project, which extends from State Road 806 (Atlantic Avenue) to Lake Ida Road, in response to numerous complaints from residents. Ms. Barletto noted that while the area is undergoing changes, the turn radius has remained the same and was designed in accordance with the City\rquote s Complete Streets Policy adopted in 2016. She emphasized that this federally funded project aims to enhance bicycle and pedestrian safety. Additionally, Ms. Barletto discussed several other planned improvements for the area and addressed the residents' concerns, explaining that many issues stem from the project being in the mid-construction stage. She assured them that the designs were developed to ensure consistency with established best practices and roadway standards. The project is anticipated to be completed by the summer of 2026. Ms. Barletto provided a website to view the project: \cf1\ul Barwickproject.com\ulnone . \cf0 The Commission thanked Ms. Barletto for her comprehensive report.\par
\par
Mr. Moore mentioned that there was one additional update regarding the renovations of the Delray Beach Municipal Golf Course that Ms. Barletto wanted to share with the Commission.\par
\par
Ms. Barletto informed the Commission that, upon clearing the land on the golf course, they encountered a Banyan Tree with a base covering half an acre and likely the largest in the South County area. She stated that this issue is causing problems because it crosses the canal. The City is working with the Lake Worth Drainage District to obtain permits for the golf course and they are asking the City to remove the Banyan Tree. Ms. Barletto mentioned that if she were to go before the Board of the Lake Worth Drainage District to seek a variance for the permit, it might delay the renovations of the golf course. However, she noted that the course designer and contractors are committed to preserving the tree and are willing to do whatever it takes to make up for the time lost due to the efforts to save the tree. Ms. Barletto also discussed the potential consequences if the tree is allowed to remain.\par
\par
Sam Mettott, Parks and Recreation Director, joined Ms. Barletto and stated that the renovations have made tremendous progress thus far.\par
\par
The Commission discussed whether to preserve the tree or remove it. There was consensus to keep the tree. \b\f1\par
\par
\b0\f0 The Commission thanked Ms. Barletto and Mr. Metott for their presentation.\cf2\f2\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mayor Carney introduced the agenda item and passed the gavel to Deputy Vice Mayor Burns so that he could make a nomination. He nominated Yvonne Odom, praising her long-standing community involvement. \par
\par
With no other nomination, Vice Mayor Burns closed nominations and requested a vote.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale requested to speak before the vote. She mentioned that someone from Mayor Carney's camp approached her between December 5\super th\nosupersub and December 8\super th,\nosupersub asking her not to support Ms. Odom. The person also requested that she ask Commissioner Markert not to support Ms. Odum. She added in exchange for not voting, things were offered to her; however, she declined. She reported this incident to the City on Monday morning because she was concerned about a possible Sunshine violation and her part in it. Commissioner Casale expressed her appreciation for Ms. Odum and said that she would love to work with her but did not feel an unelected person should be the determining vote on all matters moving forward for the next 2 months.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated the allegation was untrue and no one from his camp contacted Commissioner Casale because he did not want anyone to know what he was going to do. \par
\par
Commissioner Markert then expressed broader concerns about appointing an unelected commissioner and suggested postponing the decision. \par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns asked the City Attorney to weigh in. Ms. Gelin stated that the nomination could not be postponed because the charter requires a vote at two (2) regular meetings; if they are not able to appoint someone today, then the Commission would proceed with four members until the election in March.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns requested a roll call vote. Commissioner Market wished to abstain. Ms. Gelin stated that he could not legally abstain and since there was no conflict of interest, he would have to vote. \par
\par
\b\fs20 A roll call vote was taken for Mayor Carney\rquote s nomination of Ms. Odum. The nomination failed by the following tie vote:\par
\par
Yes: \b0 2 - Deputy Vice Mayor Burns and Mayor Carney\b\par
\par
No: \b0 2 - Commissioner Markert\b \b0 and Commissioner Casale\b\fs24\par
\b0\par
Mayor Carney resumed the gavel and called for decorum.\par
\par
The Commission then recessed at 6:31 p.m.\par
\par
The Commission reconvened at 6:37 p.m.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par

minutes_note:

{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Ms. Gelin read Ordinance No. 35-25 into the record. \par
\par
She presented revisions to the proposed Noise Control Ordinance, replacing the existing \ldblquote plainly audible\rdblquote standard with objective decibel-based measurements using calibrated sound meters. The ordinance includes standards for measuring noise at property boundaries, training for staff, and limited use of the subjective standard only when sound meters are unavailable.\par
\par
Updates included:\par
\par
- Clarification of landscape maintenance hours and exceptions for City owned or - operated properties.\par
- Plans to purchase sound meters and calibrators and train Code Enforcement and Police staff.\par
- A warning and public outreach period before enforcement begins, with anticipated full enforcement in May 2026.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin requested postponement of adoption because a required Business Impact Estimate (BSE) had not been published for the statutory 10-day period. \par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor for public comment and reiterated that anyone who speaks at this meeting will not be permitted to comment again when the item returns to the agenda.\par
\par
City Clerk Alexis Givings administered the oath to those wishing to provide public comment.\par
\par
\ul Shannon Ewing\ulnone , 33483, employee at Good Night John Boy nightclub\par
Opposed the ordinance as originally written, arguing strict sound and bass limits and the \ldblquote plainly audible\rdblquote standard could harm nightlife businesses, reduce revenue, and create subjective enforcement. She emphasized nightlife\rquote s economic importance and urged revisions that balance residents\rquote concerns with business viability.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin clarified that the \ldblquote plainly audible\rdblquote standard would only be used when noise meters are unavailable and could result only in warnings, not citations.\par
\par
\ul John Mallon\ulnone , 33444\par
Supported stronger, science-based enforcement, stating venues had previously lowered volume significantly without losing business. He argued current measurement methods would be inaccurate and recommended 24-hour monitoring devices and data analysis instead of spot readings.\par
\par
\ul Christina Morrison\ulnone , 33483 \par
Defended the entertainment district\rquote s role but supported regulating disruptive vehicle noise and suggested transitioning city landscaping equipment to electric to reduce early-morning noise.\par
\par
\ul Andre Kulikov\ulnone , 33444 \par
Supported the ordinance overall, noting excessive noise from open-air venues near his residence and emphasizing the need for reasonable limits while preserving nightlife.\par
\par
\ul Jim Chard\ulnone , 33483\par
Questioned how the ordinance would address mobile noise sources like loud cars and motorcycles, which he described as highly disruptive.\par
\par
\ul Queen of the Socialist Civil Circle\ulnone , 33444 \par
Compared concerns about noise to broader issues of perceived disrespect and treatment by police, arguing enforcement fairness should be considered alongside noise regulation.\par
\par
Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
Mayor Carney acknowledged several strong points raised, including concerns about 24-hour monitoring, ambient noise readings, and mobile vehicle noise. He emphasized the need to balance a vibrant entertainment district with the quality of life for downtown residents, noting enforcement challenges, particularly with loud vehicles and the current inability to ticket using noise cameras under Florida law. He also expressed interest in exploring a transition to electric landscaping equipment and adjusting permitted hours.\par
\par
The City Attorney clarified that the entertainment district remains subject to the noise ordinance, though with extended hours, and that the decibel limits were based on recommendations from two (2) noise consultants. She stressed the importance of objective, measurable standards over subjective \ldblquote plainly audible\rdblquote enforcement and described the ordinance as a necessary first step that could be adjusted if needed. She also noted that portable noise meters would soon be available for enforcement.\par
\par
Commissioners discussed landscape maintenance hours (confirming an 8 a.m. start time, with limited exceptions), enforcement consistency, and the need to lead by example with city operations. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale supported moving the ordinance forward without further delay. Commissioner Markert suggested holding a town hall to gather additional public input, citing past success with that approach, and the City Manager agreed staff could coordinate community outreach.\par
\par
The Commission agreed to move forward while continuing outreach efforts. \par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mayor Carney called the joint meeting of the City Commission and the Downtown Development Authority (DDA) to order at 3:00 p.m.\par
\par
\b Present for the DDA at roll call were the following:\b0\par
\par
Dr. Alan Castello, Jim Knight, Brian Rosen, Cole Devitt , and Jule Guaglardi\par
\par
\b Alexis Givings, City Clerk, called the roll and the following were present for the City Commission:\b0\par
\par
Commissioner Tom Markert, Commissioner Juli Casale, Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns, and Mayor Thomas F. Carney, Jr.\par
\par
\b Also present were:\b0\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney,\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager,\b \b0 provided an overview of the workshop agenda, explaining that the first item focused on Atlantic Avenue beautification and the second item concerned the future operational role of the DDA at Old School Square. He stated that the beautification discussion was initiated following Commission interest in collaborating with the DDA and emphasized the importance of understanding jurisdictional responsibilities, including those involving Palm Beach County and Florida Department Of Transportation (FDOT). Regarding Old School Square, he noted that recent discussions at the DDA\rquote s January 12, 2026 meeting prompted the need for a joint dialogue about potential transitions in management responsibilities.\par
\par
Laura Simon, DDA Executive Director, introduced the beautification discussion, noting that downtown improvements have been a major focus over the past three years and that Atlantic Avenue remains central to the City\rquote s identity as it enters a milestone year. DDA board member Jule Guaglardi stated that significant private investment in downtown has elevated Delray Beach to a premier destination but that public infrastructure has not kept pace. She identified concerns including cracked sidewalks, tree root damage, faded striping, inconsistent signage, aging streetscape elements, landscaping challenges, and underutilized spaces. She referenced the Bob Gibbs Shopability Study and proposed forming a collaborative aesthetics and design committee composed of City leadership, design professionals, and stakeholders to develop both short-term improvements and a long-term plan. She emphasized that the DDA seeks partnership and a formal seat at the table.\par
\par
Jeff Oris, Assistant City Manager, presented a high-level overview of City departmental responsibilities in the downtown district. He explained that Public Works oversees traffic management, roadway maintenance, stormwater systems, seawalls, coordination with FDOT and the County, capital improvement projects, and maintenance of City-owned facilities and parking garages. Neighborhood and Community Services, including the Clean and Safe Division, handles litter and graffiti abatement, pressure cleaning, rodent control, sidewalk caf\'e9 compliance, code enforcement, and community outreach. Jeri Pryor, Director of Neighborhood and Community Services, clarified that sidewalks in the district are pressure cleaned twice per month on a rotating basis. Parks and Recreation maintains downtown parks, landscaping, irrigation systems, and fountains, including Veterans Park, Old School Square, and other public spaces. Development Services administers the Form-Based Code, reviews development applications, enforces streetscape standards, manages permits and inspections, and oversees business and alcohol licensing.\par
\par
Mayor Carney acknowledged that all parties share a common goal of enhancing Atlantic Avenue and asked specifically about the frequency of sidewalk cleaning, noting public concerns about appearance. Vice Mayor Burns asked about opportunities for broader public input beyond the workshop and inquired whether a written maintenance plan exists. Mr. Moore responded that operational maintenance procedures are in place, and the DDA indicated that future public engagement could include committees, town halls, and charrettes.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that monthly coordination meetings between the City Manager\rquote s Office and DDA leadership have resumed and would serve as a mechanism for ongoing collaboration. He also noted that any enhancements would need to be considered during the upcoming budget process.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale suggested opening the discussion to public comment before continuing Commission deliberation.\par
}

title: PUBLIC COMMENTS
JOINT DISCUSSION WITH THE DOWNTOWN DEVELOPMENT AGENCY REGARDING THE MANAGEMENT AND OPERATION OF THE OLD SCHOOL SQUARE CAMPUS

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mayor Carney invited members of the public to speak, reminding each speaker to state their name and zip code and that they would have three (3) minutes.\par
\par
\ul Annette Jackson\ulnone , 33446 \par
A longtime volunteer at Old School Square, stated that she has been involved with the campus for nearly 20 years and believes it has flourished under the DDA\rquote s management. She described increased activity at the Vintage Gym, Amphitheater, and Cornell Art Museum, including lectures, community events, art shows, wellness programs, and festivals. As a docent at the Cornell Art Museum, she shared that visitors from across Florida, the country, and internationally are drawn to the vibrancy of downtown and consistently praise the museum\rquote s exhibits. She noted that attendance and donations have increased and strongly urged the City not to change management, stating, \ldblquote If it ain\rquote t broke, don\rquote t fix it.\rdblquote\par
\par
\ul Gary Gillespie and Doreen Gillespie Beats\par
\ulnone Spoke in support of the Cornell Art Museum, highlighting a current exhibition featuring their mother\rquote s artwork. Gary, who works with museums nationwide, shared that other respected institutions have taken notice of the exhibition, reflecting positively on Delray Beach. Doreen described meaningful cultural and wellness experiences at the museum, including yoga programming, and emphasized the importance of preserving the campuses artistic and cultural value amid broader development pressures. Both encouraged continued support of the DDA\rquote s leadership.\par
\par
\ul Mavis Benson\ulnone\b \b0 33445\par
Read a letter from Glaston Leroy of the Gelareh Collective, praising the DDA and the Cornell Art Museum for their collaboration on projects such as Delray Walls, the Art & Jazz series, and immersive art exhibitions. The letter commended Executive Director, Laura Simon and Cultural Arts Director, Maruska Gatto for their leadership and vision, and emphasized the importance of the staff and volunteers in making the museum a cultural hub. Benson added that beyond attendance numbers and statistics, the greatest accomplishment has been creating a space \ldblquote where Delray comes together.\rdblquote\par
\par
\ul George Long\ulnone 33444 \par
Expressed appreciation for the wide range of educational programming held at Old School Square, including lectures hosted by the Delray Beach Historical Society. He shared personal examples of programs he attended and described the campus as active, enriching, and valuable to the community.\par
\par
\ul Christina Morrison\ulnone 33483\par
Praised the DDA\rquote s work but suggested that the campus could return to a public-private partnership model, similar to its structure in the past. She noted that while the previous arrangement was not perfect, it operated for 30 years and relied heavily on private fundraising rather than tax dollars. She expressed concern about the City\rquote s financial future and rising budget pressures, stating that Old School Square could potentially be managed by a nonprofit 501(c)(3) organization to reduce reliance on municipal funding.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comments.\par
\par
The discussion continued for WS.3.\par
\par
Laura Simon, DDA Executive Director submitted a presentation to provide historical context and highlight progress made since the DDA assumed management of Old School Square in 2021, after the City and prior nonprofit operator separated, explaining that the museum reopened first under Marusca Gatto, Cultural Arts Director, followed by the amphitheater and campus, while the City handled completion of the Creative Arts School and the Crest Theater was later removed from the DDA\rquote s management scope. She emphasized that the DDA initially agreed to a short-term arrangement but is now in the first of two possible five-year terms. \par
\par
Marusca Gatto, Cultural Arts Director, reported that despite starting with no supplies or infrastructure, the museum has hosted 29 exhibitions featuring 685 artists, attracted over 38,500 visitors, generated more than $81,000 in donations and $82,000 in store revenue, rebuilt trust with artists and the community, and established collaborations with major arts organizations through intentional curation. \par
\par
Suzanne Boyd, Marketing Director, explained that the team rebuilt branding, communications, digital platforms, media outreach, and marketing channels from scratch to counter the perception that the campus was closed, while also creating a permanent brand identity and website that will remain with Old School Square regardless of future management. \par
\par
Laura Simon added that the campus has drawn over one million visitors, hosted more than 300 events, generated about $772,000 in supplemental revenue beyond City funding, and delivered major media exposure and economic impact, stressing that investments made by the DDA stay with the campus. She stated that while the DDA is proud of its work, the complex, multi-use cultural campus requires long-term planning, specialized oversight, and possibly a strategic plan and feasibility study, noting that government alone may not be best suited to manage such a venue and that short funding horizons make long-range programming difficult. \par
\par
Marusca Gatto emphasized that maintaining continuity is critical because the museum has rebuilt credibility and is now positioned to secure major sponsorships and donations. \par
\par
Dr. Alan Costilo, DDA Board Member, praised staff for operating successfully with limited funding, reduced staff, and significant challenges, including an un repaired Crest Theater that was expected to generate revenue and warned that without stronger City collaboration and resources, continued operation may not be sustainable, though he supports whichever path staff determines is feasible. \par
\par
Brian Rosen, DDA Board Member, mentioned the DDA has built strong digital infrastructure and visibility for the campus but needs clear direction and multi-year financial commitments from the City to continue, stressing that the issue is not willingness but operational viability. \par
\par
Jule Guaglardi, DDA Board Member, argued it would be premature to transition management given the DDA\rquote s success under constraints and suggested greater support could allow the campus to reach its full potential. \par
\par
James Knight, DDA Board Member acknowledged the team\rquote s dedication but mentioned either increased funding or a structured transition plan is necessary, noting the campus cannot operate properly without adequate resources. \par
\par
Mayor Carney clarified that past nonprofit operators received roughly 25-30% of their total budgets from the City, but also generated substantial independent revenue, highlighting the financial context for comparison. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale noted that the prior nonprofit operator of Old School Square had received about $950,000 annually and control of the theater. \par
\par
Mayor Carney acknowledged the DDA did an excellent job reviving the campus after it had gone \ldblquote dark,\rdblquote criticized the former operator\rquote s exit and handling of assets, and reiterated his belief that a public-private partnership (PPP) is the best long-term management model because such entities can raise funds and operate more flexibly than government. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale praised the DDA\rquote s performance despite limited funding and said she would support increasing financial support and extending their role. \par
\par
Jule Guaglardi, suggested additional funding and a dedicated staff position could address gaps in entertainment-specific expertise. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns agreed the DDA has done outstanding work but emphasized that the key issue is sustainable funding and suggested an entity capable of raising outside revenue may be necessary. \par
\par
Mr. Moore explained that after the City partnered with the DDA, funding structures shifted to include revenue-sharing (initially 80/20, later 90/10 in the DDA\rquote s favor) and said any decision about continuing the arrangement requires evaluating total financial structure and policy direction from the commission. \par
\par
Commissioner Markert called the DDA\rquote s work \ldblquote heroic,\rdblquote urged an unbiased, fact-driven evaluation of options rather than prematurely favoring a PPP model, and said any transition would likely require at least a year, while DDA Board Member James Knight emphasized the need to set a clear timeline for decisions. \par
\par
Brian Rosen clarified that the DDA\rquote s goal is cultural programming rather than profit, noting most revenue is reinvested and little net profit exists. \par
\par
Laura Simon stressed the need for a professional feasibility study and strategic plan to determine the best long-term management structure. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale asked the City Manager to clarify what direction his office believes the City should pursue. \par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that his office\rquote s goal is to gather feedback from the commission in order to obtain clear direction. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale proposed initiating a professional feasibility study to ensure Old School Square can reach its full potential regardless of who manages it. \par
\par
Mr. Moore responded that such a study would likely cost about $50,000-$60,000 but said he was comfortable moving forward if directed, explaining that after the study the City could hold another joint workshop to review findings, evaluate options, and determine what role the City itself could play. \par
\par
Mayor Carney agreed that a feasibility review is necessary to understand what is realistically possible for the campus before deciding on any management model. \par
\par
Mr. Moore emphasized that the process would be step-by-step, combining analysis, strategic planning, and evaluation of financial and operational feasibility. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale sought confirmation that nothing would change operationally in the meantime and stressed the importance of maintaining current functionality and funding stability. \par
\par
Suzanne Boyd, Marketing Director noted that uncertainty in annual funding creates operational anxiety.\par
\par
Mr. Moore outlined a structured timeline, including a February 3rd commission meeting to discuss Crest Theater options and begin shaping strategic planning elements, followed by additional joint meetings and financial analysis to develop recommendations. He stated that full commission consensus was required before proceeding. \par
\par
Mr. Moore received consensus to move forward with planning and analysis.\par
\par
\cf0 There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 6:12 p.m.\cf1\par
}

\pard\sl276\slmult1\cf0\b\f1\fs22 \b0\f2\par
\f1 There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the workshop meeting at 4:45 p.m.\cf1\f0\fs24\par
