title: PUBLIC COMMENTS
Pursuant to Section 3.12 of the Charter of the City of Delray Beach, the Mayor has instructed me to announce a Workshop Meeting of the City Commission to be held for the following purposes:
PUBLIC COMMENTS

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 The February 3, 2026 Commission Workshop meeting was called to order at 4:04 p.m. Alexis Givings, City Clerk, called the roll and the following were present:\par
\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par
Lynn Gelin, City Attorney\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk\par
\par
\b Present: 4\b0 - Commissioner Tom Markert, Mayor Thomas F. Carney, Jr., Deputy Vice Mayor Angela Burns and Commissioner Casale\cf1\kerning0\f1 \par
\par
The Mayor stated that the workshop was a follow-up to the December 1st economic development strategy discussion.\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 Assistant City Manager Jeff Oris reported on efforts to pursue a more aggressive economic development strategy focused on financial services and technology. City staff reviewed available resources and met with the Chamber of Commerce, including Stephanie Immelman, along with Economic Development Manager Rob Evans, to discuss collaboration. The city plans to reach out to existing local firms, particularly in the tech sector, to ask what the city could do to help attract similar businesses. Oris said incentives alone usually do not attract companies; factors such as efficient permitting, available space, and assistance navigating city processes are often more important. He also noted that technology firms may offer greater long-term growth potential than smaller wealth-management firms.\par
\par
The city confirmed it has about $500,000 in its economic development fund that could be used for marketing efforts without changing the budget, and a firm that previously gathered demographic data could assist with marketing. Oris reviewed incentive approaches used by nearby cities-such as job-creation incentives, high-wage incentives, expedited permitting, Boca Raton\rquote s focus on attracting headquarters, Boynton Beach\rquote s use of its CRA, and West Palm Beach\rquote s scalable job-growth incentives. He recommended flexible, customized incentives rather than large cash payments and suggested leveraging networks of existing companies, with support from the Chamber of Commerce, to identify businesses that might consider relocating.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 Mayor Carney stated the discussion was prompted by seeing Boca Raton heavily advertised by its mayor and noted that, based on conversations with people in the corporate relocation business, Delray is largely not on their radar compared to Boca Raton or West Palm Beach. They also said the Economic Council of Palm Beach County tends to highlight Boca first, partly because it has more office space, but they believe there is still opportunity for Delray. He also questioned why the report\rquote s updated program focus and prioritization relied on Broward County statistics and asked why Palm Beach County data was not used.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
Commissioner Casale referred to a previous meeting where Ms. Smallridge said the City should determine its goals before taking further steps. She stated that the City has not yet done this and questioned what types of businesses would be appropriate for Delray, noting that the City is largely built out with limited land available. She said the City should determine what it wants to attract before spending money on advertising.\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 Mayor Carney stated the City needs to complete several steps before moving forward, noting that the Delray comprehensive and cluster analysis from 2019 has not been updated to reflect current land availability.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 Mr. Oris stated that the City is exploring ways to better identify available commercial space and vacant land. He mentioned that a subscription service used by realtors could provide this information, including details about available properties and contact information for owners.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns stated that the City needs a clearly written, structured strategy with defined objectives, measurable outcomes, responsible parties, and implementation steps.She emphasized that the Commission needs a roadmap rather than general information and expressed concern that multiple workshops have occurred without a finalized, actionable plan and asked that the next presentation include specific goals and accountability measures.\par
\par
Commissioner Markert supported obtaining the subscription service to establish baseline data and acknowledged that Delray has a limited real estate portfolio, which should help determine which industries to target, meaning technology, wealth management, and possibly AI. He suggested conducting a deeper competitive analysis of neighboring cities such as Boca Raton and Boynton Beach and consider how to structure a business development team. He added that conferences and conventions can be useful places to meet company leaders and identify potential businesses.\par
\par
Mr. Oris stated that once target industries are clearly defined, they can better determine where to focus outreach efforts.\par
\par
Mr. Moore proposed to proceed with subscribing to the commercial real estate database service; conduct a full inventory and analysis of available land and commercial space; evaluate the potential structure of a business development team; consider external marketing or consulting support as needed; and develop a more structured economic development strategy. He stated that a brief progress update would be provided at the March 9, 2026, regular commission meeting, followed by a more comprehensive workshop presentation in April outlining specific recommendations and structural proposals.\par
\par
The Commission reached consensus to proceed with the subscription service and the outlined next steps.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Jeff Oris, Assistant City Manager, stated the purpose of the Opioid Settlement Advisory Committee is to recommend how to expend funds from the statewide opioid settlement for treatment and prevention, with annual plans due July 1; the committee was asked to present by May 1st for Commission adoption in June. He noted prior allocations of $158,000, remaining funds, and anticipated future funding, and reported the committee has held six meetings, engaged stakeholders including the Drug Task Force, and is seeking Commission direction on priorities before assigning funding.\par
\par
Jeff Lefton, Board Member, stated the committee prioritized four areas and recommended focusing initial funds on a Paramedicine co-responder model, outlining a city-run program through Fire Rescue paired with a behavioral health professional, or contracting with an outside agency.\par
\par
Chuck Ridley, Board Member, shared his perspective as a recovering addict and strongly supported the Paramedicine program as an innovative, life-saving approach, noting addicts often do not seek help. He stated that alternatively, funds could be leveraged for recovery supports (employment barriers, supportive housing) and prevention, emphasizing community resources exist but require guidance and investment.\par
\par
Mr.Oris clarified the committee is requesting direction on whether to prioritize Paramedicine, which would largely consume available funds, or alternative supports likely implemented through grants, noting additional funding such as \cf1 Caron Funds \cf0 could supplement efforts.\par
\par
Commissioners expressed general support for Paramedicine while also discussing leveraging funds and emphasizing prevention. Concerns were raised about duplicating existing services, the scope of a single coordinator\rquote s role, and the value of investing in prevention programs. Discussion included the variability and limits of annual settlement funds (approximately $62,000-$92,000), current available funds ($185,000), and sustainability challenges. Commissioners requested additional information on fund allocations and hospital resource processes.\par
\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager, concluded that staff would review the feedback, clarify allowable uses of \cf1 Caron Funding\cf0 , and return to the Commission with a more structured proposal that may incorporate Paramedicine and prevention strategies. The committee will continue working with staff to develop final recommendations for the Commission\rquote s consideration.\par
\par
\pard\sl276\slmult1\f1 The meeting recessed at 7:00 p.m. and reconvened at approximately 7:06 p.m.\cf1\kerning0\f2\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Missie Barletto, Public Works Director, introduced \kerning0\f1 auditorium renovation team of architects\kerning2 , \f0 which included Michael Schnoering and Katherine Frey from Mills + Schnoering Architects, and Jody Kovalick from Schuler Shook. \par
\par
Michael Schnoering explained that the project is currently in the concept design phase, which includes a broad review of the building, its conditions, code issues, and future uses. He outlined Three Options: Base scope, Option One and Option Two.\par
\par
Option one includes significant upgrades to accessibility, a formal elevator, and theater system upgrades for better functionality in musical theater, multi-act plays, and cinema. Option two builds on the base option with basic upgrades to technology.\par
\par
Ms. Frey added the base scope work included general renovations\f1 \f0 within the existing footprint, finished upgrades, seating replacement, lighting and sound improvements, accessible dressing rooms, wheelchair lift replacement, stage ramp access, accessible seating, and balcony modifications. Mr. Kovalick noted this scope restores essential functionality and safety, including stage curtains, lighting, public address and assisted listening systems, and upgrades to acoustics, electrical, HVAC, plumbing, and structure, which currently doesn't exist. Option One expands the footprint of the building in two areas; the rear and the side. \par
\par
Mr. Kovalick presented Option Two, which builds on Option One with advanced technical upgrades, including a tension wire grid replacing the catwalk, mezzanines, expanded lighting, rigging, and audio-visual systems, including live-streaming, with supporting electrical and structural upgrades for maximum flexibility.\par
\par
Mr. Schnoering noted cost estimates are conceptual, with the base scope at approximately $3 million, Option One; adding building and technology improvements, and Option Two; providing further enhancements, with phasing options available.\par
\par
Missie Barletto noted that the items in each option basket can be moved around depending on what is desired for the auditorium. She added the directive was to bring the auditorium back to the functionality it had previously, which would be Option One.\par
\par
Commissioner Markert asked about balcony safety, and Ms. Barletto \kerning0\f1 stated she had a signed and sealed letter from the architects that say that the balcony is structurally sound for the purposes that the City wants to use it for\kerning2 . \f0 Deputy Vice Mayor Burns asked about a feasibility study, and Ms. Barletto clarified the feasibility study is for the entire campus, not just the auditorium.\par
\par
Jody Kovalick confirmed that the renovations will include most in-house theater equipment to reduce rental costs and allow revenue opportunities.\par
\par
There was consensus among the Commission to proceed with design planning toward Option Two, with flexibility to phase or adjust certain components as needed.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par

\par
\kerning0\f1 Mayor Carney read the quasi-judicial rules into the record. \kerning2\f0 He also requested that anyone intending to speak on this item and other quasi-judicial items be sworn in by the City Clerk.\par
\par
Ms. Givings swore in those that wished to speak on Item Nos. 7.C., 7.D. and 8.C.\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director entered Project File No. PZ 000347-2025 into the record. \par
\par
Mayor Carney asked his colleagues to disclose any ex-parte communication.\par
\par
\ul Mayor Carney\ulnone : None \par
\ul Deputy Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone : None \par
\ul Commissioner Casale\ulnone : None \par
\ul Commissioner Markert\ulnone : None\par
\par
Bettina Stepan, representative for the applicant, stated the waterfront residential lot in the Lake Ida area has approximately 80 linear feet of canal frontage and the home is fully permitted and constructed, pending seawall improvements. She explained that the request is to allow a 12 foot elevation to comply with the approved civil drainage plan due to unique site conditions where the crown of the road is much higher than the canal, requiring a finished floor over 18 feet. She added that strict compliance with the base flood elevation would create unsafe conditions such as a steep slope and hazardous drop off, while the proposed seawall supports shoreline stabilization, erosion control, and aligns with approved engineering plans and regulatory approvals. It is consistent with similar elevations in the area, emphasizing that the waiver is necessary to meet drainage, safety, and code requirements without creating unsafe conditions. She noted that all regulatory approvals from the Florida Department of Environmental Protection and the Army Corps of Engineers are in compliance, with no anticipated adverse impacts.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes confirmed that there is a uniqueness to the situation with the yard, where the crown of the road slopes downward and even at 12 feet the sea wall is only the height of the middle elevation of the yard, explaining that the limitation on height is typically meant as a balance between resiliency and protecting neighboring properties. She noted that the existing yard has a dramatic slope from about 18.5 down to 8.75, emphasizing that this uniqueness prevents the request from being a special privilege.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to public comment. Seeing no one present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
There was no rebuttal from either the applicant or the City.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale raised a question regarding potential adverse impacts on neighboring properties, particularly whether the increased seawall height could affect adjacent yards. Ms. Gianniotes responded that the surrounding properties have similar elevations and that the conditions are consistent across the area.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Ms. Gelin read Resolution No. 10-26 into the record.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked for anyone who had not been sworn in previously to be sworn in.\par
\par
Ms. Givings swore in those that had not been sworn in.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes entered two files into the record: 2025-110, which is the conditional use and 2025-109, which is the accompanying level four site plan application.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin noted that the item is an appeal and reminded that this is a de novo hearing, meaning the Commission is not bound by the Planning and Zoning Board\rquote s decision and may consider the application anew. \par
\par
Mayor Carney asked his colleagues to disclose any ex-parte communication.\par
\par
\ul Mayor Carney\ulnone : Spoke with the applicant\rquote s representative, Brad Miller.\par
\ul Deputy Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone : Spoke with the applicant, the attorney, and the legal counsel of the homeowners association.\par
\ul Commissioner Casale\ulnone : Spoke with the applicant and whatever is on the server.\par
\ul Commissioner Markert\ulnone : Spoke with the applicants, their attorney, and have some leftover papers as well.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin mentioned that she provided a packet of emails that were on the server.\par
\par
Matthew Scott, zoning attorney on behalf of the applicant Fazio Consulting LLC, stated they are seeking approval for a conditional use application for a car wash and a level four site plan application. He explained the applicant bears the burden of showing they meet all criteria in the code through competent, substantial evidence and are entitled to approval if those criteria are met unless opposing evidence shows otherwise, clarifying this is not a rezoning request but a conditional use application, and stating the client is a long-time family-run car wash operator with over 75 years of experience in South Florida and that they believe they meet all requirements and the proposal will be an improvement for the area.\par
\par
Bradley Miller, land planner with Urban Design Studio,\kerning0 \kerning2 presented the project, explaining the parcel is zoned general commercial, allows for car washes subject to conditional use approval, and described the site plan including access from Conklin Drive, queuing, circulation, buffers, walls, landscaping, and proximity to residential areas. He stated the project design includes architecture, vacuum spaces, and shading features, and that key concerns were lighting, noise, and traffic, noting they are seeking no variances, meet code in all ways, and are proposing additional measures such as motion sensor lighting and further noise reduction to exceed code requirements.\par
\par
J.T. Stephens, noise consultant with LSA Associates, stated noise standards were met and further reduced by removing two blowers and adding noise-reducing walls and silencers, which Mr. Scott confirmed were additional refinements after Planning and Zoning Board review.\par
\par
Adam Kerr, professional enginer with Kimley-Horn & Associates, stated the traffic study was approved by Palm Beach County, confirming the project meets standards, generates less traffic than other permitted uses, requires no roadway improvements, and does not warrant a traffic signal at the location.\par
\par
Clayton Belger, BBG Real Estate, stated market analysis supports the need for an additional express car wash in the area, and Mr. Scott concluded the project meets all code and conditional use criteria with no significant detrimental impact on the neighborhood. \par
\par
Ms. Gelin put into the record a copy of the staff report. She clarified the request is a conditional use, not a permitted use, and is subject to Commission discretion, with authority to impose conditions to mitigate impacts, and noted disagreement with prior statements made by Mr. Scott. \par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes, presented the request, noting the site is zoned General Commercial, surrounded by commercial and residential uses, and located within the City\rquote s annexation area. She explained a conditional use is not permitted by right and requires findings that it is not detrimental to neighborhood stability or redevelopment, and may be revoked if impacts such as noise exceed expectations. She stated traffic is a primary concern, with County approval indicating no required roadway improvements, though trips on Conklin Drive are expected to nearly double, and reviewed site circulation and activity levels. She noted noise studies meet current standards and proposed ordinance thresholds, with blower reductions made, and discussed lighting, buffering, walls, and landscaping as mitigation measures, while raising questions about sound, safety, and design details. She concluded considerations include compatibility with surrounding uses, adequacy of mitigation measures, traffic impacts, and whether the use affects neighborhood stability, noting the Planning and Zoning Board recommended denial and the Commission may consider the request de novo. \par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item and noted that anyone that provides testimony is subject to cross examination. \par
\par
\ul Lori Vinikor\ulnone , 33446, President of the Alliance of Delray Residential Associations\par
Spoke in support of the Planning and Zoning Board\rquote s denial. Argued the project is incompatible with surrounding residential and agricultural uses. Raised concerns about traffic safety, environmental impacts, and noise traveling beyond barriers.\par
\par
\ul Hank Vogel\ulnone , 33484, Conklin Drive resident\par
Provided photos. Spoke in support of the Planning and Zoning Board\rquote s decision. Raised concerns about groundwater contamination affecting private wells. Questioned the accuracy of traffic projections and the project\rquote s financial feasibility.\par
\par
\ul Mike Caruso\ulnone , 33484\par
Described dangerous real-world traffic conditions at Military Trail and Conklin Drive, supported by video. Recounted a fatal crash at the intersection. Stated that adding more vehicles would worsen an already hazardous situation.\par
\par
\ul Dr. Marcy Weiss\ulnone , 33484, President of the Sierra Vista Homeowners Association\par
Spoke on behalf of residents. Emphasized public safety concerns, citing multiple recent crashes, and stated that traffic impacts could not be mitigated despite discussions with the applicant. Urged denial based on safety, compatibility, and community concerns.\par
\par
\ul Erin Sullivan\ulnone , 33484\par
Described a recent crash that caused major traffic delays. Emphasized concerns about congestion, environmental impacts, noise, and light pollution. Argued the project would degrade community safety and livability.\par
\par
\ul Robert Burkland\ulnone , 33484, High Point resident\par
Described heavy traffic and difficulty navigating the area, particularly due to u-turn patterns. Expressed concern that additional traffic would worsen already stressful and unsafe conditions.\par
\par
\ul David D\rquote Amico\ulnone , 33484\par
Presented video evidence of a recent crash and a similar car wash in operation, arguing that traffic accidents are frequent and that the proposed use would intensify congestion. Noted the number of nearby car washes already in the area.\par
\par
\ul Lynn Holtzman\ulnone , 33484\par
Argued the project would have a detrimental effect on neighborhood stability, citing increased traffic, noise, and potential exposure to chemicals. Stated the use is incompatible with residential living and would negatively impact health and property values.\par
\par
\ul Lauren Richards\ulnone , 33484\par
Emphasized that homes as close as approximately 41 feet would experience constant noise, light, and disruption. Stated that such proximity to an intensive commercial use would reduce property values and undermine zoning protections.\par
\par
\ul Jacqueline Wardwin\ulnone , 33484\par
Stated she lives closest to the proposed site and would experience severe impacts, including noise, loss of outdoor use, and sleep disruption.\par
\par
\ul Mitch Katz\ulnone , 33445, Planning and Zoning Board member speaking personally\par
Stated he initially supported the project but voted to deny it after recognizing significant safety concerns, particularly related to u-turn traffic and the lack of viable mitigation options.\par
\par
\ul Leia Culuso\ulnone , 33484, Registered Nurse\par
Spoke about public health risks, particularly potential contamination of private well water. Noted the absence of groundwater studies, monitoring, and fail-safe systems, and emphasized that conditional use approval is discretionary.\par
\par
\ul Eric Calcagno\ulnone , 33484, Firefighter/Paramedic Captain\par
Raised concerns about emergency access, noting that increased traffic and potential backups could hinder emergency response on a dead-end residential street.\par
\par
\ul Jeff Overstreet\ulnone , 33484\par
Argued the project does not meet multiple land development regulations and would significantly increase traffic. Emphasized safety risks, emergency access concerns, and deficiencies in the applicant\rquote s supporting studies.\par
\par
\ul Thomas Gary\ulnone , 33484\par
Described daily traffic challenges during peak hours, including blocked lanes and dangerous conditions when attempting to access Conklin Drive. Warned that additional traffic would exacerbate an already unsafe situation.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
\f1 Mr. Scott chose not to cross-examine individual residents and instead requested time for rebuttal. The Commission allowed him five minutes to respond. Mr. Scott thanked the public for input and stated the hearing must be based on competent, substantial evidence, noting public comments did not include technical expertise. He emphasized traffic as the primary concern, addressing staff and public comments regarding a projected doubling of trips, and requested clarification on overall traffic capacity and accident data.\f0\par
\par
Mr. Kerr stated that while trips may double to over 300 per day, this remains minimal compared to the roadway capacity standard of approximately 15,000 vehicles per day. He also stated that traffic studies and crash data did not indicate conditions warranting a signal or other roadway improvements.\par
\par
Jeff Fazio stated he has extensive experience in the car wash industry and explained that groundwater protection and design are strictly regulated by state and county codes, including permitting and inspections. He noted modern industry practices have significantly improved safety, including chemical handling and elimination of hazardous substances, emphasizing compliance with environmental and EPA standards.\par
\par
Mr. Scott stated public concerns were generalized and not based on competent, substantial evidence, noting the project meets all code requirements for traffic, noise, and lighting. He emphasized the conditional use standard requires a significantly detrimental impact, which staff determined does not exist, and requested approval of the application.\par
\par
\f1 At this time, the meeting recessed at 10:15 p.m. and reconvened at 10:19 p.m.\f0\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes questioned traffic capacity and access on Conklin Drive, noting it is a dead-end, while Mr. Kerr stated projected trips remain well below roadway capacity. She cited site plan standards regarding accident risks and raised concerns about traffic on a residential street, and noted noise levels are near allowable limits and must comply with current and future standards. She stated the staff report acknowledges the County traffic performance standards letter, which evaluates impacts on Military Trail and determines no roadway interventions are required, noting it does not address impacts on the local road, Conklin Drive.\par
\par
Mr. Scott was granted five minutes to cross-examine staff after their comments. He referenced the staff report regarding traffic and stated projected trips would double on Conklin Drive but remain within County-approved standards, noting the City relies on County traffic analysis and comprehensive plan policies rather than independently reevaluating roadway capacity findings.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes confirmed the County is the authority over Military Trail traffic and reiterated concerns regarding local street impacts, while discussion also addressed noise studies, with staff noting data was based on actual equipment and showing reductions but raising questions about potential sound exceedances. \par
\par
Ms. Gelin noted procedural limits of the quasi-judicial process.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale noted the decision is difficult, and raised concerns about traffic, neighborhood impacts, and potential noise mitigation measures, while acknowledging possible buffering and design options.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns stated the project would have a significantly detrimental effect on neighborhood stability.\par
\par
Commissioner Markert stated opposition due to multiple concerns.\par
\par
Mayor Carney expressed concerns regarding noise and traffic impacts on Conklin Drive, noted broader site plan considerations beyond conditional use, and stated the project may negatively impact the neighborhood due to circulation and congestion issues.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\par
David Millage, applicant\rquote s representative, explained that the property consists of three parcels with five existing office warehouse buildings totaling approximately 102,000 square feet. The request sought to change the land use designation from Congress Avenue Mixed Use (CMU) to Commerce (CMR) and rezone the property from Mixed Residential, Office, and Commercial (MROC) to Mixed Industrial and Commercial (MIC). He provided historical context, noting the site was originally approved for light industrial use, later rezoned in 1990, and then changed again in 2006-2007 as part of a city-initiated corridor update. He stated that the current MROC zoning creates nonconforming uses, making it difficult to attract and retain tenants, especially those in industries such as cabinetry, HVAC, and manufacturing.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes supported the request, explaining that the City has limited industrial space, only 4% of land allows industrial use and about 2% is actively used for it, and emphasized the importance of preserving existing industrial clusters. She also noted that the proposal would result in a significant decrease in traffic and help resolve conflicts between existing building design and current zoning restrictions. Additionally, she explained that if spaces remain vacant too long, they lose their nonconforming status, further limiting viable uses.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to public comment for Item Nos. 8.B. (Ordinance No. 05-26) and 8.C. (Ordinance No. 04-26). Seeing no one present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale asked about the impact on Live Local Act development potential. Ms. Gianniotes clarified that the change would not increase development intensity and that Live Local provisions would still be governed by the highest density and height standards, meaning the practical effect would remain the same.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale expressed support for the item. Mayor Carney commented that the zoning change would likely make the property more economically viable and reduce the likelihood of it being sold.\par

\par
Terrence Moore, City Manager\par

\par

Mayor Carney stated that the sole purpose of the meeting was to discuss the situation regarding the banyan tree at the golf course. He opened the floor for public comment and advised that speakers would have three (3) minutes each.\par
\par
\ul Jim Chard\ulnone , 33483\par
Stated that he had consulted with arborists who indicated that removing the banyan tree could potentially cause more damage to the canal bank than leaving it in place. He explained that the tree\rquote s root structure reinforces the integrity of the bank and provides additional environmental benefits. \par
\par
He addressed concerns that the tree is invasive, stating that the banyan cannot reproduce in the United States because it lacks the specific wasp required for pollination. Therefore, he asserted it is technically incorrect to classify the tree as invasive. He further noted that its growth can be managed and directed through proper maintenance practices.\par
\par
He concluded by encouraging the City to preserve and maintain the tree, suggesting it could continue stabilizing the bank for decades.\par
\par
\ul Gail Clark\ulnone , 33483\par
Stated that the banyan tree had likely gone unnoticed for many years until surrounding trees were removed. She expressed concern that the tree is now being targeted despite its long-standing presence.\par
\par
She referenced discussions with an arborist who supports preserving the tree through risk mitigation and ongoing maintenance. Ms. Clark also suggested that the tree could potentially qualify as a \ldblquote legacy tree\rdblquote if deemed one of the largest of its kind in the area, thereby warranting preservation and recognition.\par
\par
She encouraged the Commission to seek additional expert input and explore management options before making a final decision regarding removal.\par
\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\fs24 Mayor Carney requested to pull Consent Item No. 6.I. for discussion. It became Item No. 7.C.C. on the Regular Agenda.\par
\par
\cf1 Mayor Carney wanted to discuss the interlocal agreement between Palm Beach County and the City of Delray Beach for traffic control authority, noting he had previously discussed concerns with staff about the City having limited input under the agreement. He asked whether there were opportunities to negotiate greater involvement, as some other cities appear to have more influence over traffic control decisions.\par
\par
Missie Barletto, Public Works Director, explained that she had only recently received the Mayor\rquote s question and had not yet had sufficient time to fully explore options. She clarified that while some cities, such as Boca Raton, operate their own traffic control divisions with dedicated staff and equipment, Delray Beach relies on the County, which maintains control over traffic devices and decision-making. She added that this agreement had been negotiated with the County over approximately a year and a half, and attempts to modify terms were largely not accepted. The current agreement is an update to the original 1992 agreement, and one notable concession gained was allowing public art wraps on County-owned traffic control boxes, which had been a longstanding request.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale emphasized that while traffic control is often a public concern, taking over responsibility from the County would require significant staffing, equipment, and long-term financial commitment. She noted that such a transition would be costly and may not yield substantial improvements given existing constraints like traffic volume and infrastructure limitations.\par
\par
Mayor Carney clarified that he was not advocating for the City to assume full control, but rather exploring whether adjustments-such as improved signal timing-could be negotiated within the existing framework. Ms. Barletto confirmed that coordination with the County and FDOT on traffic timing is ongoing.\par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mayor Carney read the quasi-judicial rules into the record. \par
\par
\cf0 Ms. Givings swore in those individuals who wished to provide testimony on this item.\par
\par
\pard\sl276\slmult1 Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, entered Building Permit File No. 22-00204096 and Planning and Zoning File PZ000448-2026 into the record.\fs22\par
\pard\par
\fs24 Mayor Carney asked his colleagues to disclose any ex-parte communications for this item.\cf1\par
\par
\pard\sl276\slmult1\cf0\ul Mayor Carney\ulnone : Disclosed that he had spoken with members of the Beach Property Owners Association (BPOA), City staff, and the City Attorney several times regarding the permit process. He clarified that he had not had any direct communication with the applicant. He also noted that there was extensive correspondence received by the Commission, including numerous letters and supporting materials, all of which would be entered into the record as part of the ex parte communications. Acknowledged that, in addition to prior discussions, any emails or materials already included in the public record would also be considered as part of the record for this item.\par
\pard\ul Deputy Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone : Stated that she had not spoken with anyone recently regarding the item. She then clarified that any prior discussions occurred earlier when the matter first arose, but no recent communication had taken place.\par
\ul Commissioner Casale\ulnone : Spoke to the owners representative, and members of the community. Spoke to the former representative, Ms. Andrea Keiser on this at some point.\par
\ul Commissioner Markert\ulnone : Spoke to both gentlemen.\cf1\par
\par
Ms. Gelin read Resolution No. 57-26 into the record.\par
\par
The applicant was represented by Michael Stamm and Sean McAllister of Stamm Development, who explained that a building permit had originally been approved in 2023 under prior regulations allowing a larger structure. They stated that substantial costs were incurred in reliance on that permit. After new regulations reduced the allowable FAR, they redesigned the project to reduce the size from approximately 9,112 square feet (1.06 FAR) to 7,330 square feet (0.85 FAR), arguing this was a reasonable compromise. They also cited a belief that the original permit remained valid and emphasized their effort to meet updated building codes and FEMA requirements while seeking an equitable resolution.\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, clarified that the original permit was issued as an owner-builder permit, which became invalid when the property ownership changed to an LLC without notification to the City. She explained that such permits cannot transfer to a corporate entity and that a new permit would be required under current regulations. She also provided context on FAR standards, noting that the surrounding neighborhood consists of homes with significantly lower FARs, generally at or below 0.65, and that the proposed 0.85 FAR would exceed the established neighborhood character.\par
\par
\cf0 Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item.\cf1\par
\par
\ul Hal Stern\ulnone , 622 Seasage Drive, 33483 \par
Spoke as President of the BPOA, in opposition of the item and submitted a letter into the record. He stated that the BPOA supports the intent of the FAR ordinance adopted in March 2024 to preserve neighborhood scale and prevent oversized homes. He argued the requested 0.85 FAR represents approximately a 30% increase above the adopted 0.65 standard and would materially alter neighborhood character. He further stated that granting the waiver would set a precedent encouraging similar requests, weakening the ordinance, and that no hardship exists because a compliant home of approximately 5,500-6,000 square feet could still be built.\par
\par
\ul Joe Schlow\ulnone , 1005 Brooks Lane, 33483\par
Spoke representing himself and multiple nearby residents, including homeowners on Brooks Lane and White Drive who yielded their time. He stated that residents are full-time Delray Beach residents and strongly oppose the waiver due to its scale and inconsistency with the FAR ordinance. He argued the proposal represents a significant deviation that undermines the intent of the regulations adopted to preserve neighborhood compatibility. He reiterated that no hardship exists and that approval would set a precedent affecting surrounding properties.\par
\par
\ul Ned Wehler\ulnone , 1010 Ingraham Avenue, 33483 \par
Spoke as the Vice President of the BPOA, and testified in opposition of the item. He recalled prior involvement in the drafting of the FAR ordinance, stating it was developed over several years in collaboration with staff, residents, and developers to reflect existing neighborhood character. He emphasized that the adopted FAR standards were based on measured existing conditions across barrier island neighborhoods and were not arbitrary. He stated the proposed FAR exceeds neighborhood norms and is inconsistent with the intent of the adopted regulations.\par
\par
\ul Tom Kustura\ulnone , 1010 Brooks Lane, 33483\par
Stated that he lives directly next to the subject property and expressed concern that granting the waiver would create precedent for similar requests, including for his own property. He cited state law requirements that waivers be justified and argued no legal hardship exists. He also raised concerns about construction impacts and code compliance issues at the site and stated the applicant is a speculative developer rather than a full-time resident.\par
\par
\cf0 Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\cf1\par
\par
In rebuttal, Mr. Stamm reiterated that their situation was unique due to reliance on a previously issued permit and argued that granting the waiver would not create a harmful precedent. Ms. Gelin responded that the validity of the original permit was not relevant to the waiver decision and confirmed that the permit was no longer valid due to the ownership change. She emphasized that the Commission must evaluate the request solely based on the waiver criteria.\par
\par
During Commission discussion, Commissioner Markert, Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, and Commissioner Casale all expressed that, despite sympathy for the applicant, they could not support the waiver because it conflicted with the ordinance they had adopted to protect neighborhood character. Mayor Carney focused on the legal implications of the ownership change and agreed that the original permit no longer conferred rights.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mayor Carney explained that the City had not initially received a full presentation and that the purpose of the item was to formally request reconsideration in light of additional work and information now available. Ms. Gelin confirmed this understanding, and Mr. Moore provided an update explaining that, following direction from a prior special meeting, the City secured a new contractor, Baker Landscape Services, to prepare a technical report regarding the banyan tree and related conditions. This report, along with other supporting documentation, had been distributed to the Commission and would be included in the reconsideration request. He stated that the goal was to obtain Commission approval to submit a formal letter to the Lake Worth Drainage District requesting reconsideration, accompanied by the new technical findings.\par
\par

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Ms. Gelin read Ordinance No. 35-25 into the record. She explained that the ordinance updates and modernizes the City\rquote s noise regulations to establish clearer and more objective standards for measuring and enforcing allowable noise levels within the City. She noted that the City previously held a town hall meeting on February 5, 2026, with staff participation to gather community input. If adopted, staff would proceed with purchasing noise meters and begin training with a consultant, followed by community outreach. Implementation was anticipated for April-May 2026. Ms. Gelin addressed several misconceptions raised by the public. She clarified that the City does have an existing noise ordinance that has been in place since approximately 2012, with a prior update in 2013. She explained that the current standard, plainly audible at 100 feet, is subjective, and the proposed ordinance introduces objective decibel-based measurements to improve consistency and fairness in enforcement, while still retaining the plainly audible standard when meters are unavailable. She further clarified that noise is measured at the property boundary (generally near the sidewalk) rather than inside private property, in accordance with Florida law, and that the ordinance accounts for properties with boundaries close to buildings, particularly in downtown areas. She explained that different zoning districts, including entertainment districts, are assigned varying allowable decibel levels, with higher allowances for industrial and entertainment areas. Ms. Gelin also addressed concerns about how the decibel standards were developed, explaining they were based on a professional sound study conducted over approximately two weeks. The study included both objective measurements using noise meters placed throughout the City and community volunteer input. She stated that the standards were developed by an acoustic consultant experienced in other municipalities, including Miami Beach, and were further reviewed by additional consultants and legal counsel. She emphasized that the ordinance is not intended as a revenue generator and that Code Enforcement prioritizes compliance over fines. She noted that enforcement will likely begin with warnings and that fines are established by state law rather than the City Commission. She also explained that enforcement may ultimately involve the Special Magistrate if compliance is not achieved.\par
\par
Regarding vehicular noise, Ms. Gelin explained that enforcement is governed by Florida Statutes and involves coordination with state agencies. She noted that the City will rely on decibel measurement tools and law enforcement training to address complaints, particularly regarding loud mufflers and vehicle noise. She clarified that the ordinance defers to state law for vehicle related noise enforcement.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin concluded by recommending adoption of the ordinance, emphasizing the extensive work of staff and consultants to develop balanced standards that support both residents and businesses. She recommended a follow-up report to the Commission in 120 days to evaluate implementation, assess effectiveness, and determine whether adjustments are necessary based on real world enforcement data. Mayor Carney affirmed support and acknowledged the work involved.\par
\par
\cf0 Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item.\par
\par
\ul Alex Burns\ulnone , 33445\par
Shared that the noise ordinance issue is personal to him as a business owner, noting that noise is an expected part of downtown life. He expressed concern that regulating noise too strictly could negatively impact businesses and the vibrancy of downtown. He also discussed broader issues of economic inequity, stating that historically undeserved communities have been left behind and suggesting that expanding opportunity and economic development across all areas of the city would benefit Delray Beach as a whole.\par
\par
\ul Angela Hill\ulnone , 33445\par
Spoke about the historical context of segregation in Delray Beach, referencing past policies that separated communities along racial lines. She stated that these historical boundaries continue to influence present day expectations around neighborhoods and entertainment. Ms. Hill argued that extending the entertainment district west of Swinton would be a step toward correcting historical inequities and ensuring equal opportunity for cultural and business activity across the city.\par
\par
\ul Lucika Suarez\ulnone , 33444\par
Spoke as a realtor and raised concerns about the financial viability of businesses operating under stricter noise regulations. She explained the high cost of commercial space in the downtown area and warned that additional restrictions could make it difficult for tenants and business owners to succeed. She emphasized the importance of balancing regulation with economic sustainability and noted that downtown convenience comes with expected trade-offs, including noise.\par
\par
\ul Michael Tyche\ulnone , 33444\par
Stated that the ordinance appears more restrictive and may not align with residents\rquote original concerns, which he believes were primarily focused on vehicle noise, especially motorcycles. He expressed concern about reduced quiet hours and increased enforcement affecting neighborhood gatherings and community life. He also warned that the ordinance could negatively impact downtown vibrancy and create a perception of overregulation.\par
\par
\ul Chuck Ridley\ulnone , 33444\par
Provided historical context on the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) and the development of downtown Delray Beach. He stated that past revitalization efforts focused on bringing life to a previously inactive downtown. He also described the historical presence of Black-owned entertainment venues east of Swinton Avenue and argued that redevelopment efforts contributed to the decline of those spaces. Mr. Ridley urged consideration of how current policies affect the survival of businesses and called for renewed support of a vibrant entertainment district.\par
\par
\ul George Long\ulnone , 33444\par
Stated that discussion of expanding the entertainment district is separate from the noise ordinance itself. He acknowledged concerns about noise levels but said he personally has not been impacted. He suggested that some venues may be using excessively large sound systems and recommended exploring technical solutions such as improved speaker placement or acoustic engineering. He concluded that the ordinance is unlikely to harm the city but encouraged thoughtful enforcement and data-driven evaluation.\par
\par
\ul Laura Simon\ulnone , 33483\par
Representing the Downtown Development Authority, expressed concern about the potential impact of the ordinance on the nighttime economy. She noted that the entertainment district is currently limited in scope and that changes to hours and noise levels could affect multiple areas of downtown. She supported evaluating expansion of the entertainment district and encouraged further testing and review of the proposed standards before final implementation.\par
\par
\ul Ellen Beyda\ulnone , 33483\par
Stated that vehicular noise, particularly motorcycles and cars on Atlantic Avenue, is her primary concern. She described the noise as frightening for pedestrians, especially children. She expressed appreciation for the discussion and stated she was previously unaware of the broader components of the ordinance.\par
\par
\ul Rhonda Miller\ulnone , 33444\par
Questioned who is defining the complaints about noise and expressed concern that newcomers may be driving increased regulation. She raised skepticism about enforcement tools such as noise meters and suggested that noise enforcement could be uneven or targeted. She argued that noise is a natural part of community life and that enforcement should focus specifically on problem sources rather than broader restrictions affecting the entire city.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin explained that the proposed 120-day period is not a true pilot program, because we can\rquote t do a pilot program unless there\rquote s something in the code, and the city has to have regulations in order to test it out. She stated that the choice is to either maintain the current subjective approach, which doesn\rquote t work, or adopt the proposed ordinance and implement it in phases. She added that, similar to our red speed cameras, the city is still in a phased approach and may extend the period if needed. She also noted that the goal is to move away from a standard where what\rquote s noise to you may not be noise to me. She explained that the 120-day period is necessary because the city must purchase the noise meters, schedule the trainings, and do our education at the outset. This would be followed by a structured implementation period where staff are trained, the equipment is tested, and enforcement begins gradually, starting with a warning period similar to other traffic citation programs. She emphasized that the meters require technical use, including adjustments for ambient noise and proper positioning, and staff must be fully trained to ensure accurate readings. After this period, staff will return to the Commission with an update on whether the numbers are where they should be and whether the ordinance is being applied fairly. Ms. Gelin further stated that our goal is compliance, and Code Enforcement works to achieve compliance through education and coordination with businesses. She referenced prior issues with noise impacts and explained that staff previously held meetings with businesses to address concerns, noting that once people understand what the requirements are and why they\rquote re in violation, it leads to a much better relationship between the city and the business. She added that Code Enforcement and Development Services often work with businesses on mitigation measures, including operational adjustments and site-based solutions. She also explained that enforcement requires proper legal standards and cannot rely on hearsay. If there is a noise complaint, the city has to have personal observation to issue a citation. She described how other jurisdictions, including Miami Beach, used a task force approach where officers were trained on noise meters and stationed in known problem areas, similar to speed traps, allowing them to issue citations based on observed violations.\cf1\par
}

{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\fs24 Ms. Gelin read Ordinance No. 10-26 into the record.\cf1\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, explained that the changes address inconsistencies created by a 1990 citywide rezoning, where many existing lots, particularly in older neighborhoods, do not meet current dimensional standards but remain legally established. The ordinance recognizes properties defined by metes and bounds, especially in the northwest and southwest areas, and aims to correct long-standing inequities by allowing these parcels to be more easily developed. A new legacy property designation applies to parcels owned by the same family for at least 30 years, allowing redevelopment for family members without workforce housing restrictions, while still requiring workforce housing if the property is sold outside the family. Additional amendments clarify development standards and simplify previously confusing code language. A provision that would have required workforce housing when subdividing certain lots is removed due to concerns about unintended impacts on property owners and neighborhood character. The ordinance also introduces adjustments such as reduced setbacks, height limits for workforce housing, allowances for porches and driveways, and clearer rules for alley access. Ms. Gianniotes noted that these updates are intended to reaffirm property rights, support infill development, and expand workforce housing opportunities while maintaining neighborhood compatibility, and recommends approval of the ordinance as amended.\par
\par
\cf0 Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item.\par
\par
\ul Yvonne Odom\ulnone , 33445\par
Spoke as a resident and president of the Delray Beach Community Development Corporation, and in support of the ordinance, stating it will correct long-standing issues that have prevented families from building homes on legally existing nonconforming lots. She shared that two (2) housing opportunities for young men and families were previously blocked due to lot configuration issues and expressed that the ordinance will help advance homeownership opportunities. She emphasizes the importance of homeownership as part of the American Dream and argues that current residents should not be penalized for historical platting practices. She urged approval of the ordinance and thanked staff, specifically acknowledging Barbara Pinkston.\par
\par
\ul Chuck Ridley\ulnone , 33444\par
Supports the ordinance and commends staff and leadership for addressing what he describes as a historical inequity tied to past segregation-era land development patterns. He states that the changes represent corrective action and encourages continued leadership on similar issues to benefit future generations.\par
\par
\ul Jeff Costello\ulnone , 33444\par
Spoke as a planning consultant, and in support of the ordinance and noted his involvement in assisting with its development. He expressed support for provisions allowing redevelopment of metes and bounds lots without replatting, as well as changes that support workforce housing adjustments and the removal of certain restrictive provisions affecting R1A properties. He stated that the amendments provide broader flexibility for property owners. \par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns stated that she was initially pleased with the ordinance but now feels uncertain due to the changes, saying she believes it may be more appropriate to return to first reading. She requested a simplified explanation of what removing \ldblquote number four\rdblquote does.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes explained that under current rules in the R1A district, lots that are under the standard 60-foot requirement (often 50-foot lots from historic plats) can be developed, and in R1A those lots can already be split and developed as market-rate homes. The removed provision would have required that, when those lots are divided, a portion be designated as workforce housing instead of all being market rate. She explained that this proposal was intended to increase workforce housing but created a major policy shift and conflicted with other parts of the ordinance. She added that it also risked unintended impacts in other zoning districts by increasing nonconformities in neighborhoods with larger lots. She concluded that eliminating number four restores consistency with the rest of the ordinance and avoids introducing broader density changes at this time.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Burns confirmed her understanding, noting that the change removes a requirement that would have affected larger or higher-value lots by requiring workforce housing.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale asked whether the revisions were based on county practices regarding parcels not originally platted, and staff confirmed that the intent was consistent with how legally described properties are treated, particularly those conveyed through metes and bounds rather than subdivision plats. She clarified that the changes are relatively limited, mainly adjusting setbacks and clarifying rules for legacy properties and lot definitions. She also asked whether allowing redevelopment of legacy properties could expose owners to potential exploitation or pressure, and staff responded that the changes primarily streamline the permitting process by recognizing legal property descriptions and reducing procedural barriers such as plat exemptions. Commissioner Casale stated she is generally supportive and believes the changes are long overdue, referencing prior small-scale amendments that frequently came before the Commission.\par
\par
Mayor Carney expressed support for the amended version, stating it is an improvement. He acknowledged concerns about potential exploitation but emphasized that the ordinance helps legacy families, primarily in northwest and southwest neighborhoods, build wealth and benefit from increased property values. He concluded that he supports the amended ordinance and believes it provides meaningful opportunity for long-standing property owners.\cf1\par
}

\par

\par

\par
City Attorney, Lynn Gelin, explained that this is City initiated, so staff will present first. Typically, applicants go first and carry the burden of proof. She read the resolution into the record.\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, read File No. 2023-073 into the record, which is the original in-lieu parking request. She stated the property was approved as a restaurant and maintains that use, but its functional use has shifted toward assembly or meeting space, raising parking concerns. Resolution 62-23 granted five in-lieu parking spaces for the designated restaurant use, noting most customers stay under 15 minutes for grab and go coffee. Since 2023, there have been concerns about property function, code violations, including use violations, an insufficient life safety plan, and a stage shown on the floor plan but not the life safety plan, unapproved special events, traffic impacts to the surrounding area, and parking impacts to the surrounding community. \par
\par
She explained the parking requirements for the Subculture location, noting that the current parking arrangement is non-conforming. The property requires thirteen parking spaces, with five in-lieu. If it were reviewed a place of assembly, it would have required forty-four spaces. The use of the property is questioned, with Ms. Gianniotes clarifying that the zoning maintains its approval as a restaurant and the extra uses are not approved. She added the Commission must determine whether the use has expanded or changed in a way that requires additional parking spaces.\par
\par
John McClary, attorney for Mr. Mayo, requested a continuance, having recently been retained to represent Mr. Mayo. The Commission approved a continuance for a Special Meeting scheduled for March 31, 2026 at 4:00 p.m.\par
\par
\b\fs22 A motion was made by Commissioner Casale, seconded by Deputy Vice Mayor Burns, to postpone Resolution No. 64-26 until March 31st at 4:00 p.m.\par

\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, entered File No. 2025-082 into the record.\f1\par
\cf1\kerning0\f2\par
Bradley Miller from Urban Design Studio, representing the applicant, stated the existing 1949 building has back-out parking onto 4th and 6th. The proposal, approved in Art Deco style by the Planning and Zoning Board, includes eight residential condo units over four stories, just under 1,200 sq. ft. of commercial space, and 20 total parking spaces with tandem resident parking and alley access. A pull-off/loading area was expanded to 5x30 feet for deliveries, maintaining alley clearance. Floor plans include retail, lobby, bike and personal storage, two-bedroom units, and two three-bedroom units with balconies, terraces, and rooftop pool.\par
\par
The key Art Deco feature (a finial/tower element) encroaches slightly into the setback at 17'11" versus the 20' requirement, separating terraces and adding style. The corner clip dedication maintains paved area and design integrity. The team is ready for construction.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes mentioned questions that arose from the Palm Trail neighborhood about height. She explained that downtown allows four stories up to 54 feet, measured to the eave of a pitched roof or top of a flat roof; this project\rquote s flat roof is 49 feet. Downtown encourages amenities and landscaping to reduce urban heat, with air-conditioned fifth-story access allowed up to 25% of the roof. She stated the project meets code for height, design, and site plan criteria, including landscaping, pedestrian paths, and a mix of housing types. The Planning and Zoning Board recommended approval 6-1, and praised the Art Deco architecture and responsiveness to input.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the meeting to public comments. Seeing no one present, public comments was closed. There was no rebuttal or cross-examination.\par
\par
The Commission discussed the corner clip dedication for public safety, which avoids a setback problem. Tandem parking for residential units was also discussed. Overall, the project was considered manageable in terms of parking, loading, and urban design.\par

Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, entered two File Nos into the record: 2023-207 (Conditional Use) and 2024-127 (Level One Site Plan).\par
\par
Jeff Costello, JC Planning Solutions, represented the applicant, ABC Supply Company. He gave a brief presentation regarding the existing 2-acre site at the NE corner of Poinsettia Drive and Lime Lane, an existing facility approved in 1999 with a 2006 outdoor expansion. It has a commerce land use designation and zoned MIC, surrounded primarily by industrial with some residential along Royal Palm.\par
\par
The proposal is a lumber yard type of use including existing outdoor storage to the east, a 6,500 square foot outdoor storage area to the west, and proposed truck parking on the north side, with some paved area removed and landscaping installed The Planning and Zoning Board recommended approval on January 26th with a condition to provide trees and a hedge per a revised landscape plan.\par
\par
He stated findings can be made that the use is consistent with zoning, land use, LDRs, and the comprehensive plan, and will not have a significantly detrimental effect on the neighborhood. It includes screened storage and truck parking with extensive landscaping, and meets all applicable standards with no areas of concern.\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, explained that the reason this is a level four is because there is a conditional use attached to minimal exterior improvements. Landscaping and buffer changes are typically administrative level. She clarified that parking is along Royal Palm Drive with existing and additional outdoor storage areas. She stated for the record that instead of moving the applicant through a similarity of use determination, the project is being reviewed holistically to streamline, with the resolution deciding the use is akin to a lumber yard allowed as a conditional use, involving little change to buildings but expanded outdoor storage, landscaping, and truck parking.\par
\par
She noted the project has been analyzed and can be approved with conditions. The Planning and Zoning Board recommended an augmented buffer adjacent to the house. It is in mixed industrial zoning surrounded by other industrial uses. For the site plan, it is a roofing material distribution warehouse and is seeking additional exterior storage and overnight truck parking.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the meeting up to public comments. Seeing no one present, public comments was closed.\par
\par
There was not cross-examination or rebuttal.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par

\par
Jeff, Oris, Assistant City Manager, noted that the funding agreement with the Delray Beach Public Library has no expiration date or fixed amount but includes an annual allocation. The City\rquote s 2025 internal grants policy outlines procedures for most grants, excluding programs such as the Community Development Block Grant (CDBG), State Housing Initiative Partnership (SHIP), Urban Development Action Grant (UDAG), and recurring City grants.\par
\par
Ms. Bowens stated that if a competitive grant process is implemented, it would require eligible applicants to be 501(c)(3) nonprofits operating at least two years in Palm Beach County, financially accountable, align with funding priorities, and, if a new applicant, not have received City funding within the past year. She outlined a five-phase process for a potential competitive system; planning and design, Notice of Funding Opportunities (NOFO) or RFP development, solicitation and outreach, proposal and evaluation by a committee, award, monitoring, and closeout. She noted that grant administration is currently decentralized across City departments, while Finance and Purchasing oversees monitoring, financial reporting, reimbursements, and closeout. The City Commission must decide the nonprofit funding structure after the 2026 agreements expire.\par
\par
Three potential funding approaches were presented: maintain the current annual agreements, as the Commission could not bind future Commissions to multi-year commitments; implement a fully competitive grant process, where the Commission would set funding priorities and require organizations to apply through a formal process. Lynn Gelin, City Attorney, clarified that multi-year agreements are possible but must include termination provisions and cannot guarantee consistent annual funding. Staff noted nonprofits' concerns about funding instability under annual or competitive models and emphasized that City funding helps support their operations as well as stewardship of city-owned properties. However, a competitive process could improve accountability through clearer performance standards and financial documentation requirements, including upfront financial verification and end-of-year receipts. Option three; a hybrid approach, allowing the City Commission to maintain some level of existing funding while introducing competitive elements, adjusting funding levels over time, or prioritizing certain applicants, depending on the Commission\rquote s goals.\par
\par
Mayor Carney inquired if nonprofit funding could be allocated based on the type of services provided, differentiating between organizations that provide services directly to the City and suggested that funding policies could reflect these differences. He also inquired whether the City has policies that tie funding amounts to factors such as a nonprofit\rquote s revenue, operating budget, or per capita formulas. Mr. Oris responded that the current policy is general and such specific criteria would be defined in a request for proposals. Mayor Carney further asked how Delray Beach compares to other municipalities in terms of nonprofit funding levels. Mr. Oris indicated no formal analysis has been conducted, though practices vary widely across cities, with some providing no funding and others offering significant support through formal programs. Additional discussion highlighted that Delray Beach provides relatively substantial support, including leasing city-owned historic properties to nonprofits, which is less common in other municipalities. Mayor Carney also sought clarification on total funding amounts following the transition of Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) responsibilities to the City, noting that the City has now assumed full responsibility for those funds.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale estimated direct City nonprofit funding at approximately $1.9 million, or $2.2-$2.3 million, including lease values, excluding the library, lease-only arrangements, and certain smaller or externally funded entities, and emphasized that lease support and direct funding should be considered separately. \par
\par
Mayor Carney questioned whether the City has evaluated the value of benefits received, particularly for below-market leases. He indicated a preference to maintain the current funding approach in the short term while developing a more structured policy and allowing for a transition period if moving to a competitive process, while Commissioner Casale raised concerns about funding allocations and budget impacts.\par
\par
Discussion ensued among the Commission that highlighted the need to determine the total budget allocation for nonprofits before deciding on funding methods.\par
\par
Mr. Oris emphasized the need to strengthen performance standards in grant agreements, citing the agreement with the Arts Garage as a model that requires nonprofits to specify how funds will be used and to provide detailed end-of-year reports, including receipts and measurable outcomes. He noted that current standards are too general.\par
\par
Mr. Moore recommended maintaining the current funding approach for the upcoming fiscal year due to timing constraints with the budget process, while incorporating performance measurement improvements and addressing policy updates during an upcoming annual goal-setting session anticipated in May. He further advised against increasing the overall funding allocation at this time and suggested continuing with existing funding levels as a practical and financially responsible approach.\par
\par
The Commission discussed the importance of establishing clear goals, priorities, and accountability measures before implementing significant changes, with consensus to proceed with the current group of funded nonprofits and maintain existing funding levels for the next fiscal year. It was also clarified that no new organizations would be added during this period, and that further policy development, including performance standards and funding strategies, would occur alongside the budget and goal-setting processes.\par
\par
\kerning0\f1 There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 4:45 p.m.\cf1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Sheryl Trent with Raftelis thanked the Mayor, commissioners, community members, and steering committee for their work on Vision 2035 and provided a brief overview of the 72-page report and presentation highlights. She noted the community\rquote s strong engagement, thoughtful and participatory process, including hands-on activities, visual facilitation, and contributions from experienced participants and the Raftelis team. She emphasized that Delray Beach is a special community with much to preserve while planning for the future, and presented a working vision statement reflecting its heritage, sustainability, vibrant neighborhoods, and quality of life.\par
\par
She outlined key focus areas; economic development, education, environment, historic preservation, and strategic development captured through visual summaries, discussed extensively by the steering committee of over 100 community participants who helped shape and prioritize broad, long-term goals. She noted the report included detailed definitions developed through community discussion. She reviewed examples of goals within each area, emphasizing they are flexible, long-term, and may take years to accomplish, while not implying the City is not already addressing them.\par
\par
She described next steps, using the plan as a living framework to guide priorities, budget decisions, operations, aligning projects with strategic goals, and making note of how agenda items connect to those priorities. She also recommended communicating the plan through visuals, the City\rquote s website, and ongoing community engagement to keep it active and relevant.\par
\par
Mayor Carney thanked Raftelis, noting the process was well run, highlighting the interactive format where participants moved between tables to discuss issues, while the Commission observed. \par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert praised the high level of diverse citizen participation, emphasizing that hearing every voice was critical to reaching the right outcome.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale noted the repetition of goals from past efforts and questioned how to translate the vision into actionable steps, performance metrics, and financial alignment. She expressed concern that the document does not clearly define how to move forward, suggesting models like regular strategic plan check-ins. Ms. Trent responded that recurring themes reflect strong prior planning, that many goals are long-term or ongoing, and implementation, metrics, and budget integration will evolve over time and require careful development.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns thanked the team and emphasized the need for the City to clearly define and communicate a small set of priorities, noting that identifying and focusing on key priorities is essential before moving on to others.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica noted that she participated in the visioning process as a citizen. She stated that earlier discussions included more solution-oriented ideas, and suggested using those identified ideas to work back toward implementing the broader goals, and commended the team for keeping the process on track.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that following discussions on economic development synergy and recommendations for external consultancy services, representatives from the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA), Delray Beach Chamber of Commerce, and Downtown Development Authority (DDA), joined together to support planning and marketing efforts. He asked Assistant City Manager, Jeff Oris, to introduce the consultancy teams.\par
\par
Mr. Oris introduced Craig Agranoff from Grip LLC and Kevin Crowder from BusinessFlare, explaining their roles in economic development.\par
\par
Mr. Agranoff proposed that Grip LLC would focus on data-driven, highly targeted economic development strategy for Delray Beach, targeting specific businesses identified by BusinessFlare's analysis. Efforts include aligning stakeholders on ideal businesses, preparing clear information on sites and opportunities, and crafting a tailored \ldblquote Why Delray\rdblquote message for executives and investors. He added the goal is to attract the right businesses, create jobs, and drive long-term economic growth.\par
\par
Mr. Crowder highlighted the importance of understanding local assets, amenities, capacity, the need for competitive advantages, uncovering hidden local strengths, and combining data with intuition. He explained the importance of generational talent and the evolving economic landscape; focusing on quality of life and future-proofing economic development strategies. He stated that the outcome would be a concise, targeted implementation strategy aligned with the City\rquote s realities and growth potential.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale raised concerns about space availability and stressed close collaboration with the Chamber, DDA, and CRA. Mr. Crowder explained his experience includes work with Miami DDA and CRAs with strong collaboration across chambers and partner organizations.\par
\par
The Commission thanked Mr. Crowder and stated they are looking forward to the findings.\par
\par
Mr. Agranoff added insights on the types of companies that could benefit from Delray Beach's unique environment, including private equity, professional services, and remote-first companies.He noted an indirect growth from data center industries, with executives and related firms (family offices, boutique investment) choosing Delray for lifestyle.He highlighted the rise of remote-first tech and AI companies, attracted to a strong lifestyle and unique identity over traditional headquarters needs.\par
\par
The costs related to the consultants were addressed. Mr. Moore indicated that the costs would include two contracts; one with BusinessFlare, nearly $60,000 and the other for the marketing aspect with Grip at about $64,000. Both agreements will be fully financed and supported via the City's economic development fund.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale also questioned the solicitation process. Mr. Oris advised the City stayed close to the procurement rules and reached out to about ten firms for each category. The City received three responses for marketing and two for the plan; others did not respond or declined.\par
