\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\ul\b\f0\fs24 Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone\b0 : \par
Requested consensus to present the Haitian Church of God of Prophecy with a recognition for its 45th anniversary, noting that she attended the anniversary celebration and was honored by the church. There was consensus for the recognition.\par
\par
Requested consensus to have the Palm Beach County Impact Film Initiative make a presentation regarding a proposal to create a community impact feature film produced in Delray Beach and Palm Beach County. She explained that the project would raise awareness of issues affecting older adults, including social isolation, depression, financial vulnerability, and access to health and supportive services, while partnering with the City to engage residents, provide workforce development and training opportunities, and showcase the City. She noted that the initiative may seek funding and services from the City, Palm Beach County, and private entities. Mayor Carney offered to introduce Vice Mayor Burns to Michelle Hillary with the Palm Beach County Film Commission. There was consensus for the presentation.\par
\par
\ul\b Commissioner Casale\ulnone\b0 :\par
Encouraged everyone to attend the Walk with the Chief Event on July 18 at 9:00 a.m. at Barwick Park. \par
\par
Thanked the Fire Department for their heroic response to a significant neighborhood fire and also recognized the Police Department for its presence.\par
\par
Thanked Human Resources for the biometric screening fair and breakfast provided to staff. \par
\par
Requested confirmation on placing a plaque, including Mr. Hadjimiry\rquote s name and picture on the new water treatment plant to recognize his contributions. It was confirmed.\par
\par
Thanked the Parks and Recreation Department for their work during the Fourth of July holiday, noting that staff worked while away from their families and continued to represent the City well. \par
\par
Requested consensus to place a memorial sign on a chess table at the park on Atlantic Avenue honoring Willie James McCray (\ldblquote Chess James\rdblquote ), who played chess with children at the park. Mr. Moore confirmed consensus and stated the City would be happy to proceed.\par
\par
Wished Nohemi Morgan, Executive Administrative Assistant, a happy birthday and thanked Ms. Gelin for bringing cakes and recognizing her birthday.\par
\par
Expressed concern regarding the Delray Beach Municipal Cemetery that specific complaints brought forward by residents were not adequately addressed during the presentation. She stated that when residents bring specific complaints, presentations should provide the solutions for these complaints and explain the next steps, including concerns about cleaning cemetery stones. She emphasized that addressing the complaints would also allow staff to receive the appreciation they deserve for their work. Mr. Moore agreed and stated the City would proceed accordingly moving forward.\par
\par
\ul\b Deputy Vice Mayor Markert\ulnone\b0 : \par
Requested consensus for the City Manager to begin a thorough review of all options for the future of tennis, including short-term needs at the existing facility, longer-term community needs, potential development opportunities, and naming rights options. He emphasized that tennis has long timelines and that he wanted the process to begin early so the community could be involved.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale noted that naming rights may be restricted by the center court agreement and clarified that the previously submitted P3 (Public Private Partnership) application was denied. Ms. Gelin explained that the City\rquote s P3 Policy allows either unsolicited or solicited P3s and recommended a workshop to consider long-range planning for the tennis center. She noted that the tennis management contract would be coming forward in August. \par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert expressed concern about addressing the matter in little bits and pieces and requested a comprehensive review of the options, including costs, benefits, and potential property uses. Mr. Moore recommended a workshop to consider the tennis center holistically, including current commitments, the current state of the facility, potential improvements, and possible solicited P3 opportunities. \par
\par
The Commission discussed the timing of the workshop. Deputy Vice Mayor Markert urged the City to begin immediately, noting that professional sports have long timelines and that waiting could put the City at a disadvantage. Ms. Gelin explained that staff would need time to prepare a needs assessment, determine necessary facility upgrades and costs, and assemble information necessary for any potential solicitation. Mr. Moore stated that staff would begin the process and provide updates, with a workshop anticipated in the early part of the new fiscal year.\par
\par
Mr. Moore noted that the Yellow Ball Tennis/Match Point/Barron agreement does not expire for another four years, while Deputy Vice Mayor Markert emphasized that four years is nothing in the sports world and that the City should not give the tournament an opportunity to leave. Mayor Carney agreed that the contract renewal is critical and that redevelopment of the facility should also be considered.\par
\par
The Commission reached consensus to begin the process and hold a workshop in the early new fiscal year. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale noted that repairs, upkeep, and other financial considerations related to the current tournament contract should be addressed separately and sooner. Mayor Carney requested that Mr. Moore speak individually with Commissioners regarding ideas for the contract, including potential revenue enhancements. Mr. Moore agreed. \par
\par
\ul\b Commissioner Mollica\ulnone\b0 :\par
Stated she believed in using best practices from other cities and referenced Boca Raton\rquote s practice of emailing agendas to residents and providing a brief description and video clip of each agenda item following meetings. She said this would streamline information, strengthen communication and transparency, and requested consensus to direct staff to explore implementing a similar process. Commissioner Casale suggested first meeting with Gina Carter to review what the City currently provides and returning at the next meeting for discussion. Commissioner Mollica agreed.\par
\par
Requested consensus to prepare a factual sheet/webpage regarding the proposed property tax constitutional amendment, including the provisions and timeline, exemption revenue impact, spending restrictions, and the City\rquote s estimated fiscal impact, with the City Attorney\rquote s Office reviewing the information. Mr. Moore confirmed the request aligned with the City\rquote s education and outreach efforts, and consensus was provided.\par
\par
Requested consensus to hold a noticed meeting with downtown business owners, along with Laura Simon and the City Manager, to provide education and solutions regarding code enforcement issues, including illicit water discharge, and other concerns raised by businesses. Commissioner Casale suggested making the meeting public so all Commissioners could attend. Consensus was provided.\par
\par
\ul\b Mayor Carney\ulnone\b0 : \par
Stated he was pleased the City was addressing the cemetery issue, noting there was no excuse if people do not know where their relatives are buried and that, if the City dropped the ball, it must admit it and fix the problem. He supported an audit of the records to determine the information regarding burials.\par
\par
Raised concerns regarding the property at 240 Northwest Eighth Avenue, stating code enforcement should address the issue if people are living in or entering the property, as it is unsafe for the neighborhood. Mr. Moore stated it would be a collaboration between law enforcement and code enforcement.\par
\par
Discussed his communication with the Mayor of Panama City regarding ways municipalities could work together to save money and stated he would follow up and report back to the Commission.\par
\par
Raised concerns regarding City employees working from home and requested that the City\rquote s policy be reviewed. Mr. Moore stated the policy has generally been tightened, with limited instances for specific reasons and reasonable accommodations, which are governed by applicable protections.\ul\b\f1\par
}

title: Pursuant to Section 3.12 of the Charter of the City of Delray Beach, the Mayor has instructed me to announce a Workshop Meeting of the City Commission to be held for the following purposes:
PUBLIC COMMENTS

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that staff had engaged with the City Commission on numerous budget scenarios to maintain current service levels and that the presentation would review proposed budget econometrics and a tentative millage rate. He highlighted general fund expenditures, including increased personnel services, street maintenance, fuel costs, police and fire pension contributions, CRA tax increment financing payments, and decreased transfers to Neighborhood Services. He then invited Chief Financial Officer Henry Dachowitz to present historical and proposed operating millage rate considerations and related budget adjustments.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
Mr. Dachowitz reviewed historical and proposed millage rate considerations, noting the rate decreased from 6.9611 mills in 2017 to 5.9063 mills in 2025 as taxable values increased to offset the tax burden on residents while the Municipal Cost Index (MCI) and City expenditures rose due to labor, contracts, and inflationary costs. \cf0\kerning2\f0 He explained the City had managed costs while lowering the millage rate but was now working to address ongoing operational pressures. \cf1\kerning0\f1 He also reviewed the proposed FY 2026-2027 budget, including increased revenues, a proposed millage rate increase from 6.1611 mills to 6.4371 mills, and higher property tax revenues from increased taxable values and the proposed millage rate increase.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz stated that Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) payments and net property tax revenues would increase. He then reviewed the proposed $8.4 million fund balance drawdown reducing reserves to 18% which remained within the Government Finance Officers Association best practices. He explained that the additional property tax revenue and fund balance drawdown balanced the proposed $219.8 million General Fund budget. He also reviewed General Fund revenues and departmental expenditure increases, concluding the proposed budget was balanced. Commissioner Casale expressed concern about reducing reserves below 20% and suggested using other methods to balance the budget.\par
\par
Mr. Moore highlighted proposed resource commitments supporting the Vision 2035 key focus areas, including continued funding for GRIP \cf0\kerning2\f0 to support the next step of marketing opportunities\cf1\kerning0\f1 , federal and state lobbyist representatives, an additional lifeguard position, a Fire Rescue Special Services Manager through reorganization, additional planning resources in Development Services \cf0\kerning2\f0 with only a portion of the cost supported by the General Fund due to building fund-related activities\cf1\kerning0\f1 , and staffing adjustments in Parks and Recreation and the Creative Arts School.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that the proposed millage rate of 6.4371 maintained the current levels of service while striking the balance discussed during the afternoon presentation. He reviewed the estimated impact on the average Delray Beach resident, noting the proposed adjustment averaged about $28.52 per month, and highlighted that no millage rate adjustments had occurred over the last 10 years, along with the rollback from two years prior, which had impacted the City's fund balance position. \cf0\kerning2\f0 He discussed the MCI, describing it as synonymous with the municipal rate of inflation, and stated that municipal inflation exceeded available revenue offsets\cf1\kerning0\f1 . He stated that maintaining a stable millage rate allowed increases in property values and revenues to support fund balance growth and offset inflationary pressures and other municipal commitments.\cf0\kerning2\f0 He reviewed the fund balance policies of several municipalities, noting that the benchmarking information had recently been provided by the City Auditor and was included for transparency. He advised\cf1\kerning0\f1 that an 18% unassigned General Fund balance target was reasonable, \cf0\kerning2\f0 based on benchmarking and the City's overall position. He \cf1\kerning0\f1 asked Mr. Dachowitz to provide an overview of property tax and homestead exemptions as of June 2026.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz presented an analysis of property tax and homestead exemptions, explaining that taxable value, after exemptions, was used with the millage rate to determine real estate revenue. He reviewed taxable value by property type, noting that homestead properties represented about one-third of the City's total taxable value. He summarized FY 2027-28 and FY 2028-29 projections, explaining that if the November referendum passed, proposed legislation would reduce ad valorem revenue by an estimated $7.35 million in the first year and $12.77 million in the second year, prohibit reductions to Police and Fire and Rescue budgets, limit General Fund budget flexibility, and create increasing budget challenges as the homestead exemption expanded each year.\par
\par
Mr. Moore discussed the potential implementation of fire emergency medical service (EMS) fees and the other fee-based revenue streams to mitigate revenue loss. Commissioner Mollica asks about the time frame for implementing new fees, and Mr. Moore stated that he would be initiating administrative consultancy services and educational efforts. Commissioner Casale requested clarification on the budget levels of service and resident impacts. Mr. Moore committed to providing updated information within the next few days. Vice Mayor Burns asked about improvements residents can expect from the additional funds. Mr. Moore stated the additional funds would support continuation of major projects and maintain levels of service without compromising City work.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that the proposed budget and tentative millage rate review had been substantially accomplished during the workshop. He outlined the next steps in the budget process, including the submission of a tentative millage rate and the preparation for the first public hearing. He outlined the City's communications plan for the property tax referendum consideration, including educational materials and public outreach. He stated that the effort would continue through early November to address resident questions.\par
\par
Mayor Carney suggested considering signage similar to the County\rquote s approach to educate residents that parks and other City services are funded by property taxes. He emphasized the importance of informational outreach while ensuring it remains non-promotional. Additionally, he stated reserve requirements should be based on each municipality\rquote s circumstances rather than a fixed percentage. He noted that the City\rquote s resources can be redeployed during emergencies, and the City\rquote s increasing property values and ability to raise revenue provide flexibility. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Markert expressed concerns about reducing reserves, noting their importance for interest income, bond ratings, major projects, and emergency preparedness given uncertainty regarding future FEMA assistance.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz added that referendum funding for public safety and parks allowed the City to borrow and spread project costs over 30 years, benefiting residents through completed capital projects. He emphasized the importance of accessing the bond market, noting the City's audited financials looked good, the City remained conservative, and the capital projects would be presented with the Capital Improvement Program (CIP).\par
\par
There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the Budget Workshop Meeting at 4:52 p.m.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Moises Ariza, CBIZ CPAs, presented the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025 audit. He reported a clean, unmodified opinion, stating that the financial statements were fairly presented and congratulating the elected body, City Manager, and City personnel. He highlighted the Management Discussion and Analysis as a recommended section for review and reported total government-wide net position of more than $521 million, including $335.3 million for governmental activities and $186.2 million for business-type activities. The General Fund had $49.1 million in unassigned fund balance, and governmental funds had an ending fund balance of $189.5 million.\par
\par
Mr. Ariza also highlighted the City\rquote s $83.9 million investment portfolio, the issuance of $148 million in water and sewer revenue improvement bonds, and subsequent issuance of $32.1 million in public improvement revenue bonds. The City expended $6.9 million in federal awards and received a clean federal single audit, with $5.4 million tested under the major program and no items of non-compliance or exceptions to report\b . \b0 He noted one recommendation regarding implementation of a new payroll module, which is expected to be completed prior to the end of calendar year 2026.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale noted that general fund expenses increased by 2.7 percent, revenue fell by 1 percent, fund balance declined by $1.7 million, and long-term debt increased from $70.7 million to $229 million, primarily related to the water and sewer revenue bond.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns thanked the Finance Department, City Manager, and staff for their work and asked whether there were any other trends or patterns the Commission should be aware of. Mr. Ariza stated that the City\rquote s clean opinion with only one recommendation was not typical and represented a high mark for the City.\kerning0\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mayor Carney opened the floor to public comment, passed the gavel to Vice Mayor Burns and left the dais stating he had to make a call a 5:30 p.m.\ul\f1\par
\par
Shannon Grice\ulnone , 33445, Principal of Carver Middle School \par
Reported that, for the first time since 2012, Carver Middle School earned a B rating. She highlighted an increase of 16 points in eighth-grade science, 10 points in math achievement, and seven points in reading achievement. She noted that Carver offers three career academies: pre-IT, pre-medical, and criminal justice, in addition to the arts, world languages, music, and IB program. She invited the Commission to attend student pickup on August 5 and the first day of school on August 10.\par
\par
\ul Gary Eliopoulos\ulnone\par
Requested that the Commission consider reviewing the review process for projects, particularly comments that are insignificant and do not affect concurrency or LDRs. He stated that reducing unnecessary delays could help projects move to the board for approval and allow clients to offset front costs. He also expressed concern that staff accountability requirements may limit creativity and encouraged the City to consider ways to move projects more efficiently toward site plan certification and building permits.\par
\par
\ul Daniel Rose\ulnone , 33444\par
Requested that the Commission address an ongoing parking and easement matter involving Albert Richwagon. He cited more than 90 days, and approximately two years, of delays, and alleged reckless defamatory posts, harassment, vandalism, threats, and intimidation. He stated that he followed the City\rquote s process for his own business and asked that the matter be resolved and the applicable requirements enforced.\par
\par
\ul George Long\ulnone , 33444 \par
Proposed using garage rooftops at night for a type of skeet shooting involving biodegradable, bioluminescent targets. He asked the Commission to take the proposal more seriously than his previous event proposals.\par
\par
\ul Marjorie Waldo\ulnone , 33444, Arts Garage\par
Reported that the organization was in week three of its summer camp, with approximately 12 participants each week and 60 percent of participants receiving scholarships. She highlighted completed programs in technical theater, playwriting, and improvisation, and upcoming musical theater and acting programs. She also presented photos from Arts Garage\rquote s 15th anniversary ribbon cutting and reported that downtown Delray Beach attracted more than 9.3 million visitors and generated approximately $130 million in credit card spending during the year.\par
\par
\ul Kween Miller\ulnone \par
Expressed concerns regarding transparency and the condition and management of the Delray Beach cemetery. She requested that the Mayor not participate in budgeting or decision-making related to the cemetery, citing concerns about an alleged conflict of interest, and requested a budget for the cemetery and improvements to ADA compliance. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns stated that the City was moving forward with the concerns regarding the cemetery.\par
\par
\ul Chris Jensen\ulnone , 33445 \par
Spoke in support of the DDA and highlighted community events and charitable activities conducted through his business with the support and encouragement of the DDA. He noted events supporting local charities, including City House, the YMCA, and a foster care program, and thanked the DDA for its support of downtown businesses and community events.\par
\par
\ul Neil Schiller\ulnone , 33444\par
Representing Ultra Luxury Townhomes LLC, requested that the Commission reconsider the denial of the application for 47 townhomes on North Federal Highway. He cited the performance standard, the conditional use that could be conditioned to make the project more compatible with surrounding properties, and the Economic Development Strategy identifying North Federal as an opportunity for smaller, high-touch firms and talent-oriented residential infill. He stated that, if allowed to return, the applicant would present additional information and proffer conditions of approval to make the project more compatible.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin stated that, because the Mayor was not present, the Commission could undertake a motion for purposes of efficiency, although it was a little bit out of order.\par
\par
\f0 Vice Mayor Burns passed the gavel to Deputy Vice Mayor Markert. \par
\par
\b\fs20 A motion was made by Vice Mayor Burns, seconded by Commissioner Mollica, to reconsider the denial of the Ultra Luxury Townhomes application from the previous week.\b0\f1\fs24\par
\par
Commissioner Casale requested a discussion and stated that the reconsideration was highly unusual and expressed concern that it could be viewed by residents as circumventing the process, but stated that she would support her colleague. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns stated that, if there was new information that needed to be better understood, the applicant should be given a chance to present it.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin clarified that reconsideration would allow Mr. Schiller to present new evidence that could potentially change the Commission\rquote s opinion, but the site plan would not be changed. Any changes to the application would require a new application, TAC comments, and a new process before the Planning and Zoning Board. She explained that the local rules provide an opportunity for reconsideration, although it is unusual.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert asked for clarification regarding the options. Ms. Gelin explained that one option was reconsideration, allowing the applicant and staff to present additional information regarding the existing application. The other option would be for the applicant to go back to the drawing board, potentially adjust the application based on Commission comments, and begin a whole new application process.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale stated that she respected Mr. Schiller and her colleagues and would hear what was presented, but expressed concern that the public would view the matter as highly unusual.\par
\par
With no further discussion and a motion on the floor, Deputy Vice Mayor Markert called for a vote. \par
\par
\b\fs20 The motion carried by the following vote:\par
\par
Yes: \b0 3 - Commissioner Mollica, Commissioner Casale, and Vice Mayor Burns\b\par
\par
No: \b0 1 - Deputy Vice Mayor Markert\par
\par
Mayor Carney was absent from the dais during the vote.\b\par
\par
\b0\fs24 Ms. Gelin stated that the item would be on the agenda for August 18th.\b\fs20\par
}

action_text: A motion was made by Commissioner Mollica, seconded by Deputy Vice Mayor Markert, to approve the proposed millage rate at 6.4371 mills for operating and .0289 mills for debt service for a total of 6.4660 mills. The motion carried by the following vote:
minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that the proposed operating millage rate of 6.4371 mills was based on the City\rquote s desire to maintain and, to some extent, expand levels of service, following the prior workshop and financial discussions. Public hearings were scheduled for September 8 and September 22. \par
\par
Henry Dachowitz, Chief Financial Officer, explained that the millage rate cap is based on the rollback rate and a 10% increase. Ms. Gelin clarified that the Commission may adopt up to 110% of the rollback rate by a supermajority vote of four (4) out of five (5), while exceeding 110% requires a unanimous vote. She confirmed that the proposed 6.4371 mills is within the 110% threshold. Mr. Moore stated that the maximum 110% rate, considering the Community Redevelopment Agency, would be 6.5452 mills, compared with the proposed 6.4371 mills. \par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that he did not support increasing the millage rate and preferred maintaining the existing millage rate while finding other ways to save money in the budget. He supported scrutinizing overtime, delaying non-essential new hires, deferring non-critical capital purchases, and consolidating administrative functions. He stated that the City should look for areas where it can save money and not overburden taxpayers. \par
\par
Mayor Carney and Mr. Moore discussed the City\rquote s zero-based budgeting process, with Mayor Carney stating that it was not a pure zero-based budget and that additional savings should be pursued. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale stated that zero-based budgeting should be conducted one or two departments at a time and that the City had already been scrutinizing overtime. She stated that revenue and expense discussions should occur well before the tax conversation. She emphasized that the City must remain financially strong in future years, noting that expenses consistently outpace revenues, reserves and fund balance have declined, long-term obligations have increased, and critical infrastructure requires investment. Commissioner Casale stated that a modest millage increase was not about growing government but about protecting essential services, maintaining infrastructure, and avoiding passing today\rquote s costs onto future taxpayers. She stated that the Commission must balance affordability with long-term fiscal responsibility. \par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert stated that, if cuts were made, the Commission should identify exactly what those cuts would mean for roads, the water treatment plant, and cemetery improvements. He expressed concern about using reserves and deferring major projects and requested a list of proposed cuts so the Commission could make an informed decision. He supported holding 6.4371 mills as the ceiling and lowering the rate if possible. Vice Mayor Burns stated that she would save her comments for the budget discussion. \par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Ms. Gelin read Resolution No. 108-26 into the record.\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, presented Resolution No. 108-26, stating that the co-designation would recognize the Weatherspoon family while allowing residents to retain their existing addresses. The street is a City right-of-way, originally platted in 1925, with approximately 30 properties facing it. Ms. Gianniotes highlighted Reverend Elsie Weatherspoon\rquote s contributions to Delray Beach, including founding Elsie Weatherspoon Paving, employing migrant farmworkers, paving many City streets, increasing voter registration and civic participation among Black residents, and founding and building Community Primitive Baptist Church. She also noted that his son, Jimmy Weatherspoon, served as Vice Mayor and received the NAACP Community Service Award. Reverend Weatherspoon passed away in April 1988, satisfying the City\rquote s requirement that a person be deceased for at least five years before a street can be named in their honor. Ms. Gianniotes stated that, if approved, City staff would replace the street signs, coordinating with FDOT if necessary. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale asked whether the co-designation would affect Google directions or emergency services. Ms. Gianniotes stated that it would be recognized similarly to Martin Luther King Boulevard.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns stated that the co-designation was not creating a new honor, as the City had granted the honor decades ago, but the name had been misspelled. She stated that correcting the spelling would have placed a burden on residents and that the co-designation was a practical compromise. Vice Mayor Burns stated that an unveiling would be planned once the Weatherspoon family confirmed when their out-of-town relatives could attend. She invited the Commission to attend and thanked the Weatherspoon family. \par
\par
Mayor Carney commended the Weatherspoon family.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

action_text: There was consensus from the Commission to proceed as outlined.
minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Jeff Oris, Assistant City Manager, introduced Kevin Crowder, a consultant from BusinessFlare.\par
\par
Mr. Crowder provided an update on the City\rquote s economic development strategy, noting that Delray Beach has historically had a passive economic development model, with wealth coming to the City through tourism, migration, and its quality of place. He recommended shifting from attracting wealth to building it by increasing visibility of the City\rquote s existing founder and startup economy, visitor economy, and professional services. Mr. Crowder noted that Delray Beach has approximately 252 home-based business licenses, 112 knowledge-based businesses, and approximately 800 businesses within four catchall business tax receipt categories. He emphasized that these founders and entrepreneurs should be engaged and their stories better communicated. He also identified a visibility gap and stressed that economic development is ultimately about stories, belonging, and creating places where people want to live, work, and build businesses. Mr. Crowder discussed land-use challenges, particularly along Congress Avenue, noting that the area is already 51% residential and that recent projects have created vertical suburbs rather than true mixed-use development. He emphasized protecting commercial land, improving regulatory efficiency, and ensuring available properties align with future economic development opportunities. He also recommended maintaining a high-touch boutique concierge approach and building relationships with founders and developers before they need assistance from the City. Mr. Crowder discussed demographic trends, noting that Delray Beach\rquote s population over 65 is approximately double that of a city its size, while the Gen Z population is approximately half and the millennial population is between two-thirds and three-quarters of the expected level. He emphasized the importance of generational talent, belonging, flexibility, and creating opportunities that meet the needs of younger generations. Mr. Crowder recommended three tiers of target sectors: Tier One: founder-led professional services, boutique consulting, remote-first businesses, hospitality, and experiential concepts; Tier Two: wealth management, family offices, FinTech, digital health, creator economy infrastructure, and related opportunities; and Tier Three: emerging and adjacent activities, technology niches, and AI-enabled micro firms. Mr. Crowder outlined a plan of work in the first ninety days beginning with protecting the commercial land base, particularly Congress Avenue; serving existing founders; and claiming the high-touch boutique economic development lane. Months four through six would focus on more aggressive engagement, creating visibility and opportunity profiles, particularly for N. Federal, and working with the Community Redevelopment Agency (CRA) on West Atlantic. Months seven through nine would focus on refining the approach with partners, followed by a one-year review of what is working and what is not. Mr. Crowder requested consensus to adopt the operating framework, affirm the target sectors, and authorize the plan of work, beginning with commercial land-base protection, especially along Congress Avenue.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale expressed support for moving forward and emphasized the pressure to convert commercial land use to residential. She supported updating the studies for N. Federal Highway and stated that it is an untapped area where the City can create what it wants and needs.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns thanked Mr. Crowder for the presentation and supported concentrating on the Congress Avenue corridor, noting that she was surprised but not surprised that it is 51% residential.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert found the presentation enlightening and agreed that Congress Avenue deserves more attention. He identified private equity as a priority and noted that the City has already attracted private equity firms. He also expressed interest in attracting AI businesses, particularly those focused on security.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica agreed that zoning changes and guardrails are needed because businesses are being converted to townhomes, stating that the City could otherwise lose offices and high touch businesses.\par
\par
Mr. Crowder clarified that the City\rquote s previous passive economic development model meant that the City had done the right things to set the table for the market to come in rather than actively having to find opportunities.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked what Delray Beach is not providing for Gen Z. Crowder explained that Gen Z is seeking belonging, empathy, and a sense of safe haven, and that younger generations are more willing to leave places where they do not feel they belong. Mayor Carney also expressed interest in reviewing the six-month timeframe for nonconforming uses and prior Congress Avenue studies and stated that the City has a great opportunity to capture markets that others are not pursuing.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that the City Commission\rquote s support and consensus are needed to proceed with the next step of having BusinessFlare and GRIP.D work together on economic development and marketing. The goal is to aggressively market and promote opportunities available in Delray Beach externally.\par
\par
Mayor Carney expressed support for moving forward but requested continued interaction with Mr. Crowder as the final plan is developed. Mr. Crowder agreed, stating that the migration, tourism, and startup city stories each stand alone as strong stories while also working together in a manageable workplan.\kerning0\par
}

action_text: A motion was made by Commissioner Casale, seconded by Vice Mayor Burns, to approve Ordinance No. 34-26 as amended. The motion carried by the following vote.
attachments: City of Delray Beach Impact Fee Justification Study
Simple Legal Review Ord 34-26 Impact Fees
BIE Form Ord. No 34-26 lg rev - 07.13.26
minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Ms. Gelin read Ordinance No. 34-26 into the record. \par
\par
Mr. Oris provided an overview of the ordinance. He explained that impact fees are one-time charges regulated by state statute, used to fund public facilities and infrastructure impacted by growth, and are not intended to cure existing deficiencies. The fees would apply to new development and expansions exceeding 1,000 square feet, with credits provided for existing structures. Mr. Oris explained that the Florida Impact Fee Act requires a rational nexus between the fees and anticipated impacts, a study based on updated costs, and generally prohibits changes for four years. Fees collected must be used for identified capital expenditures and facilities and maintained in separate funds for each fee category. The study establishes maximum fees, but the City Commission may adopt fees below the maximum. Proposed fees include city administration, police, fire, parks, water, wastewater, and stormwater management. Hassan Hadjimiry, Utilities Director, recommended setting water and sewer fees at one-half of the maximum due to existing bond funding. Mr. Oris stated that the ordinance establishes the impact fee section, adopts the required study, moves the parks fee from Chapter Five, provides calculation methods and credits, and requires an annual review and report to the City Commission regarding fees collected and expenditures. He explained that future increases could not exceed 50%, with increases above 25% phased in over four years, and increases could not be applied retroactively. Mr. Oris provided an example of a proposed development with residential, clubhouse, and industrial components, including credits for the existing building to be demolished, resulting in $2,077,145 in impact fees. He stated that approval requires a finding that the amendment is consistent with the Comprehensive Plan and explained that impact fees are intended to fund infrastructure and equipment needs resulting from future growth rather than alleviate General Fund pressures. Mr. Oris reported that the Planning and Zoning Board found the ordinance in conformance with the Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Regulations and recommended approval, with a recommendation to consider relief for workforce and affordable housing, historic preservation, and infill construction.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked whether the proposed fees could be phased in at initial adoption. Ms. Gelin clarified that the City does not have to adopt the maximum fees and may set them lower, then review and increase them after four years. Commissioner Casale expressed concern that starting too low would limit future increases and stated that the City is already well behind and that the impact fee process should have been done years and years and years ago.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item. Seeing no present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale stated that Delray Beach is starting in a deficit because surrounding communities have implemented impact fees for years, and without adopting the recommended maximum fees, residents would continue to supplement future infrastructure needs. She supported relief for historic preservation but stated that workforce housing and infill relief should be considered carefully and, on a case-by-case basis.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns supported the impact fees and relief for workforce housing, historic properties, and infill, with consideration on a case-by-case basis.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert supported the proposed exceptions on a case-by-case basis and questioned whether impact fees could be lowered during the four-year period. Ms. Gelin stated that the ordinance was structured to remove discretion and avoid favoring one developer over another, and noted that certain entities, including the Delray Beach Community Land Trust and CRA, could have fees waived consistent with the Code.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that relief should apply to designated historic structures and not simply properties within a historic district or contributors. Ms. Gelin suggested a uniform 50 percent discount for designated historic homes/buildings, which Vice Mayor Burns supported. Commissioner Casale agreed that the discount should apply only to historic properties and not contributors.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica questioned the definition of infill. Mr. Oris explained that infill generally refers to a vacant lot surrounded by development and suggested limiting the designation to property that has been vacant for a period of time. Commissioner Casale questioned why vacant infill lots should receive a discount, stating that she did not believe infill should be included.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes explained that the Planning and Zoning Board recommended consideration of relief for historic structures and affordable housing. She recommended specifically exempting the Housing Authority and CRA from impact fees and discussed whether affordable housing that is deed restricted as part of a density bonus should also be exempt.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale requested consensus on the proposed relief categories. The Commission reached consensus to not provide relief for infill. \par
\par
Regarding historic properties, Commissioner Casale supported relief only for designated historic properties, noting that applying relief broadly would not incentivize property owners to designate their homes. The Commission discussed establishing a uniform percentage discount, with 50% discussed for designated historic properties.\par
\par
Regarding affordable housing, Ms. Gelin stated that the language from the existing Code could be incorporated to identify the applicable partners and nonprofit organizations, including the Community Land Trust, CRA, Housing Authority, and Delray Housing Group.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica asked whether impact fees could only be used for capital expenditures identified in the justification study. Mr. Oris confirmed that the fees could be used for the portion of capital expenditures attributable to new growth or new construction, provided the expense is outlined in the justification study.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes noted that, based on the most recent legislative session, the administrative fee should not be calculated as a percentage of building permit fees. Staff would review neighboring jurisdictions and revise the fee schedule to a specific dollar amount.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\ul\b\f0\fs24 Commissioner Mollica\ulnone\b0 :\par
Requested a workshop to conduct a thoughtful, comprehensive review of the Development Services Department and the development and permitting process, including staffing, compensation, training, workload, outdated processes, performance metrics, bottlenecks, customer service, and process improvements. She stated that the goal was continuous improvement and not criticism.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes explained that the permit and development review process involves multiple departments, including Public Works, Utilities, and Fire, and recommended that all departments involved in the workflow participate.\par
\par
Consensus was reached to hold the workshop.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert recommended that the City consider AI applications for development services, including whether AI could assist with reading plans. Commissioner Mollica stated that AI could be part of the workshop discussion.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica requested consensus to direct staff to create a resident communication piece similar to Boca Raton\rquote s, including agenda information before meetings and a post-meeting summary of each agenda item with what was discussed or decided and a video clip of the relevant discussion. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale stated that the City already provides agenda items and timestamped meeting videos through Legistar but questioned whether the proposed communication could be completed without additional technology and staff resources. Gina Carter, Director of Communications, explained that the proposed newsletter would be a Clerk\rquote s function, would require staff time to review meetings and prepare timestamps, and would involve additional resources. She noted that the City\rquote s videos are already available on YouTube and timestamped through the agenda. She suggested creating a tutorial explaining how residents can access City Commission meetings and individual agenda items through Legistar. Mayor Carney supported increased transparency and providing residents with information about City activities and matters affecting them.\par
\par
Mr. Moore proposed working with the Office of the City Clerk, Communications, and the Chief Technology Officer to evaluate the resource allocation, organizational structure, and technological capabilities needed for expanded resident communication, including benchmarking with Boca Raton. He proposed returning to the Commission with a presentation in the coming weeks, potentially at the first September meeting.\par
\par
Consensus was given for Mr. Moore to proceed as outlined. Mr. Moore stated that the discussion would include existing Legistar links, current capabilities, what would be required to advance the initiative, and resource allocation. \par
\par
Ms. Carter clarified that social media outreach regarding the existing Legistar capabilities could begin immediately.\par
\ul\b\par
Commissioner Casale\ulnone\b0 :\par
Apologized for missing the Walk with the Chief Event and stated that the events have been amazing for community engagement. She requested consensus to continue the community engagement efforts and schedule the next Run with the Chief Event on the next leg of Atlantic Avenue.\par
\par
Requested an update on the City\rquote s visioning efforts, including outcomes, timelines, and costs. She noted that significant resources had been invested in the visioning and goal-setting processes and stated that the City should provide residents with the outcomes, expectations, and actions resulting from those efforts. She requested that the City identify accomplishments, dates, and amounts of money allocated toward implementing the visioning.\par
\par
\ul\b Deputy Vice Mayor Markert\ulnone\b0 : \par
Commended Chief Hunter and Chief Martin for their community outreach efforts, stating that the community really appreciates it. He highlighted the fire department\rquote s community engagement, including children visiting the station and the disaster preparedness session conducted with the Red Cross at the Boys and Girls Club, which was very well attended and provided important emergency preparedness information. He thanked the Chiefs and their teams for their work.\par
\par
\ul\b Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone\b0 :\par
Requested that the City identify and periodically post the top three to five goals to remind the Commission and community of what the City is trying to accomplish over the next one to five years. \par
\par
Requested a status update on registering Airbnbs and other transient residential uses. Ms. Gelin stated that an ordinance for registration would be brought forward, subject to checking current statutes, with a limited fee for cost recovery, emergency contacts, and an initial inspection.\par
\par
Requested an update on the chicken/rooster issue and stated she would wait for further information. \par
\par
Shared her experience in Winter Park and proposed a kindness campaign in Delray Beach, beginning in the schools. She challenged the Commission to demonstrate intentional acts of kindness and presented each Commissioner with a white rose, symbolizing respect, with a challenge to perform an act of kindness for three people within 20 days and ask them to pass it on to three others.\par
\par
\ul\b Mayor Carney\ulnone\b0 :\par
Expressed appreciation for Vice Mayor Burns\rquote gesture. \par

minutes_note:

{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Ms. Brandon read Ordinance No. 32-26 into the record. \par
\par
The Development Services Management Group (DSMG) is an administrative group codified in the Land Development Regulations, consisting of the Building Official, Director of Planning and Zoning, and City Engineer. DSMG reviews technical matters, recommends LDR changes, considers interpretations and technical adjustments, and reviews certain special event applications.\par
\par
This ordinance would streamline the process by allowing the Director of Development Services, in consultation with the City Engineer, to approve certain right-of-way dedication and setback adjustments. It would also allow the Board to make minor adjustments to development standards of up to 5% or one foot. Appeals of the Director\rquote s decisions would go to DSMG and then to the Commission. The Planning and Zoning Board recommended approval, 6-0, on June 15th.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to public comment. Seeing no one present. Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked whether the change of up to 5% or one foot would trigger a Board of Adjustment review.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes explained that a threshold that small does not require Board of Adjustment review. If it exceeds the threshold, it would go into notice and to the Board of Adjustment rather than DSMG.\par
}
title: ORDINANCE NO. 32-26: AN ORDINANCE OF THE CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF DELRAY BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING THE LAND DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS OF THE CITY OF DELRAY BEACH CODE OF ORDINANCES BY AMENDING CHAPTER 2, “ADMINISTRATIVE PROVISIONS,” ARTICLE 2.1, “REVIEWING OFFICIALS AND AUTHORITIES,” SECTION 2.1.1, “ADMINISTRATIVE OFFICIALS,” SUBSECTION (B), “DIRECTOR,” TO PROVIDE THE DIRECTOR OF DEVELOPMENT SERVICES THE AUTHORITY TO ADMINISTRATIVELY APPROVE REQUESTS TO ADJUST SETBACK REQUIREMENTS UP TO FIVE FEET WHEN RELATED TO A RIGHT-OF-WAY DEDICATION, AND BY AMENDING SECTION 2.1.2, “REVIEW AUTHORITIES,” SUBSECTION (B), “DEVELOPMENT SERVICES MANAGEMENT GROUP (DSMG),” TO PROVIDE THE DEVELOPMENT SERVICES MANAGEMENT GROUP THE AUTHORITY TO APPROVE DEVIATIONS UP TO FIVE PERCENT FROM A DEVELOPMENT STANDARD, DUE TO UNIQUE SITE CONSTRAINTS; PROVIDING A CONFLICTS CLAUSE, A SEVERABILITY CLAUSE, AND AUTHORITY TO CODIFY; PROVIDING AN EFFECTIVE DATE AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES. (SECOND READING / PUBLIC HEARING)

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Ms. Brandon read Ordinance No. 33-26 into the record. \par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes explained that site plans, conditional uses, and subdivision plans currently have a 24-month approval period, with a project considered established at 25% completion or upon issuance of a certificate of occupancy.The amendment would clarify expiration requirements for recorded plats, including fee-simple townhomes, and extend the deadline for certain City and CRA public projects from two years to five years to allow time for required bidding and procurement processes. For site plans approved on or after October 1, 2022, where a plat is recorded, the deadline would run from the date of plat recordation, with a one-time two-year extension available under existing criteria. The amendment would also extend the approval period for City of Delray Beach and Delray Beach CRA projects. The Planning and Zoning Board recommended approval, 6-0, on June 15.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to public comment. Seeing no one present. Mayor Carney closed public comments.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale asked about the current 24-month approval period and whether the proposed amendment could allow private projects to remain undeveloped longer. Ms. Gianniotes explained that site plans currently expire two years from approval. For certain fee-simple townhouse developments, the proposed amendment would establish the expiration period from the date of plat recordation.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale expressed concern about changing the rules for private projects and stated that she was comfortable proceeding with the public-project provision while leaving the townhouse provision unchanged. Ms. Gianniotes proposed an alternative under which fee-simple townhouse developments with an approved plat would have a 24-month approval period beginning upon plat recordation. Mayor Carney stated that he supported staff\rquote s recommendation and noted that staff must address conflicts between site plan and plat approvals that can require projects to go back through the process.\par
\par
Ms. Brandon requested that the item be postponed to allow additional review of this portion of the amendment. Staff indicated that the item would be re-advertised.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica made a motion to table this item.\par
\par
all were in favor\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Jeff Oris, Assistant City Manager, informed the City Commission that the nonprofit organizations receiving funding from the City were presenting their annual reports.\par
\par
\ul\b Delray Rocks\ulnone\b0\par
Claretta Pickett, Park Representative, presented the organization's history and activities. She highlighted her nineteen (19) years of volunteer service and noted that the organization was celebrating its 60th year. The organization has eight (8) football teams and seven (7) cheer squads, with a focus on mental health and community cleanups. She expressed appreciation for the City of Delray Beach\rquote s continued support and requested $100,000 in funding, with additional waived special event costs and fees.\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\ul\b The Boys and Girls Club of Palm Beach County\ulnone\b0\f1\par
\cf1\kerning0\f0 Pablo Tejada, Chief Impact Officer, presented the club's mission and services, including after-school programs, summer camps, and mental health initiatives. Frankie Pierre Paul, Executive Club Director in Delray, highlighted specific programs like the Ocean Guardians Sea Turtle Adventure and Florida Youth at Risk. Mr. Oris advised that they receive a grant in the amount of $25,000 from the City.\par
\par
\ul\b Spady Cultural Heritage Museum\ulnone\b0\par
Charlene Farrington, Director of the Spady Cultural Heritage Museum, shared that the museum focuses on preservation and education, protecting source material, documents, artifacts, structures, and stories. Additionally, she highlighted its new dementia program. The museum works with young volunteers and interns to maintain its collections and inspire the next generation of history and preservation workers.\par
\par
\ul\b Achievement Center\ulnone\b0\par
Stephanie Seibel shared that since 1969, the Achievement Center had served the Delray Beach community through early learning, after-school, summer, teen, and family support programs. She highlighted student achievements, leadership, internships, and community engagement.They plan to renew their tri-party agreement with the City of Delray Beach and the school district, subject to annual commission approval.\par
\par
\ul\b The Arts Garage\ulnone\b0\par
Marjorie Waldo, President and CEO, presented the Arts Garage's diverse programming, including music, visual arts, comedy, and theater. Ms. Waldo expressed gratitude for the City\rquote s support, noting that funding allowed the Arts Garage to expand programs and provide additional services to the community. She also highlighted the Arts Garage\rquote s 15th anniversary and ongoing community outreach, including its podcast featuring local artists, leaders, and organizations.\par
\par
\ul\b Delray Beach Historical Society\ulnone\b0\par
Winnie Edwards, Director, recognized her fellow teammates who were present and presented the Society\rquote s history and mission, including the preservation of Delray Beach\rquote s heritage. She shared that they have served the community for 62 years and was entering their 40th year working with the City. They preserved three historic cottages and nearly 200,000 archival items while providing history exhibits, heritage tours, educational workshops and community events. The garden and archives remained key assets, supported by ongoing projects, fundraising efforts, and partnerships.They requested $200,000 in City funding for FY 2026-2027.\par
\par
\ul\b Sandoway Discovery Center\ulnone\b0\par
Danika Sanborn, Executive Director of Sandoway Discovery Center, highlighted the center's impact on environmental education, tourism, and community engagement. Sandoway welcomed thousands of visitors, including school groups and tourists, provided hands-on experiences with Florida's unique wildlife, cared for over 50 rescued animals, and provided environmental education to thousands of students, including students from Title One schools, with grant funding covering all costs. Fundraising included the Pub Crawl, ($10,000 raised) and Muscle on the Beach ($81,000 raised) which generated economic activity for Delray Beach. Sandoway organized two beach cleanups that removed hundreds of pounds of trash. To help offset increased operating costs and continue serving residents, students, and visitors, Sandoway requested an increase in its annual City grant from $31,200 to $35,000.\par
\par
Mr. Oris added that Sandaway House is a historic property. It is owned by the County, leased to the City, and the City subleases it to Sandaway.\par
\par
\ul\b Delray Beach Public Library\ulnone\b0\par
Michael Banza, Executive Director, acknowledged his board members and teammates before highlighting the library\rquote s essential role in Delray Beach. He emphasized the library\rquote s significant circulation, visitor, reference, collection, and programming activity, including free adult, children\rquote s, teen, and technology programs supported by numerous community partners. He noted that the City's grant represents the majority of the library\rquote s budget, with fundraising primarily restricted to programming. He explained that direct City funding exempted Delray Beach residents from the Palm Beach County library tax, which would otherwise represent a significant annual cost to residents. The library requested a 3% increase on their $1.78 million base grant, totaling $53,596. The commission agreed to review the budget requests in their next meeting.\par
\par
Mr. Banza also announced necessary construction happening at the library at the end of August, lasting about three (3) weeks, in which the library will be closed during the that time.\par
\par
The City Commission thanked all the nonprofit organizations for their presentations.\par
\par
In closing, Mr. Moore outlined the process for finalizing the fiscal year 2026-2027. The City Commission reached a consensus to maintain current funding levels for the nonprofit organizations. Mr. Moore will meet individually with each member of the City Commission to discuss the impact of the requested increases from the nonprofit organizations.\par
\par
There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the Workshop Meeting at 4:44 p.m.\par
}

\ul Laura Simon\ulnone , Downtown Development Authority (DDA) Director\par

\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comments.\cf1\kerning0\f2\par

{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mayor Carney requested that Item No. 6.I.1. be pulled for discussion. It became Item No. 7.A.A. on the Regular Agenda.\par
\par
\cf1\kerning0 Sam Metott, Parks & Recreation Director, explained that the item was a renewal of the tennis management contract for the Delray Beach Tennis Center and the south-side tennis facility. He stated that Dubin Associates had been a longtime contractor and that a formal RFP was conducted over the summer, with five bidders. He noted that price and experience were key factors in the scoring and that the recommended award offered a significantly reduced price compared to other proposals.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that he had received several letters and phone calls expressing dissatisfaction with the current management and concerns about the selection process. He suggested allowing the Commission and public to hear presentations from the bidders to better understand their proposed services before proceeding with the award. He noted that managing a tennis facility involves more than price and that different perspectives may influence how proposals are evaluated.\par
\par
Mr. Metott clarified that the scoring process was conducted through the Purchasing Department, not Parks and Recreation, and that the solicitation was a formal process rather than a request for three quotes. He reiterated that experience was a significant factor in the evaluation.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin noted that, unlike the previous Pompey Park selection, which had a one-point scoring difference, the tennis management proposals had a substantial scoring difference. She stated that the selection committee consisted of staff with the training, experience, and professional capacity to evaluate the proposals and recommended giving staff\rquote s judgment significant consideration, while acknowledging that the Commission could request public presentations.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that he would view the process differently if it were conducted solely by Parks and Recreation staff. Mr. Metott clarified that the evaluation involved independent representatives from other departments and Parks and Recreation did not obtain three quotes. Ms. Gelin stated the scoring difference almost fifty points.\par
\par
Mr. Metott stated that he had received calls both supporting and opposing the proposals during the selection process but was restricted by the cone of silence from discussing the matter. \par
\par
Mayor Carney reiterated that he was raising the concerns based on letters received and asked the Commission for direction on whether to proceed with public presentations, inviting Commissioners to share their thoughts.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale noted that several concerns involved responsibilities of the City rather than the management company, including funding capital improvements such as the bathrooms. She emphasized the importance of clarifying the management company\rquote s responsibilities and ensuring proper attribution of accountability. She acknowledged the current management company\rquote s efforts to address facility issues, including taking responsibility for problems caused by City procurement processes. She noted her respect for both the current management and potential new management. She stated that she would support the Commission\rquote s decision but wanted any presentations to provide the public with a clear understanding of the respective responsibilities.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns recognized the importance of the facility to the City and would support her colleagues\rquote decision.\par
\par
Commissioner Markert suggested that Mr. Metott present the RFP results to the Commission. He agreed that clarifying the management company\rquote s responsibilities versus the City\rquote s would benefit the Commission and ensure a level playing field.\par
\par
Mr. Metott compared the tennis center\rquote s challenges to those of the golf course, explaining that the aging facility was built in the 1990s and had received limited capital funding. He stated that the City had prioritized court renovations and stadium lighting while addressing other improvements as funding allowed. He noted that the management company\rquote s ability to address facility issues was constrained by the annual budget but that participation and revenue streams had increased over the years.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that he planned to provide an initial written summary of the proposed path forward for the Delray Beach Tennis Center, following the Commission\rquote s consensus the previous month, and that he and Mr. Metott would meet to begin developing the structure and focus. He suggested that Mr. Metott explain the price differences among the submitted proposals to clarify the recommendation.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that, given the importance of the tennis facility to constituents he believed the Commission should hear the management companies\rquote visions and proposed approaches before making a decision.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica noted the distinction between management and maintenance and asked whether maintenance was included in the proposals and whether the evaluation was budgetary.\par
\par
Henry Dachowitz, Chief Financial Officer, clarified that the RFP specified the scope of activities and did not request proposals for a vision of the facility. He explained that the selection committee evaluated the proposals and that Mr. Metott did not select the vendor independently.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica stated that she would support the staff recommendation. \par
As a courtesy, Mayor Carney opened public comment for the individuals who had misunderstood the public-comment process.\par
\par
\ul Joel Schlecker\ulnone \par
Reported that many people left the center to join other clubs resulting in lost membership revenue, plus losses from lessons, clinics, and court fees. He attributed the departures to mismanagement of the tennis center and teams and the mistreatment of players and pros, rather than cost, and urged the Commission to delay renewing the incumbent management company's contract until the fall or review membership and revenue trends over the past three years, particularly the losses following May. \par
\par
\ul Glenn Udine\ulnone , 33445\par
Stated that the courts were poorly maintained, unplayable, and unsafe due to tripping and sliding hazards. He identified court maintenance as a key management company responsibility and noted that his team stopped hosting home games at Lavers because it was embarrassing to have other clubs play there. He urged the Commission to reconsider the contract and hear presentations from the management companies.\par
\par
Mayor Carney noted that public comment instructions should be clarified to explain when speakers may address matters and when they may not.\par
\par
\ul Sharon Painter\ulnone , 33445, CEO of the current management company\par
Acknowledged the complaints and stated that she had met with several players. She explained that some players left due to dissatisfaction with team placements and match results. She stated that revenues had increased, participation was growing, and the management company\rquote s responsibilities included programming for all ages, special events, and additional revenue-generating activities. She cited evidence of its experience and contributions. She encouraged the Commission to review the City's revenue records and the management team's performance, stating that the company had been selected based on what was best for the City.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale acknowledged the need for significant investment in the Lavers facility and confirmed that players and pros had left, some dissatisfied with their experiences. She noted that the tennis center involved multiple components, including two locations, pickleball, and a stadium, and that management experience and cost were important considerations. She stated that opening the process to further presentations could provide additional information but would require the City to consider potentially higher management costs.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that hearing presentations would help the Commission understand the facility's management needs, maintenance costs, and required investment to make it a world-class facility. Ms. Gelin clarified that management and maintenance were separate responsibilities, although management could recommend necessary maintenance, with the Commission determining the budget.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert requested additional information on the facility's maintenance needs. Mr. Metott explained that maintenance included capital improvements, structural maintenance, and daily court maintenance. \par
\par
Following discussion, the Commission reached consensus to hold a special meeting for presentations from all five firms.\f1\par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f2\froman\fprq2\fcharset2 Symbol;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\f0\fs24 Ms. Gelin stated that Vice Mayor Burns had a conflict of interest and would not participate. Vice Mayor Burns left the dais.\par
\par
Jeff, Oris Assistant City Manager, presented a proposed temporary amnesty program for 44 unpaid special event invoices involving 23 producers, including invoices more than 12 months old. He explained that some producers had previously been allowed to waive costs, while others were unaware of the payment requirements or were no longer operating. The program would apply to events held before September 30, 2024, offering discounts of up to 90% for payments made by October 30, 2026. Producers who failed to pay by the deadline would owe the full amount. Participants who subsequently became delinquent under the City\rquote s receivables policy would be required to pay outstanding balances and would lose the right to host events for at least five years, with reinstatement subject to Commission approval. Mr. Oris stated that the program would help collect outstanding amounts and noted that the City had improved invoice processing and collection since hiring a special events manager. He also discussed proposed policy changes, including a 1.5% monthly late fee and additional penalties for producers with more than two delinquent invoices.\par
\par
Mayor Carney expressed concerns about writing off outstanding costs, noting that event producers were aware that fees would be due, even if the final amounts were unknown. He acknowledged that some debts might be uncollectible but maintained that event costs should be paid by the producers rather than taxpayers.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale opposed the amnesty program, stating that the City already had a mechanism for writing off debts owed by deceased individuals or defunct organizations. She cited unpaid invoices, continued event approvals despite nonpayment, and costs incurred by taxpayers, arguing that active organizations should not receive amnesty and that existing policies prohibiting new events until outstanding balances are paid should be enforced.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica supported the program, citing problems with the City's historical invoicing and collection processes, including invoices that were not sent and payments that were not recorded. She noted that some organizations had been told there would be no expenses before receiving bills and stated that the City needed to address these issues.\par
\par
Mayor Carney acknowledged that some older invoices would be difficult to verify.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert asked whether the overdue invoices could be referred to a collection agency. Mr. Oris stated that the City's collection agency could not collect invoices more than five years old. Deputy Vice Mayor Markert suggested considering write-offs for those invoices and questioned why full payment was not collected before events. Mr. Oris explained that the City now collects a 50% deposit, noting that final costs are not known in advance and some producers rely on event revenues to cover expenses.\par
\par
Mr. Moore explained that the 50% upfront deposit is based on estimated costs and is a best practice for municipalities and special event venues. He stated that policy updates over the past two years had improved collections, with final estimates adjusted to cover expenses and secure payment. He noted that the City had not experienced collection issues since implementing the policies and recommended allowing the current process to continue.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale asked whether the outstanding Old School Square Center for the Arts balance remained above $31,000. Mr. Moore confirmed that the City's calculation remained approximately $31,000, noting continued discrepancies and the absence of identifying cash checks or corresponding transactions in the City's system. He stated that efforts to resolve the discrepancy were ongoing.\par
\par
Mayor Carney acknowledged that the older Old School Square invoices were more than five years old and questioned whether writing off portions of the outstanding balances and moving forward would be more productive than continuing collection efforts. He expressed uncertainty about the ability of some organizations to pay and noted that most special event producers had paid their outstanding costs.\par
\cf0\kerning2\par
Mr. Moore stated that the City had updated its policies and procedures to address previous concerns regarding outstanding special event payments and that the process was working well. Mr. Oris credited the Special Events Manager position, noting that Allie Behrman was effectively following up with event producers and ensuring invoices were issued.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz explained that he and Sherry Dungey had reviewed outstanding amounts owed to the City and categorized them into three groups: current projects, amounts more than five years old, and politically sensitive cases. He stated that the collection agency advised that Florida law prohibits pursuing amounts more than five years old. He noted that payments had increased as the City addressed outstanding invoices and expressed confidence in the current process.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz emphasized the importance of collecting amounts owed to the City and establishing penalties for nonpayment. He proposed retaining records of written-off accounts to identify unpaid debts and restricting individuals and nonprofits with outstanding debts from booking new special events or receiving City grants. He also recommended identifying key individuals associated with organizations to prevent them from circumventing restrictions by changing names or establishing new entities.\par
Regarding Old School Square (OSS), Mr. Dachowitz stated that internal accounting records and payment vouchers did not establish that payments had been made and that canceled checks or wire transfers were needed for verification. Commissioner Mollica noted that attempts to obtain canceled checks were unsuccessful because the records were too old.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz expressed concern that the proposed temporary amnesty could become a permanent practice and stated that the City should prioritize collecting outstanding funds and implementing policies before considering service reductions. Mr. Moore responded that the City had successfully implemented policies and procedures over the past two years and was working to address historical issues.\par
\par
Mayor Carney emphasized that restrictions should apply to individuals and affiliated entities to prevent organizations from avoiding payment obligations by changing names. Mr. Moore confirmed that these measures were already part of the City's process.\par
\pard\brdrb\brdrs\brdrw20\brsp20 Mr. Dachowitz stated that commissioners' conflict-of-interest disclosures should be obtained individually for each entity rather than relying on group approval. He stated that the process should identify potential conflicts before approval. Commissioner Casale and Mayor Carney confirmed for the record that they had no conflict of interest.\par
\pard\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
\cf0\kerning2\f0 Deputy Vice Mayor Markert questioned why current outstanding debts were not referred to a collection agency, noting that organizations could change their LLC names. Mr. Dachowitz clarified that current debts were being collected, debts older than five years could not be pursued, and the proposed amnesty concerned the remaining accounts.\par
Mr. Oris explained that Finance participates in the Special Events Technical Advisory Committee (SETAC), reviews its agendas, and has identified applicants with outstanding debts.\par
\par
Commissioners discussed whether organizations receiving amnesty should be reinstated to conduct future events. Deputy Vice Mayor Markert opposed allowing organizations with unpaid bills to conduct additional events, while Commissioner Mollica noted that some nonprofits may not have received invoices or been informed of payment requirements. Mr. Moore stated that departments had worked collaboratively to develop options in response to concerns raised in early 2026.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz expressed concern that amnesty could undermine collection efforts and stated that the City should pursue outstanding payments before considering service reductions. Mayor Carney acknowledged that some organizations may not have received invoices or may have believed payment was not required, and questioned whether the City had made sufficient efforts to collect the debts earlier. Mr. Moore stated that amounts more than five years old would be written off in accordance with applicable law and that debts involving deceased organizational leadership would be addressed administratively. He also clarified that organizations receiving amnesty would not automatically regain the ability to conduct business with the City. Mayor Carney proposed pursuing collection of debts less than five years old and reviewing uncollectible accounts individually rather than granting blanket amnesty. \par
\par
Ms. Gelin outlined the following approach:\par
\pard\fi-360\li720\tx720\f2\fs20\'b7\tab\f0\fs24 Debts more than five years old would be written off, with organizations required to obtain City Commission approval before submitting future event applications.\par
\pard\fi-360\li720\f2\fs20\'b7\tab\f0\fs24 Debts less than five years old would be referred to a collection agency. If collection efforts were unsuccessful, staff would return to the Commission with a resolution requesting a write-off and explaining the reasons.\par
\f2\fs20\'b7\tab\f0\fs24 Organizations with outstanding debts would be required to satisfy their obligations before conducting future events with the City.\par
\f2\fs20\'b7\tab\f0\fs24 Requests to return following a write-off would be considered on a case-by-case basis.\par
\pard\li720\par
\pard The Commission reached consensus regarding the outlined approach. Mr. Oris clarified that, under the City's receivables policy, staff may write off amounts up to $10 without additional approval; write-offs exceeding $10 require Commission approval. Mr. Moore confirmed that staff would proceed as outlined.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}
