\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 Elena Georgiev, Internal Auditor, presented the results of a review of educational incentive compensation payments to Fire Department command staff, initiated at the Mr. Moore\rquote s request to determine why certain employees received the payments and what supported their continuation. The review examined records for five current command staff members, three of whom received the payments and two who did not. The common issue was that payments continued after employees were promoted to command positions not covered by the supervisory collective bargaining agreement. The review identified weaknesses in reassessing and documenting eligibility when employees change positions. Management is aware of the issue and are implementing changes. Internal Audit will evaluate corrective actions as part of a future follow-up. No Commission action was requested.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Casale's questions about whether the issue affected other employees and whether incentives were pensionable, Ms. Georgiev clarified that the review focused on current command staff and that reviewing current documents was insufficient to establish the payment history. She noted that others had received these benefits in prior years.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns returned to dais.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale thanked Ms. Georgiev and Fire Chief Martin for their work and expressed concern about potential financial losses to taxpayers from payroll errors and benefits attributed to pensions. She recalled requesting a review of the Fire and Police Department payroll processes in 2021 but not receiving consensus. She emphasized the importance of carefully reviewing complex contracts to safeguard residents and avoid unnecessary payments, noting that the City could not recover amounts paid over many years and that those benefits could become an issue in future negotiations.\par
\par

Michael Covelli presented a request for a conditional use permit for evening dining within the Sundy Village project in the OSSHAD district. He requested that outdoor dining be permitted from dusk until midnight in designated areas of the restored historic buildings. Mr. Covelli explained that the proposed dining areas, including decks, porches, and patios, were included in the approved site plan and constructed during reconstruction. Outdoor dining is already permitted in these areas during daytime hours; the request would extend their use to midnight without adding new areas. He reviewed the proposed dining locations in Buildings A, B, C, E (Cathcart House), F, and G, including front and rear porches, patios, raised decks, and a breezeway.\par
Regarding the required conditional use findings, Mr. Covelli stated that the site plan process had established compliance with the land use map, concurrency, Comprehensive Plan, and Land Development Regulations. He further stated that evening dining would support neighborhood stability by attracting more people, providing natural surveillance, and boosting the economy. He added that the request would not hinder nearby development or redevelopment and could serve as a catalyst for redevelopment in the area. Mr. Covelli requested approval, stating that positive findings could be made for all criteria.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes explained that evening outdoor dining requires conditional use approval because the OSSHAD district includes residential properties. She noted that the proposed use would not require additional parking, as parking is already provided for daytime operations. The primary consideration is whether evening activity until midnight would affect nearby residents. Ms. Gianniotes stated that the closest residences are within 250 feet of Coda Townhomes and that any request to operate beyond midnight would require further Commission approval. She noted that conditional use approvals may be revoked or adjusted if acoustical problems arise and cannot be rectified. She agreed that Sundy Village could serve as a catalyst for similar renovations to properties east of Swinton Avenue. Ms. Gianniotes confirmed that the Historic Preservation Board and Planning and Zoning Board unanimously recommended approval of the request.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to public comment.\par
\par
\ul George Long\ulnone , 46 N Swinton, 33444\par
Stated that he attended the Historic Preservation Board meetings where nighttime dining was discussed and supported the request. He noted that the commercial property, historic houses, and two-story office buildings provided substantial blockage and said he did not anticipate problems with nighttime dining.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
The Commission spoke in support of the request. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale wished Mr. Long a happy birthday and thanked him for his dedication. \cf1\f1\par

Kim Dwyer requested two waivers to reduce the minimum lot size from 9,500 to 9,000 square feet, a 5% reduction. She stated that the required 75-foot width and 100-foot depth would be met, along with all setbacks, and no other variances or waivers were requested. The applicants were not seeking to restore the three original 50-foot lots. Ms. Dwyer noted that they acquired the property in June and were addressing overgrown landscaping. She explained that the property was originally platted into 50- and 60-foot lots, before the current R1AA zoning requirements. She stated that 61% of the lots in the two comparable blocks are 75 feet or smaller and that the proposed division would be consistent with the existing streetscape. She said the division would remove an oversized void, reestablish the streetscape rhythm and setback pattern, support neighborhood connections, and promote compatible infill and walkable neighborhoods, consistent with the City's Comprehensive Plan. She noted that the Historic Preservation Board unanimously supported the request two weeks earlier and that the proposed designs would return to the Board for review. Ms. Dwyer also referenced neighbors' support expressed at the prior meeting and through letters and requested approval of the waivers.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes clarified that the request was to approve two 9,000-square-foot lots, where the current minimum is 9,500 square feet, and noted a typo in the agenda cover memo. She explained that the original plat consisted of 50-foot-wide lots, but only properties in the R1A zoning district may revert to that configuration. Under City regulations, lots created after October 1, 1990, must meet the minimum lot area, necessitating the requested waivers. Ms. Gianniotes stated that the neighborhood contains a mix of lot sizes representative of its historic pattern and that the proposed waivers would not create a condition contrary to that pattern. She explained that approval would allow the applicants to proceed with designing two infill homes without first investing significant time and resources before knowing whether the lots could be divided. The existing historic structure would be subject to demolition review through the subsequent Certificates of Appropriateness (COA) applications. The Historic Preservation Board would review the structure's integrity, alterations, and condition, as well as the proposed new construction. Ms. Gianniotes noted that staff generally does not recommend demolishing contributing structures and that the City has a performance measure to avoid reducing their number. The Commission was asked to determine whether the waivers would adversely affect neighboring properties, grant a special privilege, and whether dividing the lots was necessary and appropriate. She noted that the Historic Preservation Board unanimously recommended approval.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to public comment.\par
\par
\ul George Long\ulnone , 46 N Swinton, 33444\par
Urged the Commission to approve the request, stating that the 150-foot lot could be viewed as two 75-foot lots and that the division made sense. \par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
The Commission spoke in support of the request.\cf1\f1\par
}

\cf0\kerning2\f1 Dan Edwards, property owner, stated that preservation and progress do not have to be at odds and that he was choosing preservation over demolition. Mr. Edwards stated that the original submittal was made to the Historic Preservation Board (HPB) on March 5, 2025, and, following HPB input, the project was approved by the HPB in 2025 but was subsequently denied by the Commission. He stated that the project addressed the Commission\rquote s concerns by removing the third story, front balcony, and side setbacks, and by lowering and reducing the pool so that a variance was no longer requested. Mr. Edwards presented the revised two-story project, which includes the historic home, a carport providing access to the garage, a three-bedroom second floor, and a hyphen between the existing structure and the addition. He stated that the hyphen would allow the back addition to be removed in the future while leaving the 1928 home intact. Mr. Edwards stated that the project meets standards 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, and 10, and that standards 4, 6, 7, and 8 are not applicable. He stated that he was not requesting any variances and that standard 9 concerns massing. Mr. Edwards stated that he could go up to 35 feet in the district but chose 24 feet, removed the third floor, and lowered the two floors by one foot each to keep the project under 25 feet. He stated that he was requesting a two-story project and a smaller home while addressing access and cars off the street. Mr. Edwards stated that he had over $3 million invested and expected to have over $7 million invested in the project when completed. He also stated that the property has water and termite damage and that he intended to fix it. Mr. Edwards stated that his goal had always been preservation, not demolition and requested approval.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes stated that the application requires a certificate of appropriateness, including demolition of a rear contributing accessory structure, relocation of the existing house by elevating it in its current location and constructing a carport underneath, two waivers, and two variances for the front and side setbacks. Ms. Gianniotes stated that the accessory structure is less than 300 square feet, is located in the rear, is not visible from the street, and is not considered one of the last remaining types of its kind. She stated that the house is required to be elevated to meet flood requirements and that the ongoing flooding is affecting the integrity of the structure. Ms. Gianniotes stated that the main issue under the Secretary of the Interior Standards is whether the new work is compatible in massing, size, and scale. She stated that the hyphen achieves differentiation, but there is concern about the size of the rear addition and whether it can be achieved while maintaining the main house as the focal point. Ms. Gianniotes explained that the building height plane is a technique for keeping the height and scale of new projects in keeping with the street. She stated that elevating the historic house requires it to enter the building height plane, but the Commission should evaluate whether the rear addition also needs to come forward into the building height plane. Ms. Gianniotes stated that the second waiver concerns the requirement that secondary and subordinate additions shall be secondary and subordinate to the massing of the historic building and shall not overwhelm the original building, noting that the addition is taller and wider. Ms. Gianniotes stated that the two variances are required to maintain the historic house in its current position when elevated and to construct the carport underneath it. She stated that the new structure meets all required setbacks and that the variances being considered are only for the historic house and its elevation and the carport underneath it. Ms. Gianniotes summarized that the application requests two setback variances for the original structure and carport, demolition of a rear contributing accessory structure, approval of the relocation, and two waivers to visual compatibility standards.\par

\f0 Neil Schiller, Government Law Group, representing the applicant, stated that the reconsideration involved new information concerning the commercial viability of the property and sidewalk safety. He stated that an economic development presentation identified North Federal Highway as a location for talent-oriented residential infill and that information received through a public records request identified Walmart as a primary obstacle to retail development on North Federal Highway. He stated that the proposal had been improved by adding a curb sidewalk around the interior loop, changing sidewalk colors and materials to create visual separation from driveways and streets, increasing the separation between the townhomes and clubhouse from 12.5 feet to 25 feet, and providing speed bumps at stop signs. Mr. Schiller requested conditional use approval for 47 townhome units, a Level 4 site plan, internal adjustment, loading determination, off-street parking, and four additional waivers. He stated that the project included 39 two-story and eight three-story townhomes, a two-story clubhouse, a private internal access drive, pedestrian walkways, guest parking, site lighting, landscaping, and a 10-foot right-of-way dedication along North Federal Highway. He noted that the Planning and Zoning Board unanimously recommended approval on May 18 and that a 2022 rezoning application from General Commercial to Automotive Commercial had been denied by the City Commission.\par
\par
Jeff Costello stated that positive findings could be made regarding the Comprehensive Plan, North Federal Highway Redevelopment Plan, landscape plan, and development standards. He stated that the project complied with the General Commercial zoning district regulations and substantially complied with the performance standards for multifamily development. He noted that the project proposed 167 new trees, 10.7 units per acre, and a 0.79 floor area ratio. He also addressed the requested waivers concerning townhouse offset, decorative fencing, drive aisle width, stacking distance, landscaping, and distance between buildings, stating that the proposal met the intent of the applicable design standards and that conditions of approval could be provided.\par
\par
Mr. Schiller compared the proposal to the recently approved Tropics Delray project, stating that the projects were similar and that both required waivers. He stated that the proposal was consistent with the North Federal Highway Redevelopment Plan, the 2014 North Federal Highway Market Study, and the 2026 Economic Development Plan. He stated that the applicant agreed to conditions of approval addressing sidewalk colors and materials and other project changes. He concluded by noting that the Planning and Zoning Board recommended approval and that the project was consistent with the applicable plans.\par
\par
\f1 Ms. Gelin requested a three-minute recess to correct the resolution and reread it into the record. Vice Mayor Burns stated the meeting would reconvene at 9:57 p.m. \par
\par
Upon reconvening, Ms. Gelin stated that Resolution No. 96-26 had already been executed as a denial of the application and could not be reused; therefore, Resolution No. 139-26 was assigned. She read the caption for Resolution No. 139-26 into the record.\par
\par
\cf1\kerning0\f0 Ms. Gianniotes entered the presentation provided by staff on July 14, 2026, for the item. She stated that the proposal was a residential use in the General Commercial District and that freestanding multifamily housing was allowed as a principal use, subject to RM regulations, except for setback and height. She stated that the proposed density in Section 4.3.3(B)(3)(e), requires a number of different unit types, sizes, and floor plans to accommodate households of various ages and sizes. She stated that, if considered multifamily, the development provided a mix of bedroom units with varying floor plans, and if considered single-family housing, it provided a mix of three- and four-bedroom units with varying floor plans.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns opened the floor to anyone who wished to provide public comment. \par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\ul David Toll\ulnone\f1 , 915 Orchid Lane, 33483\par
A zoning lawyer, stated that he was speaking as a neighbor and supported the project. He stated that the project met all requirements, did not harm the neighborhood, would help mitigate noise, and would not have lights at night. He also stated that the impact of Walmart on commercial development along Federal Highway was absolutely true and that the project would finish that section of Federal Highway.\par
\par
\ul\f0 Jim Chard\ulnone\f1 , 401 SE 4\super th\nosupersub Ave \par
Stated that demand for commercial use was down and unlikely to return for structural reasons, citing big-box companies, e-commerce, and the gig economy. He stated that recent zoning revisions allowed more housing on underused commercial corridors and that selective redevelopment of aging or vacant commercial parcels could address housing needs while preserving the city's economic viability.\par
\par
\ul\f0 Sam Perlman\ulnone\f1 , 800 Tangerine Way\par
As a representative of the Place Au Soleil Homeowners Association Board, stated that he strongly supported the proposed townhome development. He stated that the current site plan made an effort to minimize intrusion on neighboring properties by creating a gradual step down from commercial to multifamily townhomes and then to single-family townhomes. He noted that the lot had been vacant for roughly 20 years and stated that the project was a residential project recommended unanimously by the Planning and Zoning Board and fit the character of the surrounding development. He stated that the Commission could approve the waiver with conditions addressing loading configuration and curb heights.\par
\par
\ul\f0 Trey Nazaro\ulnone\f1 , Town Manager for the Town of Gulfstream\par
Stated that the Town Commission unanimously voted to send him to support the development project. He noted that the parcels were zoned General Commercial but had been vacant for several years and stated that the nearby Walmart could impact the development opportunity for the site as a commercial property. He stated that the project was compatible with neighboring uses and consistent with development in the area, and that he did not believe it would have a significantly detrimental impact on the surrounding area.\par
\par
\ul\f0 Ann Bennett\ulnone\f1 , 2522 Avenue Au Soleil\par
Stated that she had watched the land sit idle for approximately 23 years and supported the proposed townhomes. She stated that the development would be an improvement and that nothing other than the car dealership had been presented for the property in 20 years.\par
\par
\ul\f0 Neil DeJesus\ulnone\f1 , Address exempt under F.S.S. 1179.09\par
The owner's representative for the former auto dealership, stated that after the denial of the rezoning, they considered developing the property as a commercial strip mall with a fast-food chain but ultimately sold the property to the current owners. He stated that he believed a residential community was the best use for the property and that commercial did not fit for a multitude of reasons, including Walmart and the conflict between a residential community and commercial development.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Vice Mayor Burns closed public comment. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns opened for rebuttal. \par
\par
Mr. Schiller thanked staff for meeting with him and Mr. Costello to discuss improving the project, safety, and potential conditions of approval. He stated that residential use in General Commercial had been in place since at least 1998 and that the applicant was open to including four-bedroom or two-bedroom units as a condition of approval. He stated that the unit mix was a performance standard requiring substantial compliance and that the project substantially complied with the performance standards. He noted that residents from Gulfstream, business owners in Delray Beach, and the developer of the Tropics supported the project, and that no one had spoken in opposition.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes stated that if the Commission was inclined to approve the project with conditions, the change from crape myrtle to Dahoon Holly along the North Federal sidewalk should be included to provide more shade. She stated that the project provided a good transition from single-family to the commercial corridor and that the adjustments made the project more positive, particularly the distinction between areas where people were walking and cars were driving.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin stated that changing the configuration from three-bedroom to four-bedroom units would constitute a redesign. She stated that if the Commission required a mix of bedroom types, the applicant would have to submit a new application. She noted that if the Commission found the project substantially complied with the performance standards, that would be different.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale stated that she did not see new information in the presentation. She discussed the importance of protecting commercial property and stated that the Federal Highway plan had not been updated, leaving the Commission without guidance from professionals. \par
\par
Commissioner Mollica stated that she considered the potential impact of a strip mall on neighboring residents but was not basing her opinion on the residents. She stated that the project was a good project on a neglected, unused parcel, supported conditions addressing concerns, and remained in favor of the project. She added that the market has spoken about developing that parcel commercially.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert stated that he walked the property and met with Anthea Gianniotes. He thanked the applicants for addressing concerns regarding backing out, separation, and curbs, and supported the addition of stop signs and speed bumps for safety. He stated that all units were three bedrooms and that the project did not meet the multifamily requirements for a mix of units. He discussed changing some units to one- and two-bedroom units to address boundary issues and move the project closer to conformity. He also supported the proposed railing along Federal Highway from a security and landscaping standpoint.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes stated that the Commission should consider whether the absence of smaller units affected the project's ability to substantially comply with the performance standard. She stated that the applicable standards called for a mix of three- and four-bedroom units if considered townhouse-like and a mix of one-, two-, and three-bedroom units if considered multifamily. She noted that some performance standards may not be entirely applicable to small infill residential sites and that the Commission should consider the proposed density, applicable performance standards, and the transition to single-family development. She stated that the proposed stop bars, stop signs, and speed limit signs addressed a technical item identified by staff concerning pedestrian safety and that the applicant was showing how it intended to respond to the item.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns stated that commercial zoning did not guarantee commercial development and that a commercially designated property did not mean a business would relocate there. She stated that she did not believe the project adversely affected the neighboring area, significantly diminished public facilities, created an unsafe situation, or granted a special privilege. She stated that the City Commission had not accepted or adopted a plan for the North Federal Highway corridor.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Ms. Gelin read Ordinance No. 34-26 into the record. \par
\par
Mayor Carney returned to the dais. Vice Mayor Burns returned the gavel to Mayor Carney.\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f1 Ms. Gelin explained that the ordinance\rquote s effective date was changed to January 1, 2027, because Florida Statutes require the City to provide a minimum of 90 days\rquote notice before implementing impact fees. \par
Vice Mayor Burns indicated she would be inclined to postpone the item until after the November election. Mayor Carney stated he had received calls concerning the timing and that stakeholders wanted to weigh in on the impact fees. Commissioner Casale stated that the City had held a public meeting and workshop and had discussed the impact fees at several meetings. Mr. Moore noted that the impact fee study was adopted in January 2026 and that direction was needed. Vice Mayor Burns asked whether the City would have time to implement the fees after the November election. Mr. Moore stated that the November 3 election and the 90-day notice requirement could potentially pose an issue. Commissioner Mollica questioned delaying the fees and stated that the City knew it wanted the fees. Commissioner Casale stated that delaying the fees could require restarting the process and supported moving forward with the study\rquote s recommended fees. Commissioner Casale, Deputy Vice Mayor Markert and Vice Mayor Burns expressed agreement with moving forward.\par
\par
\b\f0\fs20 A motion was made by Commissioner Casale, seconded by Vice Mayor Burns, to allow extending the meeting beyond 11:00 p.m.\par
\par
all were in favor\b0\f1\fs24\par
\par
Mr. Oris presented the impact fee ordinance, noting that impact fees are one-time charges on new development used to fund public facilities and infrastructure and are not intended to cure existing deficiencies. He stated that the fees would apply to new development and expansions over 1,000 square feet and could only be used for capital expenditures identified in the study. The study recommended fees on a square-footage basis, with water and sewer fees reduced to 50 percent of the study recommendation. The ordinance establishes the fees, calculation methods and credits, an appeal process, and an annual review and report to the Commission. A 50 percent discount was included for historic properties and affordable housing.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale asked whether the affordable housing discount would apply to developments receiving density bonuses. Mr. Oris stated that affordability controls apply to dwelling units with restrictions on price or purchaser or lessee income to ensure the units remain affordable to very low or moderate-income households. Mayor Carney clarified that workforce housing would still pay the fees.\par
\par
Mr. Oris stated that the City cannot apply impact fees greater than the study recommends and may reduce them. Future increases would require a new study and could not be retroactively applied. He noted that the Planning and Zoning Board recommended approval by a vote of 6-0 and requested discounts for workforce housing, historic preservation, and infill construction. The Commission did not include an infill construction discount but included an affordable housing discount.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin stated that applications submitted after the effective date would be subject to the impact fees. She explained that the ordinance required at least 90 days\rquote notice and that January 1, 2027, provided a buffer and time to program the City\rquote s software. The Commission reached consensus on January 1, 2027, as the effective date.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to speak on this item. \par
\par
\ul\f0 Tyler Knight\ulnone , 33445 \par
Stated that the impact fees could have a significant impact on smaller builders and suggested that the City get everyone together to discuss the fees further. \f1\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\cf1\kerning0\f0\par
}

title: Pursuant to Section 3.12 of the Charter of the City of Delray Beach, the Mayor has instructed me to announce a Workshop Meeting of the City Commission to be held for the following purposes:
PUBLIC COMMENTS

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Public Works Director Missy Barletto, accompanied by Utilities Director Hassan Hajimiry and Parks and Recreation Director Sam Metott, presented an initial draft of the Capital Improvement Budget. Ms. Barletto stated that the full budget, including project descriptions, would be provided after Commission comments and voted on in September. The total CIP request was $343,143,389, allocated to the Utilities Department for the water treatment plant, the General Construction Fund, and Stormwater Fund.\par
\par
Ms. Barletto stated that the budget highlighted tree plantings and continued Parks and Recreation efforts to update playgrounds. Statutory changes, including Senate Bill 180 signed into law by the Governor, precluded using building funds for infrastructure such as the proposed City Hall annex, so the City returned to considering a reconfiguration to address employee seating needs in the north end of City Hall.\par
\par
CRA-funded projects include Pompey Park construction, Northwest and Southwest Neighborhood Improvements, limited implementation of the Old School Square Master Plan, and courtyard improvements at Fire Station 111.\par
\par
Ms. Barletto noted that the Public Safety Government Obligation Bond Improvements included completing design of the new police department headquarters and improvements to some fire stations, including exterior painting, roofs, and restroom facilities to make them more equitable between male and female firefighters.\par
\par
Ongoing Metropolitan Planning Organization (MPO) projects include the Brant Bridge Connector, which would connect the Brant Bridge and Lindell Boulevard projects with continuous sidewalks, bicycle lanes, and improved roadway conditions. A new round of public meetings was planned for Barwick Road Phase 2, following additional studies, including one on guardrails. The community had initially requested removal of the guardrails but had since strongly supported keeping them, and the City believed it could provide favorable news on that issue. Another MPO project planned for the coming year was design work for safety improvements along NE 4th Street between Swinton and Federal Highway.\par
\par
Mr. Metott discussed the new turf, noting that the artificial turf field projects were already approved and were set to break ground in the new fiscal year. Construction at Merritt Park is expected to begin in November, followed by fields at Seacrest and Hilltopper, and a small practice artificial field as part of the first phase of the Catherine Strong Park renovation. The four fields were bid together to obtain the best pricing from the artificial turf vendor, but they remained two separate projects: sports turf and the Catherine Strong Park renovation.\par
\par
Mr. Hadjimiry added that construction on the new water treatment plant had started early, with groundbreaking on January 29. Two deep injection wells were being constructed simultaneously. The City had pre-purchased items with long delivery times, and completion was expected in early 2028.\par
\par
The Marine Way seawall, roadway, and drainage improvements project were in the process of establishing a guaranteed maximum. The Thomas Street pump station rebuild is underway and slightly over budget due to unforeseen environmental conditions in the water table. Guaranteed maximum price negotiations were also beginning for Tropic Isle neighborhood improvements. Vehicle and equipment replacements totaled approximately $4 million in the coming year\rquote s capital improvement budget to keep the fleet current, minimize maintenance costs, and save the City money. The Special Projects Fund included $65,000 to complete the current tree planting program contract.\par
\par
Mr. Metott stated that the Parks and Recreation impact fee was expected to generate approximately $200,000, earmarked for continued park pavilion replacements. Approximately $50,000 was allocated for playground updates, primarily to replace worn playground parts.\par
\par
Ms. Barletto explained that the Capital Improvement Program budgeted for the coming fiscal year, with four-year projections and funding sources to be determined. Five-cent and six-cent gas taxes were dedicated to transportation, sidewalks, mobility, and roadway reconstruction, including approximately $100,000 for ADA improvements and $300,000 for roadway reconstruction. An additional $1 million was transferred to the General Construction Fund as matching funds for MPO grants. The Building Fund included $5 million to improve working conditions for the Building Department, with another $5 million reflected in the following year. The Beach Restoration Fund was supported by state and federal funds, Palm Beach County through an interlocal agreement, state appropriations, and a prior-year surplus. Approximately $110,000 was allocated to complete the Reef Institute baby coral project, including reef planting and monitoring.\par
\par
The General Construction Fund expenses were primarily ongoing projects previously presented. A new $1 million dollar allocation was included for replacement of police department laptops, which had become critical. The Crest Theatre Auditorium renovation would complete design in the coming fiscal year, with construction planned for fiscal years 2028-2029.\par
\par
Mr. Metott advised that the Recreation General Obligation Bond included turf installations, along with $500,000 earmarked for additional public restroom renovations. Approximately 13 or 14 restrooms were slated for renovation as part of the bond-funded public restroom renovation project.\par
\par
The Public Safety General Obligation Bond included the police department headquarters and major renovations at the Ocean Rescue headquarters at Anchor Park. The renovations would move locker rooms and showers downstairs into the garage area, with the upstairs converted to conference rooms and office space.\par
\par
Mr. Hadjimiry indicated that 2026 revenue was projected at $55.4 million and 2027 revenue at $62.4 million, due to rate increases and utility efficiency measures, positioning the City to make revenue bond payments for the water plant beginning in two years. Most CIP projects, except the water treatment plant and Lift Station 50, were underground and had been presented at the May 19th Workshop. The fiscal year 2027-2028 amount for the water treatment plant would be $108 million. The water plant cost is approximately $280 million, with nearly $30 million spent to date, and most funds expected to be spent beginning in January as equipment and the building are received. He projected pursuing a second revenue bond toward the end of the year to finance the remaining portion of the water plant.\par
\par
Stormwater utility revenues include approximately $40 million in state resiliency bonds, a utility assessment pending Commission approval, and a planned revenue bond for major stormwater projects. Projects include the historic Marine Way seawall, Thomas Street pump station, Tropic Isle neighborhood, stormwater master plan update, seawall replacements, George Bush Boulevard drainage improvements, pump station repairs, and establishment of a stormwater maintenance program. The City also plans to purchase a CCTV truck and establish its own telemetry system to monitor stormwater pumping stations.\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f1 The City Garage budget included $4 million in new equipment purchases for city vehicles. The City had used a lease-to-own program for the past two years to modernize the fleet and minimize maintenance. As the automobile market recovered, the City planned to purchase vehicles based on job needs, resulting in more pickup trucks and Ford Explorers and fewer Chevrolet Tahoes. The presentation concluded with an invitation for questions, directions, and requested changes.\cf1\kerning0\f0\par
\par
The City Commission thanked staff for their presentation.\par
\par
Prior to adjourning, Mr. Moore informed the Commission that there will be a presentation by the consultants regarding the Crest Theatre during the regular meeting on September 22nd.\par
\par

title: Pursuant to Section 3.12 of the Charter of the City of Delray Beach, the Mayor has instructed me to announce a Budget Workshop Meeting of the City Commission to be held for the following purposes:
PUBLIC COMMENTS

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that the workshop was an opportunity for the Commission to provide final expectations for the FY 2026-2027 proposed budget ahead of the September 8\super th\nosupersub 1\super st\nosupersub Public Hearing and September 22\super nd\nosupersub Final Hearing. He noted that staff had provided an initial draft presentation and continued updating it to provide the most up-to-date information, data, analytics, and metrics, and requested the Commission\rquote s support and latitude in doing so. He emphasized the importance of maintaining service levels and making sound decisions based on the City\rquote s financial realities, current operations, and future expectations.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that the Commission\rquote s role was to give direction and that the workshop would allow each Commissioner to publicly share budget priorities, potential cuts, and areas for savings or expansion so the Commission could understand the different perspectives and reach a path forward.\par
\par
Henry Dachowitz, Chief Financial Officer, reviewed the Florida statutes and City Charter regulations governing the budget process and outlined the FY 2026-2027 budget timeline, including prior workshops, and the upcoming public hearings. He noted that the Finance Department is very lean and that staff continues updating data and documents as information is received.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz stated that the City\rquote s proposed operating millage rate is 6.4371, plus debt service for an aggregate 6.4660, and that the proposed 2027 millage is down 10.3% since 2016. He compared Delray Beach with peer municipalities and noted that most leverage fire assessment fees and maintain stable millage rates, while Delray Beach does not collect a fire assessment fee and continues to maintain a low millage rate.\par
He explained that proposed revenues increase to $205.8 million, with net property tax revenues increasing from $92.7 million to $103.5 million, and a projected $8.1 million fund balance drawdown, resulting in total revenues of approximately $219.6 million. He stated that the projected fund balance would decrease from $47.13 million to $39.024 million, or 18.17% of expenditures, and that the drawdown was necessary to juggle the different demands of the FY 2026-2027 budget.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz reviewed departmental budgets and reductions, primarily through attrition, while retaining COLAs and essential positions, programs, supplies, training, and services. He described the projected operating budgets for each department, with the grand total at $219.6 million.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert asked for clarity regarding attrition. Mr. Dachowitz stated that from a budgeting perspective, the City historically budgeted every position for the full year but recognized savings from turnover. He stated that Finance reviewed historical turnover and department heads\rquote expectations for the coming year to tighten the budget and gain savings.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns asked whether the attrition period was the same for every department. Mr. Dachowitz explained that it depends on the department, based on how quickly positions can be filled, historical trends, and department heads\rquote assessments of critical positions.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz explained that efficient computer systems allow employees to work faster and more accurately but require investment in upgraded software and training. He noted that the City is operating on older systems, while transitioning to new systems, and stated that increased efficiencies could result in real attrition, allowing tasks to be combined and headcount reduced.\par
\par
Mayor Carney expressed concern about a 30% increase in personnel over approximately seven or eight years without a corresponding population increase. He stated that the City should discuss ways to reduce personnel costs, including privatizing certain components and outsourcing functions such as inspections. Mr. Dachowitz noted that 53% of the City\rquote s expenses are police and fire and suggested that a cost-reduction study should begin by examining headcount by department to determine appropriate staffing and noted that some departments are already lean. \par
\par
Mayor Carney opposed raising the millage and urged the City to find ways to trim costs, while Commissioner Casale emphasized declining reserves and the costs of Commission-approved compensation and contracts.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz explained that reducing the recommended millage would have a compounding negative effect by reducing current revenues and establishing a lower base if the November referendum passes, while strengthening reserves through identified savings could be an approach. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale identified potential savings in overtime, travel and training, professional services, equipment, leases, maintenance, supplies, and other expenditures. Mr. Moore identified approximately $600,000 in fire rescue overtime and $800,000 in police overtime reductions, for $1.4 million in savings, and endorsed the reductions. He also stated that the budget discussion would help provide direction, identify efficiencies, and strengthen the fund balance before the September 8\super th\nosupersub hearing.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns asked whether, absent a supermajority consensus, the millage rate would revert to the rollback rate. Mr. Moore confirmed that four of five Commissioners must agree on a millage rate; otherwise, the rollback rate of 5.8555 would apply, resulting in a general fund revenue loss of more than $5 million. Vice Mayor Burns expressed concern about sustainability and maintaining an appropriate level of service.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica supported eliminating the $35,000 special events vehicle and reducing overtime and questioned the utilization and cost of the Teen Center. Mayor Carney stated that approximately $473,000 was spent on the Teen Center for roughly 18 children.\par
\par
Sam Metott, Parks & Recreation Director, explained that the $473,000 is an all-encompassing amount, including staffing, FICA, insurance, supplies, and facility operations; the Teen Center also hosts Women\rquote s Club meetings and operates as a skate park. He stated that teen programming typically averages 10 to 30 participants per program, primarily afternoons, summers, and school breaks, and that participation numbers do not include skate park users. Mr. Metott provided the staffing levels of the center and noted that staff are utilized at other locations, including Catherine Strong, to cover activities and avoid hiring additional personnel. He cautioned that reducing staffing further could prevent the facility from functioning effectively and noted that utilization varies by time of day, similar to other Parks & Recreation facilities.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert supported the cuts, noting that more than half of the budget is police and fire, and supported holding the millage and maintaining reserves. Mayor Carney supported additional police and fire savings and stated that he wanted to review contracts and expenditures, including library salaries the City was paying contrary to the agreement, to identify additional ways to save money. Mr. Moore supported the adjustments and requested direction on the millage rate and fund balance before the September 8 and September 22 readings.\par
\par
Mayor Carney supported reducing the millage rate. Commissioner Casale supported maintaining a 21% fund balance based on the City\rquote s audit and expressed concern about reducing reserves or police staffing given public safety needs.\par
\par
Mr. Moore proposed reducing the operating millage rate from 6.4371 to 6.3501 based on $1.4 million in public safety overtime savings, while using additional savings to improve the fund balance. Mayor Carney sought further savings to provide greater relief to taxpayers, while Commissioners Casale and Mollica emphasized maintaining reserves and preparing for potential future revenue losses.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica asked whether the City\rquote s library could levy a separate millage. Mr. Moore explained that the City\rquote s library could become part of the Palm Beach County Library system, which has a separate millage rate of .5411 and would include library personnel salaries. Mayor Carney stated that he values having the City\rquote s own library.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz explained that higher reserves maintain financial flexibility and support bond ratings. He noted that if the November referendum passes the City will have a hit of revenue right off the top, and will have a limit as to what can be cut, which will be a problem because they can't raise the millage rate. \par
\par
There was further discussion among the Commission regarding the proposed millage rate, reducing the millage rate and maintaining reserves.\par
\par
Mr. Moore proposed returning with a proposed 6.3501 operating millage rate on September 8\super th\nosupersub , incorporating the identified $1.4 million in public safety overtime savings and updated fund balance. Deputy Vice Mayor Markert requested a detailed accounting of proposed cuts, and Mayor Carney supported identifying additional savings.\par
\par
The Commission reached consensus to proceed with a proposed 6.3501 millage rate recommendation with the adjustments and updated fund balance as discussed.\par
\par
\kerning0 There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 5:57 p.m.\cf1\par
\cf0\kerning2\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mayor Carney stated that the City should not raise the millage rate above the current year\rquote s rate. He noted that maintaining the current millage would result in approximately a 6.9% increase in what taxpayers pay, compared with a 10.2% increase at the recommended rate of 6.3501. He added that the City will generate an additional $6.4 million in revenue if the millage rate stayed the same.\par
\par
He stated that services were not impaired under the rollback rate and that there is no empirical evidence that services would be disrupted. He also noted that 77 properties have received COs this year, representing approximately $77 million in increased value to the City, with additional properties expected to be added to the tax rolls next year, and that the City should manage costs internally rather than increase taxes and that taxpayers should receive relief from increased insurance, grocery, and other costs.\par
\par
Mr. Moore asked to proceed with the prepared presentation for this item and that the proposed millage rate was based on a consensus from the previous meeting.\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2 Mr. Dachowitz\f1 presented the proposed FY 2026-27 budget, explaining that total expenditures were approximately $217.3 million, including increases for police, fire, parks and recreation, public works, salaries, benefits, pension contributions, and CRA funding. He compared Delray Beach\rquote s proposed operating millage rate and taxable values with surrounding municipalities, noting that most peer cities use separate fire assessment fees while Delray Beach does not. He stated that the proposed \f0 6.3501 operating millage rate, plus 0.0289 debt service, would produce a total millage rate of 6.3790 and reduce \f1 the projected fund balance from 22% to 19% of expenditures.\par
\par
Mayor Carney argued that Delray Beach\rquote s 57% increase in its tax base over five years, compared with an 11% millage reduction, did not represent sufficient relief for taxpayers. He maintained that the City should pursue a rollback or not increase the millage rate, and require structural changes rather than rely on reserves or future development.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns stated she would support the lowest millage rate that can be provided without affecting the current levels of service.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale stated that Delray Beach\rquote s cost increases were consistent with other cities, noting increases in fire, police, and general-fund budgets since 2016. She noted that she had identified approximately $2.854 million in cuts, and explained that this produced only a $43.50 reduction per $500,000 of taxable value. She warned that the City was using reserves despite a policy calling for 21%. She challenged the Mayor to identify specific cuts. She noted that the fund balance was below the City\rquote s 21% policy, and opposed reducing reserves further and supporting the proposed millage-rate.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica added that police and fire costs were contractually required, while other departments had already been reduced to bare-bones budgets. She acknowledged that Mr. Dachowitz and Mr. Moore had worked to maintain adequate reserves. Although she opposed raising the millage and preferred keeping it unchanged, she stated that the rollback the City had two years ago, in fact, hurt.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that the millage set for fiscal year 2026-27 would serve as the baseline for fiscal year 2027-28. He noted that the recommendations had considered the potential outcome of Amendment 3 in November 2026 and the need to strike a balance rather than make drastic changes. He noted that he had been listening to feedback to help achieve a reasonable middle ground. \par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert stated that the City was not out of step with surrounding cities when the math was properly considered. He noted that fire and police assessments might be worth considering. He was opposed to drawing down reserves, stating that doing so would leave the City vulnerable. He stated that the City had already cut to the bone and added that further cuts would affect noticeable. He noted that police and fire reductions could affect safety and that union contracts had to be honored. He was not closed-minded to lowering the budget further but wanted the specific impacts of those cuts presented before the vote, stating that they would be draconian.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to public comments.\par
\par
\ul\b\f0 Greg Page, 33444\ulnone\b0\f1\par
\cf1\kerning0\f0 Raised concerns about property overvaluation. He compared property taxes from 2010 to 2026 and questioned how property valuations had increased so significantly. He also stated that short-term rentals and properties converted to private schools or daycares were not contributing their fair share of taxes and suggested these could provide additional tax revenue.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comments.\par
\par
Mr. Moore asked for direction from the City Commission. He advised that the millage rate tentatively adopted would establish the maximum rate that may be adopted at the final budget hearing, which could be equal to or lower than the tentative rate. He requested that the matter be resolved that evening and explained that if no millage rate received enough votes, the first budget hearing would not be completed and would need to be recessed and continued until a tentative millage rate and budget were adopted.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin recommended tentatively adopting the current millage rate, noting that the rate could still be lowered at the next budget hearing but could not be increased. She proposed returning with the exact cuts needed to achieve a lower millage rate so the Commission could make an informed decision based on specific impacts to personnel, programs, and projects. She also noted that PFAS funds could be an option but were not recommended as a recurring funding source.\par
\par
Mayor Carney suggested a millage rate of 6.2249, keeping the reserves at 18%.\par
}

title: Pursuant to Section 3.12 of the Charter of the City of Delray Beach, the Mayor has instructed me to announce a Workshop Meeting of the City Commission to be held for the following purposes:

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mr. Moore provided a PowerPoint presentation of the Department of Communications' role and capabilities in external communication and outreach in response to a consensus initiated by Commissioner Judy Mollica, highlighting marketing, media relations, executive communications, creative services, crisis communications, emergency alerts, public meetings, outreach, social media platforms, digital newsletters, the My Delray Beach app, publications, digital displays, city podcasts, the City website, and AI chatbot Piper. \par
\par
Jay Stacy, Chief Technology Officer, explained that the City has the technology to produce post-meeting recaps through Legistar, a comprehensive meeting management system supporting agenda creation, review and approval, packet preparation, live meeting management, video streaming, and post-meeting transparency.\par
\par
He noted that Legistar retains agendas, backup materials, outcomes, recorded video, and indexed discussion points that link directly to the corresponding video segments. As a short-term solution, he suggested sending post-meeting Legistar links to existing newsletter subscribers. IT can also use Legistar\rquote s interface to extract data and create a more readable recap or traditional newsletter. He also highlighted upcoming AI capabilities to improve search features and provide summaries of lengthy agenda items.\par
\par
Commissioner Markert asked whether the recap would summarize meeting discussions or only the pre-meeting agenda, and raised concerns about AI accuracy. Jay explained that he had explored using AI to create brief, factual summaries of discussions without opinions or quotations, while directing residents to the video for the full discussion. He noted that Legistar already provides official item titles, backup materials, and video clips.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin added that AI-generated content should be reviewed for authenticity, clarity, and accuracy before publication. She recommended human fact-checking or, at minimum, a disclaimer that AI-generated content may not be entirely accurate.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica expressed strong support, calling the approach \ldblquote brilliant\rdblquote and noting that receiving the information directly would be much easier than having to find it. She supported sending the video so residents can review what was said.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that the presentation was intended to secure the Commission\rquote s support and that staff would move forward with making the opportunities available.\par
\par
Ms. Givings reported that the City\rquote s agenda newsletter has 1,207 subscribers.\par
\par
Mayor Carney encouraged expanding the subscriber list, noting the opportunity to reach a much larger portion of the community.\par
\par
\cf0 There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the Workshop meeting at 4:27 p.m.\cf1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that he had a couple of items to discuss. He explained that adjustments to parking fines were made to comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) following a complaint regarding blocked public sidewalks. Ms. Gelin stated that the U.S. Department of Transportation issued a letter of finding requiring a compliance plan within 90 days and that failure to comply could jeopardize federal grant funding. The City submitted its plan, which was accepted, and received a letter of closure on August 27, 2026. \cf0\kerning2\f1 She stated that the City increased the fine for blocking a sidewalk from $35 to $250, consistent with the fine for a handicap parking violation\cf1\kerning0\f0 . She noted that reducing the fine would require returning to the U.S. Department of Transportation. Full enforcement is scheduled to begin October 1st, following public education and outreach.\par
\par
Concerns were raised about limited residential parking and residents parking on sidewalks or grass. Mr. Moore stated that residents could apply for permits to extend or modify driveways, subject to the permitting process.\par
\par
Mr. Moore then introduced a presentation on the RedSpeed school zone speed camera program. Neil Schiller, representing RedSpeed, reported that enforcement began August 10, 2026, with violations issued for exceeding the posted speed limit by more than 11 miles per hour during designated enforcement periods. From August 10th through September 18th, nearly 5,000 notices were issued. He reported that violations had decreased by 81% compared with the speed study conducted in 2024-2025. Mr. Schiller explained that a timing discrepancy occurred at Banyan Creek because the flashing beacons and cameras operated on different schedules. The City requested that Palm Beach County adjust the beacon times. Notices issued in error were dismissed, and refunds were issued to individuals who had already paid.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked whether additional public education was needed to clarify that cameras remain active outside the flashing-light periods. Chief Darrell Hunter stated that the City had conducted public outreach through social media, television, and school flyers. He addressed questions regarding the program's functionality and implementation. Deputy Vice Mayor Markert requested that education efforts continue through the return of seasonal residents. Mr. Moore confirmed that outreach would continue through the end of the calendar year. Mayor Carney requested updated statistics in one month to evaluate the program\rquote s effectiveness in reducing speeds.\par
\par
Following the RedSpeed discussion, Commissioner Casale made a point of order and requested that notifications be sent when agenda items change, including a brief explanation of the changes. Mr. Moore stated that we would endeavor accordingly. \par

\ul Elizabeth Chance, 33444\ulnone\par
Proposed allowing dogs off-leash on the beach north of the sailboats during early morning hours until approximately 8:45 a.m. or 9:00 a.m. and beginning around 4:30 or 4:45 p.m. She suggested an annual dog beach pass and stated that she and others would be willing to pay a fee. Mayor Carney stated that the proposal would be taken under advisement.\par
\par
\ul Billy Roach, 33483\ulnone\par
Criticized the additional proposed spending on the Old School Square assessment, stating that the City should return to a model that had previously worked, provide consistent events, and maximize the campus for residents and visitors.\par
\par
\ul Martin Dorow, 33483\ulnone\par
Stated that he would defer his comments until the millage rate discussion.\par
\par
\ul Mike Tang, 33445\ulnone\par
Read a statement on behalf of the Sable Lakes Homeowners Association regarding the Barwick Road North Improvement Project from Lake Ida Road to the L-30 Canal. The board thanked the City for proposed safety improvements, including a split-rail fence, curbing, and swales, and for removing the crosswalk from the northern Sable Lakes Road North entrance. The board requested additional turning-radius tolerance at the southern entrance to accommodate larger vehicles, including bulk trash trucks, fire trucks, and work trailers to prevent property damage and vehicles entering oncoming traffic.\par
\par
\ul Adam Greenberg, 33436\ulnone\par
Questioned whether the school-zone speed limits were set too high and discussed signage requirements. He stated that school-zone signs could identify the school zone or display the applicable times and suggested that the signage could help address concerns regarding enforcement.\par
\par
\ul Jim Chard, 33483\ulnone\par
Questioned the need for additional spending on the Old School Square assessment, stating that the City already had the knowledge, experience, and history to develop a plan. He recommended bringing the community together to prepare a proposal and stated that he had sent the Commission a proposal for moving forward.\par
\par
\ul Mariska Gato, Cultural Arts Director at the Cornell Art Museum\ulnone\par
Reported that the museum held nine new exhibitions during the last fiscal year, featured 358 artists, including 250 youths, had 32 artists consigning artwork in the museum store, welcomed 14,375 visitors, collected $25,000 in donations, and conducted more than 30 tours. She announced upcoming exhibitions beginning October 1st and October 11th, and stated that the museum was preparing fine art shows for November and February.\par
\par

Announced downtown Delray Beach Restaurant Month through September 30th with nearly 60 restaurants participating. She stated that the DDA continued operating the Old School Square campus under its interlocal agreement, that nearly 500,000 visitors attended the campus during the year, and that funding and a long-term sustainable operating model were needed. She reported that the outdoor amphitheater event infrastructure cost approximately $25,000 to $30,000 per event and emphasized the need to work together on a plan to reopen the Crest Theater.\par
\par
\ul Dr. Allen Costillo, 33483\ulnone\par
Criticized the City\rquote s enforcement of illicit water violations, stating that the $5,000 fine was excessive for minor activities such as air-conditioning condensate dripping or restaurants washing mats. He stated that the law was intended to address egregious abuse of the system and that warnings and education should be provided for first-time offenses.\par
\par

Provided the City Clerk with a copy of his email to the City Commission and requested that the City consider addressing short-term rentals, noting that the other municipalities already do so.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, public comment was closed.\par
\par

\par
Mayor Carney read the quasi-judicial rules into the record. \par
\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk, swore in those individuals who wished to provide testimony on this item.\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, entered file PZ 000360-2025 for the Site Plan and PZ 000359-2025 for the Conditional Use into the record.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked his colleagues to disclose any ex-parte communications.\par
\par
\ul Commissioner Casale\ulnone : Spoke to Mr. Costello.\par
\ul Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone : Spoke to Mr. Costello.\par
\ul Commissioner Mollica\ulnone : Spoke to Mr. Costello.\par
\ul Deputy Vice Mayor Markert\ulnone : Spoke to Mr. Costello.\par
\ul Mayor Carney\ulnone : Spoke Mr. Costello and anything on the server.\par
\par
Jeff Costello, representing the applicant for Lenny\rquote s Car Wash, presented a proposal to redevelop the existing car wash on North Federal Highway and Northeast 22nd Lane into an approximately 3,300-square-foot, single-tunnel automated car wash. The proposal included 16 on-site parking spaces with individual vacuums, five proposed on-street spaces along Northeast 22nd Lane, a central vacuum system inside the insulated building to mitigate noise, right-of-way dedications, and elimination of the curb cut along Federal Highway. Mr. Costello stated that the Planning and Zoning Board recommended approval on August 17th, with the condition that windows be added to the north elevation of the east tower. The applicant incorporated the windows into the proposed design. He stated that positive findings could be made regarding land use consistency, conditional use, concurrency, Comprehensive Plan consistency, Land Development Regulations compliance, site plan standards, and building elevations. He also discussed a waiver request to allow one-way traffic circulation despite the code requirement for two-way traffic flow for a 24-foot drive aisle. He stated that the circulation pattern would support customer flow and business operations, would not create a safety concern or affect the adjacent area, and would be supported by signage. He noted that the landscape plan preserves trees along Northeast 22nd Lane and provides landscaping around the site.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked why the car wash required a new conditional use approval when the existing use remained a car wash, noting that the waiver was understood but questioned the need for the additional process.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes explained that the application was processed together to avoid multiple presentations before the Commission. She stated that the existing car wash use would remain, but the proposal required a new application. She noted that the process could be reviewed in the future to establish minor and major conditional uses. She explained that the location was compatible with the proposed use. She supported the waiver for one-way traffic circulation, noting that it could prevent vehicles from entering the car wash in the wrong direction. Lastly, she discussed limitations on vacuum-only access and noted that excess queuing remained.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to provide public comment. \par
\par
Seeing no one present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
There was no cross-examination or rebuttal from either side.\par
}
