action_text: A motion was made by Commissioner Casale for the City's recommended operating millage rate of 6.3501 and a debt service of 0.0289 with a total millage of 6.3790, seconded by Deputy Vice Mayor Markert. The motion carried by the following vote:
attachments: Resolution157-26 City final Millage FY2026-27 09.22.26 lg rev
minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Ms. Gelin read Resolution No. 157-26 into the record. She added that the proposed operating millage rate of 6.3501 mills required approval by a two-thirds vote (a super majority) of the full membership of the City Commission. The City Commission also intended to adopt a debt service millage rate of 0.0289 mills, for a total City millage rate of 6.3790 mills for Fiscal Year 2026-27.\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f1 Mr. Dachowitz reviewed historical millage rates, which decreased from 6.9611 mills to the 2025 rollback rate of 5.9063 mills, the current-year rate of 6.1611 mills, and the proposed Fiscal Year 2027 rate of 6.3501 mills. He discussed the municipal cost index and actual City expenditures, which increased from $117 million up to $200 million over a 10-year period, while the City decreased its millage rate in eight of the last 10 years, even though the City's actual expenditures and the statistic municipal cost index has been increasing over that time period.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f0\par
Projected revenues totaled $214.9 million, beginning with $206.5 million at the proposed operating millage rate of 6.3501 mills. Additional revenues included $8,502,795 from increased taxable property values, $3.88 million from the millage rate increase, and a projected $4.5 million General Fund balance drawdown.\par
\par
The Fiscal Year 2025 fund balance was $49.13 million. The projected drawdown for Fiscal Year 2026 was $2 million, leaving a projected fund balance of $47.131 million, or 22.42% of expenditures less transfers. For Fiscal Year 2027, the projected fund balance drawdown is $4.523 million, leaving a projected year-end fund balance of $42,607,731, or 20.27% of projected expenditures less transfers of $210,179,465.\par
\par
General Fund expenditures included $211,981,960, excluding the CRA TIF, just under $2.1 million in CRA TIF funding from taxable values, and an additional $840,000 in CRA TIF funding resulting from the millage rate increase. Total expenditures were projected at $214,921,795, resulting in a balanced budget.\par
\par
Taxes decreased by $1.567 million, or 1.2%. Permits, fees, and special assessments increased by less than $79,000, or 0.8%; intergovernmental revenue increased by $117,000, or 1%; and charges for services increased by 4.6%. Judgments, fines, and forfeitures remained relatively flat, while miscellaneous revenues increased by approximately $2.5 million, or 14%. Other sources decreased by $6.76 million because the planned fund balance drawdown was not included in that line item.\par
\par
Additional projected revenues included $8.5 million from increased taxable property values, $5.667 million from the millage rate increase, and a projected fund balance drawdown of approximately $4.5 million. Police and Fire were identified as the City\rquote s two largest departments. Police expenditures were projected to increase from $56.699 million to $58.49 million, or 3.2%. Fire expenditures increased from $50 million to $54.11 million, an increase of $4.1 million, or 8.2%. Parks and Recreation, including recreation and other facilities, special events, and the cemetery, increased from $22.95 million to $24.52 million, an increase of $1.57 million, or 6.8%. Public Works Engineering increased from $10.96 million to $12.57 million, an increase of $1.6 million, or 14.7%. Other departments increased by less than $500,000, with Neighborhood and Community Services increasing by $499,705, or 11%. Finance decreased by $594,947.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz explained that departmental expenditure changes reflected reorganizations. Purchasing moved from Finance to its own department reporting to the City Manager; Internal Audit moved from the City Commission to its own department; Education moved from the City Manager to Neighborhood and Community Services; Risk Management moved from Human Resources to Finance; and Pension Administration moved from Finance to Human Resources. These changes affected departmental comparisons.\par
\par
Subtotal expenditures increased from $201 million to $211.6 million, an increase of $10.5 million, or 5.2%. He explained that CRA TIF payments increase as taxable values and the millage rate increase. Total expenditures were projected to increase from $201.1 million to $214.9 million, an increase of $13.8 million, or 6.9%.\par
\par
Across all funds, the General Fund increased by $13.8 million, or 6.9%; Special Revenue Funds decreased by $4.2 million; Enterprise Funds increased from $140.8 million to $156.6 million, an increase of $15.85 million; Debt Service remained flat; Capital Funds increased from $224.6 million to $269.7 million, an increase of $45.1 million, or 20%; and Internal Service Funds decreased by $3.3 million. The adopted budget was $648.5 million, and the tentative budget was approximately $715.8 million, an increase of $67.3 million. Mr. Dachowitz noted that most of the increase was attributable to Capital Funds and Enterprise Funds. The General Fund represented 30% of the budget, Capital Projects 37%, and Enterprise Funds 21.9%.\par
\par
The proposed combined millage rate for all taxing authorities was 18.591 mills: Delray Beach at 6.3790 mills (34.3%), public schools at 6.2870 mills (33.8%), Palm Beach County at 4.5210 mills (24.3%), and other independent districts at 1.4040 mills. A homeowner with an average taxable home value of $481,794 would pay approximately $3,073 in City ad valorem taxes.\par
\par
Mr. Dachowitz noted that growth in taxable property values may slow due to cooling market conditions, bond market concerns, stock market, and declining real estate values in some areas. He stated tht assessed and taxable values increased this year, the rate of increase has declined. He stated that recent tax levy and budgeting changes to Florida law effective July 1st, 2026, limited the ability to increase millage rates by imposing higher voting thresholds. He mentioned that assuming taxable value remains flat next year, the proposed rollback rate would be 6.3501 mills. A 10% increase above the rollback rate (0.63501 mills) would be the maximum increase requiring a two-thirds vote. An increase beyond that amount next year would require a unanimous vote. He noted that if taxable value increases while the millage rate remains at 6.3501 mills, the rollback rate would decrease.\par
\par
General Fund fund balance policy, which requires an unassigned fund balance of 21% to 25% of the current fiscal year\rquote s budgeted operating expenditures, excluding transfers. Compliance is reviewed annually during the budget adoption process, including the amounts of restricted, committed, assigned, non-spendable, and unassigned fund balances.\par
\par
Regarding new construction, he explained that Florida property values are assessed annually based on their status and market value as of January 1st. New construction substantially completed or having received a certificate of occupancy by January 1st is added to that year\rquote s tax roll. He explained that the Property Appraiser submits the preliminary tax roll on July 1st. Notices of proposed property taxes and assessments (TRIM notices) are mailed around August 24, and official property tax bills are mailed in November, when revenue collection begins.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to provide public comment.\par
\par
\ul Martin Dorow\ulnone , 33483\par
Thanked staff and the Commission for their work on the budget. He stated that property value times millage equals the revenue and that increased property values can increase property taxes even when household incomes do not increase. He suggested freezing the previous year\rquote s budget, adjusting for inflation of approximately 3.5%, and slightly lowering the millage rate. He also suggested reviewing expenditures for potential cuts and questioned the $412,000 annual cost of the teen center, stating that he does not see much activity there.\par
\par
\ul Billy Roach\ulnone , 33483\par
Stated that the City\rquote s tax base has grown by over 50% while the Commission has asked taxpayers for more money for two consecutive years. He criticized the City\rquote s response to Amendment Three, stating that officials warned of service and community event cuts if taxpayers received tax relief. He questioned claims that the budget had no remaining areas for cuts and cited the holiday parade, the partially lit Christmas tree, Fourth of July fireworks, Old School Square amphitheater, and the pavilion rebuild costing nearly $1 million due to a procurement mistake. He stated that City revenue had increased while services remained flat or worsened. He urged the Commission to hold the City Manager accountable for identifying budget cuts before increasing taxes and asked officials to represent taxpayers rather than their own political interests.\par
\par
\ul Greg Page\ulnone , 33444\par
Suggested collecting short-term rental revenue, stating that the City was leaving 13% of the revenue uncollected while asking residents to pay more. He questioned the budget increase given the rise in property values and suggested using increased revenue more effectively. He proposed considering tax relief for long-term rental properties that provide lower rents for the workforce, similar to homestead exemptions for residential properties and exemptions for businesses.\par
\par
\ul Mitch Katz, \ulnone 33445\par
Stated that the City\rquote s budget increased from $118 million to $214 million in less than 10 years, while total City expenses increased from $266 million to $715 million. He acknowledged improvements in planning and zoning, building, police, and fire services but questioned the growth in expenditures. He cited a prior $3.5 million deficit that was resolved without service cuts and supported having the City Manager and staff identify how the budget reached its current level. He questioned using $4.5 million from reserves, warning that future withdrawals could deplete the reserves. He urged the City to review its spending and make expenditures more streamlined and effective.\par
\par
\ul Jason Bodnick\ulnone , 407 SE Fourth Avenue\par
Stated that his review of the City\rquote s financial audits from 2014 to 2024 showed that inflation and population adjusted operating spending per resident increased by 40% from 2015 to 2024. He stated that administrative expenses increased by 157%, with the steepest increases in administrative overhead rather than services delivered to residents. He described this as a decline in operational efficiency and suggested reviewing staffing and internal operations, increasing automation, and delivering services with fewer resources. He also stated that reserves decreased by 1.8% year over year and questioned why the City was spending rather than increasing reserves.\par
\par
\ul Chuck Ridley\ulnone , 33444\par
Expressed support for tax relief but emphasized the need to protect neighborhoods with a history of neglect. He highlighted the importance of CRA investments, the Northwest Improvement Plan, parks and recreation, and housing repairs. He cautioned against staffing cuts affecting blue collar workers in Public Works, sanitation, and parks, noting that these employees work hard and earn below what it takes to live in South Florida. He urged the City to pursue efficiency without placing the burden on neglected neighborhoods or workers who deserve greater consideration.\par
\par
\ul Leonard Searles\ulnone , 33444\par
Stated that he and his family have paid millions of dollars in taxes and that he values Delray Beach. He expressed concern about rising property taxes on non-homesteaded properties, describing how increasing taxes on his commercial property at 140 NE Fourth Avenue contributed to his inability to continue operating his business. He warned that rising taxes could force property owners and businesses out of the area. He also discussed selling a property to the land trust, which serves people with basic jobs.\par
\par
Seeing no one present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f1 Mayor Carney stated that the number one thing that everyone's worried about is affordability. He cited Florida has the highest property insurance in the country, rising gas and food prices, and interest rates add additional burdens to the people who can least afford it.\par
\par
He stated that the City's taxes have gone up like the revenues have gone up, 45% in the last five years. He cited $350 million in increased properties coming onto the record following the rollback rate and $1.5 billion in taxable value increase from 2024 to 2025, and from 2025 to 2026 each year. He also cited 77 certificates of occupancy issued through the end of June, representing close to $100 million in value, and stated that more properties would come online in fiscal years 2027 and 2028.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f0\par
\cf0\kerning2\f1 He stated that maintaining the current rate would result in property owners paying approximately 7% more due to increased taxable values. He stated that Mr. Moore had assured him that the City could continue operating without cutting salaries or staff if the operating millage rate remained at 6.1611 mills and the debt service millage was adopted.He projected that the fund balance ratio would fall to 18.9%, and that S&P\rquote s rating criteria began at a 15% reserve level, which he stated remained above the level needed for the City\rquote s credit rating, and represented approximately 2.2 months of operating expenses. Additionally, he stated that maintaining the current rate was expected to generate approximately $6.9 million in additional revenue from increased taxable values.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f0\par
Mayor Carney stated that the reserves percentage should not be in isolation and should be considered alongside continuing revenues, future development, unused taxing capacity, and the ability to redeploy staff and equipment or reprioritize capital projects during emergencies. He suggested additional revenue sources, including business tax receipts for LLC-owned rental properties and changes to Development Services fees. He also compared taxable property value increases in Delray Beach, Boca Raton, and Boynton Beach, citing 16.58%, 14.22%, and 12%, respectively.\par
\par
He concluded that he opposed increasing the operating millage rate and favored maintaining it at 6.1611 mills, along with adopting the debt service millage. He preferred the rollback rate so residents would pay no more than they had the previous year. \par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f1 Commissioner Casale asked City Manager Moore whether maintaining the 6.1611 millage rate was his recommendation. Mr. Moore clarified that his recommendation was 6.3501 mills. He explained that maintaining the 6.1611mill rate would result in a reserve balance of 18.9%, as opposed to 20.27%. She questioned the reduction in reserves and referred to a study done by the City's auditor suggesting a 21% reserve level. She noted that voting on things creates a cost, and that contractual obligations totaled approximately $10.54 million. She cited a staffing increase of 17.28% and that fiscal responsibility required examining spending decisions throughout the year, not only during budget discussions. She stated that she had proposed $4.4 million in cuts, including approximately $1.4 million in overtime reductions and other proposed reductions. She commented that Mayor Carney voted for the contractual obligations\par
\par
She added that Mayor Carney also voted in favor of ratifying the police contract, which she stated would cost approximately $7.7 million in the current fiscal year. Mayor Carney disputed her statement, stating he had voted against the contract; however, Commissioner Casale maintained that the vote was recorded in the minutes and that he had voted in favor of it. Mayor Carney ruled Commissioner Casale was out of order and asked Ms. Gelin to rendition what the vote was to ratify the contract. \par
\par
Ms. Gelin explained that during the impasse, the City Commission presented an offer in the middle of the impasse, that was accepted and subsequently needed to be reduced to writing. She stated that the vote during the impasse was 3-2, with Mayor Carney and Commissioner Casale voting against the offer. Regarding the subsequent ratification, she stated that the minutes indicated that the Mayor indicated he was voting against the contract. She explained that, at that stage, the Mayor was required to vote. Commissioner Casale told the Mayor that he could not vote yes on everything and then question why costs were increasing at the end of the year. She mentioned some of the things that the Mayor voted for. She noted that the Mayor was talking about reducing the millage from 6.3 to 6.1, which was a cost savings of $7.88 per month, and going through the City's reserves. She then asked Mr. Dachowitz to explain the City\rquote s reserves, given that the City would be funding four major projects, and what the determination that day would mean for both the present and the future.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f0\par
Mr. Dachowitz disagreed with the Mayor's assessment that S&P considered all reserve levels above 15% equal, stating that reserve size compared to the expenditures was a major factor in S&P's assessments. He stated that Florida\rquote s credits were under a microscope due to potential revenue challenges from Amendment Three, with no replacement of revenues. He also stated that the City was also subject to inflation and rising costs. He noted that police and fire accounted for 52% of the budget and questioned whether staffing and compensation were being scrutinized, despite community support. He also discussed the challenges of union-based layoffs and called for reviewing departmental expenses, special projects, and events. He stated that the City needed to cut costs and prioritize the City\rquote s interests. \par
\par
During Mr. Dachowitz's explanation, Mayor Carney stated that it was not Mr. Dachowitz's role to educate him and referred to the City Manager. Mr. Moore asked to have the floor, which was granted by the Mayor. However, Mr. Dachowitz asked to be allowed to finish responding to Commissioner Casale, stating that the interruption was rude and improper. Mayor Carney agreed. Mr. Dachowitz concluded that elected officials needed to prioritize the City\rquote s interests over their political constituencies and make difficult, potentially unpopular spending cuts to get the City\rquote s finances in order.\par
\par
Mr. Moore asked everyone to settle down and stated that staff had presented its recommendations, supporting analysis, and different millage and fund balance scenarios. He noted that the Commission had tentatively adopted a millage rate of 6.3501 on September 8th and that staff had considered Commissioner Casale\rquote s suggestions and made additional adjustments. He requested Commission direction so staff could proceed with the fiscal year 2026-2027 budget and beyond.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica asked what difference an 18.9% reserve versus a 20.27% reserve would make to the City\rquote s ability to borrow money, and what the interest rate on a loan or bond would be, with or without Amendment Three, assuming everything else remained the same. Mr. Moore stated that for S&P Global Ratings and Moody\rquote s Investor Service, the impact would probably not make much of a difference at all, as long as the City continues to replenish its fund balance. He agreed that rating agencies are primarily concerned about the aggregate impact of Amendment Three and will assess whether the City can identify alternative revenue sources, raise fees, and make expenditure adjustments to address the resulting revenue challenges.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale stated that Mr. Moore's explanation was fiscally irresponsible and expressed concern that the City was blowing through its reserves and emphasized the importance of protecting them. She noted that reserves were at 35% in 2023, and the policy had been changed from 25% to a flexible 21%-25% to make the rollback rate work. She added that the City also decided to forego a $2 million paving program for over two years and did not hire staff. She stressed that the real effects would come when the City borrowed, noting that reserves were at 30% when bond ratings were obtained.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that Commissioner Casale was basing the reserve when on a different taxable value and that the taxable values have gone up so much in the last four years. Mr. Moore asked to answer the question; however, Commissioner Casale stated that as the financial professional, she thought the Commission should be referring financial questions to Mr. Dachowitz. \par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that he is a financial professional and that the analysis is \ldblquote not fiscally irresponsible\rdblquote but \ldblquote actually responsible.\rdblquote He noted that rating agencies consider multiple metrics, outcomes, variables, and points of analysis. He emphasized the need for municipalities to prepare for the potential passage of Amendment Three, which may require operational adjustments and additional fees to offset revenue losses.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert requested an opportunity for himself and Vice Mayor Burns be heard.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns stated that she was prepared at the previous meeting to support the adjusted millage rate of 6.350, based on the information available at the time. However, two additional points of information led her to support maintaining the millage rate at 6.1, one being the fact that Mr. Moore indicated that the City could operate at the same millage rate, which would take reserves to 18.9%, and the discovery of $1.5 million. She asked whether the $1.5 million was used to reduce the millage rate or increase reserves. Mr. Moore's response was that it increased the reserves. Vice Mayor Burns stated that residents and the City are feeling the economic impact. She noted that if the City can operate at the same millage rate without cutting services, she would support holding the rate at 6.1611 to avoid placing an additional burden on residents.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert thanked Mr. Dachowitz for pulling the budget numbers together and praised the police and fire departments, noting that they represent the bulk of the budget and that their union contracts account for significant costs. He expressed concern that the City was losing its financial edge and could lose its bondworthiness or face significantly higher borrowing rates due to reduced reserves. He emphasized that reserves should not fall below 20%, citing concerns about FEMA assistance and the need for reserves to restore City operations following a major disaster. He stated that significant cuts to events, parks, and other services would be required to balance the budget if further reductions were pursued. He also highlighted the upcoming golf course opening, water treatment facility, and Pompey Park renovations as important investments benefiting the City. He stated that he supported the 6.3501 millage rate and urged the Commission to carefully consider the consequences of reducing reserves, emphasizing the importance of being fiscally responsible for future residents and commissions.\par
\par
Mr. Moore referenced the Development Services Workshop meeting regarding identifying additional positions and opportunities. He stated that recommendations were based on the Commission\rquote s communicated expectations, goals, objectives, and desired outcomes, including continuing major projects, elevating services, and maintaining high service standards, while recognizing that these expectations must be paid for. He committed to reviewing additional opportunities over the next couple of weeks, balancing the Commission\rquote s expectations and requests with building fund resources and current economic realities, and returning with recommendations.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica asked about the required vote to approve a millage rate. Ms. Gelin stated that approval required four out of five votes and that failure to agree on a rate above the rollback rate would revert to the rollback rate, in which Mr. Moore stated was 5.855 mills. Mr. Moore stated that the rollback rate would result in a general fund revenue loss of nearly $5 million and that the budget could not support that loss. He stated that the law should not dictate the future of this community for fiscal year 2026-2027. He emphasized the Commission\rquote s high expectations and noted that the City was receiving statewide and national recognition for its ongoing work. He added that staff had developed scenarios to strike a balance and would work through the resulting challenges in the best interest of the community. He emphasized that the direction should not be based on a rollback rate position.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin explained that advertising requirements for the millage rate and tentative budget prevented incorporating two positions requested by Mr. Moore without a budget amendment. She stated that, based on the earlier discussion, there appeared to be room in the budget at the 6.3501 millage rate to fund the additional positions shown on Anthea\rquote s slide. She clarified that not all positions were building fund positions and that some would require General Fund monies. She appreciated the Mayor\rquote s goal of providing residents tax relief but emphasized that improving processes involved two prongs: staffing side and LDR side. She stated that staffing would need to be addressed in the budget and that the City could consider AI, software, and other alternatives. She cautioned that solving one problem could create an issue somewhere else and emphasized that achieving faster, better, and more efficient processes would cost money. She concluded that the positions would not come free and could not all be funded by the building fund.\par
}

title: Pursuant to Section 3.12 of the Charter of the City of Delray Beach, the Mayor has instructed me to announce a Workshop Meeting of the City Commission to be held for the following purposes:

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mayor Carney made brief remarks before turning the meeting over to Commissioner Mollica, who's idea it was to call the Workshop Meeting. He explained that the first portion would be public comment, focused on ideas for improving the process. He added that comments about individual permit delays should only be raised in the context of proposals for process improvements.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica stated that the spirit of the meeting was to help get to the best place possible for consumers of services and employees, and that nothing said or done was intended to blame anyone or complain about the past. She noted the focus should be on moving forward, with the goal of making the Building Services Department inviting, cordial, and most importantly, efficient and responsive to residents and businesses.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to public comments.\par
\par
\ul James Williams, AW Architects, 33487\ulnone\par
Stated site plan approval required a lot of detail information before architects had a fully developed permit set for the building. He explained that things sometimes shift and change during permit drawings, and that some of those things shouldn\rquote t force you back to the beginning. He added there should be a way of stating how much of a change will draw a new review of everything.\par
\par
\ul Steve Michael, 33483\ulnone\par
Delray Beach resident and developer for 26 years. He stated the permitting process, particularly in the historic district, had been slow to unpredictable and called for consistent decisions, accountability, and standards. He stated the City Center project faced multiple review holds despite following staff guidance, committing time and money, and then faced different directions. He added that minor adjustments should not become an excuse to reopen an approval process, and the City should distinguish the difference between limited administrative amendments and restarting a new approval process. He noted that mandatory requirements should cite the code and staff preferences should be identified as preferences. Mr. Moore stated staff would follow-up with him.\par
\par
\ul Mike Cavalli, 33344\ulnone\par
Read a speech that he had prepared. He stated staff comments sometimes use the Comprehensive Plan to add personal design requirements that aren\rquote t included in the zoning code, and that staff should not create standards beyond Land Development Regulation (LDRs). He suggested clearly defining what applicants were required to comply with under the zoning code.\par
\par
\ul Roger Cope, 33483\ulnone\par
Stated historic preservation should be protected while maintaining an efficient review process. He praised staff for their architectural and historic preservation expertise, and the existing system was working well but could be refined.\par
\par
\ul Sam Caliendo, 33445\ulnone\par
Stated the permitting process takes too long and the City is under-staffed and needs to invest in additional personnel. He cited Boca Raton and Palm Beach County as examples of jurisdictions that had improved permitting through automation and encouraged the City to learn from other communities.\par
\par
\ul Jim Chard, 33483\ulnone\par
Stated the City has smart, dedicated staff but needed specific goals for historic preservation. He suggested that the City proactively advocate for preserving historic properties, including several properties on Marine Way and Federal Highway, and work to expedite preservation efforts.\par
\par
\ul Christina Morrison, 33483\par
\ulnone Stated the City had excellent staff but needed more personnel. She suggested identifying potential delays during pre-submittal meetings, provide alternate paths and clearer timelines, and improve process efficiency. She supported getting additional building staff and process-mapping expertise.\par
\par
\ul Anne Gannon, 33444 - Palm Beach County Tax Collector\par
\ulnone Stated staff had been exceptionally helpful during her historic home project but believed the City should update its LDRs and give staff clearer administrative authority, rather than requiring a hearing through a board. She suggested finding a person who does process mapping, and offered to have her staff work with City staff, explaining that her agency uses green belt, yellow belt, and black belt process mapping to examine every transaction and save money. She emphasized that exceptional service is the goal.\par
\par
\ul Dr. Alan Costello, Big Al Steaks & member of Downtown Development Authority (DDA)\ulnone\par
Described the DDA\rquote s role in enhancing downtown economic vitality and advising the City on business development projects. For 53 years, projects came before the DDA for review and any recommendations, but two years ago, the City Manager no longer allowed Development Services' employees to present at DDA monthly meetings. He characterized the DDA\rquote s role as almost adversarial when advocating for businesses after process issues, and maintained that the process that worked for 53 years was a good one. He asked the City Manager to please reinstate the process.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica announced that Mr. Rick Castor submitted emailed comments for the record.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Mayor Carney closed public comments.\par
}
title: PUBLIC COMMENTS

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that the goal of this meeting was to constructively receive and respond to feedback from the City Commission, work collaboratively across departments, and provide the best service possible. He added that understanding how the process works and who is responsible for each part will help establish realistic expectations and improve outcomes. He noted that the public comments were consistent with staff\rquote s goals and objectives.\par
\par
He introduced Director of Development Services, Anthea Gianniotes; Director of Utilities, Hassan Hadjimiry; Fire Rescue Chief, Ronald Martin; Director of Public Works, Missie Barletto; Chief Technology Officer, Jay Stacy, and Chief Building Official, Steve Tobias.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes provided a brief history of the department\rquote s transition from paper-based reviews to electronic processing through ProjectDox, following a failed software implementation in 2018 and modernization efforts beginning in 2021. The multi-year implementation included Project Docs, Code Enforcement, Planning and Zoning, and full integration in July 2025, allowing simultaneous reviews, online submissions, and better tracking of turnaround times.\cf0 \cf1 Service improvements include a 24/7 customer portal, cross-trained staffing, a development permit manager, a dedicated IT strategist, and process changes to reduce board approvals. She noted the Historic Preservation Board is a one-stop shop, Planning and Zoning provides all-day walk-ins and a Planner on call every day, and single-family permits now take 30 days, with transparent timestamps and durations to identify delays and measure performance.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes provided statistics on new Zoning Certificates of Use (ZCU) applications and Business Tax Receipts (BTRs), including processing times. Approximately 9,000-10,000 building permits were in flux, representing $600-$700 million in permit value, with 39,500 inspections completed to date. Under the new system, intake time improved, and permits completed within 10 days increased from 15% to 43%. State regulations establish review time frames, with the system targeting a 10-day turnaround. The system showed where delays occurred, including staff workload and applicant re-submittals, helping identify staffing needs and distinguish applicant delays from staff delays.\par
\par
She explained that Utilities was the longest review stop, with delays caused by incomplete site verification and plans, deficient designs, missing shop drawings, and resistance to reclaimed water connections. Planning, Zoning, and Historic staff faced competing deadlines across building permits, development reviews, boards, code enforcement, and pre-application meetings, contributing to staff burnout and slower development reviews. She identified potential improvements including additional staffing, a public-facing eServices help desk, permit administration reorganization, AI-assisted application review, and additional building inspectors, and using data to identify and address delays.\par
\par
Mayor Carney thanked Ms. Gianniotes for the presentation and agreed with the data, while suggesting that changes to the application process could improve efficiency.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica asked about response-time standards, application notifications, staff suggestions, and inspection window times. Ms. Gianniotes stated calls were generally returned within 24 hours, staff reviewed process issues monthly, and inspections had a four-hour window. They also discussed adding owners to application notifications.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated applications were slowed by multiple departments and minor issues requiring additional reviews. He supported master permits, more administrative review for de minimus matters, and reviewing application and pre-application fees based on staff time. He also supported using AI to improve permitting. Ms. Gianniotes explained that reviewers worked simultaneously but that changes could cause previously completed reviews to be reopened. She identified additional staff needs, including an IT/customer-service position, Business Tax Receipt (BTR) staff, planners, and building inspectors, and said AI and other technology were being explored. She emphasized that faster service would require either additional resources or changes to the process.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns asked whether applications exceeding review targets were flagged. Mr. Tobias stated that staff monitored them and used red flags to identify priorities. When somet\cf0 hing got stuck in the system, the applicant would contact the department. She then asked which positions would have the most immediate impact on turnaround time and customer service. Ms. Gianniotes stated an IT/customer-service position would help because staff were currently assisting applicants with portal and application issues, taking time away from their regular work.\cf1\par
\par
Commissioner Casale supported identifying process changes to improve efficiency. Additionally, she supported hiring additional staff, particularly where building fund resources were available. She urged the City to include the positions in the current budget, particularly to address staff burnout and improve the permitting process.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert supported adding the requested staff positions as an immediate solution. He emphasized that AI could improve the permitting process, particularly information flow and application review.\par
\par
There was consensus amongst the Commission to include the additional staff requested by Ms. Gianniotes. Mr. Moore concluded that additional positions would come back in October through a budget amendment. He noted that two positions were already included in the proposed budget.\par
\par
There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 5:04 p.m.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 The Commission discussed establishing education and workforce development task forces following the education roundtable. Mayor Carney proposed defining each task force\rquote s goals, membership, timeline, and performance measures, noting that the education and workforce development initiatives should work hand in hand. He suggested a workshop to establish the task forces and begin the appointment process.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin explained that the task forces would serve as fact-finding groups to gather information, report community needs, and provide recommendations to the Commission without delegated decision-making authority. She noted that keeping the groups informal would provide flexibility and avoid the notice, meeting, and minutes requirements applicable to formal boards. Mayor Carney agreed that the groups should have flexibility to communicate and exchange ideas to move the initiatives forward.\par
\par
Janai Bowens explained that the roundtables began in 2024 in collaboration with the Chamber and brought together school district, business, and nonprofit partners. Prior initiatives included the Pacesetters program recognizing outstanding teachers, principals, and students; kindergarten registration drives that registered 300 families for the 2025-2026 school year; and industry tours for Atlantic High School and Village Academy students in hospitality and tourism, automotive, and medical fields.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica stated that the education task force could recommend revisions to the comprehensive plan related to education and propose implementation ideas. She noted that the goal was to bring back an education board without the restrictions of a formal board. Commissioner Casale reported that the workforce development group had identified workforce challenges, employer needs for credentials and certifications, and measures of success. The group planned to increase awareness of available programs among students and families, connect employers with available workers, expand participation by nonprofit partners and employers in targeted industries, and develop future outreach events and a marketing program.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert emphasized the need for clear objectives, agreed timelines, and measurable outcomes for task forces. Vice Mayor Burns noted that previous roundtable efforts had produced kindergarten readiness registration drives and a school showcase. The Commission discussed maintaining flexibility for fact-finding and information gathering while ensuring clear direction and accountability.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin stated that groups involving City staff must be formally established, which could be done through a resolution, and that the Commission could appoint individuals already participating. Mr. Moore proposed a workshop before the November 2, 2026 Regular Commission Meeting to formalize the task forces and establish their direction.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Deputy Vice Mayor Markert provided an overview of Florida e-bike laws, local regulatory flexibility, and regulations adopted or considered by neighboring municipalities. He explained that state law establishes three e-bike classifications, with maximum assisted speeds of 20 mph for Classes 1 and 2 and 28 mph for Class 3. E-bikes generally have the same rights and duties as bicycles, and the state does not require licensing, registration, titles, or insurance. Class 3 riders must be at least 16 years old. He outlined local options, including setting minimum ages, accepting school-issued IDs, requiring safety training, establishing rules for streets and sidewalks, and restricting e-bikes on bike paths, trails, beaches, dunes, and in parks. He noted that municipalities commonly consider minimum ages of 15 to 16, speed limits on multi-use paths, helmet requirements for riders under 16, and restrictions on sidewalk riding. He also discussed safe passing, audible signals, stunt riding, traffic-law compliance, and civil fines for violations. He reviewed neighboring municipalities\rquote approaches, noting differences in sidewalk rules, park restrictions, safety training, and parking regulations. He also discussed e-bike battery fires and potential parking considerations, noting that fires are statistically rare and may result from uncertified replacement parts, damaged management systems, unregulated voltage, physical damage, or extreme temperatures. \par
\par
Commissioner Casale requested that the City expedite an e-bike ordinance, identifying pedestrian-priority areas, sidewalk speed limits, restrictions in downtown Atlantic Avenue, the beach/A1A area, Pineapple Grove, parks, playgrounds, and sensitive areas. Deputy Vice Mayor Markert noted safety concerns involving e-bikes traveling at high speeds near driveways with limited visibility.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin explained that state law limits local regulation but allows the City to establish minimum age, identification, and training requirements. The Commission generally supported a minimum age of 16 and discussed whether to accept school-issued IDs, require government-issued identification, and mandate helmets. Commissioner Casale recommended requiring helmets if permitted by law. Ms. Gelin stated that the City\rquote s code already groups motorized scooters, bicycles, and e-bikes as micromobility devices and that additional requirements could be added to the existing framework. She agreed to prepare an ordinance for the Commission\rquote s review.\par
\par
\ul\b Commissioner Casale\ulnone :\ul\par
\ulnone\b0 Expressed concern about ongoing complaints regarding Subculture, stated that the situation was problematic and requested that Mr. Moore find a solution. She also stated that the City needs to follow its processes and procedures if violations existed. Mr. Moore said he would provide an update.at the next Commission meeting.\par
\par
Asked about the status of the Financial Review Committee and whether applications were available online. Mr. Moore stated that the City Clerk\rquote s Office was facilitating applications online and that Commission appointments were expected in the coming weeks. Commissioner Casale noted she had not seen the opportunity publicized and requested an email notifying commissioners of the application deadline so they could encourage qualified candidates to apply. Mr. Moore agreed.\par
\par
Congratulated Danielle Pearson for receiving her CFEE certification.\par
\par
Addressed the $500 public records request fee, acknowledging the request was extensive. Suggesting that information regarding the possible locations of individuals within the cemetery be shared free of charge as it becomes available. Ms. Gelin explained that the request sought extensive Police Department records, including body-worn camera footage that would require hours of redaction. Commissioner Casale clarified that she was not disputing the fee but wanted the public to understand it resulted from the request\rquote s extensive scope.\par
\par
Clarified her comments from the previous meeting regarding the millage rate and the financial impact of Commission decisions, including police collective bargaining wage increases. She acknowledged that the exchange with the Mayor was not respectful and stated that the official record showed the Mayor voted for the wage increases at impasse on August 21, 2025 and to ratify the contract on September 15, 2025. She emphasized the importance of providing residents accurate information, taking responsibility for votes, and holding all Commission members accountable. She requested that the documents she provided be entered into the record and attached to the minutes.\par
\par
\ul\b Mayor Carney\ulnone\b0 :\par
Stated that he voted to ratify the police contract because the City Attorney advised it was legally required, although he did not support the contract. \par
\par
Regarding the workforce development task force, he requested regular reports to the Commission on discussions and proposed that commissioners be allowed to attend meetings, with appropriate public notice if necessary. \par
\par
Requested that Mr. Moore arrange a discussion on the City\rquote s dedication policies to clarify their purpose and determine whether modifications were needed, noting that dedications can affect property lines and development. \par
Stated Wellington\rquote s e-bike ordinance as a model for addressing e-bike use and supported pursuing helmet requirements, particularly for 16-year-olds.\par
\par
\ul\b Commissioner Mollica\ulnone\b0 :\par
Thanked Deputy Vice Mayor for the e-bike presentation and all the work and research he put into it. Deputy Vice Mayor Markert credited the Metropolitan Planning Organization.\par
\par
Commended the Public Safety Open House held Saturday at the fire station.\par
\par
Thanked Chief Hunter and the Police Department for their downtown presence which makes citizens feel safe.\par
\par
Requested consensus for the City Auditor to review cemetery records, including burial locations and purchases, noting these details were beyond the cemetery consultant\rquote s scope. Mayor Carney, Vice Mayor Burns, and Deputy Vice Mayor Markert supported the request. Mr. Moore clarified that the consultant would provide aggregate recommendations, not conduct an audit, and said a status report would be available by the end of the following week.\par
\par
\ul\b Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone\b0 :\par
Provided a summary of the September 23 League of Cities meeting she attended regarding Florida Amendment Three and its potential impact on local government and property tax revenues. The panel expressed that the amendment does not specifically protect funding from services such as police and fire rescue, stressed the distinction between education and advocacy, stated that local governments and elected officials were advised that they may educate residents about how the amendment could affect municipal budgets and services, but should consult with the city attorney on legal limitations on what they can say publicly, agreed that one of the greatest challenges is public misunderstanding. That some residents believe that the amendment would eliminate their property tax bill entirely, which is not the case.\par
\par
Requested consensus to not move forward with Phase Two of the Old School Square needs assessment and market study and establish a task force of residents, stakeholders, City partners and organizations to provide recommendations. There was consensus among the Commission. The Commission discussed the need for a neutral, comprehensive analysis of Old School Square\rquote s future use and management. Mayor Carney supported a task force and stated that government should not be programming entertainment venues. Commissioner Casale expressed concern that the initial presentation did not provide the expected recommendations and questioned how to proceed without them. Ms. Gelin clarified that the consultant\rquote s contract covered Phase One and that the final report with recommendations for optimal facility concepts remained outstanding. Ms. Barletto explained that the research included interviews and was intended to inform the recommendations. Mr. Moore stated that the Phase One report would accompany a task force consideration item at a November Commission meeting, to begin developing a framework for Old School Square\rquote s future.\par
\par
Thanked residents for their comments regarding the tone and conduct of the previous meeting, emphasizing professionalism, fairness, respect, and treating employees and the public with dignity. \par
\par
Commended Mr. Wise for locating her father\rquote s burial site at the cemetery using old documents after years of unsuccessful searches by her family. She thanked the consultant for receiving public comments at the September 30 meeting and reiterated her support for an audit of the cemetery. \par
Ms. Gelin read Resolution No. 148-26 into the record. \par
\par
Alexis Givings, City Clerk, swore in those individuals who wished to provide testimony on this item and on Item No. 7.B.\par
\par
Vice Mayor asked her colleges to disclose any ex-parte communications.\par
\par
\ul Commissioner Mollica\ulnone : None \par
\ul Deputy Vice Mayor Markert\ulnone : None\par
\ul Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone : None\par
\ul Commissioner Casale\ulnone : Only if there is anything on the server.\par
\ul Mayor Carney\ulnone : None\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, entered File 000646-2026 into the record.\par
\par
Leo Carneiro of Luxcon Builders presented a proposal to build a two-story family home in the Lake Ida neighborhood. He stated that the existing home was built in 1956 and that the proposed home would reduce the footprint by over 500 square feet, improve landscaping, and include a wraparound porch and outdoor areas. He explained that the garage would be under air and that the floor area ratio calculation did not reflect the full garage area. He stated that the proposed home would fit the neighborhood, meet the criteria, and not adversely affect the neighborhood or public facilities. He requested approval of the waivers and comments from the neighbors.\par
\par
Aaron Fishman, Mr. Carneiro's business partner, stated that the home was designed for families, included a wraparound porch, and was shifted to the corner. He stated that the existing sea grape tree would remain.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin stated that the Commission was considering only two waivers and asked the Commission to disregard the additional comments.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes explained that the Lake Ida Neighborhood Overlay guidelines were adopted in 2008 to ensure compatibility and protect neighborhood character through measurable criteria. She stated that the proposed five-bedroom, four-and-a-half-bath home would have 3,824 square feet of living space and a 492-square-foot garage, compared to the existing 2,900-square-foot, four-bedroom, three-bath home. She explained that the applicant requested three waivers for lot coverage, floor area ratio (FAR), and second-floor size. Ms. Gianniotes stated that the proposed lot coverage was 2,880 square feet, or 34.9%, exceeding the 30% limit by 405 square feet. The proposed FAR was 0.49, compared to the 0.35 limit, exceeding the allowable area by 1,253 square feet. She explained that the second floor was 88.6% of the first floor, exceeding the 75% maximum, and that the regulations build on each other, so granting a larger first floor also allows a larger second floor. She stated that the proposed home would remain a single-family house and that public facilities and Florida Building Code requirements were not applicable to the waiver criteria. She explained that the Commission would primarily consider criteria A and D. Ms. Gianniotes raised concern that the code provisions should be loosened for everyone if they were considered too restrictive, rather than for one case. She stated that the proposed home had not been built and was still a drawing.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns opened the floor to anyone who wished to provide public comment.\par
\par
\ul Jen Davis\ulnone , 1502 Northwest 14th Street\par
Stated that she initially supported the proposed design but agreed with the Development Services Director\rquote s concern that allowing a larger first-floor footprint would result in a larger second floor. She expressed concern that the proposed house was too large, noting that the second floor would be 88.6% of the first floor and describing the design as a box.\par
\par
\ul Andrea Sherman\ulnone , 222 Northwest 15th Street \par
Stated that she participated in developing the Lake Ida Overlay guidelines in 2008 and noted there was a reason for the guidelines. She expressed concern that the proposed house would be too large for the small lot and would be a massive piece of property.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Vice Mayor Burns closed public comment. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns opened the floor for rebuttal.\par
\par
Mr. Carneiro stated that the purpose of the proposal was to reduce the mass of the building. He explained that the 2D rendering did not show the perception of depth and that the garage was 20 feet from the road to where the second floor started. He disagreed that the home would be a box and stated that the proposed architecture was a mixture of styles in the area. He presented four pictures of homes similar to the proposed home and noted that there had been 32 other waivers. He asked the Commission to consider approving the home for his client.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin reminded the Commission that each waiver and variance stands on its own and that the applicant must establish the criteria presented by Anthea Gianniotes to justify approval. She stated that waivers granted on other properties were irrelevant.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes clarified that staff audited multiple properties but did not find 32 waivers granted. She stated that approximately four or five properties had been brought forward, with each potentially having one or two waivers, depending on the mistakes discovered.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that the property had nothing special about it to justify waivers from the overlay guidelines. He questioned whether the other homes presented had been analyzed to determine whether they exceeded the FAR and stated that the proposed home could still be beautiful without waivers. Commissioner Mollica stated that she would not support the waivers because the home did not fit within the overlay guidelines. Commissioner Casale stated that the overlays were developed with community input and that the Commission should enforce its regulations. She questioned whether the neighborhood should revisit the guidelines adopted in 2008. Deputy Vice Mayor Markert stated that the overlays were in place to guide growth and that the proposed home was outside the guidelines. He supported revisiting the guidelines at some point. Vice Mayor Burns agreed that the neighborhood established the overlays for a reason and that the Commission needed to respect them. She stated that granting the waivers would be a special privilege and would have an effect on the neighboring area.\par

\par
\ul Commissioner Mollica\ulnone : Spoke with Jordana Jarjura.\par

\ul Mayor Carney\ulnone : Spoke with Jordana Jarjura.\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, entered File 2025-116 into the record. \par
\par
Jordana Jarjura, Government Law Group, representing VF Realty, requested Site Plan Level 2 approval for five townhomes on Southwest Third Avenue and a landscape waiver for the street tree locations. She stated that the project was unanimously approved by SPRAB and met 23 Comprehensive Plan goals, objectives, and policies, as well as the applicable LDR requirements, except for the street tree locations. She stated that the project met the required findings for site plan approval and the criteria for granting the waiver. Ms. Jarjura described the approximately half-acre vacant property, located in the RM zoning district within the West Atlantic Southwest neighborhood. She explained that the proposed development included five townhomes, with a height of just under 24 feet compared to the 35-foot maximum, a density of 10.71 units per acre, and open space of 51.1%, twice the required amount. She stated that the project was below the maximum FAR and met the applicable performance standards for infill development. She stated that the project provided 25 trees and two palm clusters, exceeding the 17 required trees. The requested street tree waiver was due to an existing eight-inch sewer line and the requirement for trees to be at least 10 feet from underground utilities. She explained that the proposed tree locations would avoid conflicts with the sewer infrastructure and provide canopy coverage and visual enhancement along Southwest Third Avenue. Ms. Jarjura stated that similar street tree waivers had been approved by SPRAB and offered to answer questions.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes stated that each property stands on its own and that density and waivers are considered case by case. She explained that the project was a Level 2 site plan for five two-story fee-simple townhomes with a waiver to reduce and relocate street trees. SPRAB approved the project unanimously, 4-0, but did not have a full board present. Ms. Gianniotes explained that the RM district has a base density of six units per acre and that higher density must substantially meet LDR Section 4.3.3.BB. She stated that the existing sewer line prevented street trees from being planted in the public right-of-way, so they were shifted to five-foot landscape buffers between driveways. She noted that the staff report identified vehicular and pedestrian conflicts at each driveway. She explained that the alley was unimproved and not scheduled for improvement, and that the well-field area added complications. She stated that the project would introduce a new housing type to an area primarily consisting of duplexes and single-family homes. She noted that the code calls for a mix of unit types, including three- and four-bedroom single-family attached and detached units, while the proposed townhomes were all three-bedroom units. Ms. Gianniotes stated that the project would diversify the neighborhood\rquote s housing stock, was not maximizing density at 10.7 units per acre, and was limited to two stories. She explained that the Commission should consider whether the infill development was reasonable given the property\rquote s constraints.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns opened the floor to anyone who wished to provide public comment.\par
\par
\ul Carolyn Young\ulnone , 15112 Tall Oak Avenue, Delray Beach \par
Stated that she owns multiple properties on Southwest Third Avenue. She expressed concern about the density of five townhomes but stated that the project would be an improvement to the area. She noted that there were no two-story units on the street between First and Southwest Second Street and wanted to ensure the density would not negatively impact the neighborhood. She stated that the area had low traffic, other than City trucks and residents, and that she would have no objection and would be in favor of the project.\par
\par
Seeing no one else present, Vice Mayor Burns closed public comment. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns opened the floor for rebuttal. \par
\par
Ms. Jarjura stated that traffic concurrency was found by the County and the engineers\rquote report showed a de minimis impact on trips to the area. She explained that front-loaded parking was permitted because the alley was unimproved, had a substandard right-of-way, and lacked a stabilized base to support vehicular traffic. She stated that Wellfield Zone Two was required and unbuildable, making driveway and garage access through the well-field area infeasible. Ms. Jarjura stated that requiring a single-family home instead of the allowable density would impose on the property owner\rquote s property rights. She explained that the code allows up to 12 units per acre and provides for front-loaded parking when there is no dedicated access to the side or rear. She noted that the entire street was front-loaded and included a mix of uses, including the police station and courthouse. She stated that delaying the property owner for seeking allowable density was a poor precedent and respectfully disagreed with staff\rquote s position and the public hearing concerns.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes stated that additional density could be achieved through a different typology with a single vehicular access point and a larger front yard. She explained that options included workforce housing, fewer units in a different pattern, and more room for trees in the front yard. She stated that the Commission could determine whether the proposed infill pattern was acceptable for this part of the City and approve it.\par
\par
\f1 Commissioner Casale stated that the project was not consistent with the neighborhood, which did not have similar two-story homes. She noted concerns in the staff report regarding front-loaded parking, vehicular-pedestrian conflicts, and trees. She stated that the applicant could return with three units, larger yards, and more trees, and that residents wanted less development, more green space, and more trees. \cf0 She expressed concern regarding the ability of residents to hear the presentations and provide their input.\par
\cf2\par
\cf1 Mayor Carney stated that the project would add value to the neighborhood and that the property was across from the building\rquote s back parking lot. He noted that the alley was not expected to be developed in the near future and that the well field limited access for deliveries. He stated that the project could start a development trend in the neighborhood and that he supported it. \par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert stated that he reviewed the project and drove the area. He supported the project and noted that constraints involving utility lines and tree relocation had been addressed. \par
\par
Commissioner Mollica stated that she supported the project and had no problem with the waiver. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns stated that the project is great and that the neighbors would appreciate it and that it would do wonders for the neighborhood.\par
\f0\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 This item was moved to be addressed first. It became Item No. 7.A.A. on the Regular Agenda.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin read Resolution No. 107-26 into the record. \par
\par
Ms. Gelin explained that the City issued the solicitation in March and received five proposals. The selection committee reviewed all five proposals, and the Purchasing Department initially announced that they were responsive and responsible. Ms. Gelin stated that, after the Commission\rquote s August 18 decision to hear presentations from all proposers, she reviewed the proposals and identified concerns regarding the minimum qualifications for 10 years of management and operational experience and tournament experience. Purchasing requested additional information from the three remaining proposers: Barrel Group, FM Tennis, and JCD Sports Group. Following further review, Ms. Gelin provided Mr. Moore with a memorandum stating that two of the three proposers did not meet the minimum qualifications. Mr. Moore subsequently determined that Barrel Group and FM Tennis were not responsive and not responsible, leaving JCD Sports Group as the only remaining provider. Ms. Gelin explained that the current solicitation increased the management experience requirement from five to ten years and changed the contract term from five to ten years compared with the 2021 solicitation. She stated that Mr. Moore had authority under the City\rquote s purchasing policies and procedures to evaluate responsibility at any point and that the process did not violate those policies. She noted that the selection committee\rquote s scoring showed a difference of more than 50 points among proposals. Ms. Gelin outlined two options: award the contract to JCD Sports Group under the solicitation\rquote s five-year term with five one-year renewals, or cancel the solicitation and begin the process again. She noted that the current agreement expires in December and that revising the solicitation would require further Commission discussion. She also stated that the agreement includes a termination-for-convenience clause.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns asked whether repeating the solicitation without changing its requirements would produce the same result. Ms. Gelin stated that she did not think the result would change. Commissioner Mollica questioned the 10-year experience requirement and asked about the prior contract terms. Sam Mettot, Parks & Recreation Director, explained that the City sought to make the RFP more thorough and consistent with the golf course management solicitation. He stated that the golf course contract included a five-year agreement with an additional five years and that the prior tennis contract was three years with two additional years. Ms. Gelin stated that all proposals were considered by the selection committee and that the proposals were publicly available. Deputy Vice Mayor Markert supported the staff recommendation, stating that only one company met the criteria and that a five-year term with one-year renewals was appropriate. Mayor Carney disagreed, stating that the Commission should have a role in determining RFP requirements. He questioned the 10-year experience requirement, stating that it excluded companies with five years of experience and resulted in only the current provider qualifying. He recommended canceling the RFP and issuing a new solicitation with a five-year experience requirement. Ms. Gelin stated that the Commission could direct staff to change the requirement. Commissioner Casale supported a fair and transparent process but stated that changing the experience requirement would not change the scoring and that the same group would score the proposals. Vice Mayor Burns supported the staff recommendation.\par
\par
\b\fs20 A motion was made by Mayor Carney to cancel the current RFP and issue a new RFP requiring five years of management experience, seconded by Commissioner Mollica.. The motion failed by the following vote:\par
No:\b0 3 - Deputy Vice Mayor Markert, Commissioner Casale, and Vice Mayor Burns \par
\b Yes:\b0 2 - Commissioner Mollica and Mayor Carney \par
\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that following the May 8, 2026 goal-setting session, the workshop would provide an overview of performance and activity metrics to support Vision 2035 related goals and objectives, connecting the FY 2026-2027 budget\rquote s allocation of resources to the specific goals and objectives. He introduced Interim Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Carmen Aleman to provide a brief overview. Additionally, he noted that Urban3 would present on the financial impact of land use and public policy in Delray Beach, as a result of consultancy services commissioned by the Department of Development Services. \par
\par
Carmen Aleman provided an overview of how the FY 2026-2027 budget supported Vision 2035\rquote s five focus areas: economic development, education, environment, historic preservation, and strategic development. Economic development initiatives included marketing strategies, expanded Creative Arts School offerings, workforce housing and assistance programs, infrastructure improvements, Freebee transportation, the Arts Garage, and business expos and career fairs. Education initiatives included student shadowing and internships, after-school and youth programming, library support, and the planned education and workforce development task forces. Environmental initiatives included advocacy for funding, progress toward the 28% tree canopy goal, reef planting, dune management, sea turtle nest monitoring, beach nourishment, an additional lifeguard, and bioswale installations. She mentioned that the City added a pavement preservation program to maintain roads, and new positions in the Development Services Department would strengthen historic preservation and strategic development. She concluded that these initiatives reflected the City\rquote s continued commitment to advancing Vision 2035 through the FY 2026-2027 budget.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale emphasized the need for real developed goals and objectives that carry out into the future and an action plan outlining what the City plans on doing in the next five - ten years. She expressed support for the City\rquote s economic development, education, and environmental initiatives but stressed the need for a greater plan to establish where the City is going, what it needed in the future, and how to communicate what the City is working towards.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert supported a three-year strategic plan communicated to residents.\par
\par
Mr. Moore explained that following the FY 2026-2027 budget process, the City wanted to introduce the first steps toward an alignment with the different categories outlined in Vision 2035, noting that much of what was talked about had already been initiated, and that alignment is a continuous process moving forward.\par
\par
The City Commission thanked Ms. Aleman for the presentation.\cf1\f1\par

title: PRESENTATION - OVERVIEW OF PERFORMANCE AND ACTIVITY METRICS TO SUPPORT VISION 2035 RELATED GOALS AND OBJECTIVES

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}
{\colortbl ;\red0\green0\blue0;}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Development Services Director, Anthea Gianniotes, explained that development decisions raised concerns about residential uses cutting in on commercial land use, providing workforce housing, and the cost of infrastructure. She stated that she reached out to Urban3 to provide a financial analysis of development decisions and their impacts. She introduced Joe Minicozzi, noting his design background, education at Harvard University, and public and private sector experience. She explained that the presentation would provide a story about the City, the different development patterns, land use and information to just provide data moving forward, with a final report to follow. She encouraged the Commission to let the whole story unfold before asking questions.\par
\par
Mr. Minicozzi began by describing his hometown of Asheville in the 1980s and 1990s as completely boarded up and explained that they we were too poor to tear anything down. He discussed using money to fix buildings and start businesses through a revolving fund to do rehab. He noted that political discussions often failed to understand the actual mechanics of how it operated. He explained that we\rquote ve basically lost this sense of civics and we don\rquote t understand how this whole system operates. Referring to a 1959 Florida third grade teacher\rquote s guide, he highlighted that counties often had a duplication of services and overlapping jurisdictions, and a lack of coordination between the county and the local communities.\par
\par
He presented an analysis of how land use, property taxation, and infrastructure costs affect the financial health of Delray Beach and Palm Beach County. He emphasized measuring property value and tax revenue per acre rather than total property value alone. Using examples of existing businesses along Atlantic Avenue, including Shoes and More and Big Al\rquote s, he demonstrated how small commercial buildings, walkable downtown development, townhouses, and mixed-use properties can generate substantial value and tax revenue on relatively small parcels compared with large commercial properties with extensive parking. He highlighted Delray Beach\rquote s historic downtown as a productive development pattern and presented findings that historic and non-historic properties along the studied corridor have generally tracked similarly in value per square foot in recent years. He encouraged officials to identify and replicate successful local development patterns and explore opportunities for additional neighborhood centers, including along Congress Avenue and in western areas of the city.\par
\par
He also explained how Florida\rquote s Save Our Homes Amendment and property tax exemptions affect taxable values and local government revenues. He illustrated the growing gap between market values and taxable values and compared revenue growth with rising costs for infrastructure and public services, including asphalt, police vehicles, and fire trucks. He emphasized that Delray Beach\rquote s development contributes to Palm Beach County\rquote s tax base and encouraged greater coordination between the City and County. He further stressed the importance of evaluating the full lifecycle costs of roads, utilities, and stormwater infrastructure, noting that maintenance and replacement obligations accumulate over time. Drawing on his work in Orange County, Florida, he demonstrated how local governments can compare the revenue generated by development with the costs of providing services and maintaining infrastructure to determine whether projects produce a fiscal surplus or deficit. He concluded by urging officials to know their financial statistics, measure land productivity, replicate productive development examples, account for long-term infrastructure costs, and use clear maps and data to help residents understand the financial consequences of public policies and development decisions.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns stated the data presented was some of the best, in the last four years.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale indicated that the presentation was very informative and wished it had been presented prior to the budget, as there have been inquiries about reasons for rising costs. She added that the City's expenses are out pacing the revenues and it's a concern. She noted that the wherever the City can get mixed use, it should, just based on this presentation.\par
\par
The City Commission thanked Mr. Minicozzi for the presentation and are looking forward to reviewing the hard copy.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes stated that the key takeaways were how strong mixed-use is performing and the unexpected surprise of how strong the townhouses and row houses are. She noted that there is an opportunity to regroup and determine where to focus. She stated that staff would be reaching out to Orange County because a model was built that has the inputs on infrastructure costs, and they are using that to weigh different development proposals for their long-term benefit costs. She wants to find out how they are using it and how effective it is.\par
\par
There being no further business to discuss, Vice Mayor Burns adjourned the meeting at 5:00 p.m.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore introduced a presentation on the City's municipal bond ratings, citing interest in the City's rating history and anticipated financing needs in 2027. He explained that municipal financings involve ratings from agencies such as S&P Global Ratings and Moody's Investor Services and noted that the City had received several ratings and adjustments over the past few years. Mr. Moore introduced the City's external financial advisor, Jay Glover, Managing Partner of PFM Financial Advisors, to provide an overview of the City's ratings history and recent activity. \par
\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
Mr. Glover reviewed the City's credit ratings, noting that Moody's upgraded the City's general obligation (GO) bond rating from AA2 to AA1 in 2024, while S&P assigned a AAA rating. In 2025, S&P downgraded its rating from AAA to AA+, while Moody's affirmed its AA1 rating. He explained that the ratings were aligned and that the downgrade did not affect borrowing costs because investors price bonds based on the lower rating. He also reviewed the City's water and sewer bond ratings of AA from Moody's and AA- from S&P. Mr. Glover discussed anticipated financing needs for parks, the public safety complex, stormwater improvements, water and sewer projects, and CRA projects. He stated that the City would continue working with Moody's and S&P and that the current ratings have a stable outlook. He also explained that further downgrades could increase borrowing costs and that maintaining reserves is an important factor in the City's credit ratings.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale questioned the City's use of reserves, the impact of the downgrade on borrowing costs, and the failure to provide the Commission with the October 2025 S&P rating report. She stated that the information was relevant to budget decisions and taxpayer costs. Mr. Glover clarified that the downgrade reflected the City's use of reserves to bring its unassigned fund balance closer to its adopted policy target of 21% to 25% of budgeted operating expenditures. He confirmed that the downgrade did not affect borrowing costs because Moody's already held the equivalent rating, but further downgrades could increase interest costs.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica stated that she had received information regarding the downgrade and discussed it during the budget meeting. Vice Mayor Burns requested clarification regarding the reserve policy and the impact of the split ratings. Deputy Vice Mayor Markert emphasized the importance of maintaining reserves for borrowing costs, long-term financial stability, and potential emergencies.\par
\par
Mayor Carney asked whether reducing expenditures would improve the City's rating. Mr. Glover confirmed that both increased revenues and decreased expenditures could contribute to a surplus and improve fund balances. He also clarified that rating agencies conduct surveillance at least every two years without an ongoing fee.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale reiterated that the City Manager's October 2026 letter acknowledged that the October 28, 2025, S&P rating documents had not been provided. Mr. Moore accepted responsibility and committed to providing rating agency materials and updates as part of the 2027 financing process. Mayor Carney emphasized the importance of transparency when credit ratings change. Mr. Moore reaffirmed his commitment to providing the information moving forward.\par
}
