\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\fs24 Ms. Gelin identified Item Nos. 9.C. and 9.D. as additional quasi-judicial hearings.\par
\par
\cf0\kerning2\f1 Ms. Givings swore in those individuals who wished to provide testimony on Item Nos. 7.B., 9.C. and 9.D.\cf1\kerning0\f0 \par
\par
Mayor Carney read the quasi-judicial rules into the record.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin read Resolution No. 163-26 into the record.\par
\par
Anthea Gianniotes, Development Services Director, entered File Number PZ 000773-2026 into the record. \par
\par
Mayor Carney asked his colleagues to disclose any ex-parte communications.\par
\par
\ul Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone : None\par
\ul Commissioner Mollica\ulnone : None\par
\ul Commissioner Casale\ulnone : None\par
\ul Deputy Vice Mayor Markert\ulnone : None\par
\ul Mayor Carney\ulnone : He followed up with Ms. Gianniotes to obtain an update. \par
\par
Kristen Ritchie, First Water Building & Design, requested a waiver for the retaining wall located at the corner of Basin Drive and Lowry Drive. She explained that the new home was elevated to NAVD 9 feet due to its location in a FEMA AE-8 flood zone. The Land Development Regulations require the wall height to be measured from the undisturbed grade. The Basin Drive measurement was 2 feet, resulting in a measured wall height of 7 feet, although the actual concrete wall is 6 feet from top to bottom. She stated that the Lowry Drive measurement was 2.9 feet and did not require a waiver. Ms. Ritchie presented photographs showing the wall, surrounding vegetation, and neighboring property. She stated that the neighboring wall measures approximately 9.1 feet and that approval would be consistent with surrounding properties. She explained that the family requested the higher wall for safety and stated that the waiver would not adversely affect neighboring properties, public facilities, or create an unsafe situation. She respectfully requested approval and offered to answer questions.\par
\par
Ms. Gianniotes explained that properties on the Barrier Island are in an AE-8 flood zone and must meet the required elevation criteria. She stated that the wall exceeded the allowable height by one foot and that mature landscaping was preserved, with additional landscaping along Basin Drive. She noted that the design was not out of character with the neighboring property. Ms. Gianniotes stated that the Commission could grant the waiver or require removal of the concrete cap and lowering the wall, which would result in a five-foot wall. She explained that the City\rquote s administrative adjustment ordinance allows a 5% or one-foot adjustment, whichever is less, and that the request could not be handled administratively under the current language. She also noted that the City had hoped to adopt a fill ordinance but was unable to do so due to Senate Bill 180.\par
\par
Mayor Carney opened the floor to anyone who wished to provide public comment.\par
\par
Seeing no one present, Mayor Carney closed public comment.\par
\par
Mayor Carney confirmed there was no cross-examination.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale noted concerns about similar cases involving substantially greater wall heights and stated that the City should address after-the-fact issues. Ms. Gianniotes stated that the Building Division now has a floodplain manager who coordinates with contractors during construction to address these issues. She noted that the contractor nearly met the requirements and that maintaining the mature vegetation was important to the neighborhood. Mayor Carney noted that FEMA may make additional changes affecting the Barrier Island and that similar cases may arise more frequently. He stated that the adjustment should have been handled administratively and suggested making a correction to the administrative process.He requested consensus.\par
\par
\b\fs20 A motion was made by Commissioner Casale, to approve Resolution No. 163-26, seconded by Vice Mayor Burns. The motion carried by the following vote:\b0\par
\par
\b Yes\b0 : 5 - Deputy Vice Mayor Markert, Commissioner Mollica, Commissioner Casale, Vice Mayor Burns, and Mayor Carney\fs24\par
\par
Consensus was given directing staff to return with a corrective Ordinance.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\cf1\ul\b\fs24 Commissioner Mollica\ulnone\b0 : \par
Requested consensus to have the City Manager, staff, and Jay Stacy evaluate a company offering AI technology for zoning. She stated that the City should explore using AI to avoid falling behind other cities. Commissioner Casale, Vice Mayor Burns, and Mayor Carney expressed support. Mayor Carney noted that AI could review plans, shorten response times, and improve customer satisfaction.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that staff would evaluate available tools and return to the Commission with an update on potential options and implementation. He noted that the organization was evolving in its AI training. Ms. Gelin reminded the Commission that the City must follow its purchasing policies. Mr. Moore stated that staff would consider the applicable policies and provide an update in the coming weeks.\par
\par
\ul\b Deputy Vice Mayor Markert\ulnone\b0 :\par
Requested that staff evaluate the possibility of allowing dogs off leash at Cornell Park for a set period of time, following requests from Lake Ida residents. He asked staff to review available options and practices in other major cities.\par
\par
Mr. Moore stated that staff would examine the proposal, including potential liability concerns, and clarify that the request was not to designate the park as a dog park. He offered to provide an update to the Commission in December. The Commission reached consensus to proceed with the evaluation.\par
\par
\ul\b Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone\b0 :\par
Stated that Straghn & Son successfully held its Trunk or Treat event after resolving issues with the City. She requested a process to simplify approvals for longstanding private events that remain on the same property and do not require road closures. Ms. Gelin stated that language could be added to the Special Events Policy to make the process easier for recurring events with minimal City impacts. The Commission reached consensus to direct the City Attorney to develop language for the policy.\par
\par
\ul\b Commissioner Casale\ulnone\b0 :\par
Commended Utilities Department employees, including William, Mr. Hadjimiry, and two other employees, for their thoughtful and accommodating response to an after-hours emergency call. \par
\par
Acknowledged additional opioid litigation settlement money.\par
\par
Requested a review of the nonprofit funding agreements, expressing concern about the documentation requirements and the timing of reimbursements. Ms. Gelin stated that the reimbursement process should be rolling and could be addressed administratively. She explained that the documentation requirements were intended to ensure that funds were used consistently with the program mission and could be supported during an audit. Ms. Gelin offered to revisit the requirements if directed by the Commission. Commissioner Casale requested copies of the agreements for review.\par
\par
Recognized the City\rquote s nomination for Best Holiday Tree Display in USA Today.\par
\par
Requested a workshop to review the Code Compliance Department\rquote s processes, including how cases are handled, fines are assessed, and liens are collected. She cited approximately $2.8 million in closed cases, with an expected collection of $1 million, and $5.3 million in open cases, with an expected collection of $500,000. Mayor Carney supported a full review, including citation timelines and enforcement practices. Vice Mayor Burns commented on the amount of daily fines. Ms. Gelin explained the statutory requirements for code enforcement, the use of daily fines and liens, and the legal considerations involved in foreclosure. Mr. Moore stated that the City was reorganizing the Department of Neighborhood and Community Services and the Department of Code Compliance and updating department leadership. He proposed a workshop with the new leadership in early 2027 to review expectations and potential policy changes. Commissioner Casale requested that the workshop revisit the prior report prepared by Calvin Giordano and review its recommendations. The Commission reached consensus to hold the workshop in early 2027.\par
\par
\ul\b Vice Mayor Burns\ulnone\b0 : \par
Requested consideration of using Caron funds to support Alpha Star Academic Enrichment Inc., led by Marcelia Kelly, to provide SAT preparation for local high school students. She stated that the six-week Saturday program costs $10,000 and can serve 35 to 40 students. Ms. Gelin explained that the program must include a component related to substance abuse training to meet the funding criteria. Mr. Moore stated that staff would need to review the application to ensure compliance. Vice Mayor Burns stated that she would contact Ms. Kelly and request a proposal.\par
\par
\ul\b Mayor Carney\ulnone\b0 :\par
Thanked the Utilities and Public Works Departments for their responses to issues caused by the recent weather.\par
\par
Invited the public to the Mayor\rquote s Chess Challenge on Saturday, November 7, at 10:00 a.m. at the Community Center. \par
\par
Expressed support for the quarterly reporting requirements in the nonprofit funding agreements and the reorganization of Code Compliance as a separate department.\par
\par
Requested consensus to direct the City Attorney to draft an amendment to Section 96.12 of the Code of Ordinances to allow the City Manager or designee to waive provisions of the AED requirements when a waiver would not adversely affect public health, safety, and welfare. He explained that some properties would be required to purchase numerous AED units, including one example involving 30 units, despite being near a fire station. Commissioner Casale expressed concern about reducing AED requirements and questioned whether waivers were appropriate for a public health and safety requirement. Ms. Gelin explained that the amendment would allow the Fire Chief to review requests, consider the circumstances of each building, and establish a compliance schedule or reduce the number of units when appropriate. Fire Chief Ronald Martin stated that AED units cost approximately $700 to $1,250 new and $550 to $850 refurbished. He reported that 13 multifamily residential occupancies had come into compliance, there had been 13 out-of-hospital cardiac arrest incidents, and AED use had been attempted nine times. He also reported one case in which bystander CPR and medical interventions restored the person\rquote s pulse, and the person returned to normal life without neurological deficit. Mayor Carney clarified that the intent was to provide flexibility based on the circumstances of each building. Vice Mayor Burns and Commissioner Mollica expressed support. The Commission supported allowing the City Manager and designee flexibility to review AED requirements. Commissioner Mollica asked about the assistance provided to churches regarding the AED requirements. Vice Mayor Burns stated that the Fire Department visited the churches and provided counseling and assistance. She added that staff was still working on a manual to distribute to each church.\par
\par
\ul\b Commissioner Casale\ulnone\b0 :\par
Reported receiving three or four complaints about private parking lots, including instances where individuals received tickets despite having paid for parking. Vice Mayor Burns described an incident in which several family members received tickets at the Throw Social parking lot and had to obtain bank records to prove payment because the machine did not provide receipts.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin explained that state law preempts the City from enforcing regulations against private parking lots, and the City\rquote s authority is limited to requiring signage. Mayor Carney asked whether the City had inspected the signs for compliance with the ordinance. Mr. Moore confirmed that inspections had been completed. Mayor Carney suggested reviewing the signage further. Commissioner Casale stated that she would continue encouraging people to use City parking lots and avoid private lots.\par
}

{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\froman\fprq2\fcharset2 Symbol;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore introduced Janai Bowens, Director of Neighborhood & Community Services. Ms. Bowens was accompanied by Tavarous Parks, Neighborhood Services Administrator.\par
\par
Ms. Bowens provided an overview of the Neighborhood Resource Center (NRC), located at 141 SW 12th Avenue, and requested Commission direction on future occupancy and programming. The current agreements with four community-serving organizations expire in January 2027:\par
\pard\fi-360\li720\tx720\f1\fs20\'b7\tab\f0\fs24 Cros Ministries: Provides food pantry opportunities, hot meal distribution, and homebound meal services.\par
\pard\fi-360\li720\f1\fs20\'b7\tab\f0\fs24 Legal Aid Society of Palm Beach County: Provides legal services related to the Fair Housing Act and resident workshops.\par
\f1\fs20\'b7\tab\f0\fs24 Urban League of Palm Beach County: Provides housing counseling and first-time homebuyer workshops for low- and moderate-income residents.\par
\f1\fs20\'b7\tab\f0\fs24 Delray Beach Community Land Trust: Provides affordable and workforce housing and community development opportunities for qualifying households.\par
\pard\par
Ms. Bowens stated that according to the 2024-2025 annual report, Cros Ministries served 4,173 residents, the Community Land Trust served 465, Urban League served 113, and Legal Aid Society served 70. The current revocable license agreements provide temporary, non-exclusive office space and equipment for authorized services. The City maintains the building, covers utilities and security expenses, and provides administrative support. Each organization pays a $1 annual fee. The agreements were executed in January 2022 for an initial two-year term with three optional one-year renewals and are now in the final renewal year.\par
\par
Ms. Bowens presented three considerations for Commission direction:\par
\pard\fi-360\li720\tx720 1.\tab Renew or negotiate agreements with existing tenants, including updated terms, performance expectations, reporting deliverables, and revised renewal fees based on usable square footage, pro rata share of office and common areas, or a base fee.\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 2.\tab Establish a tenant selection process through a formal request for proposal or application, inviting qualified nonprofit and community-based organizations to apply. Applicants could be evaluated based on proposed services, community impact, and alignment with City priorities.\par
3.\tab Develop an alternative service model as deemed appropriate.\par
\par
\pard Ms. Bowens requested direction on the facility's intended use, whether to maintain existing agreements or consider new tenants, and whether organizations should provide service and impact reports and how frequently.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale expressed support for keeping the existing tenants and renewing the agreements.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica expressed support for support for keeping the existing tenants, but wanted more information about the Legal Aid Society. Ms. Bowens responded that their hours of operation are based by appointments and standardizing hours of operation could be a consideration for the new revocable license agreements for the existing organizations. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns questioned the Legal Aid Society's appointment-only schedule and requested a commitment to at least one day of on-site office hours per week. She also questioned Urban League's facility use, since its services were sometimes provided at the Swinton Operations Complex (SOC) or library, and requested that the space be made available to organizations that can provide services that the community can use. \par
\par
Ms. Bowens offered to consult with City Attorney regarding establishing operating hours and program deliverables in the new agreements. She also suggested quarterly reporting requirements for all organizations, similar to those provided by the Community Land Trust.\par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns requested exterior signage identifying the organizations housed at the NRC.\par
\par
Mayor Carney supported quarterly performance expectations and deliverables for all tenants, as well as established office hours with the option for appointments. He emphasized the need to measure the services provided, particularly given the limited space available. Vice Mayor Burns suggested allowing additional organizations to share office space on days when existing tenants are not present. Ms. Bowens stated that staff could explore a shared or hoteling arrangement for agencies with varying schedules. Mayor Carney supported maximizing the available space to expand services to residents.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica inquired about the square footage. Ms. Bowens responded that she would get the information. \par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert supported continuing the program but emphasized the need for performance metrics and reporting to ensure organizations serve the community in accordance with City priorities. He suggested working with the organizations to establish metrics and providing quarterly or annual reports to monitor performance and make adjustments as needed.\par
\par
Ms. Bowens summarized the Commission's direction to continue facility use for existing NRC tenants while considering standardized operating hours, shared use of the space by additional agencies, and performance metrics and deliverables for each organization. The Commission confirmed their direction. Mayor Carney reiterated the need for exterior signage identifying the services available in the building. \par
\par
Vice Mayor Burns congratulated Ms. Bowens on her appointment as Director of Neighborhood and Community Services.\par
}
title: FUTURE USE AND TENANT SELECTION FOR THE NEIGHBORHOOD RESOURCE CENTER

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Ms. Bowens presented proposed approaches for establishing Education and Workforce Development Task Forces and requested Commission direction on their composition, membership, appointments, terms, and goals. She reviewed the Education Roundtables held in August 2024 and 2025 in partnership with the Delray Beach Chamber of Commerce, Chamber Education Fund, and School District of Palm Beach County. The priorities focused on were kindergarten readiness, grade-level reading proficiency, and career readiness. Those priorities carried into 2025 which resulted in a voluntary pre-kindergarten transition resource fair, school readiness screening campaign, and a school and career showcase at Atlantic High School. This year\rquote s visioning exercise identified five priorities: restoring the Delray Beach Education Board, expanding youth internship opportunities, developing a Haitian Creole dual-language program, expanding mentorship and after-school programs, and advancing workforce development in collaboration with the City's economic development team. The education board task force was one of the recommended paths forward. Some of their recommendations were to review and update the education element of the Always Delray Comprehensive Plan, as well as to house all of the other priorities from the visioning exercise within this task force, so that included developing pathways to youth internship opportunities through partnerships with local businesses, assessing the feasibility of a Haitian Creole dual language program, and identifying opportunities to expand available after-school programming, transportation access, and community partnerships. The primary recommendation for the workforce development task force, was to establish formal partnerships among employers, workforce training providers, the Delray Chamber of Commerce, the school district, our city, and local universities to strengthen career pathways.\par
\par
Ms. Bowens presented two considerations:\par
\pard\fi-360\li720 1.\tab Formal City Commission-appointed task forces: Establish standing and Commission-appointed members with professional qualifications and experience in education, workforce development, and economic development; establish term limits, goals, and performance measures; and allow the task forces to propose policy considerations and recommendations for Commission review. Updating the Comprehensive Plan would require collaboration with Development Services.\par
2.\tab Flexible stakeholder work groups: Allow education and workforce development partners to convene based on emerging priorities, available resources, and specific initiatives. Membership could vary based on interest, experience, expertise, and goals. Work groups could meet quarterly or biannually, develop events and partnerships, and conduct fact-finding, while City staff would prepare policy recommendations. \par
\pard\par
Ms. Bowens requested Commission direction on formal appointments versus flexible work groups, Commission participation, responsibility for policy recommendations, designated positions for core partners, and specific deliverables, performance measures, and reporting frequency. She noted that Commission participation would trigger Sunshine Laws.\par
There was discussion among the Commission regarding the Sunshine Law. Ms. Gelin explained that delegating authority to a group would trigger Sunshine Law requirements, while groups convening to provide recommendations without delegated authority could operate in a more informal setting.\par
\par
Mayor Carney supported the informal approach to encourage communication and progress, while allowing any Commissioner to participate. He stated that meetings would need to be publicly noticed when Commissioners attended.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale stated that the workforce development group had been operating before the roundtable and breakfast and commended Stephanie Immelman for her work. She explained that the task force designation was intended to recognize the group's qualified members. She also expressed interest in continuing to participate in the workforce development group, if permissible.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin explained that staff participation should be directed by the City Manager and that the level of City staff involvement could affect whether a group is considered a formal board subject to Sunshine Law requirements. She stated that groups could informally develop education goals and recommendations, including reviewing the Comprehensive Plan, and present them to the Commission for consideration without delegated authority. She emphasized that the focus should be on the groups' functions rather than their titles.\par
\par
Mayor Carney supported continued Chamber involvement in the workforce development group, noting its longstanding efforts and established network of business contacts. He suggested that City staff, including the Economic Development Director, participate on an as-needed advisory basis rather than as permanent members.\par
\par
Ms. Gelin agreed that the group could remain Chamber-led, with the City Manager designating a staff representative to serve in an advisory capacity. She noted that Commissioners could participate in meetings, but not vote and Mayor Carney noted that in those instances the City Clerk's Office would be notified to meet public notice requirements.\par
\par
Commissioner Casale clarified that the Economic Development Director had attended only one meeting and that the group would likely meet four to six times annually. She expressed enthusiasm for the initiative. \par
\par
The Mayor stated that the Commission was in agreement.\par
\par
Deputy Vice Mayor Markert supported the flexible work group approach and recommended formal quarterly updates to the Commission, with additional updates as needed. He favored an oversight role for Commissioners, allowing the groups to work independently and present findings and recommendations for Commission review.\par
\par
Commissioner Mollica supported Commission participation, acknowledged that the Workforce Task Force has already been working, and asked how to establish the Education Task Force. Vice Mayor Burns expressed interest in participating on the Education Task Force.\par
\par
The Commission discussed what to call the task force related to workforce development. It was determined it would be called the Workforce Task Force.\par
\par
Mayor Carney stated that the Education Task Force did not have an established group and that interested participants needed to be identified. He recommended Vice Mayor Burns spearhead the effort and expressed interest in participating while keeping the group informal. Commissioner Mollica noted that individuals at the prior Education Roundtable had expressed interest in participating and offered to provide their names. \par
\par
Ms. Bowens asked whether the Commission wanted a formal, appointed structure with qualifications and standing members. The Mayor supported flexibility so participants could speak freely without concerns about violating rules.\par
\par
Ms. \kerning0 Bowens asked whether both task forces could be housed under the Delray Beach Chamber, with the City coordinating participation and providing a City representative to share institutional knowledge. The Mayor noted the Chamber's involvement in education efforts and suggested asking Stephanie Immelman to have the Chamber provide a recommendation on how to proceed.\par
\par
\kerning2 Ms. \kerning0 Immelman stated that the Chamber Education Fund is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit focused on raising money for public schools and that the Chamber had previously organized education roundtables, which it could continue in coordination with the City. She requested City staff participation to remain informed. \par
\kerning2\par
\kerning0 Following discussion, the Commission reached consensus to use a flexible structure for the \kerning2 Education Task Force. Ms. \kerning0 Immelman stated that the group would be based on the Vision 2035 initiatives. \kerning2 Ms.\kerning0 Gelin advised that the group's function, rather than its title, was the determining factor\kerning2 for requirements\kerning0 .\par
\kerning2\par
At this time, Jim Chard was allowed to speak as a Chamber Member.\par
\par
\ul Jim Chard\ulnone , 33483\par
\kerning0 Asked how the results of the two task forces would be used. He suggested incorporating recommendations into the Comprehensive Plan and an interlocal agreement with the County. Mayor Carney supported the suggestions and stated that proposals could be brought before the Commission for discussion and consideration, including recommendations to the School Board and incorporation into an interlocal agreement. \kerning2 Mr. \kerning0 Chard noted that this would provide measurable results\kerning2 and thanked the Commission for allowing him to speak.\par
\par
Ms. \kerning0 Bowens \kerning2 asked if it was the Commission's direction that she work with Stephanie Immelman and all appropriate stakeholders in order to provide quarterly updates regarding the work groups. \kerning0 The Mayor \kerning2 responded yes\kerning0 , provided there were no legal or procedural issues, and stated that City staff would be available on an as-needed basis. \par
\par
Commissioner Mollica \kerning2 asked who should interested \kerning0 Education Task Force participants contact\kerning2 .\kerning0 \kerning2 Ms.\kerning0 Bowens \kerning2 responded that they can contact her, she works closely with Ms. Immelman and would \kerning0 coordinate \kerning2 appropriately.\par
\cf1\kerning0\f1\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\kerning2\f0\fs24 Mr. Moore stated that Palm Beach State College would present the Panther Partner Award in recognition of the City's continued support of workforce development, student success, and community engagement. He cited the City's partnerships with the College in public safety training, the summer internship program, and other workforce development initiatives. \par
\par
The meeting recessed at 4:27 p.m. pending the expected arrival of the College representatives. It reconvened at 4:35 p.m. \par
\par
Mr. Moore introduced Matthew Lenihan, Director of Academic and Business Partnerships, and Natacha Nettles, Assistant Dean of Student Services, at Palm Beach State College, for the presentation of the Panther Partner Award. Mr. Lenihan, speaking on behalf of the College's president and provost, recognized the City as a longstanding community partner committed to serving students, supporting the Palm Beach County workforce, and building a vibrant community. He noted that Delray Beach residents have attended the College and pursued successful careers in the County and City. He thanked the City for its feedback on current and future workforce needs and stated that the College remains a resource for the City.\par
\par
Natasha Nettles, Assistant Dean of Student Services at Palm Beach State College, thanked the City for its continued community support and presented the Panther Partner Award and requested a photograph with the Commission. Mayor Carney welcomed the presentation and agreed to take a photograph. \par
\par
There being no further business to discuss, Mayor Carney adjourned the meeting at 4:42 p.m.\cf1\kerning0\f1\par

title: ORDINANCE NO. 43-26: AN ORDINANCE OF THE CITY COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF DELRAY BEACH, FLORIDA, AMENDING THE LAND DEVELOPMENT REGULATIONS OF THE CITY OF DELRAY BEACH CODE OF ORDINANCES, CHAPTER 4, “ZONING REGULATIONS,” ARTICLE 4.4, “BASE ZONING DISTRICT,” SECTION 4.4.13, “CENTRAL BUSINESS (CBD) DISTRICT,” SUBSECTION (I), “CBD PARKING STANDARDS,” SUB-SUBSECTION (2), “MINIMUM NUMBER OF OFF-STREET PARKING SPACES,” TO EXTEND THE PARKING EXEMPTION FOR CHANGES IN COMMERCIAL USE WITHIN EXISTING COMMERCIAL BUILDINGS AND ASSOCIATED OUTDOOR AREAS WITHIN THE WEST ATLANTIC NEIGHBORHOOD SUB-DISTRICT OF THE CENTRAL BUSINESS DISTRICT THROUGH DECEMBER 31, 2031 AND TO EXPAND THE GEOGRAPHIC AREA OF AVAILABILITY FOR THE EXEMPTION; PROVIDING A CONFLICTS CLAUSE, A SEVERABILITY CLAUSE, AUTHORITY TO CODIFY, PROVIDING AN EFFECTIVE DATE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES. (FIRST READING)
